units.la: Hait[?] ait Doctor Gentium. Quidni igitur ego ambas vos, florentissimas sorores, Charitatis osculo nunc salutem denuo, quas pariter Veritatis zonâ cingere ex animo cupio, & amplexari? Quam autem veritatem prosi- teamur, omnium interest scire; eòque magis, quòd Edmundus Campianus, Jesuiticæ familiæ alumnus primarius, mihi jam obstrepere videatur, in Præfa- tione illa sua ad utramque Aca- demiam data: in qua Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Doctores omnes, in- credibili jactantiâ, ad certamen Theologicum lacessivit, in hæc verba , {*}Equidem occîdi possum, superari non possum. Iis[?] enim Do- ctoribus insisto, quos ille Spiritus e- rudiit, qui nec fallitur, nec vinci- tur. Hoe ille [illegible, ~7 letters] ebuccinavit ante victoriam, ipse falsus vates, qui non itâ multò post in turri Londi-
units.tr: Thus says the Teacher of the Gentiles. Why, then, should I not greet you both again with a kiss of charity, most flourishing sisters, whom I earnestly wish to gird with the belt of truth and embrace? What truth we profess, however, concerns everyone to know, and all the more so because Edmund Campion, the leading alumnus of the Jesuit family, already seems to me to be clamouring against us in that preface of his, addressed to both Universities. In it he challenged all the teachers of the English Church, with incredible boasting, to a theological contest, in these words: I may indeed be killed, but I cannot be overcome. For I rely on those teachers whom that Spirit has taught, who is neither deceived nor overcome. He trumpeted this before the victory, the false prophet himself, who not long afterwards was in the Tower of Lond-
DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

units.la: Londinensi in Quæstione de Iu-stificatione, tam certo à Doctori-bus nostris victus erat, quàm non multò post pro merito acceptus.
units.tr: London, in the dispute on Justification, was as surely defeated by our Doctors as he was soon afterwards received for merit.

units.la: Quem tamen non puduit Præfationem illam splendido ex-polire mendacio. Responderunt postulatis meis (inquit) Hammerus & Charcus. Quid tandem? Otiosè omnia. Nullum enim respon-sum, præter unum, honestè dabunt, Quod numquam dabunt: Conditiones amplectimur, Regina spondet; Ad-vola. Quasi vero omnem cum illo disputationem detrectâssent Doctores hi, quorum argumen-torum pondere ille penitus ob-ruebatur, ut constat ex Tracta-tu, qui, eo tempore, omnium manibus versabatur. Quan-
units.tr: Yet he was not ashamed to dress up that Preface in a splendid lie. "Hammer and Charcus," he says, "have answered my demands. Well then? All idle. For they will give no honest answer, except one, which they will never give: 'We accept the conditions; the Queen promises; Advola.'" As if these Doctors had refused all debate with him, though the weight of their arguments utterly overwhelmed him, as is plain from the Treatise that at that time was in everyone's hands.

units.la: Quanquam quid hic tam au-dax Promissor feret tanto hiatu dignum? Et quænam illa autori-tas est, quâ potissimùm niti videri voluit? Dicam. Patres, Patres crepat inculcátque Romanensis illa Philomela, Vox, & præterea nihil. Quam tamen volupe est au-dire.{*} Ad Patres (inquit) si quan-do licebit accedere, confectum est præliùm, tam sunt omnes nostri, quam Gregorius Decimus Tertium (Pa-pa) filiorum Ecclesiæ pater amantissimus. Ain? Omnes nostri? Pro-culdubio hoc ab illo Athenien-si non multùm abludit, qui omnes naves in Pyræo sibi proprias vendicabat, cùm nè ad unam quidem scapham jus illi erat. Et quidem ementita hæc gloriatio debet censeri, nisi verè Patres ip-sos designet, de quibus dixit, Tam nostri sunt, quàm Pontifex Romanus Gregorius Decimus Ter-tius. Et huc sanè incumbit ambi-tiosus ostentator: nam {*}Regnet in Anglia, inquit, fides illa, utinam regnet, quàm hi Patres ex Scriptura extruunt, Cyprianus, Athanasius, Nazianzenus, Ambrosius, Hie-ronymus, Chrysostomus, Augusti-nus, & Gregorius Latinus.
units.tr: But what is there here, so bold a promiser's offering, worthy of such a gaping? And what is the authority on which he chiefly wished to seem to rest? I will tell you. "The Fathers, the Fathers," that Roman nightingale keeps shrilling and repeating: "Voice, and nothing else." Yet it is pleasant to hear him. "As for the Fathers," he says, "if ever it is permitted to approach them, the battle is won; they are all ours, just as Pope Gregory XIII is the most loving father of the sons of the Church." Do you say so? All ours? Surely this is not far from that Athenian who claimed all the ships in the Piraeus as his own, when he had no right even to a single skiff. And indeed this boastful claim must be judged false, unless he means exactly the Fathers, of whom he said, "They are as much ours as the Roman Pontiff Gregory XIII." And here the ambitious show-off certainly presses: "Let that faith reign in England," he says, "would that it reign, which these Fathers build from Scripture: Cyprian, Athanasius, Nazianzen, Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine, and Gregory the Latin."

units.la: Hos ille Patres recensuit (De-us bone!) in hac causa nostra (nisi insanissimè fallor) ipsissi-mos Patronos nostros, quibus [illegible, ~9 letters] adjunximus octo alios, Origenem, Tertullianum, Hila-rium, rium, Nyssenum, Theodore-tum, Prosperum, Fulgentium, Remigium: ut taceam Bernardum, Bedam, Anselmum, quos auctarii vice adjecimus: (quorum omnium Testimonia oculatâ fide allegavimus, non solùm meâ, sed & aliorum.) De quibus verè pronunciare possum, eos in hac controversia nostra contra Meritum de Condigno, tam nostros esse, quàm erat (cujus etiam ibidem meminit Campianus) Pontifex Gregorius Latinus totus noster. Gregorius, inquam, qui, non modò alios erudiens, statuit vitam æternam non Propter, sed Secundum opera redi: verumetiam, ut sibi conscius,
units.tr: These Fathers, good God, he has enumerated as our very own patrons in this cause of ours (unless I am gravely mistaken), to whom we have added eight others: Origen, Tertullian, Hilary, Nyssen, Theodoret, Prosper, Fulgentius, Remigius; not to mention Bernard, Bede and Anselm, whom we added by way of an appendix. (The testimonies of all of these we have cited with an honest eye, not only my own but also that of others.) Of these I can truly declare that in this controversy of ours against the Merit of Condignity they are as much ours as Gregory the Latin, wholly ours, was (as Campian also mentions in that place) the Pontiff. Gregory, I say, who, not only teaching others, decreed that eternal life is rendered not on account of works but according to works; and indeed, being conscious of himself,

units.la: Ad vitam, aiebat, non ex meritis, sed ex venia convalesco. Sic noster Gregorius, Gregorio Decimo Tertio multis nominibus præ-stantior; utpote tempore longè prior, & ideo istius nominis Pri-mus designatus: pietate multò clarior; ex quo erat insignitus Sanctus: Denique omnium æsti-matione illustris; unde cognomento hoc, Magnus, adornatus est.
units.tr: "I recover for life," he used to say, "not from merits but from pardon." So our Gregory is far superior to Gregory XIII in many respects: far earlier in time, and therefore designated "the First" of that name; far more distinguished in piety, from which he was marked as "Saint"; and finally illustrious in the esteem of all, whence he was adorned with the surname "the Great."

units.la: Anglicanam Ecclesiam quod attinet, Regnet, inquit ille; nos autem, Imo regnat, inquimus, (Deo gratias) in Anglia, atque uti-nam etiam perpetuo regnet fides illa, quam hi Patres ex Scripturis extruunt. Cujus veritatis, cum in aliis
units.tr: As for the English Church, "Let it reign," he says; but we, on the contrary, say, "Indeed it reigns" (thanks be to God) "in England, and would that the faith also reign forever which these Fathers build from the Scriptures." Of this truth, since in other

units.la: aliis controversiis palàm exhi-buimus, tum in nuper editis de Ecclesiae Romanae (quatenus se Catholicam Ecclesiam esse ja-ctitat) Grandi Impostura, & altera De Missa Romana, nonnul-lum specimen dedimus; tum etiam in hoc conflictu luculenter præstare præ me fero.
units.tr: controversies we have openly demonstrated, and in recently published works, the Great Imposture of the Roman Church (insofar as it boasts of being the Catholic Church) and the other, On the Roman Mass, we have given some specimen; and in this conflict too I openly profess to set it out clearly.

units.tr: Into this, above all, that zeal [ζῆλος] towards both universities impelled me (with St Paul as my adviser), lest any of the adversaries catch someone from either by their tricks and deceptions. What these might be like, grant me, I beg, the indulgence that I may at least conjecture, as it were by certain omens.
I. Names
Dedicatory

units.la: 1. Nomina haec ἀρετή & Me-reri, apud Patres, bonis operibus tribui sæpe jactitant: nec hoc dis-simulamus; sed in lata illa signi-ficatione, quam etiam ab Eth-nicis mutuati sunt, pro τυγχάνειν[?], Latinè, Acquirere, consequi, obti-nere, nusquam verò in vero & præciso (quanquam pestifero) sensu Exigendi vitam æternam ex æqualitate justitiæ apud Deum. Facessat igitur omnis verborum [illegible, ~8 letters] nec enim ab externo co-lore, sed ab exitiali malitia inter-na venenum discernitur.
units.tr: 1. These words virtue [ἀρετή] and to merit are often claimed by the Fathers as ascribed to good works, and we do not deny this. But they use them in the broad sense, which they borrowed from the heathen too, of to obtain [τυγχάνειν], in Latin to acquire, to attain, to obtain, and never in the true and strict sense (however pernicious) of earning eternal life by the equity of justice before God. Let all wrangling over words therefore cease, for poison is distinguished not by its outward colour but by its deadly inner malice.

units.la: 2. Jamdudum Pontificios Pro-testantium autorum fastidium cepit, altúsque despectus; quia nimirum isti (Jesuitæ præsertim)
units.tr: 2. For some time now the Papists have incurred the disdain and deep contempt of Protestant authors, because, of course, these men (the Jesuits especially)
EPISTLE

units.la: sibi solis in omni disciplina primas deferendas esse venditare[?]: quamvis ex Protestantium fontibus (expertus loquor) hortulos suos sæpe rigare soleant. In quo, quantum Calvino debeant, ex eo quis facilè auguretur, quod ex Stapletoni testimonio de-prompsimus: "Calvinus (inquit) quoad literam, ità Interpres diligens, ità moralis, ità elegans, & suavis est, ut—etiam ab ipsis Orthodoxis avidè interdum legatur—quos etiam aliquando excipere audivi, ut resectis, quæ contra Ecclesiam disputantur, castratus prodiret, sic enim Commentarios ejus persuasiles[?] fore." Quod quàm verè dixerit facile videre est, non modò ex Melchiore Cano, qui integram pa-ginam ex eo transcripsit, sed multò magis ex Salmerone & aliis: qui dum literalem sensum expiscari cupiunt, interdum o-perté, itá tamen ut deprehendi facilè possint, interdum [illegible, ~6 letters] Calvini interpretationem usur-pant. Quam, si fateri hoc vellent, mutuatos eos; sin nollent, suffuratos esse dixerim.
units.tr: They are wont to claim the first place in every branch of learning for themselves alone, though (I speak from experience) they often water their own little gardens from the springs of the Protestants. How much the Papists owe to Calvin one may easily guess from the testimony of Stapleton, which we have taken from him: "Calvin, he says, as far as the letter goes, is so diligent an interpreter, so moral, so elegant and pleasant, that he is even sometimes eagerly read by the Orthodox themselves. I have even heard some of them say that they would like to take him up with the parts that are argued against the Church cut out, so that he would come forth castrated, for in that way his commentaries would be persuasive." How truly he spoke is easy to see, not only from Melchior Cano, who copied out a whole page from him, but much more from Salmeron and others, who, while they wish to draw out the literal sense, sometimes openly, yet in such a way that they can easily be detected, and sometimes [illegible], make use of Calvin's interpretation. If they were willing to admit this, I would say they had borrowed it; if they were unwilling, I would say they had stolen it.

units.la: 3. Enimvero controversiis di-rimendis Pontificiorum mirus consensus & conspiratio esse di-citur: nempe Andabatarum instar, quod cùm in controversiis aliis, tum sanè in hac Quæstione liquidò constet, in qua fundamenta illa omnia, quæ alii eo-rum rum summo cum artificio pro Merito posuerint, ab aliis nullo cum negotio labefactantur illico. Quod nos ipsius veritatis victo-riæ tribuendum existimamus. Itâ tamen, ut in hosce sophistas optimè quadret illud Catonis scitum, Miror cur Haruspex non riserit, cùm Haruspicem viderit.
units.tr: 3. Indeed, the Papists are said to have a remarkable agreement and conspiracy in settling their controversies, like the Andabatae, who fight blindfolded. That is plainly clear in their other controversies, and certainly in this question, in which all those foundations which some of them have laid down for Merit with great skill are at once overthrown by others with no trouble at all. We think this must be ascribed to the victory of truth itself. Yet the saying of Cato fits these sophists very well: "I wonder why one haruspex does not laugh when he sees another haruspex."

units.la: 4. Est tamen ubi se prolixè ja-ctitant, ex Merito suo Gloriam Christi amplificari omnino, eò quòd afferant, Ex meritis Christi se accepisse illam suam virtutem merendi, per justitiæ æqualitatem apud Deum. Quem nos proba-vimus esse fucum multò perni-ciosissimum; perinde ac si quis eò prorumperet insaniæ, ut (quæ singula sunt Prærogativæ Chri-sto σωτῆρι[?] propriæ) Redimendi, immediatè illuminandi, Regenerandi, gratiam primam conferendi, justificandiq virtutem, tanquam ex Christi Meritis, sibi arrogaret. Quod absque nefando sacrilegio fieri non posse, vel Pontificii ipsi concedunt ultro.
units.tr: 4. Yet there are places where they boast at length that the glory of Christ is altogether magnified by their Merit, because they affirm that "from the merits of Christ they have received that power of merit of their own, through the equality of justice before God." We have shown this to be a far more pernicious deception; it is just as if someone were to break out into such madness that he would claim for himself, as from the merits of Christ, those things which are each proper to Christ the Saviour [σωτῆρι]: redeeming, immediately enlightening, regenerating, conferring first grace, and the power of justifying. Even the Papists themselves freely concede that this cannot be done without a foul sacrilege.

units.la: 5. Hâc arte non succedunt: Novo fascino tenera ingenia corripere satagunt. Solifidianorum Hæresis scilicet Protestantibus impingenda est, quippe sublatâ opinione Meriti de condigno, bonorum operum gloriam omnem obfuscari, necessitatem bene operandi tolli, & nihil non flagitii perpetrandi licentiam horum summo cum artificio pro Merito posuerint, ab aliis nullo cum negotio labefactantur illico. Quod nos ipsius veritatis victo-riæ tribuendum existimamus. Itâ tamen, ut in hosce sophistas optimè quadret illud Catonis scitum, Miror cur Haruspex non riserit, cùm Haruspicem viderit.
units.tr: 5. They do not succeed by this art; they strive to seize tender minds with a new charm. The heresy of the Solifidians, it seems, is to be thrust upon the Protestants, since, with the opinion of merit de condigno removed, all the glory of good works is said to be obscured, the necessity of doing good is taken away, and the licence to commit every kind of wickedness is granted. In this, too, they have the same skill; they set this up as Merit with great art, and it is at once overthrown by others with no trouble at all. We think this must be ascribed to the victory of truth itself. Yet the saying of Cato fits these sophists very well: "I wonder why one haruspex does not laugh when he sees another haruspex."

units.la: singula sunt Prærogativæ Chri-sto θεανθρώπῳ[?] propriæ) Redimendi, immediatè illuminandi, Regenerandi, gratiam primam conferendi, justificandiq; virtutem, tanquam ex Christi Meritis, sibi arrogaret. Quod absque nefando sacrilegio fieri non posse, vel Pontificii ipsi concedunt ultro.
units.tr: (which) are the peculiar prerogatives of Christ the God-man [θεανθρώπῳ]: to redeem, to enlighten immediately, to regenerate, to confer first grace, and to have the power of justifying, as if from Christ's merits he were arrogating these to himself. Which, without unspeakable sacrilege, cannot be done, as the Papists themselves freely concede.

units.la: 5. Hâc arte non succedunt. Novo fascino tenera ingenia corripere satagunt. Solifidianorum Hæresis scilicet Protestantibus impingenda est, quippe sub-latâ opinione Meriti de condi-gno, bonorum operum gloriam omnem obfuscari, necessitatem bene operandi tolli, & nihil non flagitii perpetrandi licentiam ho-minibus minibus indulgeri ad ravim ufq; clamitant & vociferantur. Sed quid (malùm!) mentiendi hoc Cacoëthes sibi vult? Esse enim hoc insigne ac pellucidum men-dacium ex ingenuis ipsorum Pontificiorum confessionibus itá evicimus, ut si quam voluptá-tem illi falsò nos criminando ce-perint, eam Doctorum suorum confessionem veram audiendo amittant. Nec tamen satis erit hoc modo adversariorum no-strorum criminationes obtrivif-se, nisi etiam ex Patribus probe-mus, Protestantes bonorum o-perum necessitatem haud mino-rem, dignitatem verò longè il-lustriorem, & veræ pietatis pro-ventum
units.tr: 5. They do not succeed by this device. They labour to seize tender minds with a new charm. The heresy of the Solifidians, forsooth, is to be fastened upon the Protestants, since, once the opinion of merit of condignity is removed, they cry out and shout themselves hoarse that all the glory of good works is obscured, the necessity of doing good is abolished, and men are granted licence to commit every kind of wickedness. But what, good heavens, does this itch of lying mean for them? For we have shown from the Papists' own candid confessions that this is a notable and transparent lie, so that if they have taken any pleasure in falsely accusing us, they will lose it by hearing the true confession of their own teachers. Yet it will not be enough to have crushed our adversaries' accusations in this way, unless we also prove from the Fathers that Protestants hold the necessity of good works to be no less, and their dignity far more illustrious, and the fruit of true piety
Dedication.

units.la: proventum uberiorem, felici-orémque profiteri, juxtà ac promovere.
units.tr: to profess a more abundant and happier fruit of true piety, and to promote it as well.

units.la: Ad vos tandem redeo (Viri clarissimi) quorum interest prospicere, non modò nè cæremonias, veluti Ecclesiæ phylacteria, improbè quis arroserit: sed multò etiam magis, nè articulos ejus, tanquam spiritus vitales, eliserit. Ex his facilè intelligatis cur vobis hoc, quicquid est opellæ, nunc dico, consecróque. In qua causam hanc uberiùs disserui, ut facilius effugerem Adversariorum calumniam, præsertim cùm (ut scitè cautéque Cicero) Quæ angustiùs & breviùs concluduntur, ea ferè apertiora & aptiora sunt ad reprehendendum. Quin hæc vos (quæ est vestra παρρησία[?], Viri Ornatissimi) æqui bonique consuletis, nullus dubito. In CHRISTO Jesu valete, qui vos conservet in gloriam Gratiæ ipsius. AMEN.
units.tr: I return at last to you, most distinguished gentlemen, whose concern it is to watch over the Church. Let no one wrongly scrape away not only its ceremonies, which are like the phylacteries of the Church, but much more its articles, which are like its vital spirits. From these remarks you will easily understand why I now dedicate to you whatever this little work is. In it I have argued the case more fully, so that I might more easily escape the calumny of my opponents, especially since (as Cicero says wisely and cautiously) what is concluded more narrowly and briefly is generally clearer and better suited to being found fault with. Indeed, I do not doubt that you will take these things in good and fair part, you whose candour [παρρησία] is well known, most excellent gentlemen. Farewell in Christ Jesus, who keep you to the glory of his grace. AMEN.
THOMAS OF DURHAM.
The State of the Controversy. CHAP. I.
Concerning merit of congruity.
Three questions. Its use is rejected.
CHAP. II.
Concerning merit of condignity:

units.tr: Six classes of Scriptures objected by the Papists and answered, sect. 3 to 8.
CHAP. III.

units.la: Objectiones ex Patribus pro nomine Meriti solvuntur, sect. 2, & 3.
units.tr: The objections from the Fathers in favour of the term merit are answered, sect. 2 and 3.
CHAP. IV.
Against merit of condignity, from the sacred letters.

units.la: Tria Argumenta contra Meritum de Condigno ex Pontificiorum ipsorum principiis & confessionibus.
units.tr: Three arguments against merit of condignity from the Papists' own principles and confessions.
CHAP. V.
Our first argument,

units.la: Quia bonum opus caret æqualitate justitiæ apud Deum, tum commutativa, sect. 2. tum distributiva, sect. 3. tum etiam utriusque, sect. 4.
units.tr: Because a good work lacks equality of justice before God: both commutative, sect. 2, distributive, sect. 3, and also of both together, sect. 4.
CHAP. VI.
Our second argument

units.la: Ex Pontificiis, contra Meritum de Condigno: Quia opus bonum caret omni fundamento Condignitatis. Contra præextum primum Liberi arbitrii, sect. 2, 3. Spiritûs sancti, ac membri Christi, sect. 4. Atque etiam Pacti, sect. 5, 6, & 7.
units.tr: From the Papists, against merit of condignity: because a good work lacks every foundation of condignity. Against the first pretext of free will, sect. 2, 3; of the Holy Spirit and of the member of Christ, sect. 4; and also of the compact, sect. 5, 6, and 7.
CHAP. VII.
Our third argument

units.la: Ex Pontificiis, Quia vita æterna redditur ex digna-tione, tione & acceptatione Dei, juxta confessiones Pontificiorum locupletissi-mas, sect. 21.
units.tr: From the Papists, because eternal life is bestowed by the gracious regard and acceptance of God, according to the most copious confessions of the Papists, sect. 21.

units.la: Argumenta tredecim ex Scripturis & Patribus simul adversus Meritum de Condigno. CAP. VIII.
units.tr: Thirteen arguments from Scripture and the Fathers together against the Merit of Condignity. CHAP. VIII.
Our first argument,

units.la: Quia bonum opus est donum Dei. Scriptura, sect. 2. Patres, sect. 3.
units.tr: Because a good work is a gift of God. Scripture, section 2. The Fathers, section 3.
CHAPTER IX.
Our second argument:

units.la: Quia omne opus bonum est Deo debitum. Scrip-tura, sect. 2. Patres, sect. 3.
units.tr: Because every good work is owed to God. Scripture, section 2. The Fathers, section 3.
CHAP. X.
Our third argument:

units.la: Quia omne opus nostrum indignum est tantâ re-muneratióne. Scriptu-ra, sect. 2. Patres, sect. 3.
units.tr: Because every work of ours is unworthy of so great a reward. Scripture, sect. 2. The Fathers, sect. 3.
CHAPTER XI.
Our fourth argument:

units.la: Quia Deus esse nequit proprie debitor hominibus. Ex Scripturis, sect. 2. Ex Patribus, sect. 3. Ex ipsis Pontificiis, sect. 4.
units.tr: Because God cannot be properly a debtor to men. From the Scriptures, section 2. From the Fathers, section 3. From the Papists themselves, section 4.
CHAPTER XII.
Our fifth argument,

units.la: Quia ipsa vita æterna est Dei donum. Scriptura, sect. 2. Patres, sect. 3.
units.tr: Because eternal life itself is the gift of God. Scripture, section 2. The Fathers, section 3.
CHAPTER XIII.
Our sixth argument,

units.la: Quia vita æterna est donum hæreditarium. Ex Scripturis, sect. 2. & 3. ex Patribus, sect. 4. Objectio, Regnum cœleste est venale, sect. 5. Solut. triplex, triplex, sect. 5, 6,7,& 8.
units.tr: Because eternal life is an inheritance gift. From the Scriptures, section 2 and 3. From the Fathers, section 4. Objection, The heavenly kingdom is for sale, section 5. Threefold solution, threefold, sections 5, 6, 7 and 8.
CAP. XIIII.
Our seventh argument,

units.la: Quia vita æterna est supra Condignum operis cu-juscunque. Ex Scriptu-ris, sect. 2. ex Patribus, sect.3. Objest. sol. sect.4.
units.tr: Because eternal life is above the merit of any work whatsoever. From the Scriptures, section 2; from the Fathers, section 3; objection and solution, section 4.
CHAPTER XV.
Our eighth argument,

units.la: Quia opus bonum nihil quicquam Deum juvat. Scriptura, sect. 2. Patres, sect. 3.
units.tr: Because a good work does not benefit God in any way. Scripture, section 2. The Fathers, section 3.
CAP. XVI.
Our ninth argument

units.la: Quia talis venditatio apud homines esset odiosa & execrabilis. Ex Scriptu-ris, sect. 2. ex Patribus, sect. 3. ex Ethicis, sect. 4. Ex Philosophis, sect.5. & ex Pontificiis, sect. 6. Contra Pontificiorum ul-timum refugium, quasi Christus meruerit nobis virtutem merendi.
units.tr: Because such bartering would be odious and detestable among men. From the Scriptures, section 2; from the Fathers, section 3; from the ethical writers, section 4; from the philosophers, section 5; and from the Papists themselves, section 6. Against the Papists' last refuge, as if Christ had merited for us the power of meriting.
CAP. XVIII.
Our tenth argument,

units.la: Quia prætextus iste est derogatorius propriis Christi meritis: probatur per Theses quatuor, sect.3,4,5,6. Quia Protestantium doctrina magis amplificat Christi merita, sect.7.8,9. Quia Patres Pontificiis adversantur, sect.10, & 11. Vindicatio sententiæ Augustini, sect.12. Quia antiquæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ fidei repugnat, sect.13. Et hodiernæ Ecclesiæ praxi, sect.14.
units.tr: Because this pretext detracts from the proper merits of Christ: proved by four theses, sect. 3, 4, 5, 6. Because the doctrine of the Protestants magnifies the merits of Christ more, sect. 7, 8, 9. Because the Fathers are opposed to the Papists, sect. 10 and 11. A vindication of the opinion of Augustine, sect. 12. Because it is contrary to the faith of the ancient Roman Church, sect. 13. And to the present practice of the Church, sect. 14.
CAP. XVIII.
Our eleventh argument

units.la: Quia opus Christianitatis nobilissimum, (quod est martyrium pro Chri-sto) non est meritorium. Ex Scripturis & Patribus, sect. 2, & 3.
units.tr: Because the most noble work of Christianity (which is martyrdom for Christ) is not meritorious. From the Scriptures and the Fathers, sect. 2 and 3.
CHAPTER XIX.
Our twelfth argument,

units.la: Quia pro omni bono debetur Deo gratitudinis officium. Ex Scripturis, sect. 2. Ex Patribus, sect. 3, & 4.
units.tr: Because for every good thing the duty of gratitude is owed to God. From the Scriptures, section 2. From the Fathers, sections 3 and 4.

units.la: De profectu verae pietatis per abolitionem Meriti de Condigno.
units.tr: On the advancement of true godliness through the abolition of merit of condignity.
CHAPTER XX.
Our thirteenth argument,

units.la: Quia Doctrina de Merito ex Condigno obest plu-rimum profectui verae pietatis : Probatur per Theses varias, nempe
units.tr: That the doctrine of merit of condignity greatly hinders the progress of true piety. This is proved by various theses, namely:

units.la: 1: De necessitate bonorum operum quae à Protestantibus exigitur, sect. 2, 3. usque ad 9.
units.tr: 1: On the necessity of good works, which is required by the Protestants, sect. 2, 3 to 9.

units.la: 2. De imperfectione bo-norum operum qua-tenus à nobis, sect. 9. usque ad 13.
units.tr: 2. On the imperfection of good works, insofar as they come from us, sect. 9 to 13.

units.la: 3. De dignitate operum nostrorum quatenus per gratiam, sect. 13, 14, 15.
units.tr: 3. On the dignity of our works, insofar as they come through grace, sect. 13, 14, 15.

units.la: 4. De ipso profectu verae pietatis : Quia Protestantes adversus Meritum de Condigno pugnant iis Argumentis, quibus Patres antiqui usi sunt in hortando & suadendo ad omnem sanctitatem, sect. 16, 17.
units.tr: 4. On the progress of true piety itself: because the Protestants fight against the merit of condignity with those arguments which the ancient Fathers used in exhorting and urging all holiness, sect. 16, 17.

units.tr: 1 John 2. If anyone confesses, he is just, etc. chap. 2, sect. 8, and chap. 6, sect. 7. Rev. 2. If you overcome, I will give, chap. 2, sect. 8. Rev. 3. For they are worthy, chap. 2, sect. 3. Rev. 7. For they came out of tribulation, sect. 6.
THE STATE OF THE CONTROVERSY IN GENERAL.

units.la: PRotestantes OPERA BO-NA ad salutem necessaria esse, & destinata media defendunt.
units.tr: The Protestants maintain that good works are necessary to salvation and are appointed as means.

units.la: Pontificii Doctores EA præterea PROPRIE DICTA MERITA esse venditant.
units.tr: The Papist teachers, moreover, boast that these same works are merits properly so called.

units.la: MERITVM vero duplex esse statuunt, 1. De Congruo. 2. De Condigno.
units.tr: They lay down that merit is twofold: (1) of congruity, (2) of condignity.
Against MERIT OF CONGRUITY.
CHAP. I.

units.la: Meritum de Congruo ( definitore {a}Vega ) est Actio libera, cui congruum sit, ut par aliquod respondeat Præmium. Opiniones Eorum, de hoc Merito, ad Quæstiones tres reduci possunt.
units.tr: Merit of congruity (as Vega defines it) is a free action to which it is fitting that some corresponding reward should be given. The opinions of these men about this merit can be reduced to three questions.

units.la: QVÆST. I. An ulla Merita de Congruo antecedant Justificationem.
units.tr: QUESTION I. Whether any merits of congruity precede justification.
SECT. I.

units.la: Fuerunt in Ecclesia Romana non nullius nominis Authores, qui hoc affirmârunt; adversus quam opinionem Ecclesia nostra Anglicana Articulum suum, veluti salutiferum Antidotum praescripsit hisce verbis, ART.XIII.
units.tr: There were in the Roman Church authors of some repute who affirmed this. Against this opinion our English Church prescribed its Article as a saving antidote, in these words, Article XIII:

units.la: Ante Gratiam Christi, & Sancti Spiritus inspirationem, Opera nostra non sunt Dei grata, utpote quae non dimanent à fide in Christo Iesu, nec homines idoneos faciunt ad Gratiam recipiendam, vel (ut loquuntur Scholastici) ut mereantur Gratiam de Congruo. Imò quia non secundum Dei mandatum fiunt, non dubitamus quin in se habeant naturam peccati. At verò quàm nullius authoritatis sint contrariæ Opinionis Scholastici Authores, ex illius Refutatione discat Lector[?], non quidem nostrâ (nec enim necesse est) sed ex ipsorum Pontificiorum confessione, qui in ea refellenda diligentem operam navârunt.
units.tr: Before the grace of Christ and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, our works are not pleasing to God, since they do not spring from faith in Jesus Christ, nor make men fit to receive grace, or (as the Scholastics put it) to merit grace de congruo. Indeed, because they are not done as God has commanded, we do not doubt that in themselves they have the nature of sin. But how little authority the contrary opinion of the Scholastic authors has, the reader may learn from its refutation: not from ours (for there is no need), but from the confession of the Papists themselves, who took diligent pains in refuting it.

units.la: Summa est, Quòd omnes absq;[?] fide in Christo sub maledictione sunt, Gal.3. Quidni igitur Adversarios nostros tandem resipiscere patiamur, & nobiscum, quoad licèat, in gratiam redire? quippe (siqua Stapletono fides) {b}Meritum de Congruo, respectu primæ Gratiæ (inquit) jam olim explosum est. Et paulò pòst, Vtcunq; igitur vel olim Scholastici aliqui, vel circa initium hodierni Schismatis Scriptores aliqui Catholici de hac præparatione hominis ante Gratiam, & consequenter de viribus humanæ naturæ nondum sanatæ imprudenter scripserunt; non est illud hodie ab aliquo Authore Catholico defensum: sed juxta Concilii Tridentini definitionem, & plurimorum hodieTractatorum Catholicorum consentientes sententias, in confesso omnibus est, Vires naturæ sic per peccatum Originale fractas esse & debilitatas, ut sine habituali dono, per Christi gratiam infuso, neq; Deum diligere, vel ullum opus bonum, ut oportet, & ut Meritorium esse queat, præstare valeant: neq; sine speciali Dei auxilio per liberum arbitrium ad oblatum Gratia donum acceptandum cooperari. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The sum is: That all who are without faith in Christ are under a curse, Gal. 3. Why then should we not allow our adversaries at last to come to their senses and, so far as is permitted, return to agreement with us? For (if Stapleton is to be believed) the merit of congruity, with respect to the first grace, has long since been exploded. And a little later: Therefore, however some Scholastics once, or some Catholic writers near the beginning of the present schism, rashly wrote about this preparation of man before grace, and consequently about the powers of human nature not yet healed, it is not today defended by any Catholic author. But according to the definition of the Council of Trent, and the agreed opinions of most of today's Catholic treatises, it is agreed by all that the powers of nature are so broken and weakened by original sin that, without the habitual gift infused by the grace of Christ, they cannot love God, or perform any good work as they ought, or any work that can be meritorious; nor can they, without the special help of God, cooperate through free will in accepting the offered gift of grace.* Thus he.

units.la: Nos igitur nè, veluti {*}ἀέρα δέρων[?], absq; Adversariis pugnare videamur, missum faciemus hoc Membrum speciei primæ de Merito ex Congruo.
units.tr: We therefore, lest, like those beating the air [ἀέρα δέρων], we seem to fight without adversaries, will drop this member of the first species of merit of congruity.

units.la: QUÆST. II. De Dispositionibus, quibus Peccatores ad Gratiam ex Gratia excitantur.
units.tr: QUESTION II. Concerning the dispositions by which sinners are stirred up to grace by grace.
SECT. II.

units.la: DE quibus sic statuit Bellarminus, {c}Hæ non excludunt Meritum, modo non tribuatur eis Meritum de Condigno. Rursus, Nos quidem intelligere non possumus, cur non sit hoc tempore utendum nomine Meriti, præsertim cum additione illa de Congruo, cùm agitur de Operibus, quæ fiunt ex Gratia præveniente. Idem {d} Vega contendit; qui tamen agnoscit, {e}Doctissimos quosdam & pientissimos Viros eò propendere, ut Ecclesia Meritum Congrui repellat, tanquam novum Inventum. Quinimo Gregor. de Valentia, rejectâ priùs illâ sententiâ, ut Pelagianâ, quæ docuit Hominem ex justitia mereri ut in Dei gratiam recipiatur, aliam aggreditur. {f}Non probamus, inquit, Sententiam Eorum, qui dicunt nos primam Gratiam mereri ex Congruita-te Operum, quibus nos ultimò ad illam disponi-mus. Non ità est— repugnat Meritum Congrui habere suam perfectionem, aut Congruitatem ex præmio, tanquam ex principio. Et paulò post, Longè probabiliùs diceretur, per Opera bona Mo-ralia, quibus aliquis ante acceptam Gratiam faceret quod Moraliter posset, eatenus primam Gratiam ex Congruo illam mereri, quatenus conveniens & congruum est, ut cùm talis facit quantum in illo statu moraliter potest, Deus etiam præstet id quod suarum est partium : hoc est, ei auxilia augeat, quibus adjutus possit Gratiam consequi, atque adeò consequatur, si sibi non desit.
units.tr: Of these matters Bellarmine thus determines: "These do not exclude merit, provided that merit de condigno is not attributed to them." Again: "We indeed cannot understand why the name of merit should not be used at this time, especially with that addition of congruous merit, when the question concerns works which are done from prevenient grace." Vega contends the same, though he admits that certain very learned and most pious men lean toward rejecting congruous merit as a novel invention of the Church. Moreover, Gregory of Valentia, having first rejected that opinion as Pelagian, which taught that man merits from justice to be received into God's grace, takes up another. "We do not approve," he says, "the opinion of those who say that we merit the first grace from the congruity of works by which we are finally disposed for it. It is not so: congruous merit cannot have its perfection or congruity from the reward as from a principle." And a little after: "It would be much more probable to say that through good moral works, by which someone before receiving grace does what he morally can, he merits the first grace congruously, insofar as it is fitting and congruous that when such a person does what he morally can in that state, God also supplies what belongs to his part: that is, he increases the helps by which, being aided, he may obtain grace, and so obtains it, if it is not lacking to him."

units.la: Theologus Pontificius Patavinus Paulus Benius Eugubinus multus est in hoc Argumento. Operæ-pretium erit sententias ejus, sparsim positas, in compendium reducere, ubi à præcipua Dispositione, quæ est Fides, auspicatur. {§}Quòd si Augustinus dicit (inquit) Epist. 105. fidem impetrare posse remissionem peccatorum: Et rursus Epist. 106. Posse nos per fidem mereri Gratiam bene operandi.— Ego sanè possem ad eundem Augustinum sexcentis in locis provocare; in quibus tuetur, Justificationem ullo planè nostro prævio Merito non modo non inchoari, sed nè absolvi quidem: ut Epist. 105. Qua igitur sua merita jactaturus est Liberatus? qui, si digna suis meritis redderentur, non esset nisi damnatus.— Huic Patrum sententiæ Conciliorum multorum posset addi sensus & irrefragabile judicium. Etiam Concil. Trident. Sess.6. cap.8. explicans illud Apostoli, [Justificati gratis] Gratis quidem ideo justificamur (inquit) quia nihil eorum, quæ justificationem præcedunt, sive fides, sive opera, ipsam justificationis gratiam promeretur — alioquin, ut idem Apostolus, Gratia non esset Gratia. Pòst arguit, Arbitramur hoc demonstrari posse, quia ante habitualis Charitatis adeptionem, adhuc sumus filii iræ. Hæc ille, & nonnulla alia in eandem sententiam. Sed plura Testimonia accumulare supervacaneum erit.
units.tr: The Papist theologian Paul Benius of Eugubio of Padua is extensive on this subject. It will be worth the effort to reduce his opinions, scattered here and there, to a summary, beginning from the chief disposition, which is faith. "But if Augustine says (he says), in Epistle 105, that faith can obtain the remission of sins; and again, in Epistle 106, that we can merit by faith the grace of doing good works.— I could indeed appeal to the same Augustine in six hundred places, in which he maintains that justification is not only not begun by any merit of ours, but not even completed: as in Epistle 105, 'What, then, will Liberatus boast of as his merits? Who, if they were rendered according to his merits, would be nothing but condemned.'— To this sentiment of the Fathers the sense and irrefragable judgment of many Councils could be added. Also the Council of Trent, Sess. 6, cap. 8, explaining that saying of the Apostle, [Justified freely], says: 'We are justified freely indeed for this reason, that nothing of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification itself; otherwise, as the same Apostle says, grace would not be grace.'" Then he argues: "We think this can be demonstrated, because before the attainment of habitual charity we are still children of wrath." Such is he, and several other things to the same effect. But to accumulate more testimonies would be superfluous.

units.la: QUÆST. III. An Justus in Gratia constitutus, si forte in peccatum mortale lab- atur, possit promereri Gratiam Re- parationem. SECT. III.
units.tr: QUÆST. III. Whether a man who is righteous and established in grace, if perhaps he falls into mortal sin, can merit the grace of restoration. SECT. III.

units.la: AD hanc Bellarminus, Potest homo nondum reconciliatus per opera pœnitentiæ impetrare & mereri ex Congruo Gratiam Justificationis, ut in primo libro demonstratum est. Cum igitur non poterit idem ipse, dum est Justus & amicus Dei, impetrare ac mereri, ex Congruo, reparationem, si forte labatur? Sic ille. In quo quàm turpiter labitur Cardinalis, probabimus. Primo in loco Aquinas, nempe Romanæ Scholæ Oraculum ipsum (cui tamen Cardinalis prudens scienséque adversatur) Dicendum est (inquit) quòd nullus sibi mereri potest reparationem post lapsum futurum, neque merito Condigni, neque merito Congrui — propter impedimentum peccati in eo cui quis meretur. En insuper Vasquem Jesuitam Commentatorem oppidò opportunum! Hæc Conclusio Thomæ (inquit) confirmatur Ezech. 18. [Si averterit se justus à justitia sua, & fecerit iniquitatem, omnes justitiæ ejus, quas fecerat, non recordabuntur, sed in iniquitate sua morietur.] Consensum quæris ? Idem paulò antè; De qua Conclusione nulla est apud Scholasticos controversia: in quam consenserunt Alex. Cajetan. & reliqui Thoma Interpretes. Rationem deposcise[?] —Si opus factum in Gratia esset meritorium (inquit) reparationis post lapsum, tum absq; ullo adjutorio tolleret peccatum. Sic ille. Nempe valeret ad impediendum lapsum in peccatum. Imò & Greg. de Valentia, cùm jam praestò adest, non est negligendus. {1}Reparationem vero post lapsum (inquit) Operibus ex gratia ante lapsum factis nullo modo mereri possumus— Non viget enim praeteritum Meritum, cùm quis post lapsum in gratiam restituitur: nam per lapsum fuit mortificatum. Mihi si liceret aliquid de proprio addere, dixerim ego, vix posse esse dogma (ut ita loquar) novercale magis, & ad praesumptionem in omne peccatum magis praeceps, quàm est illa Bellarmini Assertio. Ex his quis non clarè videat, in quaestione De Merito ex Congruo, Doctores Pontificii quàm parùm inter se congruant? ut taceam quàm indignè illud Meritum appelletur, quod, ex Adversariorum opinione, non habet ullam rationem proprie dicti Meriti, nec cui Praemium jure ullo debeatur. Faceßat igitur omnis Congruitatis Meritoria fictio, ut ad proprie dictum Meritum, quod de Condigno appellitant, accedamus propiùs.
units.tr: To this Bellarmine answers: "A man not yet reconciled can, through works of penance, obtain and merit by congruity the grace of justification, as was demonstrated in the first book. Since therefore the same man, while he is just and a friend of God, cannot obtain and merit by congruity restoration, if perhaps he falls?" So he. How shamefully the Cardinal slips in this, we will prove. First, in the place of Aquinas, the very oracle of the Roman school (whom nevertheless the prudent and knowing Cardinal opposes): "It must be said that no one can merit for himself restoration after a future fall, neither by merit of condignity nor by merit of congruity, on account of the impediment of sin in the one for whom one merits." Behold, moreover, the Jesuit commentator Vasquez, most opportune! "This conclusion of Thomas (he says) is confirmed by Ezekiel 18: [If the righteous man turn away from his righteousness and commit iniquity, none of his righteousnesses which he had done shall be remembered, but in his iniquity he shall die.]" Do you seek consent? The same author a little before: "Concerning this conclusion there is no controversy among the Scholastics; Cajetan and the rest of Thomas's interpreters agreed to it." The reason? "If a work done in grace were meritorious of restoration after a fall, then without any help it would remove sin." So he: namely, it would avail to prevent the fall into sin. Indeed Gregory of Valentia, since he is already at hand, is not to be neglected: "But we cannot in any way merit restoration after a fall by works done in grace before the fall. For past merit does not thrive when someone after a fall is restored to grace, since by the fall it was mortified." If it were permitted for me to add something of my own, I would say that there can hardly be a dogma (so to speak) more stepmotherly, and more headlong toward presumption in every sin, than that assertion of Bellarmine. From these things, who does not clearly see how little the Papist doctors agree among themselves on the question De Merito ex Congruo? To say nothing of how unworthily that is called merit which, by the opinion of the adversaries, has no reason of merit properly so called, nor anyone to whom a reward is due by any right. Therefore let all the meritorious fiction of Congruitatis Meritoria be set aside, so that we may come closer to the merit properly so called, which they call de condigno.
CHAP. II.
On Merit of Condignity, repugnant to the [?] state

units.la: E[?] esse dona Dei, stificati Merita Operibus, quae Christi meritum sunt, non vere ma sit. Operatem de Condig[?] fit, Pontificii al[?] finiverunt; ita recte definiunt justitiae consiste[?] ternam promere[?] sterus Jef. Me[?]
units.tr: That these are gifts of God, and that justified people's merits by works, which are the merit of Christ, are not truly [?]. The Papists have defined the work of condignity; thus they rightly define the justice that consists in [?] ... the eternal [?] ... Jesus [?] Me[?]
CHAP. II.

units.la: T O proprie dicto DE CON- Decretum Romanæ, & Ei[?] ns Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Articulus. s Controversiæ. SECT. I.
units.tr: Of Merit properly so called: the Controversy. The Decree of the Roman Church and the Article of the Church of England. SECT. I.

units.la: Ktat CONC. TRIDENT. Canon, quem boni illi Patres noviter hominum Conscientiis imposuerunt, viz. Si quis dixerit hominis justificati bona Opera ita ut non sint etiam Bona ipsius justificationis; aut ipsum justificatum bonis ab eo per Dei gratiam, & Jesu Christi, cujus vivum est membrum, mereri vitam æternam: Anathe- [illegible, ~6 letters] nostra propriè merentur felici-[?] no[?]. Sic illi. Hoc Meritum quid alii pressiùs, alii explicatiùs de-tamen ut omnes (qui illud statuant illud in Æqualitate re apud Deum, ad vitam æ-ndum. Exempli causâ, 1. Contritum de Condigno est Actio li-bera, bera, cui merces debetur ex justitia. 2. Definitio, quam suis Lectoribus dictabat Bellarminus, hujusmodi est. {P}Absolutam aequalitatem inter Meritum & Mercedem Deus constituit, ut unusquisque tantam habeat mercedem, quantam Dei judicio meretur. Dein addit; Hoc ex promissione Dei sit, sine qua non potest mercedem exigere. 3. Vasquez Jes. {q}Opera nostra non dignitatem habent à persona Christi, sed à persona à qua procedunt. Item; {r}Nostra merita ità perfectè meritoria sunt vita aeterna, ut nullum habeamus defectum, ob quem denegetur illis vita aeterna, aut digne denegari possit. Neq; hoc solùm, sed etiam; {s}Meritum est comparatione alicujus praemii obsequium, quod natura suâ exigit praemium hujusmodi, tanquam parem gratiam, illi referre. Haec ille. Denique, Suarez Jesuita pleniore accentu, ubi contendit, Vitam aeternam deberi operibus Justorum: Loquimur (inquit) de Operibus, quae ex rigore debitum Justitiae requirunt. Haec ille, (ut infrà referemus, Cap. 11. Sect.1.) & plura alia in eandem sententiam. Et profectò siquod intercederet Meritum de Condigno inter nos & Deum, tale illud esse oportet, quale isti Jesuitae nunc delineârunt: ad quod requiritur 1. ut Actio sit libera: 2. ut in Aequalitate justitia consistat, non autem aliquâ Dei benignitate aut misericordiâ nitatur: 3. ut Aequalitas ea Absoluta sit, nec Christi Gratiâ extrinsecâ egeat: 4. ut talis sit omnino, quæ apud Deum æternam vitam suo jure possit exigere: 5. supposito Pacto seu Promissione Dei. Vera hæc est, fateor, & exacta definitio proprie dicti Meriti de Condigno.
units.tr: The Canon of the Council of Trent, which those good Fathers lately imposed on men's consciences, runs thus: "If anyone shall say that the good works of a justified man are not also good works of that justification itself; or that the justified man, by the good works which he performs through God's grace and the merit of Jesus Christ, of whom he is a living member, does not truly merit eternal life: let him be anathema." ... "our works properly merit eternal happiness." Thus they. Some define this Merit more strictly, others more explicitly, but all who maintain it place it in equality with God with respect to eternal life. For example: (1) Merit of condignity is a free action, to which a reward is owed from justice. (2) The definition which Bellarmine dictated to his readers is of this kind: "God has established absolute equality between merit and reward, so that each man has as much reward as he merits by God's judgment." Then he adds: "This comes from God's promise, without which he cannot demand a reward." (3) Vasquez the Jesuit: "Our works have their dignity not from the person of Christ but from the person from whom they proceed." Likewise: "Our merits are so perfectly meritorious of eternal life that we have no defect on account of which eternal life would be denied them, or could justly be denied." And not only this, but also: "Merit is a service which, in comparison with some reward, by its own nature demands such a reward, as if repaying an equal favour." Thus he. Finally, Suarez the Jesuit, in fuller emphasis, where he contends that eternal life is owed to the works of the just: "We speak," he says, "of works which by strict justice require what is due." Thus he (as we shall relate below, chap. 11, sect. 1), and many others to the same effect. Indeed, if any merit of condignity were to exist between us and God, it must be such as these Jesuits have now outlined. For this requires: (1) that the action be free; (2) that it consist in equality of justice, and not rest on any kindness or mercy of God; (3) that this equality be absolute, and need no extrinsic grace of Christ; (4) that it be of such a kind that by its own right it can demand eternal life from God; (5) on the supposition of a covenant or promise of God. This, I admit, is the true and exact definition of merit of condignity properly so called.

units.la: Hoc illud Monstrum est, quod tum Scri-pturarum sacrâ ac divinâ, tum etiam Antiqui-tatis Catholicâ authoritate profligare ac pes-sundare conamur, juxta sententiam Ecclesiæ nostræ Anglicanæ, quæ eam, ut provida Ma-ter, & salutis [illegible, ~8 letters] solicita, nobis propinavit in Articulis xi & xii. Justi habemur coram Deo tantum ex meritis Jesu Christi, per fidem, & non ex operibus, aut meritis nostris. Quamvis autem Opera bona, quæ sunt fructus fidei, & Justificantem sequuntur, non possunt delere peccata, aut severitas Dei justitiam sustinere, sunt tamen Deo in Christo grata atque accepta [illegible, ~12 letters] Deo in Christo gratis atque accepta, [?] & à vera ac viva fide necessariò dimanant: per quam fides viva non minùs aperte innotescat nobis, quàm arbor per fructum vitæ discernitur & diiudicatur. Cum qua quàm amicè Orthodoxèque Protestantes alii conspirent [?], malim ego ex Adversariorum confessione, quàm ex ipsorum scriptis referre. Prodit igitur Vasquez, qui de Protestantibus testatur in hæc verba; {*}Opera bona necessaria esse dicunt, sicut etiam dixerunt Remunerationem necessariam esse, per fidem, spem, & charitatem, ad Justificationem: sed tamen ut justorum opera non sint digna remuneratione vitæ æternæ, nisi Deus suâ benignitate dignaretur ea remunerari. Sic affirmârunt Wittembergenses, sic Confessionistæ Augustani, imò etiam Calvinus, & Chemnitius. Hæc ille, (de quibus infrà) ubi Protestantes, ex Pontificiorum ordinibus multos, & consentientes & Advocatos sibi asciscunt.
units.tr: This is that monster which we strive to overthrow and destroy, both by the sacred and divine authority of the Scriptures and by the catholic authority of antiquity, in accordance with the judgment of our Church of England, which, as a provident mother anxious for our salvation, has offered us in Articles 11 and 12: "We are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of our Lord Jesus Christ, by faith, and not for our own works or merits. Although good works, which are the fruits of faith and follow justification, cannot put away our sins or endure the severity of God's judgment, yet they are pleasing and acceptable to God in Christ, and necessarily spring from a true and living faith; by which living faith is made known to us no less clearly than a tree is discerned and judged by its fruit." With which agreement how friendly and orthodox other Protestants are, I would rather report from the confession of our adversaries than from their own writings. Vasquez therefore brings forward one who testifies of the Protestants in these words: "They say that good works are necessary, just as they also said that reward is necessary for justification through faith, hope and charity; but that the works of the just are not worthy of the reward of eternal life, unless God by his goodness deigned to reward them. Thus the Wittenbergers affirmed, thus the Confessors of Augsburg, and even Calvin and Chemnitz." Thus he (of whom more below), where he counts among the Protestants many from the ranks of the Papists, both agreeing with them and acting as their advocates.

units.la: Veruntamen hic siste gradum (quæso te) Lector, nè forte impingas, dum hæsitabundus apud te quæras, in tanto discrimine conflictúq; Authorum, quomodo Ecclesiam ipsam Romanam impugnare videar. Dico igitur ex hac διατριβῇ[?] refelli omnes eos qui verè ac proprie dictum MERITUM hominum defendant, quod sanè Romana Ecclesia palàm fecit in Concilio Tridentino, ubi (ut jam didicimus) Anathema eum esse pronunciavit, quisquis negaverit hominis justificati bona opera verè mereri vitam æternam. Verè autem, & Proprie dictum Meritum omnino fingi nullum potest, quod non (juxta Jesuitarum definitionem accuratissimam) in Justitiæ æqualitate consistat. Sunt igitur qui opus suum bonum vel Meritorium esse credunt? Hi jam corde suo Venenum hauserunt. An verò etiam sunt qui, non id credentes, vocem tamen Meriti tamquam necessariam usurpent? Isti sanè ore saltem Venenum sumpserunt. Propterea nos, per hoc Antidotum, Lectoris nostri, non solùm cordis, verùm etiam oris sanitati studuimus. mus. Sed primo in loco, quid pro Causa sua ex Scripturis obtendant, examinabimus.
units.tr: But here, I beg you, Reader, pause a moment, lest perhaps you stumble while, doubting within yourself amid such danger and such conflict of authors, you ask how I seem to attack the Roman Church itself. I say, therefore, that by this discussion all those are refuted who defend a truly and properly so-called MERIT of men, which the Roman Church itself openly did in the Council of Trent, where (as we have already learned) it pronounced anathema on whoever denies that the good works of a justified man truly merit eternal life. But a truly and properly so-called merit cannot be imagined at all which does not (according to the most exact definition of the Jesuits) consist in equality of justice. There are, then, those who believe that their work is good or meritorious? These have now drunk poison in their heart. Or again, are there also those who, not believing it, nevertheless use the word merit as if it were necessary? Those, certainly, have taken the poison at least by mouth. Therefore, through this Antidote we have aimed at the health not only of our Reader's heart but also of his mouth. But first, we shall examine what they put forward in support of their cause from the Scriptures.

units.la: EXamen I. ex Scripturis, idque quoad
units.tr: EXAMINATION I: from the Scriptures, and that as to
1. The name
2. The sense
SECT. II.

units.la: Scripturas alias pro se proferunt & urgent
units.tr: They bring forward and press other Scriptures
The Papists. The Protestants.
I. The Papists.

units.la: SCripturæ (inquam) in quibus etiam nomen Meriti extare Pontificii somniant. Quid verò? ut Illi Meritum [illegible, ~6 letters] in Scripturis reperiant usquam? prius Locusta bovem pariet, ut est in Adagio. Sed quid ego eorum interturbo conatus? Bellarminus instar, {1}Non desunt (inquit) Scriptura testimonia, ubi ipsum nomen vel aperte continetur, vel inde facili negotio deducatur. Agè igitur, loca profer, quæ Tibi aperte denotare videantur ipsum Meriti nomen. Primus locus (inquit Bellarminus) est Ecclesiastic. 16. Omnis misericordia faciet locum unicuique secundum meritum operum suorum. Respondet Calvinus, in Græco textu non haberi nomen Meriti, sed solùm [κατὰ τὰ ἔργα?], id est, secundum opera: at illud [secundum opera] rectè vertitur, secundum Merita. Dilutum hoc Commentum & prorsus inane, quia in hujusmodi sententiis [κατά?] & [secundum] comparatio inter Operationem & Præmii collationem denotatur, non autem Causa Meritoria omnino. Potest Rex in eos, qui hastiludio praeclarè se gesserint, Beneficia ampla, secundùm eorum res gestas, conferre, ex mera sua munificen-tia. Sed de hac phrasi {*} infrà fusius, ubi ea ab Adversariis urgetur vehementiùs.
units.tr: Scriptures (I say) in which the Papists dream that even the name merit is found. But really? Will they find merit anywhere in the Scriptures? Sooner will the locust bear an ox, as the proverb has it. But why should I trouble myself over their efforts? Bellarmine, following the same pattern, says: There are not lacking (he says) passages of Scripture where the very name is either openly contained or can easily be deduced from it. Come then, produce passages that seem to you to point openly to the very name of merit. The first passage (says Bellarmine) is Ecclesiasticus 16: Every mercy will make room for each person according to the merit of his works. Calvin replies that the Greek text does not contain the word merit, but only [κατὰ τὰ ἔργα?], that is, according to the works; yet that phrase is rightly rendered according to merits. This answer is weak and utterly empty, because in such sentences [κατά?] and according to denote a comparison between the work and the bestowal of a reward, and not a meritorious cause at all. A king may, out of sheer generosity, confer ample benefits on those who have acquitted themselves brilliantly in the joust, according to their deeds. But I shall discuss this phrase more fully below, where our opponents press it more vehemently.

units.la: Agit aliter Bellarminus; {u} “Alius est locus (inquit) ad Hebr.13. Beneficentia & communionis nolite oblivisci, talibus enim hostiis prome-retur Deus. Ubi Graeca vox [εὐαρεστεῖται][?] rectissimè vertitur in [promeretur:] significat enim, Placatur Deus, aut Placetur Deo. Haec est ejusdem farinae placenta. Quasi verò voces hae, Placare, aut Placere, necessariò Meritum subindicent. Jubet Apostolus, Rom.15.2. ut Quivis placeat proximo in omnibus; ergòne singula humanitatis officia, sive gestu, nictu, nutu, risuve praestentur, inter Merita numeranda sunt? Imò, impia illa & scelerata Saltatrix dicitur Placuisse Herodi; an igitur meruit illa dimidi-um regni, aut (multis regnis pretiosius) divinum Baptistae caput? Artaxerxes, cùm illi in via obequitanti Pauper, nihil aliud habens, ambabus aquam, è vicino profluente haustam, manibus obtulisset, jucundè accepit, atque arrisit, ait Historicus: nec tamen Pauper de Condigno praemium meruit. Denique cùm mancipia faciunt, quod jure, atque etiam sine pacto, maximè debent, Dominis placent; ecquid merentur de Condigno? prorsus negabitis. In Vulgata Translatione, Psal.114.9. de Davide legitur,
units.tr: Bellarmine argues differently: Another passage (he says) is Hebrews 13: Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for with such sacrifices God is won over. Here the Greek word [εὐαρεστεῖται?] is most rightly rendered is won over, for it signifies: God is appeased, or God is pleased. This is a cake of the same dough. As if these words, to appease or to please, necessarily implied merit! The Apostle bids (Rom. 15.2) that each one please his neighbour in all things. Are then all the offices of kindness, whether shown by gesture, wink, nod, or smile, to be counted among merits? Indeed, that impious and wicked dancer is said to have pleased Herod; did she then merit half the kingdom, or (more precious than many kingdoms) the head of the Baptist? Artaxerxes, when a poor man riding up beside him on the road offered him water, scooped in his two hands from a stream nearby, gladly accepted it and smiled, says the historian; yet the poor man did not earn a reward de condigno. Finally, when servants do what they rightly owe, and indeed even without any contract, they please their masters; do they then merit de condigno? You will flatly deny it. In the Vulgate translation, Psalm 114.9, it is read of David: [I will please the Lord in the land of the living].

units.la: {u} Bellarm. ibid. §Alius legitur, [ Placebo Domino in regione viventium: ] quæ verba Bellarminus interpretatur de cœlesti regione, extra peregrinationem hanc nostram mortalem; ubi {a} Sancti (inquit) placent Deo omnibus modis: cùm tamen Sanctos beatos docuisse extra statum merendi. Et ut alibi dissertiùs; {b} Neque peccatores extra gratiam, neque Beati mereri possunt, sed solùm qui peregrinantur in terris. Atque itâ ex vocabulo [Placet] potest Cardinalis concludere, Sanctos mereri, quando mereri non possunt; quod quomodo Pontificiis aliis placeat, ipse viderit.
units.tr: {u} Bellarmine, ibid., §Alius. Bellarmine explains these words of the heavenly region, outside this mortal pilgrimage of ours, where the saints (he says) please God in every way, although he has taught elsewhere that the blessed saints are outside the state of merit. And, more clearly elsewhere: Neither sinners outside grace nor the blessed can merit, but only those who are pilgrims on earth. And so from the word please the Cardinal can conclude that the saints merit, when they cannot merit at all. How this pleases the other Papists, he himself must see.

units.la: Idem error facilè cernitur in Objectione vocis[ Placatur: ] quia infantem iratum nutrix lallando, puer patrem lacrymando, facetus quivis Adversarium jocando, aut saltem blandiendo Placat, sed Meriti expers tamen. Phinees & alii gentis Israëliticæ Proceres indignè ferunt extructum à Reubenitis Altare; sed dato ab iis responso, nempe id non Cultûs, sed duntaxat Memoriæ causâ esse erectum, protinus Placati sunt. An verò (dic amabò) ex illo Responso vel guttula ulla Meriti exprimi posset? Ad causam accedam propius. Quid enim magis aut Placere aut Placare dici potest, quàm quod reddit alium propitium? at Valentia Jesuita de Impetratorio Medio, quod à Medio Meritorio in Scholis distingui solet, loquitur: {c} Peculiari ratione precibus (inquit) propitiandi virtus in Scripturis tribuitur, quatenus Beneficia divina, ex misericordia Dei, per illas impetramus. Sic ille. Virtus igitur illa non ex Condignitate Operis, sed ex Dei com-placentia beneficia obtinet. Adhuc igitur piscati estis in aëre; vox enim hæc, Meritum, per totam Scripturam prorsus muta est; de quo tamen non adeò laboramus, modò Me-riti de Condigno ἀξίως[?] & sensum liquidum ex iis possitis elicere.
units.tr: The same error is easily seen in the objection based on the word appeased. For a nurse appeases an angry infant by babbling, a boy his father by weeping, and any witty fellow an opponent by joking, or at least by flattering; yet none of these has any merit. Phinehas and other leaders of the people of Israel took it badly that the altar had been built by the Reubenites; but when they had received the answer, namely that it had been erected not for worship but only as a memorial, they were at once appeased. But tell me, pray, could even a drop of merit be squeezed out of that answer? I shall come closer to the matter. For what can be said more to please or to appease than that which makes another favourable? But the Jesuit Valentia speaks of the Impetratory Means, which in the schools is usually distinguished from the Meritorious Means: By a peculiar reason (he says) the power of appeasing by prayers is ascribed to them in the Scriptures, inasmuch as through them we obtain divine benefits from the mercy of God. So he. That power therefore obtains benefits not from the condignity of the work but from God's good pleasure. So you are still fishing in the air. For this word merit is utterly silent throughout the whole of Scripture. Yet we do not labour much over this, provided you can draw from them a clear sense of merit de condigno [ἀξίως?].

units.la: MEritum de Condigno, quoad sensum, Pontificii ex Scripturis variis deducere-conantur; sed frustra.
units.tr: Merit de condigno, as to its sense, the Papists try to deduce from various Scriptures; but in vain.
SECT. III.
I. The First Class of Scriptures.

units.la: CLassis prima Scripturarum, quam objicit Bellarminus; Evidenter (inquit) evincitur ex Scripturis. 1. In locis, in quibus invenitur nomen Dignitatis, ut Apoc. 3. Ambulabant in albis, quia digni. Luc. 20. 35. Digni habebantur seculo illo. 2. Thess. 1. 5. Ut digni habeamini regno Dei. At Pererius vestræ Societatis Jesuita primarius, vel tacentibus nobis, ora vobis obstruet.{b} Pelagiani dicunt (inquit) Deum non dare primam Gratiam nisi dignis & merentibus. Quibus respondeo; Digni dicuntur gratiam accipere, non tanquam Condigne eam accipere merentes, sed quia per Dei gratiam facti sunt idonei & habiles, & rite præparati ad accipiendam Gratiam. Sic ille. Eóne verò, Bellarmine, vos angustiarum redactos esse, ut in nos armis utamini Pelagianis? nónne vos pudet? Quod igitur Pererius vester adversus Pelagianos, re-spectu Gratiae, id vobis, quoad Gloriam, à nobis responsum putetis: Non quia Condi-gnè merentes, sed quia Habiles & idonei, Digni appellentur. Quanquam, nè nos ipsi nobis de-esse videamur, respondemus; Sanctos Dignos apud Deum haberi, non tamen ex dignitate aliqua Meriti sui, sed ex misericordi digna-tione Dei. Cujus acceptationis exemplum liquidum extat, Act.5.41. Ibant Apostoli gau-dentes, quòd [καταξιωθέντες] digni habiti sunt pro nomine Jesu contumeliam pati. De quibus verbis Chrysostomus; {c} Καταξιωθῆναι γὰρ ὄντως ἐστὶν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ ἀτιμασθῆναι [?]; id est, Revera dignatio est (nempe Dei) eos contumeliam pati pro nomine ejus. Quam dignationem, &, ut itá dicam, honoris praerogativam, tanquam à pe-culiari gratia & dono Dei profectam esse, ex-pressissimè docet Apostolus, Philip.1.29. Vo-bis datum est, non solùm credere, sed etiam pro ipso pati.
units.tr: The first class of Scriptures, which Bellarmine objects, is this: It is evidently proved from Scripture. 1. In those places where the name of Worthiness is found, as Rev. 3. They shall walk in white, because they are worthy. Luke 20.35. They were counted worthy of that world. 2 Thess. 1.5. That you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God. But Pererius, the chief Jesuit of your Society, will stop your mouths, even if we say nothing.{b} The Pelagians say (he says) that God does not give the first grace except to the worthy and deserving. To whom I reply: They are said to receive grace worthily, not as though they received it by deserving it condignly, but because through the grace of God they have been made fit and able, and duly prepared to receive grace. Thus he. But do you, Bellarmine, come to such straits that you use the Pelagian weapons against us? Are you not ashamed? So what your Pererius answered against the Pelagians with respect to grace, you may think we answer for you with respect to glory: they are called worthy not because they deserve condignly, but because they are fit and able. Yet, lest we seem to be lacking in our own case, we also answer: the saints are held worthy before God, not by any worthiness of their own merit, but by the merciful condescension of God. A clear example of this acceptance stands in Acts 5.41: The apostles went away rejoicing that they were [καταξιωθέντες] counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus. On these words Chrysostom says: Καταξιωθῆναι γὰρ ὄντως ἐστὶν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ ἀτιμασθῆναι [?]; that is, it is truly an act of condescension (namely of God) that they suffer dishonour for his name. That this condescension, and, as I may say, this prerogative of honour, comes from a peculiar grace and gift of God, the Apostle teaches most expressly, Phil. 1.29: It has been given to you not only to believe, but also to suffer for him.

units.la: Nos, si vestram patientiam impetrare valeamus, donec causam hanc discutiemus, facilè sentietis Primaevae Antiquitatis Consensum à Papistico sensu De Merito ex Condigno, adeò abhorrere, ut nec quenquam Dignum, nec nos quicquam vitâ aeternâ proprie Dignum operari posse profiteantur. Taceo vos à nostris sæpe doceri, voces has, ἀξίως [?], & ἀξιοῦσαι [?], non Meritum, sed Dignationem significare; æquè ac 2.Thess.1.11. Cujus rei gratiâ precamur semper pro vobis, ut [ὑμᾶς ἀξίωσῃ ὁ Θεὸς [?]] dignetur vos Deus vocatione istâ [?], & compleat omnem bonitatis suæ [ἀδοξίας [?]] gratuitum beneplacitum & opus fidei potenter. Ubi singula ferè verba contra dignitatem Meritorum, pro Dei dignatione, pugnant.
units.tr: If you will bear with us long enough for us to discuss this matter, you will easily see that the consensus of primitive antiquity is so far from the Papistic sense of merit of condignity, that it professes that no one is worthy, and that we can do nothing that is properly worthy of eternal life. I say nothing of the fact that our people have often taught that these words, ἀξίως [?] and ἀξιοῦσαι [?], signify not merit but condescension; as in 2 Thess. 1.11: For which cause we also pray always for you, that [ὑμᾶς ἀξίωσῃ ὁ Θεὸς [?]] God would count you worthy of this calling, and fulfil every good pleasure of his goodness and the work of faith with power. Here nearly every single word is opposed to the worthiness of merits and in favour of God's condescension.

units.la: II. Classis Scripturarum, quæ pro Merito de Condigno objicitur.
units.tr: II. The Class of Scriptures which is objected in favour of Merit of Condignity.
SECT. IV.

units.la: Classis secunda. Objicit Bellarminus; Sunt alia Scripturæ loca, in quibus vitam æternam mereri dicimur: Matth.20.8. Reddet mercedem. Matth.5. Copiosa est vestra merces in cœlis. Disputa; Merces & Merita sunt Relata: At vita æterna est propriè Merces: Ergò, Opera sunt propriè Merita. Hæc ille pro Merito de Condigno; cui consonat illud Maldonati Enthymema; Vita æterna est propriè Merces bonorum Operum: Ergò bonum opus est propriè Meritum. Cùm Argumentum à Relatis objecisti, seriòne & ἐνθυμηματικῶς [?], Bellarmine, an ἀγωνιστικῶς [?] & tentativè disseruistis? Loquere, ut te videam. Neque Argumenta illa (inquit) à Relatione Meriti & Mercedis convincunt: fateor enim omni merito respondere Mercedem, sed sicut certum quoddam donum ex Congruo: ità Mercedem quandam dicimus esse ex Congruo, quæ magìs debeatur ex Gratia, quàm ex justitia. Quæ confessio tua vestrum pro Merito de Condigno Argumentum planè jugulat, siquidem Theologis vestris fidem ullam habeamus; de quibus Costerus Jesuita, {s} Catholici (inquit) Meritum hoc modo definiunt, ut sit Actio cui merces debetur ex Justitia. De Mercede distinguimus. Alia est Merces Æqualitatis & Commensurationis, seu Condignitatis ad opus: & sic Merces & Meritum correlativa sunt. Sed alia est Merces Munificentia & Benignitatis, quæ Dignitatem Operis infinitis modis excedit. Sed de hoc multò opportunior erit differendi locus in capitibus sequentibus De Mercede; ubi nihil nos de Mercede statuere quivis intelligat, quod non erat à Catholicis Patribus antiquitus decretum & definitum.
units.tr: The second class. Bellarmine objects: There are other passages of Scripture in which we are said to merit eternal life: Matth. 20.8, He will repay the reward. Matth. 5, Great is your reward in heaven. He argues: Reward and merit are correlatives; but eternal life is properly a reward; therefore good works are properly merits. He says this for merit of condignity, and Maldonatus' enthymeme agrees with it: Eternal life is properly the reward of good works; therefore a good work is properly a merit. When you objected the argument from correlatives, Bellarmine, did you do so seriously and enthymematically [ἐνθυμηματικῶς], or agonistically [ἀγωνιστικῶς] and tentatively? Speak, that I may see you. Nor do those arguments (he says) convince from the relation of merit and reward: for I admit that every merit corresponds to a reward, but as a certain gift from congruity. So we say there is a certain reward from congruity, which is owed more from grace than from justice. Your confession here plainly destroys your argument for merit of condignity, if we may put any trust in your theologians. Of them, the Jesuit Coster says: Catholics define merit in this way, that it is an action to which a reward is owed from justice. We distinguish about reward. One reward is of equality and commensurateness, or condignity to the work, and in this sense merit and reward are correlatives. But another reward is of munificence and kindness, which exceeds the worth of the work in infinite ways. A much more suitable place to discuss this will be in the following chapters On Reward, where anyone may understand that we decide nothing about reward that was not already decreed and defined by the Catholic Fathers of old.

units.la: III. Clasis Scripturarum objicitur pro Merito de Condigno.
units.tr: III. A class of Scriptures brought forward for merit of condignity.
Section V.

units.la: {h}Aliæ sunt loca (inquit Cardinalis) in quibus vita dicitur reddi secundum mensuram. Luc.6. Quà mensurà mensi fueritis, eadem remetietur vobis. Loquitur tam de bonis quàm malis. Et, Reddet unicuique secundum opera, malis mortem [?] aeternam, bonis vitam aeternam, Rom.2.6. Eadem est phrasis de utriusque. Cui succinit Costerus. {1}Reddet unicuique secundum opera.] Observandum est, Scripturam, quando de Retributione loquitur, eadem verborum formula uti; cum agit de reddendis praemiis Justo, atque cum improbis supplicia denuntiat: ut clarè perspiciatur, non minùs nos bonis actionibus aeternam felicitatem, quàm malis & flagitiosis aeterna supplicia promereri. Sic ille. Et certè, si eventum Praemii & Supplicii respicimus, similiter se habent: sin spectemus modum vel Condignitatis operis, ex parte hominis; vel modum divinae Justitiae Dei, in conferendis Praemiis, Supplicììsque exigendis; Illatio haec parùm distat à blasphemia; ad quam contundendam non opus est aliquâ nostrâ confutatione, cùm praesertim ipsius Costeri conscientia (quâ nihil potest esse homini magis adversarium) eum lancinet atque fodicet: nam in eodem Tractatu de Meritis veritas ipsa hanc illi confessionem extorsit: {k}Si considerantur opera (inquit) ut à voluntate nostra dimanant, hoc modo quidem peccata impiorum merentur aeternis supplicìis vindicari, quia perditio nostra ex nobis, Ose.13.9. Opera verò nostra non merentur aeternam gloriam, quòd meritum omne nostrum divinâ gratiâ nitatur. Et subindè addit; Bona opera conjunctam habent divinam promissionem mercedis aeternae: & hâc ratione digna sunt praemio, non quidem suâ naturâ, sed ex pacto Dei. Quamvis igitur Boni & Mali dicuntur Remunerationem obtinere secundum Opera, quoad effectum; tamen in genere causarum duplex discrimen cernitur: Unum, quòd Bona opera non planè nostra sunt, quia Gratia divina operatur in nobis; sic enim Deus, [?]Auxilium à me, Ose. 13. (De hac Objectione consulendus est Augustinus infrà, Cap. 3. Sect. 1.) Mala verò non nisi nostra sunt; unde dicitur, Perditio tua ex te; Ibidem. Alterum verò, quia Opera bona inferioris naturae sunt, quàm ut cum dignitate divini Praemii comparari possint. Quod nostrum responsum posthac Patrum antiquorum judiciis accuratissimis muniemus. Interea Augustini testimonium valde opportunum nullo modo praetermittendum est. {1}Deus autem in malis hominum merita eorum debita retributione persequitur; bona verò per indebitam gratiam misericordi voluntate largitur. Sic ille.
units.tr: "There are other passages" (says the Cardinal) "in which life is said to be repaid according to measure. Luke 6. With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again. It speaks of good and bad alike. And, He will render to every one according to his works: to the wicked eternal death, to the good eternal life, Rom. 2.6." The phrase is the same for both. Costerus echoes him: "Render to every one according to his works." It must be observed that Scripture, when it speaks of retribution, uses the same form of words whether it is assigning rewards to the just or announcing punishments to the wicked, so that it may be clearly seen that we merit eternal happiness by good actions no less than eternal punishments by wicked and shameful deeds. Thus he. And indeed, if we look at the outcome of reward and punishment, they stand alike; but if we consider the manner of the worthiness of the work on man's side, or the manner of divine Justice in bestowing rewards and exacting punishments, this inference differs little from blasphemy. There is no need for any refutation of ours to crush it, especially since Costerus's own conscience, than which nothing can be more hostile to a man, gnaws at him and goads him. For in the same treatise on Merits the truth itself wrung from him this confession: "If works are considered (he says) as they proceed from our will, in this way indeed the sins of the impious merit to be punished with eternal punishments, because our destruction is from ourselves, Hos. 13.9. But our works do not merit eternal glory, because all our merit rests on divine grace." And again he adds: "Good works have joined to them the divine promise of eternal reward, and for this reason they are worthy of a reward, not indeed by their nature, but by the covenant of God." Although, therefore, good and bad are said to obtain their recompense according to works as to the effect, yet in the kind of causes a twofold difference is seen. One is that good works are not wholly ours, because divine grace works in us; for thus God says, "Your help is from me," Hos. 13. (On this objection the reader should consult Augustine below, chap. 3, sect. 1.) But evil works are only ours; hence it is said, "Your destruction is from yourself," ibid. The other is that good works are of a lower nature than that they can be compared with the dignity of the divine reward. We will confirm this answer of ours later by the most careful judgments of the ancient Fathers. Meanwhile the very apt testimony of Augustine must by no means be passed over. "God, indeed, in the evil of men pursues their merits with the retribution due to them; but good things he bestows through undeserved grace by a merciful will." Thus he.

units.la: Est ubi distinguit Perkinsus noster inter Remunerationem Operum bonorum Secundum opera, tanquam à benignitate Remunerantis; & Remunerationem Propter opera, tanquam ex dignitate Operantis; & statim incurrit in falsam irrisionem Bishoppi vestri: {m}O (inquit) acutum hominis ingenium! Rectiùs in illum nos, O Cyclopicam audaciam! qui non videt isthoc suo Sarcasmo, veluti nigro sale, Gregorium Magnum
units.tr: Our Perkins, in one place, distinguishes between the reward of good works according to works, as flowing from the kindness of the one who rewards, and the reward on account of works, as flowing from the worth of the one who works; and at once he falls into a false mockery of your Bishop: {m}"O (he says) what a sharp wit the man has!" More rightly should we say to him, O Cyclopean audacity! He does not see that by this sarcasm, like black salt, he rubs Gregory the Great

units.la: {1} August. contra duas Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 6. in fine.
units.tr: {1} Augustine, against two letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chap. 6, near the end.

units.la: {m} Mr. Bishop in Tract. Angl adversus Perkins. Sect. quae est de Meritis. gnum Pontificem pariter perfricari: sic enim sanctus ille Pontifex:{n} Quod si Sanctorum felicitas misericordiâ acquiratur, ubi erit quod scribitur, [Reddet unicuique secundum opera ejus?] si secundum Opera, quomodo misericordia æstimatur?
