Sed aliud est Secundum Opera, aliud Propter Opera reddere. Hoc Romanus ille Pontisex pronunciare non potuisset, si de Meritis Operum ex Condigno vel somniasset quidem.
units.tr: {m} Mr. Bishop, in the English treatise against Perkins, section on merits. gnum, the Pontiff, equally: for that holy Pontiff says this: {n}"But if the happiness of the saints is acquired by mercy, where will be what is written, [He will repay each one according to his works]? If according to works, how is mercy valued? But it is one thing to repay according to works, another to repay on account of works." That Roman Pontiff could not have pronounced this, if he had even dreamed of merits of works by condignity.

units.la: Hic rursus, ut omnis Amphibolia removeatur, distinguendum est de voce [Secundum,] quod nonnunquam proportionem qualitatis ex Gratia inditæ denotat, ut secundum bonitatem Operis bonitas Præmii reddatur; quod liberè concedi potest, absque ulla Relatione ad ullum Meritum. Aliquando designat (ut jam Pontificii definiverunt) proportionem Æqualitatis Justitiæ, ex Condignitate Operis, ad vitam æternam. Quam acceptionem vocis nos non rejicimus modò, sed & detestamur: In quo à Catholicis Patribus consensum testatissimum habemus; qui tum Indignitatem Operis nostri fatentur, tum etiam Supra-dignitatem vitæ cœlestis adstruunt prædicántq;. De quo infrà, Cap.10. & Cap.20. Sect.11.
units.tr: Here again, so that all ambiguity may be removed, we must distinguish the word [according to], which sometimes denotes a proportion of quality arising from infused grace, as the goodness of the reward is returned according to the goodness of the work; this can freely be conceded, without any relation to any merit. Sometimes it designates (as the Papists have already defined) a proportion of equal justice, based on the condignity of the work, to eternal life. This meaning of the word we not only reject but also detest. In this matter we have the most express agreement of the Catholic Fathers, who both confess the unworthiness of our work and also assert and proclaim the surpassing worth of heavenly life. Concerning this, see below, chap. 10 and chap. 20, sect. 11.

units.la: IIII. Classis Scripturarum, quæ objiciuntur pro Merito de Condigno.
units.tr: IIII. The class of Scriptures which are objected in favour of merit of condignity.
SECT. VI.

units.la: Quartam Classem Scripturarum objicit Bellarminus; Ex locis (inquit) ubi ratio redditur, cur detur vita æterna: ut Matth. 21. Possidete regnum; Esurivi enim, & dedistis mihi manducare, &c. Et ibidem, Quia fuisti fidelis in paucis, constituam te super multa; intra in gaudium Domini tui. Et Apoc. 1. Quia venerunt è tribulatione multa, ideo sunt ante thronum. Respondet Calvinus, In Scripturis illud [Enim] sæpe notam esse Consequentia, non Causæ, & sic hîc in locis, quia Deus prius voluit bona Opera fieri ab Electis, & postea ejus regnum obtineri. At Christus eodem modo loquitur de Bonorum præmiis, & Malorum supplicîis, [Ite in ignem, non Enim dedistis mihi manducare, &c.] Nec non Salmeron; {P}Verba sunt clarissima; nam vox, Enim, causalis est, & rationem exponit. Respondemus, (quanquam Calvini responsio per se valeat) Vos, ut Causalem Condignitatem pariter in utrisque inesse constet, nunquam profecto efficietis: id quod Costeri nupera palinodia satis vos edocuit, qui postquam in idem Condignitatis præcipitium lapsus, Æquè remunerandi Bonos præmiis, & malos ac flagitiosos supplicîis, statim tamen latum discrimen agnovit ex parte Causæ, quòd nimirum dignitas bonorum Operum diuinâ gratiâ nita-tur: E contrà, Malorum supplicia, quanta quanta fuerint, ex ipsorum proprio Reatu illis debeantur. Oportet igitur, velitis nolitis, de causis ipsis distinguere, quia Impiorum perditio ex se, & tanquam à Causa solitaria, ideóque purè putè Meritoria supplicii.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects a fourth class of Scriptures: "From passages (he says) where a reason is given why eternal life is given, such as Matt. 21: Possess the kingdom; for I was hungry, and you gave me food, etc. And in the same place, Because you were faithful in a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord. And Rev. 1: Because they came out of great tribulation, therefore they are before the throne." Calvin answers that "in Scripture that word [for] is often a mark of consequence, not of cause, and so here, because God first willed that good works be done by the elect, and afterwards that his kingdom be obtained." But Christ speaks in the same way of the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked: [Depart into fire; for you did not give me food, etc.] So too Salmeron: {P}"The words are very clear; for the word, for, is causal and explains the reason." We reply (although Calvin's answer is sound in itself) that you will never manage to show that causal condignity is present in both. This the recent palinode of Costerus has taught you well enough: having fallen into the same precipice of condignity, he says that the wicked and the shameful are equally to be rewarded with prizes and the good with punishments, yet he at once recognised a wide difference on the side of the cause, namely that the worth of good works rests on divine grace. On the other hand, the punishments of the wicked, however great they are, are owed to them from their own guilt. It is necessary, therefore, whether you wish it or not, to distinguish the causes themselves, because the perdition of the impious is from themselves, and as from a solitary cause, and therefore purely meritorious of punishment.

units.la: At quævis bona opera Iustorum sunt Caufæ causatæ; acti enim pii à Spiritu Sancto aguntur, ut agant: id quod facile erit nobis discernere in eadem forma iudicii novisimi, ubi sententia pronunciatur in impios, Ite maledicti in ignem æternum paratum Diabolo & Angelis ejus. Nempe, Maledictio ut à iusto iudice, (haud aliter quàm in Diabolis) tantùm eorum malitiæ debetur. Altera, Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum; cùm enim esurivi, dedistis manducare, &c. Nunquam profecto daturi illi quicquam, nisi priùs à Deo benedicti; nec posteà remunerandi à Deo Iudice, antequam à Deo Patre habiles & præparati facti essent ad Regnum: [illegible, ~9 letters] creati in bonis operibus, inquit Apostolus, Ephes.2. ad quod ab eo erant prædestinati. Quod, ut par est, si pensitare velimus exactius, vah, quot quantæque Benedictiones Patris cœlestis præcessisse reperiemus, (viz. Electionis, Vocationis, Regenerationis, Sanctificationis, Reconciliationis, & Confirmationis in bono) priusquam æternam hanc Glorificationis Benedictionem sortiantur? Si, quæ infrà proferentur, Patrum antiquorum Judicia consulere velimus, quivis intelliget Responsum hoc omnino esse Catholicæ veritatis. Interea gustum Lector fumat ex Fulgentio super illa verba, [Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis ab initio mundi, &c.] Sed & hoc ipsum (inquit) opus est Gratia: ex Gratia enim datur non solùm justificatis vita bona, sed & glorificatis vita æterna. In hunc finem, ubi quæstio est, cur dictum erat Bonis, Venite benedicti Patris mei; non autem erat dictum Malis, Ite maledicti Patris mei; vester Tostatus Abulensis respondet, Quia Benedictio est à Patre, at Maledictionis Deus author non est: & sic apparet in Prædestinatione & Reprobatione; nam ab æterno elegit nos, ut essemus Sancti, Eph.1. ideo non est in nobis, neque ex nobis, id est, in potestate nostra, quòd habeamus bonum illud, sed ex Dei voluntate, Rom. 9. Secus in Reprobatione, causa non est ex parte Dei, sed ex se: Benedicti, quia benedictionis Ministrator est Pater; maledictionis autem unusquisque Actor est sibi. Hæc ille.
units.tr: But every good work of the just is a caused cause; for the pious are moved by the Holy Spirit so that they may act. This we shall easily discern in the same form of the final judgment, where sentence is pronounced upon the wicked: "Depart, cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels." Clearly, the curse, as from a just judge (no differently than for the devils), is due only to their wickedness. The other: "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom; for when I was hungry, you gave me food, etc." They would never have given anything unless first blessed by God; nor would they afterwards be rewarded by God the Judge before they had been made by God the Father fit and prepared for the kingdom: [illegible, about 9 letters] "created in good works," says the Apostle, Eph. 2, for which they had been predestined by him. If we wish to weigh this more exactly, as is fitting, oh, how many and how great blessings of the heavenly Father we shall find to have gone before (namely election, calling, regeneration, sanctification, reconciliation, and confirmation in good) before they obtain this eternal blessing of glorification? If we wish to consult the judgments of the ancient Fathers, which will be set out below, anyone will understand that this answer is wholly that of Catholic truth. Meanwhile let the reader take a taste from Fulgentius on those words, [Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, etc.] "But this very thing (he says) is the work of grace: for by grace is given not only good life to the justified, but eternal life to the glorified." To this end, where the question is why it was said to the good, Come, blessed of my Father, but was not said to the wicked, Depart, cursed of my Father, your Tostatus of Avila answers: "Because blessing is from the Father, but God is not the author of cursing; and so it appears in predestination and reprobation: for from eternity he chose us that we should be holy, Eph. 1; therefore it is not in us, nor from us, that is, in our power, that we have that good, but from God's will, Rom. 9. It is otherwise in reprobation: the cause is not on God's side, but from itself. Blessed, because the Father is the minister of the blessing; but cursed, since each one is the author of his own curse." Thus he.

units.la: Nec est quòd negotium ullum facessat nobis vox [ENIM] quatenus æquè utrisque inserviat, [Venite Benedicti, dedistis ENIM: &c, Ite maledicti, non ENIM dedistis:] quia pro diversitate subjecti diversa esse potest ejusdem dictì ratio: viz. Venite benedicti, dedistis ENIM, nempe per gratiam & benedictionem Dei in-debitam: debitam: &, Ite maledicti, non ENIM dedistis, nimirum, ex voluntatis vestrae pravitate. Nec enim ignoratis, frequenter vocem eandem in eadem sententia variè usurpari in Scripturis. Qui servabit vitam suam, perdet eam : ubi vita prior temporalem, posterior æternam denotat. Et 2.Cor.5. Is qui non novit peccatum, id est, legis transgressionem, factus est peccatum, id est, sacrificium pro peccato. Quæ observatio est apud antiquos Patres admodum familiaris, qui in Commentariis suis sese explicant, æquè ac nunc patuit ex illis verbis, in voce ENIM tam quoad ITE, quam quoad POSSIDETE; quam Vulgata Editio perperam reddit nudè [Possidete]& non ut est in Græcis[illegible, ~14 letters] hereditatem habete. Quæ vox indicat, Regnum Sanctis obtingere jure hereditario, quod excludit prorsus Jus omne Meritorium, ut exactè probatur infrà. Denique differentiæ Ratio hæc esse potest, Qui in uno offendit, reus erit omnium, Jac.2. 10. Ex uno igitur peccato, licèt in aliis rectè se gesserit, meretur homo mortem: non item ex uno bono opere sequitur eum mereri vitam. Necessariò igitur considerandum est discrimen Subjectorum, ut exempli gratiâ, Marc. 16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur : qui autem non, damnabitur: Æquè valet consequentia Salutis ex fide unius, atque damnationis ex incredulitate alterius. Sed Ratio consequentiæ est multùm diversa: nam damnatio non credentis est ex Merito, salus autem credentis ex Gratia ac singulari Dei indulgentia.
units.tr: Nor should the word [ENIM] cause us any trouble, since it serves both sides alike [Come, blessed ones, for you gave ENIM: etc. Go, cursed ones, you did not give ENIM:], because the sense of the same word can differ according to its subject. Thus Come, blessed ones, for you gave, namely through the grace and undeserved blessing of God; and Go, cursed ones, for you did not give, namely from the perversity of your will. You are not unaware that Scripture often uses the same word in different ways within the same sentence. He who would save his life will lose it: here the first life denotes temporal life, the second eternal life. And in 2 Cor. 5, He who knew no sin, that is, no transgression of the law, was made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin. This practice is very familiar among the ancient Fathers, who explain themselves in their commentaries, as is now plain from those words, where ENIM applies equally to Go and to Possess. The Vulgate edition renders this wrongly and bare as [Possess], whereas the Greek has [illegible] inherit. The word indicates that the kingdom falls to the saints by hereditary right, which utterly excludes all meritorious right, as is exactly proved below. Finally, the reason for the difference may be this: Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all, James 2:10. By one sin, then, a man deserves death, even if he has behaved well in other respects; but it does not follow from one good work that he merits life. It is therefore necessary to consider the difference between the subjects. For example, Mark 16: He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not will be condemned. The inference to salvation from the faith of one is as valid as the inference to condemnation from the unbelief of the other. But the ground of the inference is very different: the condemnation of the unbeliever comes from merit, while the salvation of the believer comes from grace and God's singular kindness.

units.la: Alteram vocem [Quia] quod attinet, ut Apoc.7. Quia venerunt ex tribulatione, potest subire vicem Consequentiae, perinde ut illud Christi dictum, Luc. 7.47. Dico ei remissa esse peccata multa, quia dilexit multum. Sic hunc locum intellexit Calvinus; & statim vapulat ab Orbilio Stapletono, {r}Miratur Calvinus (inquit) nostros Interpretes ita crasse hallucinari, ut dicant hanc mulierem veniam suis lacrymis promeritam. Putidus cavillator! Nemo vel veterum Interpretum, vel recentiorum verbo [Promerendi] usus est. Bona verba, quaeso. Sed agedum, huius Textus sensum germanum rimemur: {s}Calvinus vult nec Meritum, nec causam ullam subsecutae remissionis fuisse officia, quae haec mulier praestitit: sed argumentum, inquit, quo nititur Christus, non a causa, sed ab effectu sumptum est, quia prius ordine est beneficium accipere, quam gratias agere: at hic multa dilectio causa erat, non quidem meritoria, sed ad eam disponens. Inepte & absurde Calvinus; quicquid hic Magdalena fecit, adepta jam justitia signa fuisse, ad gratitudinem suam testandam exhibita. Sic ille. Nullum est certius signum cerebri male constituti, quam omne illud in aliis ut insulsum reprehendere, quod ad palatum suum non sapiat.
units.tr: As for the other word [Quia], as in Rev. 7, Because they came out of great tribulation, it may stand in the place of a consequence, just as Christ's saying in Luke 7:47, I say to her that her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. Calvin understood this passage in this way, and at once Orbilius Stapleton lashes him: Calvin, he says, wonders that our interpreters blunder so grossly as to say that this woman earned pardon by her tears. Foul jester! Neither any of the older interpreters nor any of the more recent has used the word [to earn]. Fine words, I must say. But come, let us look for the true sense of this text: Calvin wants neither merit nor any cause of the forgiveness that followed to be the services this woman performed; rather, he says, the argument on which Christ rests is taken not from the cause but from the effect, because receiving a benefit comes before giving thanks. Here, however, great love was the cause, not indeed meritorious, but disposing her to it. Calvin is foolish and absurd; whatever Mary Magdalene did, she had already attained justification, and she displayed these signs to attest her gratitude. So he. There is no surer sign of a badly constituted brain than to criticise in others as insipid whatever does not suit one's own palate.

units.la: Alii igitur consulendi sunt, quorum sen-foria[?] soria fortè paulò eruditiora fuisse videbuntur; imprimis Toletus Jes. & Cardinalis: [{t}Propter quod dico tibi, remittuntur ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multùm:] Id est, multa peccata ei remissa esse, eo signo ac argumento manifestum esse potest, quoniam multa signa dilectionis erga me ostendit. Tu enim, Simon, judicâsti, & rectè quidem, cui multum debitum est, multùm diligere, ac magis gratum esse erga creditorem oportere. Ubi ergo ista multa dilectionis signa appareant, judicandum est, magnam peccatorum ac debitorum remissionem. In quibus verbis vox [QUONIAM] causam significat, non rei, sed probationis; est enim argumentum ab effectibus & signis:— nam ex signis dilectionis erga ipsum, quasi creditorem, exhibitis, deducit mulieri peccata esse remissa. Quae expositio (vocem QUONIAM, non causam rei significare) tam est prorsus Calviniana, ac si ab ipsius Calvini Commentario desumpta verbatim fuisset. Quam etiam interpretationem ex Gregorii Pontificis judicio & authoritate stabilire conatur. Gregorius (inquit) Lib.6.Epist. 22. hac de Dilectione, quae sequitur remissionem, interpretatur: illûdq; [QUONIAM] probationem indicare sentit, quasi Argumentum sit ab effectu: ut in hoc demonstratum sit, ei remissa peccata multa, ex dilectione multa quam ostendit.
units.tr: We must therefore consult others, whose opinions will perhaps seem a little more learned; above all Toletus, the Jesuit and cardinal: [Therefore I say to you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much]. That is, that her many sins were forgiven her can be made manifest by this sign and argument, since she showed many signs of love towards me. For you, Simon, have judged rightly that he to whom more is owed should love more, and that a debtor ought to be more grateful to his creditor. Where, then, these many signs of love appear, it must be judged that there has been a great remission of sins and debts. In these words the word [BECAUSE] signifies not the cause of the thing but the proof; for it is an argument from effects and signs: for from the signs of love shown to him, as to a creditor, he infers that the woman's sins were forgiven. This explanation, that the word BECAUSE signifies not the cause of the thing, is so entirely Calvinian that it might have been taken word for word from Calvin's own commentary. He also tries to establish this interpretation by the judgment and authority of Pope Gregory. Gregory, he says, in Book 6, Letter 22, interprets this love, which follows the forgiveness, in this way: he judges that the word [BECAUSE] indicates a proof, as if it were an argument from the effect, so that it is shown that her many sins were forgiven her on account of the great love she displayed.

units.la: Nec minùs enucleatè Salmeron Jesuita hanc causam disceptat, tandemque concludit: "{u}Alii (inquit) viri docti contendunt, in, Latinè, QuoNIAM, non semper significare rei causam efficien-tem, sed interdum per illam reddi rationem ab effectu: dixit enim Dominus [Propter quod dico tibi, remittuntur ei peccata multa,] Et hujus mea affirmationis rationem (inquit) ab effectu subdo, [Quoniam dilexit multum.] Ex dilectione enim, ut effectu, causam ejus, id est, remissionem peccatorum praecessisse demonstrat; atque hic sensus tum a praecedentibus, tum a subsequentibus comprobatur. Ex praecedentibus, quia dixit, [Donavit utrisque] & quaesivit, [Quis ergo eum plus diligit?] Ex subsequentibus etiam sequitur, [Cui minus dimittitur, minus diligit.] Haec ille; & post, exempla id genus dictionum reddit plurima; v. g. Cicero doctus est, quia erudite scribit. Ex Scriptura, 1. Joan. 3. Nos scimus quod translati sumus de morte ad vitam, quoniam diligimus fratres. Et Psal. 116. Ego clamavi, quoniam exaudisti me.
units.tr: Salmeron the Jesuit debates this question no less clearly, and at last concludes: "Other learned men, he says, contend that the Latin QUONIAM does not always signify the efficient cause of a thing, but sometimes gives a reason drawn from the effect: for the Lord said, [Therefore I say to you, her many sins are forgiven]. And I add the reason for my affirmation (he says) from the effect: [because she loved much]. For from love, as an effect, he shows that its cause, that is, the remission of sins, went before; and this sense is confirmed both by what precedes and by what follows. From what precedes, because he said, [He forgave them both], and asked, [Which of them will love him more?]. From what follows also it follows, [He to whom less is forgiven loves less]. So he. Afterwards he gives very many examples of this kind of expression, for instance: Cicero is learned because he writes learnedly. From Scripture, 1 John 3: We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren. And Psalm 116: I called, because you have heard me.

units.la: Quid quòd ipsa doctrina Pontificia Stapletoniana expositioni reclamat? nam, Nunquam (teste eodem Salmerone) propter dilectionem ex charitate efficitur remissio peccati, quantum ad culpam. Locum persimilem Heb. 1.9. ex Jef. Ribera; {*}Propterea unxit te Deus, &c.] S. Thomas affirmat, cum dicitur [Propterea] non meritum indicari, sed finem. Quid multa? ut libere vobis demus, ENIM & QUIA esse terminos causales, qui denotant bona Opera esse causam, non modò sine qua non, sed etiam operantem: an igitur Meritoriam ve-stram? Imò cana & veneranda Antiquitas nunquam hoc sinet; ut eorum testimonia infrà passim demonstrabunt.
units.tr: What is more, Papist doctrine itself, as Stapleton presents it, cries out against this interpretation. For, according to the same Salmeron, the remission of sin as to guilt is never brought about by love arising from charity. Ribera, on a very similar passage, Heb. 1:9, Therefore God anointed you, says that St Thomas affirms that when the word [therefore] is used, it indicates not merit but the end. What more need be said? Let us grant you freely that ENIM and QUIA are causal particles, which denote that good works are the cause, not only the sine qua non but even the efficient cause: will that then be your meritorious cause? Indeed, the hoary and venerable antiquity will never allow this, as their testimonies will show everywhere below.
SECT. VII.

units.la: V. Classis Scripturarum, quae objicitur pro Merito de Congruo.
units.tr: V. Class of Scriptures which is objected in favour of merit of congruity.

units.la: QUintam Classem Scripturarum objicit Bellarminus. {y} Scriptura dicunt, bonis operibus praemium ex justitia esse reddendum, ut 2.Tim. 4.8. [Coronam mihi reddet justus judex] Et Heb. 6.10. [Non est injustus Deus, ut obliviscatur operis vestri] Item Apoc. 2. [Esto fidelis usque ad mortem, & dabo tibi coronam vitae.] Respondeo, quòd ex hac Justitia Dei nullâ vi ingenii ratio aliqua Meriti extrahi queat; siquidem Commentatorem vestrum Espencæum, juxtà & Augustinum, interpretem admittere velitis. {z}Justitiae genus (inquit Espencaeus) est praestare quod promiseris, quâ ratione Deus seipsum nobis quodammodo Debitorem constituit, ut si non ob merita eum nostra appellare, ob promissa tamen possimus. Quòd si nos officii nostri meminerimus, non recusat injustus vocari, si minùs praestet quod pollicitus est; hac quidem tum Scholastica, tum Erasmica. Proferam ego (inquit) meliora, quae Augustinus hujus loci (2.Tim.4.) occasione tractavit. Coronam, inquit, Paulus exposcit, ex miseri-
units.tr: Bellarmine objects a fifth class of Scriptures. {y} They say that a reward is to be paid to good works from justice, as in 2 Tim. 4:8 [The righteous judge will render me the crown], and Heb. 6:10 [God is not unjust, so as to forget your work]. Likewise Rev. 2 [Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life]. I reply that no reasoning about merit can be drawn from this justice of God by any power of wit, if you are willing to accept your own commentator Espencaeus, and Augustine too, as interpreter. The kind of justice (says Espencaeus) is to perform what one has promised. By this reason God has made himself, in a sense, our debtor, so that if we cannot call him to account on account of merits, we can at least do so on account of his promises. But if we remember our duty, he does not refuse to be called unjust if he fails to perform what he has pledged. This is both Scholastic and Erasmian. I will set forth better things (he says), which Augustine treated on the occasion of this passage (2 Tim. 4). Paul, he says, demands the crown from mercy—

units.la: {z} Claud. Espenc. Com. in 2.Tim.4. ubi omnia illa perhibet de Augustino, quae hic cordia quidem promissam, sed jam ex justitia sal-vendam: justum enim est ut reddat qui debet; debet autem qui promisit, ex gratia, licet non ex debito. Et de hac Dei justitia, qua est Dei promissio, Apostolus hic velut præsumit, & repetit, etc. tò sciens eum, cui pollicenti credidit, servaturum atque redditurum. Paulò post, ex eodem Augustino; Cui enim redderet coronam justus Judex, si non donâsset gratiam misericors Pater? Dein-de post; Coronat Deus in misericordia: constat ergò, quibus misericorditer tribuit, ut in hac vi-ta bene operentur, misericordius iisdem largitur, ut in æterna beatitudine centuplicato fructu remu-nerentur: hæc est Gratia, quam pro Gratia esse dandam Apostolus perhibet, Joh.1. ut quibus in hac vita divinitus datur gratia Sanctificationis, iis ex hac quoque in futura detur gratia æterna felicitatis.
units.tr: {z} Claud. Espenc. Com. in 2 Tim. 4, where he attributes to Augustine all those things which are said here: promised indeed out of mercy, but now to be paid out of justice; for it is just that he who owes should repay, and he owes who has promised, out of grace, although not out of debt. And of this justice of God, which is the promise of God, the Apostle here presumes and repeats, etc., knowing that he will keep and render to Him to whom he entrusted his promise. A little later, from the same Augustine: For to whom would the righteous Judge render the crown, if the merciful Father had not granted grace? Then below: God crowns in mercy. It is plain, then, that to those to whom he grants mercifully that they may do well in this life, he grants more mercifully that they may be rewarded with a hundredfold fruit in eternal blessedness. This is the grace which the Apostle says must be given for grace (John 1), so that those to whom the grace of sanctification is divinely given in this life should also receive from it the grace of eternal happiness in the future.

units.la: Utut igitur Augustinus, quoties Meriti no-men usurpat, Congruitatem aliquam suppone-re videatur; certè quidem Condignitatem Oper-um, quæ est ex Justitiæ Æqualitate, aversatur vel maximè. Sic enim apud eundem Autho-rem sequitur, ex Augustino; Si ergò, ô bone, accepturus es vitam æternam, justitia quidem pen-dium est; sed tibi Gratia, cui etiam Justitiæ (infusa) est Gratia: tibi enim tanquam debitare-deretur, si ex te tibi esset justitia cui deberetur. Necnon Barradius Jesuita citans illud Augustini in Psal.109. Fidelis (inquit) Deus, qui se no-strum strum debiterem esse fecit, non aliquid à nobis accipiendo, sed tanta nobis promittendo. Eodem modo Coloniensis Conc. Antididagma, in eisdem Augustini insistens vestigiis; {c}Ne existimes hanc Dei coronam justitiam, quòd tuis virtutibus, propter earum dignitatem, debeatur: Corona Justitia appellatur, non nostra, sed Dei. Justitia Dei ad eum modum dicitur, sicut dicimus, Domini est salus, non quà salvus est Dominus, sed quam dat iis, quos salvos facit.— Hujus justitia, nempe Dei, non sua, coronam reposcit Paulus; sed vide quà praesumptione reposcit: Scio, inquit, cui credidi, & certus sum quia possit depositum meum servare. Quia credidit promittenti, fideliter promissum repetit, suum Depositum Dei Promissum appellans; promissum quidem ex misericordia, sed jam ex Justitia persolvendum: Justum enim est ut reddat quod debet, debet autem quod pollicitus est. Singula ferè verba singulas proprie di-cti Meriti Assertiones revincunt. In eandem sententiam Augustini, Patres alii plurima tradiderunt, ut Cap.9.infrà latiùs probabitur.
units.tr: However often Augustine uses the name of merit, he seems to suppose some congruity; yet he by all means rejects the condignity of works, which arises from equality of justice. For the same author follows Augustine thus: If therefore, my good man, you are to receive eternal life, it is indeed a payment of justice; but it is grace to you, to which even justice (infused) is grace. For it would be owed to you as a debtor, if there were in you a justice to which it was owed. Also the Jesuit Barradius, citing that saying of Augustine on Psalm 109: Faithful is God, who has made himself our debtor, not by receiving anything from us, but by promising us so much. In the same way the Cologne Council Antididagma, following the footsteps of this same Augustine: {c}Do not suppose that this crown of God is owed as justice, because of your virtues and their worth. It is called the crown of justice, not ours, but God's. The justice of God is so called in the way that we say, Salvation belongs to the Lord, not because the Lord is saved, but because he gives it to those whom he saves. — It is of this justice, namely God's, not his own, that Paul demands the crown; but see with what presumption he demands it: I know, he says, whom I have believed, and I am sure that he is able to keep my deposit. Because he believed the one promising, he faithfully asks for what was promised, calling his deposit God's promise: promised indeed out of mercy, but now to be paid out of justice, for it is just that he should render what he owes; he owes what he has promised. Almost every single word refutes the assertions of merit properly so called. Other Fathers have handed down very many things to the same effect as Augustine, as will be proved more fully below in chapter 9.

units.la: VI. Classis Scripturarum, quam objiciunt Pontificii pro Merito de Condigno.
units.tr: VI. Class of Scriptures which the Papists object in favour of merit of condignity.
SECT. VIII.

units.la: SExtam Classem Scripturarum objicit Bellar-minus, {d}In multis Scripturis vita aeterna promittitur sub conditione Operis boni. Matth.19. [Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata.] Et 1.Tim.4. [Pietas est ad omnia utilis, habens promissionem, &c.] quam promisit diligentibus se. Et in his; Jac.1. [Si feceris: Apoc.2. Si vicerit, dabo.] Disputa: Promissio facta cum conditione Operis non solùm debitam facit rem promissam, ita ut Deus teneatur stare promissis suis: sed etiam facit, ut, qui opus impleverit, meruisse rem promissam, & eam ut mercedem suo jure exigere dicatur. An verò exigere mercedem? apud Deum quoq;, idque ex iure? atque etiam vi Promissionis ejus? Ecquid contrà Protestantes? Dicito. {e}Objiciunt Adversarii illud, 1.Joh.1. Si quis confitetur peccata sua, justus est Deus ut remittat nobis peccata, & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate. Sed Remissionem peccatorum, ex omnium confessione, nemo meretur, & tamen justus est Deus ut remittat peccata. Quid ais? Respondeo; Loquitur Joannes de remissione peccatorum venialium, quæ justo Dei judicio redditur bonis meritis Justorum. En putidum Commentum! sic enim dixerim potius quàm Commentarium. Nam, teste Aquinate, {f}Si peccata confitemur, ut Glossa exponit, peccata scilicet Mortalia. Atque quodlibet peccatum remissum iri, Textus palàm quodammodo profitetur, viz. [Emundet nos ab omni iniquitate] Quid hoc? dicite, Rhemenses. {g}Id est, omni Originali & Actuali, veniali & mortali, culpâ & poenâ. Pariter Arius Montanus; {h}Id est, quicunque se peccatorem agnoscit, peccata confessus, fessus, Deum sibi propitium postulabit, qui illi omnia peccata remittet. Idem largitur ex Patribus Vega; {1} Nulla major Justitia est, inquit Hieronymus, quàm ignoscere pœnitenti, & ad misericordiam revertenti sinum misericordiæ aperire. Et D. Augustinus audaciter aliquando dixit; Si Deus non reciperet confugientes ad se, esset in eo iniquitas. Et B. Anselmus; Cùm pœnis malos, justum est, quia illorum meritis congruit: cùm parcis malis, justum est, non quia illorum meritis, sed tuæ bonitati convenit.
units.tr: The sixth class of Scriptures that Bellarmine objects is this: {d}In many Scriptures eternal life is promised under the condition of a good work. Matt. 19. [If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.] And 1 Tim. 4. [Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise, etc.], which he promised to those who love him. And in these: James 1. [If he shall have done it.] Rev. 2. [If he overcomes, I will give.] Dispute: A promise made with the condition of a work not only makes the promised thing owed, so that God is bound to stand by his promises, but also makes it that the one who has fulfilled the work is said to have merited the promised thing and to demand it as wages by his own right. But does he demand wages? From God too, and that by right? And even by virtue of his promise? What do the Protestants say to this? Tell us. {e}The opponents object that passage, 1 John 1: If anyone confesses his sins, God is just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. But no one merits the remission of sins, by the confession of all, and yet God is just to remit sins. What do you say? I answer: John speaks of the remission of venial sins, which is granted by God's just judgment to the good merits of the just. Behold a foul invention! For I would call it that rather than a commentary. For, as Aquinas testifies, if we confess our sins, as the Gloss explains, namely mortal sins. And that any sin whatever will be forgiven the text plainly declares in a way, namely [it will cleanse us from all unrighteousness]. What is this? Tell us, Rheims men. {g}That is, from all original and actual, venial and mortal, guilt and punishment. Likewise Arius Montanus: that is, whoever acknowledges himself a sinner, having confessed his sins, weary, will ask God to be propitious to him, who will remit all his sins. The same is granted from the Fathers by Vega; {1} No greater justice, says Jerome, than to pardon the penitent and, returning to mercy, to open the bosom of mercy. And St. Augustine once boldly said: If God did not receive those who flee to him, there would be iniquity in him. And St. Anselm: when punishing the wicked, it is just, because it agrees with their merits; when sparing the wicked, it is just, not because of their merits, but because it befits your goodness.

units.la: Dein, nè videamur (si eo opus esset) Jesuitarum præsidio destituti, Eftius suum interponet suffragium; {k} Justus autem hic Deus dicitur, non quòd pœnitenti lege justitiæ debeatur peccati venia, quomodo bene operanti debetur merces vitæ æternæ; sed vel hâc ratione, quia servare fidem promissorum pars quædam justitia est. Sequitur; [Et ut emundet nos ab omni iniquitate] quod potest sumi distributivè: ut sit sensus; Nullam esse iniquitatem tantam, vel numero, vel magnitudine, à qua sanguis Christi nos non emundet, si eam confessi fuerimus. Objectionum & Refutationum affatim accepimus: nec tamen satis erit nobis evicisse, non probari ex Scripturis opinionem proprie dicti Meriti de Condigno, nisi etiam per sacras literas eam expugnari liquidè appareat; quod in Argumentis nostris passim copiosè appositèque præstabimus. Interea, nè vox MERITUM, quoties nobis oc-currit
units.tr: Next, lest we seem (if there were need) to be left without the support of the Jesuits, Estius will add his vote: {k} Here God is called just, not because forgiveness of sin is owed to the penitent by the law of justice, as eternal life is owed to the one who acts well; but at least for this reason, because keeping the faith of promises is a certain part of justice. It follows: [and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness], which can be taken distributively, so that the sense is: there is no iniquity so great, either in number or in magnitude, from which the blood of Christ will not cleanse us, if we have confessed it. We have received objections and refutations in plenty. Yet it will not be enough for us to have shown that the opinion of merit of condignity, properly so called, is not proved from the Scriptures, unless it also clearly appears to be overthrown by the sacred letters; this we will do fully and aptly in our arguments throughout. Meanwhile, lest the word MERIT, whenever it occurs to us

units.la: {1} Vega,O-pusc. de Merit. qu. 6.pag.791. per totam illam sextã[?] quæstionem.
units.tr: {1} Vega, Opusc. de Merit., qu. 6, p. 791, through that whole sixth question.

units.la: {k} Eftius in eundem loc. currit apud Patres, Causæ nostræ præjudicio esse possit, Adversariorum objectionibus satisfaciemus.
units.tr: {k} Estius on the same passage. It runs among the Fathers, and may be prejudicial to our cause; we shall satisfy the objections of the Adversaries.
CAP. III.
Objections of the Papists drawn from the Fathers.
I. THESIS.

units.la: Pontificios ex Græcis Patribus violenter extorquere nomen MERITI.
units.tr: The Papists wrest the name of MERIT violently from the Greek Fathers.
SECT. I.

units.la: INcipit {1}Cardinalis à Græcis Pa-tribus, sed plurimi ex nostris partibus sæpe multúmque conquesti sunt de Pontificiorum Versionibus, ceu improbis, vel ignaris: qui ex Græcis sententiis bonis reddidérunt Latinas non bonas, ut hoc pacto saltem nomen MERITI extraherent.
units.tr: The Cardinal begins with the Greek Fathers. But many on our side have often and loudly complained about the Papists' translations, as dishonest or ignorant, which turn good Greek sentiments into bad Latin, so that by this means they might at least extract the name of MERIT.

units.la: Primus Pater ab eo laudatus est Ignatius in Epist. ad Rom. Sinite me, ut bestiarum esca sim, per quam possim Deum promereri. Ubi Græca vox [ἐπιτυχῶν][?] quæ est consequi aut adipisci, Latinè coactè vertitur, Promereri.
units.tr: The first Father he praises is Ignatius in his Epistle to the Romans: Suffer me to be food for the beasts, through whom I may be able to merit God. Here the Greek word [ἐπιτυχῶν][?], which means to attain or obtain, is forcibly rendered to merit.

units.la: Secundus est Justinus Martyr Apolog.2. circa medium, in hunc modum; Homines se dignos Deo facere, & cum eo victuros meritis suis. In qua Translatione duplex σχῆμα cernitur; 1. Si se dignos [illegible, ~12 letters] id est, Si se ostenderent dignos consilio ejus per opera sua. At vocem, Dignum, nihil aliud plerunque quàm Habilem significare, Pontificii nobis supra largiti sunt, Cap.2.Sect.3. Alterum, [illegible, ~14 letters] id est, Ejus conversatione (nempe Deum) dignatum iri. Ergò hoc (inquimus) Deus hominibus indulget ex Dignatione, non ex Debito.
units.tr: The second is Justin Martyr, Apology 2, about the middle, in this manner: They make themselves worthy of God, and will live with him by their merits. In this translation two figures can be seen. (1) If they make themselves worthy [illegible], that is, if they showed themselves worthy of his counsel by their works. But the word worthy usually signifies nothing more than fit or able, as the Papists themselves have granted us above (Chap. 2, Sect. 3). (2) The other [illegible], that is, he would deign to live in fellowship with (namely God) him. Therefore (we say) God grants this to men out of condescension, not out of debt.

units.la: Ex Origene lib. 2. in Rom. cap. 2. Pro meritis reddet Deus. Responsum accepistis à nostris, Bellarmino curæ non fuisse, rectâmne Translationem sequeretur, an distortam, quia non modò in Basiliensi, sed etiam in Parisiensi editione postrema, non est [pro Meritis] sed tantùm [pro Operibus.] Vetus est hæc nostra querela.
units.tr: From Origen, book 2 on Romans, chapter 2: God will repay according to merits. You have had the answer from our people: Bellarmine did not care whether he followed a correct translation or a distorted one, since in the Basel edition, and even in the latest Paris edition, the text reads not [according to merits] but only [according to works]. This complaint of ours is an old one.

units.la: Chrysostomus Orat.4. de Lazaro: Boni & mali accipient [χρὴ τὴν ἀξίαν?] id est, prout digni sunt. Verum est; nam est etiam Dignitas spiritualis in Justis, secundum quam Remunerationem accipient. An verò igitur secundum Æqualitatem Justitiæ apud Deum? Non habetis inter Protestantes magis Adversarium quenquam, quàm se exhibiturus est hic Chrysostomus (Infrà sæpiùs.)
units.tr: Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Lazarus: The good and the wicked will receive [according to the worth?], that is, as they are worthy. This is true; for there is also a spiritual worthiness in the just, according to which they will receive reward. But does this mean according to an equality of justice before God? Among Protestants you have no greater adversary than this Chrysostom, who will show himself so again and again below.

units.la: Gregorius Nyssenus in Orat. de amandis Pauperibus. Respondemus, nullum hujusmodi Titulum extare in Nysseni libris excusis Basileæ[?] Anno 1571. nec igitur Testis mutus aliquod Responsum mereretur.
units.tr: Gregory of Nyssa, in his oration on the duty of helping the poor. We reply that no such title exists in the printed books of Nyssen published at Basel in 1571; so this mute witness does not deserve any answer.

units.la: Respondemus; Basilii & Nazianzeni testimoniis Meriti nomen abest; non sunt igitur ad Rhombum: quanquam sententia Nazianzeni alicujus videatur esse momenti. Ait enim in S. Baptisma Orat. 4. ante finem; Crede resurrectionem, judicium, mercedem ad justam Dei lancem exigendam. Quod & nos liberè profite-mur; ita ut si Hirci & Oves, id est, Justi & Injusti inter se comparentur, Judicium Dei summa Justitiæ lanx est: Sin verò Justi per se ex rigore legis examinentur, ex Æqualitate justitiæ cum Deo in judicio non ausint contendere, si vel Græcis vel Latinis Patribus credere velimus, ad quos sæpe sæpiúsq; provocamus.
units.tr: We reply: the testimonies of Basil and Nazianzen lack the name of merit; they therefore do not bear on the point, although the sentiment of Nazianzen seems to have some weight. For he says in his oration on holy Baptism, near the end: Believe in the resurrection, the judgment, and the reward to be exacted by God's just balance. This we also freely profess; so that if the goats and the sheep, that is, the just and the unjust, are compared with one another, God's judgment is the highest balance of justice. But if the just are examined on their own by the strictness of the law, they will not dare to contend with God in judgment on the basis of an equality of justice, if we are willing to believe the Greek or the Latin Fathers, to whom we often and insistently appeal.
II. Thesis.

units.la: Ex Latinis Patribus proprie dictum MERITUM DE CONDIGNO Pontificii nunquam potuerunt evincere.
units.tr: The Papists have never been able to prove from the Latin Fathers merit properly so called, merit of condignity.
SECT. II.

units.la: FAcilè agnoscimus dicta Patrum: ut Hilarii, Can.5. De nostro esse aeternitatem promerendam. Ambrosii, Lib.1. Offic.cap.15. Evidens est, Meritum praemia manere. Augustini, & Prosperi, Ex Merito justitiæ vita æterna acquirenda est. Tertulliani, Est ordo Meritorum. Cypriani, Justitiâ opus est, ut quis Deum promereri possit. Bernardi, Merita habere cures. Sequuntur testimonia, in quibus nulla est omnino mentio Meriti; Hieronymi, Pro labore pramia praparari. Et Gregorii Pont. In hac vita est discretio operum: post hanc vitam erit discretio Dignationum.
units.tr: We readily acknowledge the sayings of the Fathers, such as Hilary, Canon 5: eternal life is to be merited through our own [works]. Ambrose, On the Duties, book 1, chapter 15: It is evident that merit remains for rewards. Augustine and Prosper: Eternal life is to be acquired by the merit of righteousness. Tertullian: There is an order of merits. Cyprian: There must be righteousness, so that a man may be able to merit God. Bernard: See that you have merits. There follow testimonies in which there is no mention at all of merit: Jerome, Rewards are prepared for labour. And Gregory the Pope: In this life there is a distinction of works; after this life there will be a distinction of dignities.

units.la: Ad Testimonia, in quibus voces, MERITA, & MERERI sonant,
units.tr: As for the testimonies in which the words MERITS and TO MERIT occur,

units.la: Respondemus; Ex sententiis Patrum, proprie dicti Meriti de Condigno, sensum liquidum Pontificli[?] nunquam hactenus potuerunt extundere. Imò huic toxico, de Merito ex Æqualitate Justitiae apud Deum, suffragiis suis Orthodoxis Antidotum praescripserunt. Ubi non Metaphoricis dictis, sed claris & perspicuis Asseverationibus dicunt, Nullum esse Meritum nostrum: Nihil nos dignum facere vita æterna: sed, Eam esse supra omne Condignum nostrum; & id genus alia plurima, ut infra copiosè probabimus. Interea impropriæ acceptionis vocabuli MERITI apud Antiquos, exempla aliqua exhibemus.
units.tr: we reply: from the sayings of the Fathers the Papists have never yet been able to extract a clear sense of merit properly so called, merit of condignity. Indeed, against this poison, merit from equality of justice before God, they have prescribed an antidote by their orthodox votes. There they say, not in metaphorical expressions but in clear and plain assertions, that we have no merit; that we do nothing worthy of eternal life; but that it is above all our condign deserts; and many other things of this kind, as we will prove fully below. Meanwhile we set out some examples of the improper use of the word MERIT among the ancients.

units.la: III. Thesis. Acceptionis impropriæ vocabuli MERITI apud Antiquitatem, fatentibus Ad- versariis, Instantia aliquot.
units.tr: III. Thesis. That the ancient writers, as the adversaries admit, used the word MERIT improperly: some instances.
SECT. III.

units.la: INTER Adversarios nostros Vegæ nomen celebre est apud Pontificios. Is, Non me fugit (inquit) usurpari apud Patres nomenquam nomen [?] Meriti, ubi nulla est ratio Meriti, neq; de Congru[?], neque de Condigno. Solemus enim dicere, Felices esse eos homines, qui inter catera animalia hanc gratiam apud Deum meruerunt, ut libertate Arbitrii insigniretur. Et Cyprianus dicit, Infantes plus mereri divinam Gratiam, quòd in primo nativitatis sua ortu plorantes, nihil aliud faciunt quàm deprecantur. Haec ille. Augustinus etiam (apud P. Lombardum) ubi loquitur de Peccato in Spiritum Sanctum, {a}Hoc solum Peccatum, inquit, veniam mereri non potest. Et rursus, {o}Nemo peccator (ait) de se desperet, quandoquidem Paulus meruit Indulgentiam. Frequens est in ore omnium illud Gregorii Pontificis dictum de peccato Adae, quod nunc in Ecclesia Romana canitur, in Cerei benedictione: O felix culpa, quae talem meruit habere Salvatorem! Sed quid potest esse apud Pontificios magis familiare, quàm sua Biblia? ubi Vulgatus Interpres hanc suam Translationem evulgavit, Genef.3. tanquam ex ore Cain; Majus est meum Peccatum, quam ut veniam mereatur. Ejusdem furfuris est id, quod in solennibus Missis decantatur; {p}Ut nos qui de qualitate Meritorum diffidimus, non judicium tuum, sed misericordiam consequi mereamur. Quid ergo sibi volunt hujusmodi acceptiones Meriti? sane nihil aliud quàm obtinere, consequi, acquirere, & similia. Quod igitur Stapletonus fateri cogitur de Factis ante ju-stificatistificationem, id nos præterea etiam de aliis Operibus rectè dici facilè intelligimus:{q} Quòd si aliquis Veterum, inquit, vocabulo, Promerendi, usus est, non aliter intellexit quàm Consecutionem de facto. Optimè sanè.
units.tr: Among our opponents the name of Vega is famous among the Papists. He says: "It is not unknown to me that the word Merit is sometimes used among the Fathers where there is no ground of merit, neither of congruity nor of condignity. For we are accustomed to say that those men are happy who, among the other animals, have merited this grace before God, that they should be distinguished by the freedom of the will." And Cyprian says that infants merit more divine grace, because, weeping at the first moment of their birth, they do nothing else than beseech. Thus he. Augustine too (in Peter Lombard), where he speaks of the sin against the Holy Spirit, says: {a}"This sin alone, he says, cannot merit forgiveness." And again: {o}"No sinner, he says, should despair of himself, since Paul merited indulgence." On everyone's lips is that saying of Pope Gregory about the sin of Adam, which is now sung in the Roman Church in the blessing of the Paschal candle: "O happy fault, which merited to have so great a Saviour!" But what can be more familiar among the Papists than their own Bible? There the Vulgate translator published this rendering of his, Genef.3, as if from the mouth of Cain: "My sin is greater than that it can merit pardon." Of the same chaff is that which is chanted in the solemn Masses: {p}"That we, who despair of the quality of our merits, may obtain not your judgment but your mercy." What then do such senses of merit mean? Surely nothing other than to obtain, to attain, to acquire, and the like. Therefore what Stapleton is forced to admit about works done before justification, we easily understand can rightly be said of other works as well: {q}"But if any of the Ancients," he says, "used the word promerendi, he understood it in no other way than as attaining by the deed." Very well indeed.

units.la: Atque siquis hujus Interpretationis originem exquirere velit, reperiet usum hunc ortum suum habuisse in lingua Latina à Populo Romano, de quo dicitur; — Quem penes arbitrium est, & vis, & norma loquendi. Cujus rei Testem habemus insignem illum antiquæ eruditionis cultorem excultorémque Isaacum Casaubonum, ex Plinio secundo, in hæc verba; Ut honorem parcorum expectarent, & mererentur. Et rursus; Sequi enim Gloria, non appeti debet; nec, si casu aliquo non sequatur, idcirco quod gloriam non meruit, minùs pulchrum est. Hinc clarissimus noster Scholiastes,{r} Meruit, est, ἐντ[?] Sensus est; Præclara facta, etsi laudatores non inveniant, non ideò minùs esse pulchra. Verbum, Mereri, non semper ἀξιοῦσθαι significare, sed τὸ πραγμα, & factum notare, non jus, notius est quàm ut probatione egeat. Sic ille. Quæ Animadversio potest esse nobis λογομαχία[?], seu Controversiæ de Nomine exquisita determinatio atque dirempto. Nunc porrò contra Meritum de Condigno pugnandum nobis est, 1. Ex sacrarum literarum authoritate: 2. Ex Pontificiorum ipsorum consessionibus: 3. Ex Primitivæ Ecclesiæ patrocinio.
units.tr: And if anyone wishes to inquire into the origin of this interpretation, he will find that this usage had its origin in the Latin language from the Roman people, of whom it is said: "In whose power lie the judgment, the force and the rule of speaking." We have a notable witness to this in that famous cultivator and refiner of ancient learning, Isaac Casaubon, who quotes from Pliny the Younger these words: "that they might look for and earn the honour of the sparing." And again: "Glory ought to follow, not be sought; nor, if by some chance it does not follow, is it on that account any less fine, because it did not earn the glory." Hence our most distinguished commentator says: "Meruit (he earned) is used in the sense of ... Famous deeds, even if the praisers do not find them, are not on that account any less fine. That the verb mereri does not always signify to be deemed worthy [ἀξιοῦσθαι], but to denote the thing itself [τὸ πραγμα] and the deed, not the right, is better known than it needs proof." Thus he. This observation can be for us a settling of a war of words, an exact determination and resolution of the controversy about the term. But now we must fight against merit of condignity, (1) from the authority of the holy Scriptures; (2) from the confessions of the Papists themselves; (3) from the defence of the primitive Church.
CHAPTER IV.
SECTION I.

units.la: Brevitatis studio loca Scripturarum in compendium reducam, quæ postea à nobis perspicuitatis gratiâ tractanda sunt accuratius. Sunt autem multifaria: nam, si spectemus principium bene agendi, 1.Cor.3. Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Si prioritatem donandi, Rom.11. Quis prior dedit, & retribuetur ei? Si indignitatem Operantis in se, 1.Ioan.1. Quisquis dixerit se peccatum non habere, seipsum seducit. Si defectum operis, Rom.7.18. Perficere non invenio.
units.tr: For the sake of brevity I will reduce the passages of Scripture to a summary, which afterwards I must treat more carefully for the sake of clarity. They are many and varied. If we consider the source of good action: 1 Cor. 3. What do you have that you did not receive? If we consider priority in giving: Rom. 11. Who first gave to him, that it should be repaid to him? If we consider the unworthiness of the doer in himself: 1 John 1. Whoever says he has no sin deceives himself. If we consider the defect of the work: Rom. 7.18. To perform, I do not find.

units.la: Sed ut dignitatem Justi hominis considere-mus, Conditio ejus non est Mercenaria, sed Filialis & Hæreditaria; Joan. 1. Quotquot eum (Christum) receperunt, dedit illis potestatem filios Dei fieri. Nihilominus Opus ejus, ex præcepto Dei, debitum; Luc.17. Quod debuimus fecimus. Nec Deo Remuneratori prodest hilum; Job.22. Quid prodest Deo, quòd justus es?
units.tr: But let us consider the dignity of the righteous man. His condition is not mercenary but filial and hereditary: John 1. As many as received him (Christ), to them he gave power to become children of God. Nevertheless his work, by God's command, is owed: Luke 17. We have done what we ought to have done. Nor is it of the least advantage to God the Rewarder: Job 22. What profit is it to God that you are righteous?

units.la: Ultimo in loco Æstimatio habenda est Operis, Præmii, & Dei remunerantis. Huc spectant loca sequentia; Rom. 8. Non sunt condigna afflictiones, &c. Rom.6.23. Vita aeterna est donum Dei. Psal.102.4. Coronat nos Deus in misericordia. Et 1.Thess.6.18. In omnibus gratias agite. Harum Scripturarum apices (ut alias omittam) satis per se convellunt opinionem istam de Merito ex Condignitate secundum Æqualitatem Justitia apud Deum. Quod nos insuper duplici genere Argumentorum profligare expugnareque satagimus: quorum unum est ex Pontificiorum Confessionibus, veluti propriis ipsorum pharetris, deductum: alterum ex Sanctorum Patrum suffragiis, tanquam Antiquitatis armamentario, extractum; nec tam nostris tamen,quàm Patrum ipsorum viribus brachiisq; vibratum.
units.tr: Lastly, the worth of the work, the reward, and God who rewards must be weighed. To this belong the following passages: Rom. 8. The afflictions are not worthy, etc. Rom. 6.23: Eternal life is the gift of God. Ps. 102.4: God crowns us with mercy. And 1 Thess. 6.18: In all things give thanks. These texts (to pass over others) of themselves sufficiently overthrow that opinion of merit from condignity, according to the equality of justice before God. We strive, moreover, to defeat and storm this opinion with a twofold kind of argument: the one drawn from the Papists' own confessions, as if from their own quivers; the other taken from the testimonies of the holy Fathers, as if from the armoury of antiquity. Yet we wield these weapons not so much with our own strength as with the strength and arms of the Fathers themselves.
CHAPTER V.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum primum adversus MERITUM DE CONDIGNO, ex Pontificiorum ipsorum confessionibus; ex parte formalis Rationis ejus, quae dicitur esse Justitia Æqualitas. Argumentatio.
units.tr: Our first argument against MERIT OF CONDIGNITY, drawn from the Papists' own confessions, concerning the formal part of that merit, which is said to be the equality of justice. The argument.
SECTION I.

units.la: OMne Meritum de Condigno consistit in Condignitate Æqualitatis Justitiæ ad Præmium vitæ æternæ:
units.tr: Every merit of condignity consists in the condignity of an equality of justice to the reward of eternal life:

units.la: Sed nullum nostrum Opus bonum confiftit in Condignitate Æqualitatis Justitiæ ad Præ-mium vitæ æternæ:
units.tr: But none of our good works consists in the condignity of an equality of justice to the reward of eternal life:

units.la: Proinde nullum Opus bonum est Meritori-um de Condigno.
units.tr: Therefore no good work is a merit of condignity.

units.la: Propositionem Adversarii ipsi ultro nobis porrexerunt: Nihil amplius requiritur ad Con-dignitatem, quàm Æqualitas. Alteram enim Commutativam esse volunt, Distributivam alte-ram. (Supra, Cap.2. per totum.)
units.tr: The Papists themselves have offered us the premise unasked: Nothing more is required for condignity than equality. For they want one kind of equality to be commutative and the other distributive. (See above, Chapter 2, throughout.)
We shall pursue our argument concerning both kinds.

units.la: Nullum Opus bonum in alterutra Justitiæ Æqualitate consistere.
units.tr: No good work consists in either kind of equality of justice.
I. Not in commutative equality.
SECT. II.

units.la: CArdinal. Bellarminus, {f}Debet Deus, inquit, reddere vitam æternam ex Justitia Commutativa, vel Distributiva: Ex Commutativa, quoad substantiam; ex Distributiva, quoad modum. Sic ille. Nos verò ex diametro, Nec Commutativa (inquimus) nec Distributiva Justitia proprie intercedit inter Deum & Hominem. Agedùm, sit pedi pes junctus.
units.tr: Cardinal Bellarmine: "God, he says, ought to render eternal life by commutative or by distributive justice: by commutative as regards the substance, by distributive as regards the mode." So he. But we, quite to the contrary, say: neither commutative nor distributive justice properly lies between God and man. Come now, let the foot be joined to the foot.

units.la: 1. Commutativam aggredimur; de qua Pontificii sensum suum explicant: inter quos Coste-rus Jesuita, {e}Commutativa aequalitas est, inquit, rei cum re; qualis est in emptionibus, permutationibus, nibus, locationibus: ut, quando merces æquatur ope-ri, aut pretium rei vendita aut locata. Hanc quoque dignam esse censetis, cui Meritum de Condigno tribuendum sit: pergit enim Jesu-ita; {*}Justitia ratio quâ Deus æternam vitam justis in mercedem operum donat, ad utramq; quidem justitiæ partem aliquo modo pertinet, tum ad æqualitatem operum, tum etiam ad digni-tatem personarum. Bellarminus etiam, quid sibi videatur, significare nobis non gravabitur: {u}Absoluta æqualitas (ait) inter Mercedem & Meritum constituitur per modum justitiæ Commutativa. Deus judicium exercet per modum Commutativæ justitiæ, cujus est constituere absolutam æqualitatem inter Meritum & Mercedem, ut unus-quisq; tantam habeat mercedem, quantam Dei ju-dicio meretur. Observemus, oportet, Cardina-li nullam justitiæ æqualitatem veram videri (quæ nimirum constituat Meritum de Condigno) nisi quæ sit absoluta, quæque ex Debito Mer-cedem (sic enim dixit) possit exigere.
units.tr: 1. Let us first take up commutative justice, on which the Papists explain their view. Among them the Jesuit Coster says: "Commutative equality is thing with thing, such as is found in buying, exchanging, hiring and letting: as when the wage is made equal to the work, or the price to the thing sold or let." You also think this is the kind of justice to which merit *de condigno* should be ascribed; for the Jesuit goes on: "The principle of justice by which God gives eternal life to the just as the reward of their works pertains in some way to both parts of justice, both to the equality of the works and also to the dignity of the persons." Bellarmine too will not hesitate to make clear to us what he thinks: "Absolute equality (he says) between the reward and the merit is established by way of commutative justice. God exercises judgment by way of commutative justice, whose office it is to establish absolute equality between merit and reward, so that each one receives as great a reward as he merits by God's judgment." We must observe that the Cardinal seems to regard no equality of justice as *true* (namely that which establishes merit *de condigno*) unless it is *absolute*, and one that can demand the reward *as a debt* (for so he put it).

units.la: Quod Cardinalis decretum Præceptori suo Aquinati prorsus Paradoxon videbatur: nam {x}Commutativa justitia (inquit) non competit Deo, quia dicit Apostolus de Deo, Rom.11.35. Quis prior dedit, & retribuetur ei? Sic ille. Quem Homeru[?]m suum Cardinalis, quoties libitum est, excludit foras. Cui tamen ejusdem familiæ Jesuitæ duo [illegible, ~9 letters] occurrunt. {y}Recentiores nonnulli (inquit Jesuita Vasquez) justitiam Commutativam Deo tribuunt: nos verò ex instituti ostendimus, nullum esse Scholasticum ex antiquis, qui horum Doctorum sententiam sequatur. —Et isti Commutativa justitia definitionem à nullo ha-ctenus traditam statuunt, ità ut nominis hujus significatum quò velint detorqueant: quod sane si unicuique liberum esset, nihil firmum, nihil stabile in Theologicis disputationibus haberemus. Hæc ille. Quærat, si cui libeat, & perscrutetur tria illa Capita, quæ Vasquez in illius doctrinæ refutatione insumpsit, cui potius opinioni Valentianus Jesuita adhærerat. {1} Cùm de Merito vitæ æterna loquimur (inquit) nullus locus est Commutativa justitia. Deniq; Stapletonus (nè stri-ctam Æqualitatem justitiæ intervenire inter Deum & Hominem quis putet) {2} Ratio meriti, inquit, non ad Commutativam justitiam pertinet; non est enim opus servile aut mercenarium, sed virtutis & charitatis, quæ amicitiam ponit. Hæc illi, tam docte tamque diserte, ut ulteriori aliquâ nostrâ refutatione pars hæc nullo modo indigeat. Nostrum erit nihilominus rationes ab illis propositas memoriæ tradere. Prima, Novam esse hanc sententiam, & nullo modo tolerandam. Altera, quòd repugnat Gratiæ Dei; de qua Apostolus, Deus prior dedit. Tertia, quòd reddit opera Christianorum Servilia, & minimè Charitativa.
units.tr: This decree of the Cardinal seemed to his own teacher Aquinas utterly paradoxical; for he says: "Commutative justice does not belong to God, because the Apostle says of God, Rom. 11.35: Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?" So he. This Homer of theirs the Cardinal, whenever it pleases him, drives out of doors. Yet two Jesuits of the same family run up against him. "Some more recent writers" (says the Jesuit Vasquez) "ascribe commutative justice to God; but we have shown in our work that there is no Scholastic among the ancients who follows the opinion of these teachers." And these men lay down a definition of commutative justice that no one has hitherto given, so that they twist the meaning of the name whichever way they wish; which, if it were free to everyone, would leave us nothing firm or stable in theological disputations. So he. Let anyone who likes seek out and examine the three heads which Vasquez employed in refuting that doctrine, to which opinion rather the Jesuit Valentia adhered. (1) "When we speak of the merit of eternal life (he says) there is no place for commutative justice." Lastly Stapleton (lest anyone think that a strict equality of justice intervenes between God and man) says: (2) "The reason of merit, he says, does not pertain to commutative justice; for it is not a servile or mercenary work, but one of virtue and charity, which posits friendship." These men have said this so learnedly and so eloquently that this part needs no further refutation from us. Nevertheless it will be our task to set down in memory the arguments they put forward. The first: that this opinion is new and in no way to be tolerated. The second: that it conflicts with the grace of God, of whom the Apostle says, God first gave. The third: that it makes the works of Christians servile and not at all charitable.

units.la: II. ÆQVALITATEM, in qua ponunt Con-dignitatem MERITI, non esse secundum justitiam Distributivam.
units.tr: II. That the equality on which they base the condignity of MERIT is not according to distributive justice.
SECT. III.

units.la: Pro hac Justitia Costerus Jesuita,{b} Distribu-tiva est, inquit, quando non tantùm laboris, sed potissimùm personae habita est aestimatio: ut, ubi hi duo, Dux & gregarius miles, aquè fortiter in bello se gesserint, praemium redditur amplius Duci, non pro laboris magnitudine, sed pro dignitate personae. Justitia ratio, ob quam Deus vitam æternam justis in mercedem operum donat, etiam ad hanc justitiam pertinet. Item de Valentia Jesuita; {c}Meritum est actus bonus, quem Deus secundum justitiam Distributivam compensat. Hoc est secundum distinctionis Pontificiorum Membrum, ad quod resecandum armis nostris nil opus est; cùm praesertim intelligamus illud jamdudum à Vasque Jesuita contritum esse atque revulsum: {d}Nos ex Durando & aliis omnibus (inquit) qui justitiam Distributivam ex instituto distinguunt, probavimus hujusmodi justitiam proprie non solùm non Deo convenire; sed etiam modum illius ab eo non servari, cùm praemia justis distribuit; quia meritum tunc ex justitia Distributiva locum habet, cùm servatur Æqualitas Geometrica, quam Aristoteles ait esse inter duas personas, & duas res distribuendas: ità ut qualis sit proportio dignitatis inter personas, talis sit inter res quas acceptura sint. Cum tamen Commutativa respiciat solùm aequalitatem inter rem & rem, & unius personae ad aliam, ut, inter debitum & solutionem, inter datum & acceptum, quam aequalitatem Arithmeticam solùm appellant: recte dicimus, ut ibidem probamus, in Deo distributivam non esse. Pergit Vasquez, &, quae in contrarium objici solent, convellit. Postea Durandus, & Theologi vestri pedibus ibunt in sententiam nostram.
units.tr: In support of this justice, the Jesuit Costerus says: Distributive justice is when regard is had not only to the labour but chiefly to the person's worth, so that when a general and a common soldier have fought equally bravely in battle, the reward is given in greater measure to the general, not in proportion to the magnitude of the labour but in proportion to the dignity of the person. The reason by which God grants eternal life to the just as the reward of their works also belongs to this justice. Likewise, from the Jesuit Valentia: Merit is a good act, which God recompenses according to distributive justice. This is the member of the Papists' distinction, and there is no need for our arms to cut it away, especially since we know that the Jesuit Vasquez long ago crushed and tore it up. We (he says) have proved, from Durandus and all the others who deliberately distinguish distributive justice, that this kind of justice does not properly belong to God, and that God does not observe its manner when he distributes rewards to the just; for merit has a place under distributive justice only when geometrical equality is preserved, which Aristotle says exists between two persons and two things to be distributed, so that the proportion of dignity between the persons is the same as that between the things they are to receive. But commutative justice regards only the equality between thing and thing, and between one person and another, as between what is owed and what is paid, between what is given and what is received, which they call arithmetical equality alone. Therefore we rightly say, as we prove in the same place, that distributive justice does not exist in God. Vasquez goes on and overturns the objections usually raised to the contrary. Afterwards Durandus and your theologians will go over to our opinion.

units.la: III. Probando, nec Commutativam, nec Distributivam proprie Deo erga Homines competere. SECT. IV.
units.tr: III. Proving that neither commutative nor distributive justice properly belongs to God in his dealings with men. SECT. IV.

units.la: AD Doctores vestros rursus provocamus. Costerus Jesuita, qui jamjam utramq; justitiae aequalitatem amplexus est, post tamen, re diligenter atque exactius apud se discussa, veritatis imperio quasi coactus est fateri,quòd {*}Inter Deum & homines non potest exacta, qualis est inter homines ipsos, justitiae aequalitas intercedere. Quod ille rationibus sanis, & verè Theologicis confirmat. 1. Quia Deus non est itâ obligatus. 2. Quia factura ipsius sumus, ejúsque sunt omnia nostra. 3. Quia aliis innumeris beneficiis nos sibi obstrinxerit. Progreditur Jesuita feliciter satis, nisi quòd nonnunquam in nomen hoc Meritum impingit. Ex hac confessione superior Bellarmini defensio, de Absoluta aequalitate justitiae inter Deum & Homines, plane labefactatur.
units.tr: Again we appeal to your teachers. The Jesuit Costerus, who had already embraced both kinds of equality of justice, nevertheless, after carefully and more exactly examining the matter for himself, was as it were compelled by the authority of truth to confess that between God and men there cannot be that exact equality of justice which exists between men themselves. He confirms this with sound and truly theological reasons: first, because God is not so bound; second, because we are his workmanship, and all that we have is his; third, because he has bound us to himself by countless other benefits. The Jesuit makes good progress in this, well enough, except that now and then he stumbles upon the word merit. From this confession Bellarmine's defence of an absolute equality of justice between God and men is plainly overthrown.

units.la: Maldonatus Jesuita suam symbolam adjicit; ubi postquam has Scripturas expendisset exactius, viz. Matt.25.21. EUGE BONE SERVE, SUPER MULTA TE CONSTITUAM, &c. Rom. 8. 18. NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES HUJUS VITÆ GLORIA FUTURA; {f}Quid ergò, inquit, aliquid accepturi sumus praemii, quod meritò non fuerimus? Minimè id dico: omne enim quod accepturi sumus praemium, aut meriti erimus, aut non erit praemium. Sic ille. Sed Meritum (Deus bone!) quàm jejunum & plane ludicrum! Pergit enim hîc Jesuita: Sed quia (inquit) non ad aequalitatem, sed ad analogiam dantis & accipientis advertendum est, Praemium dicitur esse magis quàm Meritum. Nota est Alexandri vetus historia, qui cùm Poëta, propter compositum carmen, vinum magnum pecuniæ jussit dari, ísque [?] re-spondisset, hoc nimium esse Poëta: subjecit Rex, At hoc Alexandro non est nimium. Hactenus Maldonatus de Analogia, in quâ nullum est Justitiæ Æqualitatis vestigium, magis quàm inter Regis munificentissimi praemium, & carmen Poëtæ. Unde vix satis mirari quis poterit Jesuitarum eorum vecordiam, quos non puduit aequalitatem justitiae inter humanum Meritum, & Dei Praemium venditare, cùm adeò abhorreret Poëta inter suum Carmen, & Alexandri pecuniam æqualitatem ullam agnoscere; qui accepto præmio, illico exclamavit, ΝΙΜΙΥΜ[?]; quæ est apertissima Analogiæ negatio.
units.tr: Maldonatus the Jesuit adds his own opinion. After examining these passages more closely, namely Matt. 25.21, Well done, good and faithful servant; I will set you over many things, and Rom. 8.18, The sufferings of this present life are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed, he says: What then? Shall we receive any reward that we have not deserved? By no means. For every reward we shall receive will either be merited by us, or it will not be a reward. So he writes. But what a thin and utterly trifling notion of merit this is, good God! The Jesuit goes on: But since (he says) the comparison is not to be drawn in terms of equality but of proportion between giver and receiver, a reward is said to be more appropriately called a reward than merit. The old story of Alexander is well known. When a poet, for a poem he had composed, was given a large sum of money by the king, and replied that this was too much, the king answered, But for Alexander it is not too much. So far Maldonatus on proportion, in which there is no trace of equality of justice, any more than there is between the reward of the most generous king and a poet's verse. It is hard to wonder enough at the madness of these Jesuits, who were not ashamed to peddle an equality of justice between human merit and the reward of God, when the poet, in his poem, so utterly rejected any equality with Alexander's money that, on receiving the reward, he at once cried out in Greek, "Too much!" [ΝΙΜΙΥΜ], which is the plainest possible denial of any proportion.

units.la: Justitiam Distributivam quod attinet, quam definiverunt habere respectum diversarum personarum, quæ diversâ remuneratione compensantur; dicimus eam pugnare contra omnes eas formulas Judicialis Dei processûs, quas Adversarii ipsi hactenus ex Scripturis objectabant ad probandum suum Meritum de Condigno. Quæ, inquam, formulæ non ullam comparationem diversorum, sed duntaxat singulorum Operantium æstimationem designant. Formulæ ab iis propositæ (supra Cap. 2.) hujusmodi sunt; Justi vocantur digni remuneratione; Sect. 2. Et, Illis reddi præmia secundum Opera sua; Sect.4. Et, Quia bona Opera fecerunt; Sect. 5. Et denique, Juste & legitimè certantibus promittitur Corona vitæ; Sect.6. Quæ singulæ formæ respiciunt Remunerationem cujusvis justi hominis, pro se & Opere suo, nullâ habitâ relatione ad præmia in alios collata. Scripturæ phrases sunt hujusmodi; Reddet Deus unicuique secundum opera ejus. Et, Vincenti dabitur, nempe, unicuique. Nec dictum esset generaliter, Venite Benedicti Patris mei, quia fecistis; nisi judicialiter verum fuisset de singulis, Quia TU fecisti, & TU, atque itâ de reliquis. Cùm igitur modus nullus sit, nisi ratione rei modificatæ; sequitur, quòd quia nulla est proportio Geometrica & distributiva observanda in Judicio Divino, nullus esse potest Geometricus & Distributivus Remunerandi modus.
units.tr: As for distributive justice, which they define as having regard to different persons who are recompensed with different rewards, we say that it is contrary to all those forms of God's judicial process which our opponents have hitherto cited from the Scriptures to prove their merit of condignity. These forms, I say, indicate not a comparison of different persons but only the assessment of each individual worker. The forms they have put forward (above, chapter 2) are of this kind: The just are called worthy of reward, sect. 2; and, Rewards are given to them according to their works, sect. 4; and, Because they have done good works, sect. 5; and finally, To those who strive justly and lawfully the crown of life is promised, sect. 6. Each of these forms regards the reward of any just man, for himself and for his work, with no relation to rewards conferred on others. The phrases of Scripture are of this kind: God will render to each one according to his works; and, To him who overcomes it will be given, that is, to each one. Nor would it have been said in general, Come, you blessed of my Father, because you have done so, unless it were judicially true of each individual, Because you have done it, and you, and so with the rest. Since, therefore, there is no manner except in relation to the thing modified, it follows that, because no geometrical and distributive proportion is to be observed in the divine judgement, there can be no geometrical and distributive manner of rewarding.
CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum secundum, adversus Pontificiorum Meritum de Condigno, ex ipsis Pontificiis. Argumentatio.
units.tr: Our second argument, against the Papists' merit of condignity, drawn from the Papists themselves. The argumentation.
SECT. I.

units.la: CQuicunque Operi deest verum principium omne propriè dictæ Condignitatis apud Deum, illud non potest esse propriè Meritum de Condigno:
units.tr: Whatever work lacks the true principle of all condignity properly so called before God, that work cannot be properly called merit of condignity.

units.la: At omni Operi bono deest verum omne principium Condignitatis apud Deum:
units.tr: But every good work lacks the whole true principle of condignity before God.

units.la: Ergò nullum Opus bonum dici potest propriè Meritum de Condigno apud Deum.
units.tr: Therefore no good work can be properly called merit of condignity before God.

units.la: Quatuor Condignitatis suæ ad vitam æternam Pontificii Principia cuderunt. 1. Quatenus Opus bonum provenit à libero Arbitrio. 2. Quatenus à Spiritu Sancto inhabitante proce-dit. dit. bro, orit eve qui pro 17.
units.tr: The Papists have devised four principles of its condignity to eternal life. (1) Insofar as the good work proceeds from the free will; (2) insofar as it proceeds from the indwelling Holy Spirit; (3) insofar as it proceeds from the man, as a member of Christ; (4) insofar as it proceeds from God's covenant. Each of these must now be examined and refuted. But the point which others have set down as a kind of foundation, namely that Christ merited for us the power of merit, I have deferred to the chapter where it is treated at length.

units.tr: 3. Insofar as it proceeds from man, as from the merit of Christ. 4. Insofar as it comes from the grace of God. These single points must now be examined and refuted. But that which others have laid down as a kind of fundamental principle, namely that Christ by His merit gained for us the power of merit, I have deferred to the chapter where it is treated at length.

units.la: Adversus primum Pontificiorum principium Meriti de Condigno, quod est liberum Arbitrium.
units.tr: Against the first principle of the Papists concerning merit of condignity, which is free will.
SECT. II.

units.la: E Opere bono, quatenus procedit ex libero Arbitrio in statu Gratiæ, sic statuit Bellarminus; {g}Meritò merces debetur: debitum vero non oritur, nisi unus dat alteri quod suum est: ... sed alienam daret, nihil debearetur: nihil autem proprie nostrum, nisi quod pro arbitrio facere possumus, vel omittere. c ille. Quem summus Scholæ moderator Aquinas aliter multò informabat; qui, ubi loquitur de homine in Gratia constituto, {h}Primum liberum Arbitrium, inquit, nulla est Condignatio, propter summam inæqualitatem, sed tantum de Congruo. Rationem erudite explicat Bellarmini condiscipulus, Pererius Jesuita: si considerentur humana opera, sicut sunt à libero Arbitrio profecta, proculdubio haberent nullam qualitatis proportionem, vel Condignitatis ad vitam vitam aeternam: Illorum enim bonitas & prastantia, quam à libero Arbitrio accipiunt, est quiddam humanum & naturale; aeterna verò gloria est quiddam aeternum & supernaturale: Hac igitur ratione Bonum opus non est condignum vitâ aeternâ. Hæc ille. Imò, etiam ipsius Bellarmini opinione, Liberum arbitrium, per se, non valet ad Meritum de Condigno, absque altero principio Meriti, quod jam proximè sequitur, viz. Spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: Concerning good works, insofar as they proceed from free will in a state of grace, Bellarmine determines thus: Reward is rightly owed; but a debt does not arise unless one gives to another what is his own; ... but if he gave what was another's, nothing would be owed: and nothing is properly ours except what we can do or omit by our own choice. So far he. But the chief moderator of the school, Aquinas, taught quite otherwise; where he speaks of a man established in grace, he says: First, free will is not the ground of condign merit, on account of the very great inequality, but only of congruent merit. Bellarmine's fellow pupil, the Jesuit Pererius, explains the reason learnedly: If human works are considered as they proceed from free will, they would undoubtedly have no proportion of quality, or worthiness, to eternal life: for their goodness and excellence, which they receive from free will, is something human and natural; but eternal glory is something eternal and supernatural. For this reason, therefore, a good work is not worthy of eternal life. So he.
