Indeed, even in Bellarmine's own opinion, free will by itself does not avail for merit of condignity, without the other principle of merit, which immediately follows, namely the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Adversus secundum Pontificiorum principi-um Meriti de ,Condigno, quod non recte t- ribuitur Spiritui Sancto.
units.tr: Against the second principle of the Papists' condign merit, which is wrongly attributed to the Holy Spirit.
SECT. III.

units.la: HOc principium Condignitatis Meritoriæ, & sequentia alia obtrudunt nobis Pontificii, ut fucum faciant discipulis suis, quasi suam de Merito opinionem studio efferendi Dei gratiam defenderent; cùm revera non possent magis à Spiritûs Sancti & Christi gratia detrahere; ut ex sequenti disputatione liquidum fiet. Sed ad rem. Jesuita Cofterus assertor prodeat: {k}Si considerentur opera nostra, ut effecta sunt à nobis Dei filiis, atque inhabitante Spiritu Sancto; hac ratione Æqualitas, verùmque Meritum invenitur inter Opera & Mercedem. Eodem modo Pererius Jesuita; {l}Ut proficiscuntur Opera à Spiritu Sancto inhabitante, habent profecto dignitatem cum pramio vita aterna. Idem habet Valentia.
units.tr: The Papists thrust this principle of meritorious condignity, and the other principles that follow it, upon us. They do so to deceive their own followers, as if they were defending grace by promoting their opinion of merit with zeal for God's glory, when in fact they could not detract more from the grace of the Holy Spirit and of Christ. The following discussion will make this plain. But to the matter. The Jesuit Costerus, a champion of the cause, comes forward: If our works are considered as they are made by us, the sons of God, and by the indwelling Holy Spirit, then equality and true merit are found between the works and the reward. Pererius the Jesuit says in the same way: Since works proceed from the indwelling Holy Spirit, they certainly have a worth that deserves eternal life as a reward. Valentia holds the same.

units.la: Quanquam contra hanc sententiam cohors quasi Pontificiorum sese opponunt, citante Vasque Jesuita, viz. Gregorius, Gabriel, Alphonsus de Castro, Canonici Colonienses, Concil. Senonense, & Vega; Quorum opinio fuit (inquit {1}Vasquez) Opera justorum in se spe-cta, quatenus procedunt ex auxilio Dei, & posi-tá sanctitate per quam Spiritus in nobis operatur, non habere Condignitatem & relationem meriti vita aeternæ; sed tantum rationem meriti habere petitam à promissione & pacto Dei. Inter citatos Authores Vega, qui Theologus quanti nominis fuerit in Concilio Tridentino, nobis Canisius Jesuita tradidit: {m}Andreas Vega, inquit, in Tridentino Concilio doctissimos Theologos & sapientissimos Patres differentes audivit: Cum de Justificatione multis est mensibus disputatum, ipse quidem cum disputantibus aliis sua sensa studiosissimè contulit. Iste Disputator igitur (si quis alius) idoneus testis videri posset, qui judicium proferat Concilii Tridentini, cui ipse de-votissimè subjecerat suum. Ejus nos sensum deposcimus & efflagitamus. Ille, {n}Scio, inquit, non deesse Doctores, qui dicunt Opera nostra esse meritoria & condigna beatitudine, propter supernaturalem dignitatem Spiritus Sancti à quo procedunt: verum omnibus hinc inde pensitatis, adhuc crediderim ea non esse Condigna beatitudine. Licèt enim major multò sit valor operum nostrorum, ut sunt à Gratia & Spiritu Sancto, tamen adhuc non videtur aequalitas inter ipsa & beatitudi-nem, & consequenter neque Condignitas : —quo sensu credimus, verè Paulum dixisse, Non esse condignas passiones hujus temporis ad gloriam quae revelabitur in nobis.
units.tr: Yet against this opinion there stands a whole band of Papists, as Vasquez the Jesuit cites: Gregory, Gabriel, Alphonsus de Castro, the canons of Cologne, the Council of Sens, and Vega. The opinion of these men was (Vasquez says) that the works of the righteous, considered in themselves, insofar as they proceed from the help of God and from the holiness set within us, by which the Spirit works in us, do not have condignity or the character of merit for eternal life, but have only the character of merit, derived from God's promise and covenant. Among the authors cited, Canisius the Jesuit has told us how great a name Vega had at the Council of Trent: Andreas Vega, he says, heard the most learned theologians and the wisest Fathers debating at the Council of Trent. When justification had been disputed for many months, he himself most eagerly contributed his own views to the other disputants. This disputant, therefore, if anyone, might seem a fit witness to pronounce the judgment of the Council of Trent, to which he had most devotedly submitted his own. We demand and urgently seek his opinion. He says: I know that there are no lack of teachers who say that our works are meritorious and worthy of blessedness, on account of the supernatural dignity of the Holy Spirit from whom they proceed. But after weighing everything on all sides, I would still believe that they are not worthy of blessedness. For although the value of our works, as they are from grace and the Holy Spirit, is far greater, still there seems to be no equality between them and blessedness, and consequently no condignity either. It is in this sense that we believe Paul truly said, The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us.

units.la: Sed personas mittamus, rationibus concer-temus. Bellarminus, ut videatur pro Gratia pugnare,{o} In opere bono, inquit, ex Gratia procedente esse quandam aequalitatem ad pramium a-ternum, probatur ex Joan. 1.16. AB EJUS PLENITUDINE ACCEPIMUS OMNES, ET GRATIAM PRO GRATIA: id est, GRATIAM MERCEDIS, pro GRATIA MERITORUM, sive, ut Augustinus loquitur, GRATIAM PATRIAE, pro GRATIA VIAE. At inter Gratiam & Gratiam est magna proportio: GRATIAM PRO GRATIA. Sic ille. Ergòne ex meritoria condignitate operis, secundum aequalitatem justitiae? Aut hoc probate, aut causâ caditis. A qua opinione Meriti, cùm passim alibi, tum etiam in loco objecto abhorruit Augustinus: {r}EX EJUS PLENITUDINE OMNES ACCEPIMUS: Pro modulo (inquit) nostro, tanquam particulas nostras, ut bene vivamus; sicut Deus partitus est mensuram fidei, quia unusquisque donum suum habet à Deo: —GRATIAM PRO GRATIA, quando nobis aeterna vita reddetur. —Cùm prius dixisset, STIPENDIVM PECCATI MORS: merito enim STIPENDIVM, quia militia diabolica mors æterna tanquam debitum redditur. Vbi autem potuit dicere, STIPENDIVM AVTEM IVSTITIÆ VITA ÆTERNA, maluit dicere, GRATIA AVTEM DEI EST VITA ÆTERNA: ut hinc intelligeremus, non pro Meritis nostris Deum nos ad æternam vitam, sed pro sua misericordia perdu-cere. Sic ille. Nihil igitur clarius est, quàm juxta Augustini sententiam, Præmium bonorum operum (quod est vita æterna) & Stipendium peccati (nempe æternam mortem) inter se, quoad condignitatem Meriti, non minus distare, quàm Non-debitum & Debitum: Nam Stipendium peccati Debitum esse asserit; at Præmium bonorum Operum dicit esse Divinæ misericordiæ remunerationem. Citiùs ergò quis ex silice aquam eliciat, quàm ex Gratia Dei proprié dictum Hominis Meritum ex Condigno. Quanquam, genuinam Scripturæ expositionem quod attinet, Toletus Jesuita vobis erudité respondet: {r}Ista expo-sitio Augustini, inquit, non mihi visa est conve-niens. Deinde ostendit Gratiam illam, quæ dicitur, Pro quâ, & quæ est verè meritoria, significare Gratiam Christo propriam, non in nobis inhærentem. GRATIAM PRO GRATIA, {s}Quia, inquit, in ipsius Christi gratia gratiam consecuti sumus, & per eum sumus grati facti Deo. Sic ille. Attendite verò; Gratia, quâ grati facti sumus, pura puta Christi est Gratia, non nostra. Sed pergit; Idem est sensus cum illis verbis, Rom.5.15. MULTO MAGIS GRATIA DEI ET DONUM IN GRATIA JESU CHRISTI IN PLURES ABUNDAVIT: —fuit enim Christus itâ Deo gratus, ut suâ gratiâ nobis meruerit & consecutus sit gratiam: —ut ad Ephes.1. GRATIFICAVIT NOS IN DILECTO SUO FILIO: ac si dicat, IN GRATIA SUI FILII NOS GRATOS EFFECIT; hoc est, GRATIAM PRO GRATIA ACCEPIMUS. Et hic est sensus legitimus. Qualem nimirum Gratiam Paulus praedicat in cap.5. ad Rom. verf.15. Si unius delicto multi mortui sunt, multò magis Gratia Dei, & donum in gratia unius hominis Jesu Christi in plures abundavit. Hic quoque attentionem vester Toletus adhiberi sibi postulat. {e}Attende; GRATIAM DEI appellat, qua nos gratos sibi facit: (An inhærentem? nequaquam; hanc enim ab illa distinguit) DONUM verò GRATIÆ, quæ nobis ex gratia infunditur.
units.tr: But let us set aside persons and contend with arguments. Bellarmine, in order to seem to fight for grace, says: That in a good work, proceeding from grace, there is a certain equality with the eternal reward, is proved from John 1:16: "Of his fullness have all we received, and grace for grace": that is, the grace of reward, for the grace of merits, or, as Augustine puts it, the grace of the homeland, for the grace of the way. But between grace and grace there is a great proportion: grace for grace. So he says. Is it, then, by the meritorious condignity of the work, according to equality of justice? Either prove this or you fall with your cause. Augustine, both elsewhere everywhere and also in the very passage objected to, shrank from this opinion of merit: "Of his fullness have we all received." He says: "According to our measure, as our portions, so that we may live well; as God has apportioned the measure of faith, because each one has his own gift from God." "Grace for grace," when eternal life will be given back to us. Having first said, "The wages of sin is death," he calls it a wage, rightly, because eternal death is paid back as a debt to the soldiers of the devil. But where he could have said, "But the wages of righteousness is eternal life," he preferred to say, "But the grace of God is eternal life," so that we might understand that God leads us to eternal life not for our merits, but by his mercy. So he says. Nothing, therefore, is clearer than that, according to Augustine's view, the reward of good works (which is eternal life) and the wage of sin (namely eternal death) differ no less in respect of the condignity of merit than what is not owed differs from what is owed. For he asserts that the wage of sin is a debt, but he says that the reward of good works is a recompense of divine mercy. Sooner could someone draw water from flint than draw from the grace of God a man's merit, strictly so called, in the sense of condignity. Yet as regards the genuine exposition of Scripture, the Jesuit Toletus answers you learnedly: This exposition of Augustine, he says, did not seem to me suitable. Then he shows that that grace which is called for which, and which is truly meritorious, signifies the grace proper to Christ himself, not inherent in us. Grace for grace, he says: because we have obtained grace in the grace of Christ himself, and through him we have been made acceptable to God. So he says. But look closely: the grace by which we have been made acceptable is purely the grace of Christ, not ours. But he goes on: The sense is the same with those words in Romans 5:15: "Much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of Jesus Christ abounded unto many." For Christ was so pleasing to God that by his grace he merited and obtained grace for us ... as in Ephesians 1: "He has made us accepted in his beloved Son," as if he said, "He has made us acceptable in the grace of his Son"; that is, "we have received grace for grace." And this is the legitimate sense. Such, of course, is the grace Paul proclaims in Romans 5:15: If through the offence of one many are dead, much more the grace of God and the gift by the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, have abounded to many. Here again your Toletus asks that your attention be given to him. Notice: he calls it the grace of God by which he makes us acceptable to himself (inherent grace? By no means, for he distinguishes this from that), but the gift of grace is what is poured into us from grace.

units.la: Ad Augustinum revertamur, ex annotatione Peterlii Jesuitæ, Rom. 3. 24. JUSTIFICATI GRATIS PER GRATIAM IPSIUS. {u}Nomen Gratia videtur hoc loco potiùs significare gratuitam Dei bonitatem erga hominem, quàm qualitatem à Deo infusam animæ hominis: & hunc quadrat Expositio Augustini; Hæc est Gratia, inquit, quit, sine qua nec infantes, nec atate grandes salvi esse possint, qua non meritis redditur, sed gratis donatur, propter quod GRATIA nominatur. Sic ille. Si, ex sententia Augustini, Gratia nominatur, quia non Meritis redditur; tum qui Meritum suum extollunt, Gratiam tollunt. Hinc apparet Bellarminum, praetextu efferendi Gratiam, ad fabricandum Meritum contra Gratiam dimicasse.
units.tr: Let us return to Augustine, from the annotation of the Jesuit Peterlius on Romans 3:24: "Being justified freely by his grace." The name grace seems in this place to signify rather the free goodness of God toward man than a quality infused by God into the soul of man; and Augustine's exposition fits this: "This is grace," he says, "without which neither infants nor adults can be saved, which is not rendered by merits, but is given freely; on account of which it is named GRACE." So he says. If, according to Augustine, grace is so named because it is not rendered by merits, then those who exalt their merit take away grace. From this it appears that Bellarmine, under the pretext of promoting grace, fought against grace in order to fabricate merit.

units.la: Nos contrà, locum Evangelistae in Adversarios retorquebimus: Joan.1.16. De plenitudine ejus accepimus, Gratiam pro gratia. In quem locum Maldonatus, Nemo tantum Gratia habet, inquit, quantum Christus; non enim plenitudinem accepimus, sed de plenitudine: Ergò (inquimus nos) Opera nostra bona, quae procedunt ex Gratia Spiritus Sancti, finita cùm sint, non possunt esse infinitae virtutis ad vitae aeternae praemium promerendum.
units.tr: We, on the contrary, will turn the Evangelist's words back upon our opponents: John 1:16: Of his fullness we have received, grace for grace. On this passage Maldonatus says: No one has as much grace as Christ, for we have not received his fullness, but out of his fullness. Therefore (we say) our good works, which proceed from the grace of the Holy Spirit, being finite, cannot have an infinite worth sufficient to earn the reward of eternal life.

units.la: Non possum non in Argumentum Bellarmini reflectere, tanquam quod petatur ad Absurdo: quia quatenus Gratia est Dei, est donum Dei gratuitum; non igitur implicat, sed plane potius excludit Meritum nostrum: quanquam hinc facilè elicimus, quòd Deus (quae est ejus infinita bonitas) ad mensuram Gratiae fidei & sanctificationis in Via, destinavit nobis mensuram Gratiae glorificationis in Patria.
units.tr: I cannot help but turn back to Bellarmine's argument, as if it were a case for reductio ad absurdum: for insofar as grace belongs to God, it is the free gift of God; therefore it does not imply, but plainly rather excludes, our merit. Although from this we may readily infer that God (whose infinite goodness it is) has appointed for us, in the way, the measure of grace of faith and sanctification, and in the homeland, the measure of grace of glorification.

units.la: Adversus tertium Pontificiorum Principium Meriti de Condigno, quod adscribunt Christiano, ut Christi membro.
units.tr: Against the third principle of the Papists concerning merit of condignity, which they ascribe to the Christian as a member of Christ.
SECTION IV.

units.la: ENumerantur à Vasque Authores decem, quos vocat Catholicos & pios, qui ut Christo in suis Meritis honorem deferrent, dixerunt, {a}Rationem Meriti nostri esse ex merito Christi, quatenus Christus, tanquam caput in membra, influit & operatur, & meretur: ut quemadmodum Paulus dixit ad Gal.2.20. VIVO EGO, JAM NON EGO, VIVIT VERO IN ME CHRISTUS: itâ de Christiano dici posset, MEREOR EGO, JAM VERO NON EGO, SED IN ME CHRISTUS. — Quod ex eo probari potest, quia vulgò dici consuevit, Opera nostra, quatenus aspersa sanguine Christi, (Apoc.7.14.) & à meritis ejus ablata, esse digna tanto præmio.
units.tr: Vasquez enumerates ten authors whom he calls Catholic and pious, who, in order to pay honour to Christ in their merits, said: The ground of our merit is the merit of Christ, insofar as Christ, as head into the members, flows in, works, and merits; so that, as Paul said at Gal. 2.20, I LIVE, YET NOT I, BUT CHRIST LIVES IN ME, so it could be said of the Christian, I MERIT, YET NOT I, BUT CHRIST IN ME. — This can be proved from the fact that it is commonly said that our works, insofar as they are sprinkled with the blood of Christ (Rev. 7.14) and taken from his merits, are worthy of so great a reward.

units.la: Hanc tot Doctorum sibi proponit Vasquez sententiam, ut Objectionem solvendam, cui postea satisfacere conatur strenuè; præsertim ex hac parte, quòd {b}Opera nostra magis digna esse debent ex eo, quòd Christus est Caput nostrum, & itâ nos reputamur eadem persona cum Christo. Summa responsi ejus hæc est, Merita nostra dici non posse, nisi quatenus opera à nobis ipsis eliciuntur: Sed hoc modo (inquit) quæ Cajetanus, Hosius, & alii Theologi tenent, non potest defendi augmentum dignitatis in operibus nostris; quoniam opera dicuntur dignitatem & valorem accipere a persona a qua proxime procedunt; non autem a persona a qua provenit gratia. Sed cum persona Christi non elicit opera nostra, minime accipiunt incrementum dignitatis a Christo, sed ex persona eliciente secundum dignitatem iustitiae & sanctitatis: alioquin sequeretur, Opera nostra esse infiniti valoris, —ad infinitam gloriam merendam. Haec ille. Et responsum suum dilatat, remque ipsam accurate persequitur, quasi illa opinio Meritis nostris repugnet, eo quod requiratur ad Meritum, ut {e}Opera suapte natura, & in se, habeant dignitatem suam.
units.tr: Vasquez sets this opinion of so many teachers before himself in order to solve an objection, to which he afterwards strenuously tries to give an answer; especially on this point, that our works ought to be more worthy because Christ is our Head, and thus we are reckoned one person with Christ. The sum of his reply is this: our works cannot be called merits except insofar as they are elicited by ourselves. But in this way (he says), what Cajetan, Hosius and other theologians hold cannot be defended, namely an increase of dignity in our works; since works are said to receive their dignity and value from the person from whom they proceed immediately, not from the person from whom grace comes. But since the person of Christ does not elicit our works, they in no way receive an increase of dignity from Christ, but from the eliciting person, according to the dignity of righteousness and holiness; otherwise it would follow that our works would be of infinite value, so as to merit infinite glory. So he. And he expands his reply and pursues the matter itself carefully, as if that opinion were repugnant to our merits, because merit requires that works have their dignity by their own nature and in themselves.

units.la: Deinceps ad illud, Meretur in me Christus, respondet:{d} Admonet Sotus, non recte dici Deum mereri in nobis, aut per nos; quia mereri denotat rationem aliquam obsequii, respectu alicujus a quo mereantur. Et, quia Deo nullo modo convenire potest, ut per aliquod obsequium ab alio mereatur, ideo ineptè satis diceretur, Deum in nobis, aut per nos mereri— Hanc partem sententia nostra aperte docet Andreas Vega. Hactenus Vasquez; qui insuper occurrit Obje-ctioni alteri, de Operibus Iotis[?] in sanguine Agni: {c}Respondemus, Commune illud dictum, OPERA NOSTRA, QUATENUS ASPERSA SANGUINE CHRISTI, SUNT DIGNA TANTO PRAEMIO, intelligendum esse, non ratione favoris, & imputationis meritorum Chri-sti, fi, qua accedat operibus jam ex gratia factis; —sed quia ex meritis sanguinis Christi datur nobis gratia ad haec opera, qua aliàs non daretur.
units.tr: Next, to that statement, Christ merits in me, he responds: Sotus warns that it is not correct to say that God merits in us, or through us; for to merit denotes some kind of service with respect to one from whom one merits. And since it cannot in any way belong to God to merit from another through some service, it would be quite absurd to say that God merits in us or through us. Andreas Vega clearly teaches this part of our view. Thus far Vasquez; who moreover meets another objection, concerning the works of those washed in the blood of the Lamb: We reply that the common saying, OUR WORKS, INSOFAR AS THEY ARE SPRINKLED WITH THE BLOOD OF CHRIST, ARE WORTHY OF SO GREAT A REWARD, is to be understood not by reason of favour and imputation of the merits of Christ, if any be added to works already done from grace; but because from the merits of the blood of Christ grace is given to us for these works, which otherwise would not be given.

units.la: Adversus quartum Principium Pontificiorum, pro suo Merito de Condigno, de Pacto scilicet.
units.tr: Against the Fourth Principle of the Papists, concerning their merit of condignity, namely that of pact.
SECT. V.

units.la: HOc est commune Pontificiorum diverti-culum, & ad quod plurimi, omni alio fundamento destituti, tanquam ad unicum causae suae de Merito propugnaculum, confugiunt. Eò nos illos persequimur. Pro necessitate hu-jus Principii Meriti de Condigno, ex Pacto Dei, pugnat acriter imprimis Bellarminus; {f}Sive ex Justitia commutativa, inquit, reddat Deus praemia laborantibus, necessaria est promissio; neque enim qui alterius vineam sponte colit, potest mercedem exigere: —Sive ex Justitia Dei distributiva, hinc quoque necessaria est promissio; neque enim debetur praemium velocis currenti, nisi pactum promissionis praecesserit. Haec ille, ubi eò arrogantiae Cardinalem pervenisse constat, ut eam justitiam profiteatur, quae etiam exigat à Deo praemium vitae aeternae. Andreas Vega, qui in Concilio Tridentino praelarus actor & athleta extitit, caeteris Principiis rejectis, omnis est in hoc uno de Pacto.
units.tr: This is the common refuge of the Papists, and the one to which most of them, having no other foundation, flee as to the sole bulwark of their doctrine of merit. There we pursue them. For the necessity of this principle of merit of condignity from God's covenant, Bellarmine fights most fiercely. Whether God renders rewards to those who labour, he says, by commutative justice, a promise is necessary; for no one who voluntarily tends another's vineyard can demand a wage. Or whether by God's distributive justice, a promise is likewise necessary here; for a reward is not owed to the swift runner unless a promise of it has gone before. So he writes, and it is plain that the Cardinal has come to such arrogance that he professes a justice which even demands from God the reward of eternal life. Andreas Vega, who was a distinguished actor and champion at the Council of Trent, rejected the other principles and rests everything on this one, the covenant.

units.la: I. Impugnatio ex Theolog- is Pontificiis. SECT. VI.
units.tr: I. Refutation from the Papists' theologians. SECT. VI.

units.la: PLurima Argumenta adfert Jesuita Vasquez ad hanc opinionem refutandam. 1. Asserit, Quamvis operibus justorum divina promissio accesserit, illam tamen ad rationem Meriti nullo modo pertinere. 2. Ad suas partes adscicit Thomam, & aliquot alios Scholasticos. 3. Annumerat tres Theologos, qui contra Haereticos hujus seculi, inquit, egregiè scripserunt, & in eos, qui dicunt ad rationem Meriti requiri pactum & promissionem, acriter invehuntur. Objicitur, Licèt sine pacto opera digna non essent praemio; tamen, cum exiguntur ex pacto & promissione, & sine illis promissio non esset complenda, ipsamet promissione videntur effici digna tanto praemio.
units.tr: The Jesuit Vasquez brings many arguments to refute this opinion. (1) He asserts that although a divine promise has been added to the works of the righteous, it in no way pertains to the nature of merit. (2) He enrols Thomas and several other Schoolmen on his side. (3) He counts three theologians who, he says, have written excellently against the heretics of this age, and bitterly attack those who say that a covenant and promise are required for the nature of merit. The objection is raised: Although good works would not be worthy of a reward without a covenant, yet, since they are demanded by covenant and promise, and the promise could not be fulfilled without them, they seem by the promise itself to be made worthy of so great a reward.

units.la: Respondet, Frivolum hoc; quia non per promissionem opus ipsum fit magis dignum re promissâ, quàm in materia Justitiae id manifeste apparet. Nam qui promitteret equum pro obsequio, aut pecuniâ exigui valoris, non propterea augeret pretium & valorem pecuniae aut obsequii, pro quo illum esset pollicitus. {*}Ex Matth.20. Cùm Paterfamilias convenit cum operariis in vineam ex diurno denario, non facit laborem ipsorum dignum denario: sed supponit dignitatem operis pro pretio aequali. Ergo dignitas Operum non oritur ex Conventione.
units.tr: He replies: This is trivial, because the work does not become more worthy of the promised thing through the promise, as is plainly apparent in matters of justice. For someone who promised a horse in return for a service, or money of small value, would not thereby increase the price and value of the money or the service for which he had promised it. From Matthew 20: When the householder agreed with the workers for the vineyard at a denarius a day, he did not make their labour worth a denarius; rather he assumed the worth of the work for an equal price. Therefore the worth of works does not arise from the agreement.

units.la: Secunda Ratio. {*}Si Deus comminaretur gra-viorem poenam, quàm peccatum suâ naturâ juste postulat, ut leve mendacium aeternâ poenâ puniat: non inde ex ea comminatione veniale peccatum in mortale mutaretur.
units.tr: Second reason: If God threatened a heavier punishment than sin by its own nature justly demands, as for instance to punish a small lie with eternal punishment, a venial sin would not for that reason be changed into a mortal sin by that threat.

units.la: Tertia Ratio, ab exemplis. {1}Si sola Bromif-[?]fio reddit opus Meritorium, tum quia Eleëmosy-na promittitur remissio peccatorum, esset[?] ex merito (cùm tamen est ex impetratione) atque itâ dicerentur nostram justificationem condignè mereri; quod nemo concedet. Deinde Abrahamo promissus est adventus Redemptoris, Gen.22. & tamen nec Abraham, nec Patres antiqui condignè adventum ejus meruerunt.
units.tr: Third reason, from examples: If a promise alone makes a work meritorious, then, since remission of sins is promised to almsgiving, it would be from merit (whereas it is in fact from impetration), and so we would be said to merit our justification condignly; which no one will concede. Again, the coming of the Redeemer was promised to Abraham, Genesis 22, and yet neither Abraham nor the ancient fathers merited his coming condignly.

units.la: Huc usque Jesuita. Cujus Rationes sunt adeò per se solidæ & nervosæ, ut replicam nullam admittant. Quanquam non desunt nobis Rationes aliæ, quibus efficitur, Pactum nullo modo inferre Meritum de Condigno.
units.tr: Thus far the Jesuit. His reasons are so solid and vigorous in themselves that they admit of no reply. Nevertheless we have other reasons, by which it is shown that a covenant in no way brings about merit of condignity.

units.la: 1. Quia illud ex parte Dei (qui reddit præmium vitæ æternæ) prorsus Gratuitum est, ad quam Remunerationem ille se ex mera gratia obstrinxerat. 2. Ex parte Hominis, opus bonum erat prius Deo ex legali Pacto debitum. 3. Quia leve & umbratile obsequium Deus (qualis est calix aquæ frigidæ, pauperum largitio) immensâ vitæ æternæ remuneratione compensat. 4. Quia si Deus concessisset dispositionibus ante justificationem promissionem vitæ æternæ; istæ tamen dispositiones, fatenfatentibus adversariis, non fierent Meritoriæ de Condigno. 5. Quia opus proprie dignum vitâ æternâ redderet Deum homini propriè obligatum, & accipientem bonum quid ab homine, ac non modò acceptantem. Quas singulas Rationes in sequenti dissertatione sparsim persequemur infra.
units.tr: (1) Because on God's side (who gives the reward of eternal life) it is entirely gratuitous, since he bound himself to that reward by sheer grace. (2) On man's side, the good work was already owed to God by a legal covenant. (3) Because God compensates a slight and fleeting service (such as a cup of cold water, or the giving of alms to the poor) with the immense reward of eternal life. (4) Because if God had granted a promise of eternal life to dispositions before justification, those dispositions, as our opponents admit, would not become meritorious of condignity. (5) Because a work truly worthy of eternal life would make God properly obliged to man, and would make him receive something good from man, and not merely accept it. We shall pursue each of these reasons separately in the following dissertation, below.
II. Refutation from the Scriptures.
SECT. VII.

units.la: NObis operæ-pretium videtur aliquid au-xiliarii [?] vice per nos attexere. 1. Job. 1. 9. Si confitemur peccata nostra, justus est Deus, ut remittat nobis peccata. 1. SI confitemur: En Pactum. 2. justus est Deus: Ergò ex justitia præstandum. 3. Si confitemur: non autem confitetur quis, ut debet, nisi volens; & id, ut vos interpretamini, ex libero arbitrio: nec ulla fit syncera confessio absque operante gratia Spiritûs Sancti. An igitur indè propriè dictum Meritum infertur? Cardinalis ipse hoc negat. Ecqua ratio? {*}Non est (inquit) Meriti dignitas in Confessione peccati. Sed respondet, Spiritum Sanctum non esse in confitente inhabitantem. An igitur in nullo confitente omnino Spiritus Sanctus residet? Mirus hic [illegible, ~8 letters], qui Spiritus Sanctus inhabitánsne sit, an hospitans in corde confitentis, poterit dignoscere. Sed quis spiritus eum hoc docuit?
units.tr: It seems worth our while to add something by way of support. 1 John 1:9. If we confess our sins, God is just to forgive us our sins. (1) If we confess: here is a covenant. (2) God is just: therefore it is to be performed out of justice. (3) If we confess: but no one confesses as he ought unless he is willing; and this, as you interpret it, comes from free will; nor is any sincere confession made without the working grace of the Holy Spirit. Does merit properly so called follow from this? The Cardinal himself denies it. What is his reason? There is no worth of merit in the confession of sin, he says. But he replies that the Holy Spirit does not dwell in the one confessing. Then does the Holy Spirit not dwell in any confessor at all? This is a marvel [illegible], who will be able to discern whether the Holy Spirit dwells within or only lodges in the heart of the confessor. But what spirit taught him this?

units.la: In Primitiva Ecclesia adulti, qui candidati erant Baptismi flaminis, priusquam fluminis Baptismo aspersi obsignatique fuerunt, utiq; Spiritum Sanctum inhabitantem experi sunt; quia, ut ait Apostolus, Qui Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est ejus. Spiritus Sancti residentiam omnibus in abscondito orantibus deesse non affirmabit Christianus quispiam, praesertim eis qui se viva Christi membra esse suis operibus demonstrant. [illegible, ~7 letters] haec, quae ad Meritum vestrum requiri solent, singula in pię orante inesse probantur; 1. in Voluntate orantis: 2. ex Pacto Dei cum orante: 3. orantem ipsum Christi membrum esse: 4. eundem denique Spiritu Sancto inhabitante imbutum. Quaeratur igitur, Utrum ex his Meritum proprie dictum colligere necesse sit. Dicito, Stapletone; {1}E-tiamsi (inquit) preces nostra non impetrent per modum justitiae, sed per modum misericordiae, id quod petimus; ideoque hoc non debitum, sed gratuitum est, quod precibus nostris Deus largitur; ideoque Deus quod oramus saepe negat: tamen pro debito orandi modo Deum aliquid semper tribuere, manifeste Christi verba affirmarunt. Haec ille, & rectissime quidem. Deus debito orandi modo multa concedit orantibus: sed non ex debito tenetur largiri quid nobis, aut ex nostro Merito.
units.tr: In the primitive Church, adults who were candidates for baptism of the Spirit, before they were sprinkled and sealed with the baptism of water, certainly experienced the Holy Spirit dwelling in them; because, as the Apostle says, He who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his. No Christian will assert that the presence of the Holy Spirit is lacking in all those who pray in secret, especially in those who show by their works that they are living members of Christ. [Illegible] These things, which are usually required for your merit, are each shown to be present in the devout one who prays: (1) in the will of the one praying; (2) by the covenant of God with the one praying; (3) the one praying himself is a member of Christ; (4) and finally he is imbued with the Holy Spirit dwelling in him. Let it be asked, then, whether it is necessary to infer from these merit properly so called. Speak, Stapleton. Even if (he says) our prayers obtain what we ask not by way of justice but by way of mercy; and therefore what God bestows on our prayers is not owed but gratuitous; and so God often denies what we pray for: nevertheless, that God always grants something to prayer offered in the due manner, the words of Christ clearly affirm. So he writes, and quite rightly. God grants many things to those who pray in the due manner, but he is not bound by debt to bestow anything on us, nor by our merit.

units.la: Quod Suarez objicit, Hoc scilicet intelligi de operibus oneros is, futile est. Nam vera con-
units.tr: What Suarez objects, that this must be understood only of the works of the burdened, is futile. For true

units.la: {1} Prompt. Gath. Fer. 4. Cinerum. tritio, quæ est dispositio ad justificationem, & non habetur à Pontificiis pro opere meritorio ex condigno, à Patribus inter opera mo-fissima[?] numeratur: quam propterea Scriptura mortificationem nominat, nonnunquam etiam Crucifixionem hominis veteris, quæ est pravæ nostræ voluntatis absoluta abnegatio, de qua vel Ethnici testantur, cùm dicunt homines improbos Vitam suam sæpe malle quàm pravam voluntatem perdere.
units.tr: (Prompt. Gath., Wednesday of Ash Wednesday.) contrition, which is the disposition to justification, and which the Papists do not hold to be a work of merit of condignity, is counted by the Fathers among the works of mortification. For this reason Scripture calls it mortification, and sometimes also the crucifixion of the old man, which is the complete renunciation of our corrupt will. Even the heathen bear witness to this, when they say that wicked men often prefer to lose their life rather than their corrupt will.

units.la: Hîc quoque Patres habemus duces. Chry-soft. {*}Mortifica corpus tuum, inquit, & crucifige, & accipias tu Martyrii hujus coronam: nam quod illic gladius operatur, fecit hic animi alacritas. Item Gregorius Pontifex, {¤}Etsi occasio deest, inquit, tamen pax nostra habet Martyrium; quia etsi carnis colla ferro non subdimus, carnalia desideria tamen spiritali gladio in mente trucidamus. Sed superius Pontificiorum Commentum, de quatuor principiis conditionis Meritoriæ, ab antiquis Patribus abundè refutatur infrà.
units.tr: Here too we have the Fathers as our guides. Chrysostom: Mortify your body, he says, and crucify it, and you will receive the crown of this martyrdom; for what the sword accomplishes there, the eagerness of the mind accomplishes here. Likewise Gregory the Pope: Although the occasion is lacking, yet our peace has martyrdom; for although we do not submit the neck of the flesh to the iron, we nevertheless slay carnal desires in the mind with the spiritual sword. But the Papists' fiction above, concerning the four principles of meritorious condition, is abundantly refuted by the ancient Fathers below.
CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Tertium nostrum Argumentum contra Meritum de Condigno, ex Confessionibus Pontificiorum locupletissimis, ex parte Dignationis Dei remunerantis[?]. SECT. I.
units.tr: Our third argument against merit of condignity, from the most abundant confessions of the Papists, on the part of God's rewarding graciousness[?]. SECT. I.

units.la: N[?]Vllum opus, quod præmium æternæ vitæ obtinet ex bonita-te & dignatione Dei remunerantis, potest dici Meritorium de Condigno apud Deum:
units.tr: No work that obtains the prize of eternal life from the goodness and condescension of God who rewards can be called meritorious of condignity before God.

units.la: At omne opus bonum præmium æternæ vitæ obtinet ex benignitate & dignatione Dei:
units.tr: But every good work obtains the prize of eternal life from the benignity and condescension of God.

units.la: Propterea nullum opus bonum est Meritorium de condigno apud Deum.
units.tr: Therefore no good work is meritorious of condignity before God.

units.la: Majorem Vasquez clarè profitetur in Di-ctatoria Censura sua de Protestantium doctri-na: {o}Operibus bonis (inquit) secundum se dignitatem vita æterna negant, sed referunt eorum dignitatem in favorem Dei, & acceptationem per Christi merita: quod nihil aliud est, quàm veram & perfectam rationem Meriti operibus nostris denegare. Sic ille, & quidem verissimè: quia nullum Meritum quod opus habet Dei acceptatione, potest dici in Condigni-tate operantis consistere secundum Æqualitatem Justitiæ apud Deum. Tale igitur Meritum de Condigno esse oportet, quale Adversarii discipulis suis credendum propinârunt. Minoris igitur nobis incumbit probatio.
units.tr: Vasquez clearly professes in his Dictatorial Censure of the Protestants' doctrine: "They (he says) deny that good works in themselves have the dignity of eternal life, but refer their dignity to God's favour and acceptance through the merits of Christ; which is nothing other than to deny outright the true and proper concept of merit to our works." So he says, and very truly: for no merit whose worth rests on God's acceptance can be said to consist in the worth of the doer according to an equality of justice before God. Such merit of condignity must therefore be of the kind the adversaries have served up to their disciples to believe. The burden of proof for the minor premise therefore rests on us.

units.la: Contrariam Pontificiorum sententiam à vera Theologia prorsus abhorrere, ex Pon-tificiis Theologis ostendent ii, qui vel Consequentiis suis labefactârunt, vel etiam ingenuis suis Confessionibus eam rejiciendam esse duxerunt. Vasquez denuo intromittendus est, ut intelligamus, an is, qui antea Protestantes perstrinxit, sustinere velit suos Pontificios Doctores in castris nostris militare: {p} Si ratio meriti nostrorum operum, inquit, provenit ex promissione & acceptatione Dei, efficitur ut justitia, quâ redditur æterna vita bene laborantibus, non attendatur in compensatione: Item, {q} Hæ-retici, inquit, ipsi (sic enim, quæ est ejus erga nos benevolentia, Protestantes appellat) æqualitatem hanc in complenda promissione non inficiantur. Denique expresse dicit, Opinionem hanc prorsus tollere rationem Meriti. Hactenus Vasquez: In quem insurgent veteris Scholæ magni nominis Doctores, Scotus, Gregorius, Gabriel, Ockam; qui (fatente eodem Jesuitâ) tradiderunt, {r} Opera justorum in se spectata, quatenus procedunt ex auxilio Gratiæ Dei, & posità sanctitate animâ, per quam S. San-ctus in justis habitat, non habere condignitatem [?]
units.tr: Those who have either shaken the Papists' contrary opinion by their own consequences, or judged it to be rejected by their own ingenuous confessions, will show from the Papist theologians that this opinion is utterly abhorrent to true theology. Vasquez must be brought in again, so that we may understand whether he, who earlier attacked the Protestants, is willing to admit that his own Papist teachers fight in our camp: "If the reason of merit of our works," he says, "arises from God's promise and acceptance, it follows that the justice by which eternal life is rendered to those who labour well is not taken into account in the compensation." Likewise: "Heretics," he says, "themselves" (for so, from his kindness towards us, he calls the Protestants) "do not deny this equality in fulfilling the promise." Finally he states expressly that this opinion "utterly removes the concept of merit." So far Vasquez. Against him rise up the great-named doctors of the older School, Scotus, Gregory, Gabriel and Ockham, who (as the same Jesuit admits) taught that "the works of the just, considered in themselves, insofar as they proceed from the help of God's grace, and with the holiness of soul in place through which the Holy Spirit dwells in the just, do not have condignity" [?].

units.la: {p} Vasquez in 1.1.Tom. 2. disp.214. Cap.5.n.23. §Primo. & rationem meriti vita aeterna, sed totam digni-tatem & rationem meriti habere petitam à pro-missione & pacto Dei.
units.tr: {p} Vasquez, in 1.1, Tom. 2, disp. 214, cap. 5, n. 23, §Primo: and the reason of merit of eternal life, but the whole dignity and reason of merit to be sought from God's promise and pact.

units.la: Horum & aliorum sententias (illo tacente, teste tamen Hosio) nos referemus: Scotus, dist. 17. lib. 1. Sent. docet Meritum esse ultra intrinsecam bonitatem actús, ex mera gratuita Divina acceptatione.—Et qui sub idem prope-modum tempus vixit, Nic. de Lyra, in Esa. 26. Omnia nostra opera, inquit, operatus es in nobis, Domine, quia non sunt meritoria, nisi ex acceptatione Divina, et gratia, per quam sunt acce-ptabilia, à solo Deo in nobis efficitur. Quem secutus est Gabriel Biel, lib. 2. dist. 22. In eo (inquit) qui dat premium, requiritur acceptatio actús elicití aut imperati, ut premium justitia non innitatur bonitati actús, quam habet ex bonitate intrinseca & principiis suis naturalibus; sed Divina ordinationi, quae est promissio & pactum. Et in Can. Missa, lect. 86. Dignum fieri pro-pter promissionem Dei, inquit, ex liberalitate sua, tanquam Dignum, acceptantis: quemadmo-dum in lib. * Hefter legimus: HOC HONORE DIGNUS EST, QUEMCUNQUE REX VOLUERIT HONORARE. Stephanus Bruli-pher (lib. 1. dist. 17.) Scoti sententiam secutus; Nullus actus bonus, quantumvis à charitate elicitus, est dignus vitâ aeternâ, ex natura sua; —sed solùm est dignus vitâ aeternâ per passi-vam acceptationem Dei. Item Greg. Ariminens. (lib. 2. dist. 26.) dicit, Opera nostra non ex se, sed ex sola gratiosa acceptatione Divina, meritoria esse vitæ æternæ. Hactenus Hosius Cardinalis.
units.tr: We shall set out the opinions of these and others (he being silent, though witnessed to by Hosius): "Scotus, dist. 17, bk. 1 of the Sentences, teaches that merit lies, beyond the intrinsic goodness of the act, in mere gratuitous divine acceptance. And Nicholas of Lyra, who lived at about the same time, on Isaiah 26: 'All our works, Lord, you have wrought in us, because they are not meritorious except by divine acceptance; and grace, through which they are acceptable, is effected in us by God alone.' Gabriel Biel, who followed him, bk. 2, dist. 22: 'In him who gives the reward, acceptance of the elicited or commanded act is required, so that the reward of justice does not rest on the goodness of the act, which it has from its intrinsic goodness and natural principles, but on divine ordinance, which is promise and pact.' And in the Canon of the Mass, lect. 86: 'To become worthy, he says, through God's promise, from his liberality, as one worthy of the one who accepts; just as we read in the book of Esther: THIS HONOUR IS WORTHY, WHOMSOEVER THE KING WILL HAVE WISHED TO HONOUR.' Stephen Brulefer (bk. 1, dist. 17), following Scotus's opinion: 'No good act, however much elicited from charity, is worthy of eternal life by its own nature;' 'but is worthy of eternal life only through God's passive acceptance.' Likewise Gregory of Rimini (bk. 2, dist. 26) says that our works are meritorious of eternal life not of themselves, but by God's gracious acceptance alone." So far Cardinal Hosius.

units.la: Ad Vasquem redeamus, qui se testem nobis præbet de prædictis Authoribus quos nunc allegat, qui similiter nullum Meritum admittunt, nisi {a}ab acceptatione & dignatione Dei provenientes[?]. Primò Alphonsus de Castro, {b}Meritum non procedit, inquit, ex natura rei, sed ex pacto Dei inito, quo opus factum est æquale præmio: velati si duobus contendentibus in bastiludio[?] horæ spatio, Rex promiserit vincenti gemmam, seu mille aureorum summam; non diceretur vincens gemmam illam meruisse. Sequitur Vega; {c}Credidérim, inquit, non esse incon-veniens dicere cum subtili nostro Doctore (Scoto) & cum Bonaventura, Richardo, & aliis, Deum debere justis beatitudinem dare ex promissione; NON ENIM EST INJUSTUS DEUS, UT OBLIVISCATUR OPERIS VESTRI, Heb. 6.10. ET expresse Paulus: {d}REPOSITA EST MIHI CORONA JUSTITIÆ, QUAM REDDET MIHI JUSTUS JUDEX. Et rursus, {e}DEUS SEIPSUM NEGARE NON POTEST. Sed cum dicimus, Deum debere justis beatitudinem, judicamus hoc non esse ex dignitate operum, sed ex misericordia & benignitate Dei nimia.
units.tr: Let us return to Vasquez, who presents himself as a witness to the authors just mentioned, whom he now cites, and who likewise admit no merit except that arising "from God's acceptance and condescension" [?]. First Alphonsus de Castro: "Merit does not proceed, he says, from the nature of the thing, but from a pact of God entered into, by which the work done is made equal to the reward; just as if, in a contest of two combatants in a tournament [?] over the span of an hour, the King had promised the victor a gem, or a sum of a thousand gold pieces; the victor would not be said to have merited the gem." Vega follows: "I should think, he says, that it is not inconvenient to say, with our subtle Doctor (Scotus), and with Bonaventure, Richard and others, that God ought to give the just blessedness by promise; FOR GOD IS NOT UNJUST, TO FORGET YOUR WORK," Heb. 6.10. "And Paul expressly: THERE IS LAID UP FOR ME THE CROWN OF RIGHTEOUSNESS, WHICH THE RIGHTEOUS JUDGE WILL GIVE ME. And again: GOD CANNOT DENY HIMSELF. But when we say that God ought to give the just blessedness, we judge that this is not from the dignity of works, but from the mercy and excessive benignity of God."

units.la: Theologi Colonienses locum proximum occupant, ubi interponunt (fateor) hoc no- men Meritum, sed ita, ut hanc antidoti bolum immisceant, viz. Quae tamen Merita ita intelligi debeant, quòd Deus remuneret opera vitæ æternæ ex gratuita dignatione sua clementia. His succedunt Canonici Conc. Coloniensis: Non veretur Scriptura, inquiunt, æternam vitam bonorum operum Mercedem appellare: nec ut putemus bona facta nostra digna esse vitâ æternâ, seu deberi illis vitam æternam propter eorum dignitatem: (quis enim tam stupidus est, qui sic sentiat?) sed magis, quòd Deus fidei nostræ, quam per ejusmodi opera in nobis exercet, vitam æternam gratuitò est pollicitus: Concludentes tandem cum Theologis Conc. Senonensis, Locus unicuique, aiunt, juxta Merita operum, non quidem erit ex Condignitate operum, (NON ENIM SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES HUJUS VITÆ GLORIA FUTURA, Rom. 8. 18.) sed magis ex gratuita & liberali promissione. Sic illi. Non ab his abscedit Pighius, Pontificiorum Achilles adversus Lutherum, qui cùm totus noster sit in causa Justificationis, tum de Merito operis sic definivit: Clementissimus Dominus veluti beneficium sibi impensum acceptâ & tanquam benignus heros servos ad id invitat, propositis pro suo labore præmiis aliquot liberalibus, ad quod sine ullo præmio obligabentur ex sua conditione & officio.
units.tr: The Cologne theologians occupy the next place, where they insert (I admit) the word merit, but so as to mix in this pill of antidote: that these merits are to be understood in such a way that God rewards good works with eternal life from his gratuitous condescension and clemency. The canons of the Council of Cologne follow: "Scripture is not afraid, they say, to call eternal life the reward of good works; nor do we think our good deeds worthy of eternal life, or that eternal life is owed to them because of their dignity (for who is so stupid as to think this?), but rather because God has freely promised eternal life to our faith, which he exercises in us through works of this kind." Concluding at last with the theologians of the Council of Sens: "A place for each one, they say, according to the merits of works, will indeed not be from the condignity of works (FOR THE SUFFERINGS OF THIS PRESENT TIME ARE NOT WORTHY TO BE COMPARED WITH THE GLORY TO COME, Rom. 8.18), but rather from gratuitous and liberal promise." So they. Pighius, the Papists' Achilles against Luther, does not depart from these; and although our whole case turns on justification, he nonetheless defined the merit of works thus: "The most merciful Lord, having accepted what is bestowed on him as a benefit, and like a kindly hero, invites his servants to that, with some liberal rewards proposed for their labour, to which they would otherwise be bound by their condition and office, without any reward."

units.la: Neotericos duos, quia mihi jam ante oculos obversantur, nullo modo prætermittendos esse duxi, qui de Remuneratione ex Misericordia loquuntur. Jac.2.13. JVDICIVM SINE MISERICORDIA ILLI, QVI NON FECERIT MISERICORDIAM. MISERICORDIA EXALTAT SE SVPER IVDICIVM. Eftius, {f}Ex hoc loco concluditur, inquit, quod inter Theologos controverti solet, Reprobos non infra meritum, sed secundum exactam & rigidam Dei justitiam puniendos esse: alioqui enim cum aliqua misericordia judicandi essent.— At in verbis proximis, SVPEREXALTAT MISERICORDIA IVDICIVM, id est, Contragloriatur Misericordia judicio: quasi dicat, Misericordia prævalitura est in judicio: quod intelligitur de Electis, qui omnes cum misericordia judicandi sunt: nam, seclusâ misericordiâ, NON IVSTIFICABITVR IN CONSPECTV TVO OMNIS VIVENS, Psal. 142. Hæc ille. Omnis insuper in hoc est vir verè Pontificius Fevardentius: {s}SVPEREXALTAT MISERICORDIA IVDICIVM: Nulla alia re nititur causa salutis nostra, quam misericordiâ, quâ unâ contra severum illius judicium possumus gloriari & exultare. Notandum est, Augustino misericordiam Dei non absque æquitate futuram esse in extremo judicio: in eum enim qui fecit misericordiam, misericordia Dei justa est; ejus enim misericordia non est confusa: nam misericordia est, ut dimittantur peccata; misericordia, ut tribuatur vita aeterna. Itaque misericordia patet in gratia & præmio: justitia ve-rò in laborum & bonorum operum ratione. Hæc ille; qui porrò in re tam seria attentionem exigit; {*}Attende, inquit, quomodo sola Dei misericordiæ spes universa salutis nostræ prora & puppis; quando, si exacto suo judicio nobiscum agat Deus, de nobis penitus actum sit. Merito igitur supplicas Propheta, Psal. 142. NON IN-TRES IN JUDICIUM CUM SERVO TUO, DOMINE, QUONIAM NON JUSTIFI-CABITUR IN CONSPECTU TUO OMNIS VIVENS.—Denique misericordia est, quâ solâ possumus in extremo judicio Dei vti[?] consistere. Hæc Fevardentius, ore Pontificiorum omnium Scriptor laudabilis.
units.tr: I thought that two recent writers, who are already before my eyes, must by no means be passed over: those who speak of reward out of mercy. James 2:13. JUDGMENT WITHOUT MERCY TO HIM WHO HAS NOT SHOWN MERCY. MERCY EXALTS ITSELF ABOVE JUDGMENT. Eftius: "From this passage, he says, it is concluded what is usually disputed among theologians: that the reprobate are to be punished not beneath their merit but according to the exact and rigid justice of God; otherwise they would be judged with some mercy." But in the words that follow, MERCY EXALTS ITSELF ABOVE JUDGMENT, that is, mercy triumphs over judgment, as if he said that mercy will prevail in judgment. This is understood of the elect, who are all to be judged with mercy; for, mercy set aside, NO ONE LIVING WILL BE JUSTIFIED IN YOUR SIGHT, Ps. 142. Thus he. Moreover, in this same place the thoroughly Papist Fevardentius, a writer praised by all Papists, says: MERCY EXALTS ITSELF ABOVE JUDGMENT: our cause of salvation rests on nothing but mercy, by which alone we can glory and rejoice against God's severe judgment. It is to be noted that, according to Augustine, the mercy of God at the last judgment will not be without equity; for the mercy of God is just towards him who has shown mercy, since it is not confused: for mercy is that sins be forgiven; mercy is that eternal life be bestowed. Therefore mercy lies in grace and reward, but justice in the reckoning of labours and good works. Thus he. He further demands attention in so serious a matter: "Observe," he says, "how the sole hope of God's mercy is the whole prow and stern of our salvation; for if God dealt with us by his exact judgment, we would be utterly undone." Rightly therefore the Prophet makes his supplication, Ps. 142: "Enter not into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for in your sight no one living will be justified." Finally, it is mercy alone by which we can stand at the last judgment of God. Thus Fevardentius, a praiseworthy writer in the mouth of all Papists.

units.la: Quisquis igitur velit Doctrinam hanc conferre cum Confessione (ex tanta nube Testium) Doctorum & Theologorum Pon-tificiorum (qui nullum aliud quam Meritum tantùm ex acceptatione, id est, improprie Meritorium, profitebantur) quomodo de hac Pontificiorum causa jam planè conclu-matum esse non fatebitur?
units.tr: Whoever therefore wishes to compare this doctrine with the Confession of so great a cloud of witnesses, the teachers and theologians of the Papists, who professed no merit except merit by acceptation, that is, merit only improperly speaking, how will he not admit that this cause of the Papists has now been plainly concluded?
CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Argumenta contra Meritum de Condigno, ex Patrum antiquorum testimoniis lo-cupletissimis desumpta.
units.tr: Arguments against merit of condignity, drawn from the very abundant testimonies of the ancient Fathers.
[illegible, ~30 letters]

units.la: ritum de Condigno, ex parte Operis boni, ut est Dei Donum. Argumentatio.
units.tr: ...ritum de Condigno, from the side of the good work, as it is God's gift. An argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: NUllum Donum potest esse proprie Meritorium apud ejus Do-natorem:
units.tr: No gift can be properly meritorious in the eyes of its giver.

units.la: Sed omne opus bonum, conferens ad salutem æternam, est Dei Donum:
units.tr: But every good work contributing to eternal salvation is God's gift.

units.la: Proinde nullum opus bonum, conferens ad salutem æternam, potest esse proprie Meritorium apud Deum.
units.tr: Therefore no good work contributing to eternal salvation can be properly meritorious before God.

units.la: Utramque Propositionem ex Scripturis & Patribus comprobatam dabimus.
units.tr: We will give proof of both propositions from Scripture and the Fathers.

units.la: Probatio nostra ex Scripturis, tam Apo- cryphis, quàm Canonicis.
units.tr: Our proof from Scripture, both the Apocryphal and the Canonical books.
SECT. II.

units.la: Ratio manifesta est; quia nemo Accipiendo mereri dicitur; At Operari bonum conducens ad salutem, est Accipere beneficium à Deo. Primo in loco operæ erit pretium inqui-rere in Autorem boni. Autor libri Sapientiæ, cap. 8. 21. Scivi me non potuisse sapientiam obtinere, nisi Deus dederit: & hoc quoque sapientia erat, scire cujus esset donum. Nos pariter sapere discamus ex Divinis literis, ex quibus decerpsimus breviusculam feriem bonorum operum, quatenus ad salutem destinantur. Primum, quod requiritur, est cogitare de bene operando: quod quidem cogitare est bonum acceptum; 2. Cor. 3. 5. Non sumus sufficientes ex nobis ad cogitandum quicquam, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Secundum est, ut bonum salutare cognitum credamus: quod quoque est bonum acceptum; Phil. 1. 29. Deus dat vobis credere. Tertium est, velle quoque id quod credimus: & hoc pariter datum est; Phil. 2. 13. Deus dat velle. Quorsum autem velle, nisi (quod quartum est) subinde operemur? Apostolus ibidem, Das & operari; atque etiam operari, non solùm faciendo, sed & constanter patiendo; 1. Cor. 10. 13. Non patitur nos Deus supra vires tentari, sed dat victoriam per Christum Iesum.
units.tr: The reasoning is plain: no one is said to merit by receiving; but to do good that leads to salvation is to receive a benefit from God. First, it will be worth our while to inquire into the author of the good. The author of the Book of Wisdom, chapter 8, verse 21: "I knew that I could not obtain wisdom unless God gave it; and this too was wisdom, to know whose gift it was." Let us likewise learn to be wise from the divine writings, from which we have gathered a brief series of good works, insofar as they are directed to salvation. First, what is required is "to think about doing good"; and this thinking is a received good: 2 Cor. 3:5, "We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything, but our sufficiency is from God." Second, that we believe the saving good once known: this too is a received good: Phil. 1:29, "God has given you to believe." Third, that we will also what we believe: this likewise has been given: Phil. 2:13, "God gives the willing." Why, then, will, unless (which is the fourth) we afterwards work? The Apostle in the same place: "God gives both to will and to work"; and indeed to work not only by doing but also by enduring steadfastly: 1 Cor. 10:13, "God does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but gives the victory through Jesus Christ."

units.la: Ecquid habent Pontificii quod opponant? Nihil, nisi quòd bonum à nostro libero arbitrio proficiscatur, ex quo nostrum dicitur. Sic enim (Cap. 6. Sect. 2.) suprà Bellarminus.
units.tr: What have the Papists to set against this? Nothing, except that the good proceeds from our free will, by which it is said to be ours. For so Bellarmine, above (chapter 6, section 2).

units.la: Nos autem; Opus, quatenus bonum, etsi à nostro libero arbitrio fit, tamen non ab eo tanquam in se libero, sed quatenus per gratiam liberatur, procedit. Ex qua fit, ut non solùm possit homo bonum operari si velit, sed etiam ut velit; quemadmodum Apostolus docuit. Et indè est quòd omne opus bonum conferens ad æternam salutem per Christum Jesum, fit, quatenus bonum, spirituale; quatenus spirituale, supernaturale; quatenus supernaturale, gratuitum; & quatenus donum gratuitum, nihil minùs quàm Meritorium apud Deum.
units.tr: But we say: a work, insofar as it is good, although it is done by our free will, yet proceeds from it not as free in itself, but insofar as it is set free through grace. From this it follows that a man can do good not only if he wills, but also that he may will, as the Apostle taught. And hence it is that every good work contributing to eternal salvation through Jesus Christ is, insofar as it is good, spiritual; insofar as it is spiritual, supernatural; insofar as it is supernatural, gratuitous; and insofar as it is a gratuitous gift, by no means meritorious before God.

units.la: Argumentum superius ex suffragiis Sancto-rum Patrum comprobatur.
units.tr: The preceding argument is confirmed by the testimony of the holy Fathers.
SECTION III.

units.la: Eandem planè Doctrinam Sancti Patres, in Apostolica schola instituti atque edocti, scriptis suis posteritati omni commendârunt: ut {1}Origenes; EI VERO QVI OPERATVR, MERCES NON IMPVTATVR SECVNDVM GRATIAM, SED SECVN-
units.tr: The holy Fathers, trained and taught in the Apostolic school, commended this very same doctrine to posterity in their writings. Origen, for example: "TO HIM WHO WORKS, THE REWARD IS NOT IMPUTED ACCORDING TO GRACE, BUT ACCORDING TO MERIT: the eminence of the word."
[Origen's quotation continues in the same vein.]

units.la: DUM DEBITUM suadeo (inquit) ullum remunerationem Dei ipsum, quòd agere al[?] tare, vel proloqui, i[?] ciamus. Quod ergò gratia praefisit? Sic thymema necessariò est ex dono Dei; (quae est vita aeterna, Merito nostro.
units.tr: "I persuade you," he says, "that God's reward is itself a debt, since we bring about, do, or utter something. What then has grace gone before to give? Thus the argument is necessarily from God's gift (which is eternal life) and not from our merit."

units.la: Secundus erit {k} (inquit) talem vitae conv[?] digaus esse posset; sed[?] Sic Ille: Nempe, I[?] Dignum. Non minù[s] veri, inquit, est ejus ipsi auctor exstitit. Si in omnibus praedicat; juxta illu[d]
units.tr: The second point, he says, is that a life of such a kind could not be worthy. "But," he says, "it is no less true that God himself became its author." If he preaches this in all things, then according to that saying:

units.la: 12. {m}Tales nos amat ipsius dono, non quali[?] Can. 20. Multa in facit homo; nulla veri[?] Deus praestat ut faci[?] cilii Patres, Deus ig[?] Auctor, cujus ductu[?]
units.tr: 12. "God loves us as his own gifts, not as what we are..." (Can. 20.) "Man does many things in us; God gives nothing that is true..." The Councils and the Fathers: God works, God is the author, by whose guidance...

units.la: Nec minus appo[?] Sed ego, cùm considero, quòd dicit, SECUNREDDI, vix mihi peropus esse, quod ex debito depóscat, cùm etiam hoc aliquid possumus, vel cogi- ipsius dono & largitione fa- erit debitum illius, cujus ille. Ex quo hoc En- conficitur: Opus bonum Ergò remuneratio ejus non est ex debito, seu
units.tr: Nor is it less fitting. But when I consider that he says "SECOND," it seems hardly appropriate to me that he demands as a debt what we can do, or are compelled to do, only by his gift and bounty, and which is his debt, to whom we belong. From this the following syllogism is formed: a good work is God's gift; therefore his reward is not owed as a debt, or...

units.la: Chryfostomus: Nemo (in- erfationem ostendit,ut regno totum Denum est ipsius Dei. Denum Dei tollit nostrum is accuratè 1Hilarius, Me- qui meriti acquirendi sibi c ille; qui gratiæ Divinæ s bonis operibus nostris d Araufcani Deus, quales futuri sumus es sumus nostro merito. Et homine bona sunt, quæ non ò bona facit homo, quæ non at homo. Hæc istius Con- gitur primus boni operis i homo Actor. olitè exquisitéque Hieronymus, {a}Scimus, inquit, nos nihil esse, nisi quod donavit Deus.—Non sufficit quod semel mihi donaverit, nisi semper donaverit: peto ut accipiam; & cùm accepi, rursus peto. {o}Augustinus ad vivum rem resecat; Deus coronat dona sua, non operatus. Apostolus dixit, PLVS OMNIBVS LABORAVI: sed vide quid adjunxerit, NON EGO, SED GRATIA DEI MECVM. Statim introducit Apostolum quasi in soliloquio apud se dicentem, EXPECTO CORONAM QVAM DABIT MIHI JVSTVS JVDEX: Sed quare? QVIA AGONEM CERTAVI.--Sed unde certâsti[?]? Unde fidem servâsti[?]? NON EGO, SED GRATIA DEI MECVM. Hinc ipse Augu-stinus infert: Ergo nunquam fis superbus, semper lauda Dominum, noli oblivisci omnes ejus retributiones. Retributio est, cùm peccator vocatus es, ut justificareris:—cùm tibi vires subministrata sunt, ut in finem usque perseverares[?].—Omnes retributiones ejus noli oblivisci, si vis ut benedicat anima tua Domino, qui coronat te in misericordia & miseratione.. Hæc hi duo Patres; ubi non solùm primam justificationem (ut vos vocatis) per remissionem peccatorum intelligunt; sed etiam secundam illam quæ in sanctificatione consistit, usque ad ipsam Coronationem quæ est vita æterna, misericordiæ inter retributiones numerant. Denique, est ubi Augustinus sic argumentatur; Fides non est Meritum, quia est Donum Dei.
units.tr: Chrysostom: "No one..." shows this explanation, so that the whole kingdom is God's gift. God's gift removes ours. Hilary, carefully: "Me..." who seeks to acquire merit for himself... who, by the grace of God, with our good works... The Council of Arausio: God crowns... as we shall be... are our merit. And: "the good things which man does not..." Man makes good things, which man... These of that Council... the first good work is the work of man as author. Jerome, carefully and exquisitely: "We know," he says, "that we are nothing except what God has given. It is not enough that he has given once to me, unless he always gives. I ask to receive; and when I have received, I ask again." Augustine cuts the matter to the quick: God crowns his own gifts, not our works. "The Apostle said, I labored more than all; but see what he added: not I, but the grace of God with me." Immediately he introduces the Apostle as if speaking to himself in soliloquy: "I look for the crown which the just Judge will give me." But why? "Because I have fought the good fight." But whence did you fight? Whence did you keep the faith? "Not I, but the grace of God with me." Hence Augustine himself infers: "Therefore never become proud; always praise the Lord; do not forget all his rewards. The reward is when you were called as a sinner, that you might be justified; when strength was supplied to you, that you might persevere to the end... Do not forget all his rewards, if you wish your soul to bless the Lord, who crowns you in mercy and compassion." These two Fathers not only understand the first justification (as you call it) as the remission of sins, but also count among the rewards that second justification which consists in sanctification, right up to the Coronation itself, which is eternal life. Finally, there is a place where Augustine argues thus: "Faith is not merit, because it is the gift of God."
[Marginal reference:] Ad Ctesiphontem, p. 253.
[Marginal reference:] In Psalm 102.

units.la: {r}S. P Bernardus clavum figet; Non talia sunt nostra merita, inquit, ut propter ea ex jure debeatur vita aeterna. Ex communi consessione Pontificiorum, Merita de Condigno proprie dici non possunt; quia definiverunt Meritum de Condigno esse, cui vita aeterna ex justitia aequalitate debeatur. Denique idem vir Sanctus, (infra, Cap. 17. Sect. 11.) nobiscum conclusionem nostram difertissime tenuit; qui vitam aeternam bonis operibus deberi ideo negavit, quia viz. sunt Dona Dei. Praeterea, quomodo homo pariter ejusdem boni operis, qua bonum est, Autor haberi mereatur, clare expediet: {q}Dei proculdubio sunt munera, tam nostra opera, quam ejus praemia. Et infra, Verba sunt non mea, sed Apostoli [?]; qui omne, quod bonum esse potest, id cogitare, velle, & perficere, pro bona voluntate attribuit Deo, non suo arbitrio. Sic ille, in hoc Argumento Athleta strenuus, Deoq; admodum devotus.
units.tr: St. Bernard drives in the nail: "Our merits are not such," he says, "that eternal life is owed to them by right." By the common agreement of the Papists, merits of condignity cannot properly be called merits, since they have defined merit of condignity as that to which eternal life is owed by the equality of justice. Finally, this same holy man (below, chap. 17, sect. 11) held our conclusion most eloquently with us, since he denied that eternal life is owed to good works precisely because they are gifts of God. Moreover, how a man may deserve to be regarded as the author of the same good work, insofar as it is good, he makes clear: "Doubtless our works are God's gifts, and so are his rewards." And below: "These words are not mine but the Apostle's, who attributes to God's good will, and not to our own choice, everything that can be good: to think, to will, and to perform it." Thus he, a vigorous athlete in this argument and very devoted to God.

units.la: Pontificiorum aliquorum consensus aliquis, si abest, non est inquirendus; si tamen adest, non est respuendus. {s}Capreolus igitur (teste Hosio) Thomae locum hunc adducens, Opera, inquit, nostra bona, pro quanto nostra sunt & à libero arbitrio proficiscuntur, parvi valoris sunt, ut dicit S. Thomas. Si autem loquitur de bonis operibus nostris, prout sunt informata charitate & gratia, potius sunt opera Dei, quàm nostra. Sic ille.
units.tr: If the agreement of some Papists is absent, it need not be sought; if, however, it is present, it should not be rejected. Capreolus, therefore (as Hosius attests), citing this passage of Thomas, says: "Our good works, insofar as they are ours and proceed from free will, are of little value, as St. Thomas says. But if he speaks of our good works as informed by charity and grace, they are rather the works of God than ours." Thus he.

units.la: CAP. IX. Secundum nostrum Argumentum ex Patribus adversus Meritum de Condigno, ex parte Operis boni, ut est Deo debitum.
units.tr: CAP. IX. Our second argument from the Fathers against merit of condignity, from the side of the good work, as it is owed to God.
The argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: NUllum opus bonum Morale proprie Deo, ex præcepto, debitum, potest esse de Condigno Meritorium apud Deum: Sed omne opus bonum Morale est proprie Deo, ex præcepto, debitum: Propterea nullum opus bonum Morale potest esse proprie de Condign[?] Meritorium apud Deum.
units.tr: No good moral work that is owed to God properly, by precept, can be meritorious of condignity before God. But every good moral work is owed to God properly, by precept. Therefore no good moral work can be meritorious of condignity before God.

units.la: De Assumptione nulla lis erit. Probanda est Major: primò ex Scripturis.
units.tr: There will be no dispute over the assumption. The major must be proved, first from Scripture.
Proof from Scripture. SECT. II.

units.la: LUc. 17. 10. ait Christus Discipulis suis, Cùm omnia feceritis, quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite, Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Quæ verba nobis videntur omnem Meriti bonorum operum opinionem labefactare & prorsus tollere. Qui locus quantùm Pontificios torqueat, facilè ex eo cernitur, quòd, ut eludant Lectores, vertunt se in omnes facies, sed ità infeliciter, ut sibi invicem contradicant.
units.tr: Luke 17. 10. Christ says to his disciples, When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do. These words seem to us to shake and utterly overthrow every opinion of merit from good works. How much this passage torments the Papists is easily seen from this, that to deceive their readers they turn themselves in every direction, yet so unluckily that they contradict one another.

units.la: Primò Bellarminus, omnia evadendi latibula inquirens, ait primò, Dictum esse, INUTILES SVMVS, de iis, qui extra gratiam operantur; ex Ambrosio. Maldonatus & Salmeron in eum locum, Dictum esse, aiunt, de iis servis qui non sponte & ex charitate operantur. Sic illi: quamvis Christus jam non nisi servos suos, viz. Apostolos, allocutus sit, qui tunc dixerunt ei, Auge nobis fidem: nempe eos, qui tunc præ cæteris in gratia constituti erant, &, reliquis omnibus, Christum ex charitate sequebantur. Atque semper debet Protasis cum Apodosi convenire.
units.tr: First, Bellarmine, searching out every hiding place of escape, says first that it was said, WE ARE UNPROFITABLE, of those who work outside grace; taking this from Ambrose. Maldonatus and Salmeron, on the same passage, say that it was said of those servants who do not work willingly and from charity. So they; although Christ was now addressing only his servants, namely the Apostles, who then said to him, Increase our faith: that is, those who at that time were established in grace beyond the others, and who, with all the rest, followed Christ from charity. And the protasis ought always to agree with the apodosis.

units.la: Secundò ait Bellarminus, Dici INVTILES SERVOS, nempe Domino suo: sed tamen sibi utiles: ex Beda. Cui contradicit Maldonatus: Nam servus ille in Evangelio Domino utilitatem attulit: (Recte. Arabat enim, & armenta pascebat totâ die) Neque concludit Christus, DICITE, SERVI INVTILES SVMVS, quia nihil Deo utilitatis attulimus; sed quia QVOD DEBVIMVS FACERE FECIMVS. Sic ille: & in eandem sententiam Alphonsus de Castro, Tit. De Haresibus.
units.tr: Secondly, Bellarmine says that they are called UNPROFITABLE SERVANTS, namely to their Lord, but nevertheless useful to themselves, citing Bede. Maldonatus contradicts him: for that servant in the Gospel brought profit to the Lord (rightly so, for he ploughed and tended the cattle all day). Nor does Christ conclude, Say, We are unprofitable servants, because we have brought no profit to God, but rather because we have done what we ought to do. So he writes, and Alphonsus de Castro, under the title On Heresies, is of the same opinion.

units.la: Tertiò Bellarminus, INVTILES dicimur, quia nihil fecimus ultra id quod debuimus: atque ita nihil inde petere debemus, ultra mercedem ex pacto adjunctam. Sic ille, tanquam ex Augustino, Sermone tertio de verbis Domini: ubi nihil quicquam tale occurrit, nec in ullo istorum Sermonum de verbis Domini, qui ibi extant quinquaginta.
units.tr: Thirdly, Bellarmine says, We are called UNPROFITABLE because we have done nothing beyond what we ought to do; and so we ought to ask nothing from it beyond the wage attached by agreement. So he, as if from Augustine, Sermon three on the words of the Lord; yet nothing of the kind occurs there, nor in any of those fifty sermons on the words of the Lord that are extant there.

units.la: Quartò Bellarminus, Ut exponit Chrysostomus, inquit, Non dixit, DICITE, SERVI INUTILES ESTIS, UBI OMNIA FECISTIS: Sed, DICITE, SERVI INUTILES SUMUS, ut humiliter de nobis sentiamus. Rectissimè Chrysostomus. Cujus testimonio vestra, Bellarmine, arrogantia arrogantissima retunditur.
units.tr: Fourthly, Bellarmine says, "As Chrysostom explains it: he did not say, 'Say, servants, you are unprofitable, since you have done everything'; but, 'Say, servants, we are unprofitable,' so that we may think humbly of ourselves." Most rightly said by Chrysostom! By his testimony, Bellarmine, your most arrogant arrogance is refuted.

units.la: Sed quaestionem ipsam quod attinet, omnia commenta vestra hactenus sunt foedae tergiversationes, ut vim nostri Argumenti effugere possitis; quam idcirco nos latius persequemur. Dicimus nos pactum promissionis de mercede ex opere extare, Si illud fecerimus; & non separari ab obligatione praecepti, & comminatione poenae, Ni fecerimus. Ut videre est Matth. 10. 32. de confitentibus & non confitentibus Christum: Luc. 9. 24. de vitam expendente, & (cum causa exigit) non expendente pro Christo: & Rom. 8. 13. de iis qui mortificant, & qui non mortificant carnem suam: Quae omnia Consequentiam hanc nostram abunde confirmant: Nempe, Bona nostra opera, quia sunt simpliciter, ex praecepto, Deo debita, non posse ex pacto fi-eri Meritoria. Ut suprà etiam disseruimus?, Cap. 6. Sect. 5. Hactenus ex Scripturis.
units.tr: But as far as the question itself goes, all your inventions so far are foul evasions, so that you may escape the force of our argument; and therefore we shall pursue it more fully. We say that the promise of a reward from the work exists as a covenant of promise, If you have done that; and that it is not separated from the obligation of the precept and the threat of punishment, Unless you have done it. As can be seen in Matt. 10. 32, concerning those who confess and those who do not confess Christ; Luke 9. 24, concerning the one who loses his life, and (when the case requires) the one who does not lose it for Christ; and Rom. 8. 13, concerning those who mortify and those who do not mortify their flesh. All of which abundantly confirm this consequence of ours: namely, that our good works, because they are simply owed to God by precept, cannot become meritorious by covenant. As we also argued above, chapter 6, section 5. So far from the Scriptures.

units.la: Argumentum superius ex antiquorum Patrum suffragiis luculenter comprobatur.
units.tr: The argument stated above is clearly confirmed by the witness of the ancient Fathers.
SECT. III.

units.la: Testimonia tot & tantorum Autorum non tam numeranda sunt, quàm ponderanda. Quorum collectiones, ex verbis Christi, multiplices sunt. Prima, Ergò bona opera nostra sunt Deo imputanda. Secunda , Ergò omnia à Deo accepimus. Tertia , Ergò imperfectos nos esse noverimus. Quarta, Ergò major Dei bonitas, quòd nobis servis, & omnia ei debentibus, amicitiarum praemia repromittit. Quinta, Ergò cùm omnia fecimus, nil magni fecimus; & vā[?] nobis, nisi fecissemus. Sexta, Ergò non laborum Merita pensare debemus. Per quas Patrum consecutiones , Bellarmini responsis aditus omnis interclusus est. Primò, Quia loquuntur Patres de hominibus in statu gratiæ constitutis. Secundò, Quia non hic agitur de servo, quatenus est sibi tantùm utilis. Tertiò, Quia nihil etiam de mercede proponitur, quod est ultra Meritum: Juxta Chrysostomi observationem, Nempe , hæc à Christo dicta fuisse, ut si omnia fecerimus, tamen humiliter de nobis sentiamus. Quod per se solùm causam vestram jugulat. Quæ enim arrogantia arrogantior aut elatior esse potest, quàm eam jactare Condignitatem meriti, quæ ex æqualitate justitia vitam æternam exigere possit apud Deum?
units.tr: Testimonies of so many and such great authors are not so much to be counted as to be weighed. Their inferences from the words of Christ are manifold. First: Therefore our good works are to be imputed to God. Second: Therefore we have received all things from God. Third: Therefore we ought to know that we are imperfect. Fourth: Therefore God's goodness is greater, in that he promises the rewards of friendship to us, who are servants and owe him all things. Fifth: Therefore, when we have done all things, we have done nothing great; and woe to us unless we had done them. Sixth: Therefore we ought not to weigh the merits of our labours. By these consequences of the Fathers, every avenue to Bellarmine's replies is closed off. First, because the Fathers speak of men constituted in the state of grace. Second, because here the question is not about the servant as far as he is useful only to himself. Third, because nothing is proposed even about a reward that goes beyond merit, according to Chrysostom's observation, namely that these things were said by Christ so that, even if we have done all things, we should nevertheless think humbly of ourselves. This alone cuts your cause to pieces. For what arrogance can be more arrogant or more haughty than to boast of the condignity of merit, which by equality of justice could exact eternal life from God?

units.la: CAP. X Tertium nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, ratione Indi- gnitatis Operantis, seu etiam Operis.
units.tr: Chapter X: Our third argument against merit of condignity, on the ground of the unworthiness of the one who works, or also of the work.
The argument. Section I.

units.la: Nullus operans, qui itâ in se indignus est, ut, quò opera bona acceptentur, dignatione & misericordiâ Dei egeat, potest Meritum de Condigno ex operibus vendicare apud Deum: Sed quilibet operans, quamvis sanctissimus, ità est in se indignus, ut, quò opera sua bona acceptentur, misericordiâ Dei indigeat: Ergò non potest Meritum de Condigno vendicare apud Deum.
units.tr: No one who works, who is in himself so unworthy that, in order for his good works to be accepted, he needs the favour and mercy of God, can claim merit of condignity from his works before God. But every worker, however holy, is in himself so unworthy that, in order for his works to be accepted, he needs the mercy of God. Therefore he cannot claim merit of condignity before God.

units.la: Majoris consequentia à Jesuita {c}Vasque conceditur: Bonis operibus (inquit) secundum se dignitatem vitae aeternae negare, sed referre eorum dignitatem in favorem Dei, & acceptationem per Christi merita, nihil aliud est, quàm persectam rationem Meriti operibus nostris denegare. Dignum igitur est hoc nostrum argumentum in quo elaboremus, ex Scripturarum lumine, ex Patrum antiquorum autoritate, & ex Pontificiorum plurimorum liquida & ingenua confessione.
