units.tr: Concerning the major premise, the Jesuit Vasquez is cited as granting it: "To deny that good works are of themselves worthy of eternal life, but to refer their worth to the favour of God and their acceptance through the merits of Christ, is nothing other than to deny outright the true nature of merit to our works." It is worth working this argument out, therefore, in the light of the Scriptures, on the authority of the ancient Fathers, and on the clear and frank confession of very many Papists.
Proof from the Scriptures.
SECT. II.

units.la: Scripturas, quæ indignitatem etiam Justorum operum indicant atque pronunciant, quisquis sacra Biblia extremis, quod dicitur, labris delibavit, novit esse complures: præsertim, per quas instituitur quilibet Christianus petere delictorum suorum remissionem, & mendax esse judicatur, qui dixerit se non habere peccatum. Præ cæteris, Scripturæ hæ cum causa nostra sunt conjunctissimæ, Psal. 102. 4. Deus est qui coronat nos in misericordia & miseratione; Et Matth. 5. 7. Beati misericordes, quia misericordiam consequentur. At Meritum de Condigno, quod consistit in æqualitate justitiæ ad coronam vitæ æternæ, ut eam apud Deum possit exigere in die coronationis, acceptatione & misericordiâ Dei nihil opus habet. Ut hunc nodum diffindat, dissolvátve, duos cuneos adhibet Bellarminus, tanquam ab Augustino mutuò acceptos, ex lib. de Correptione & Gratia, cap. 13.
units.tr: Anyone who has tasted the holy Scriptures, even just at the edges, as the saying goes, knows that there are many passages which show and declare the unworthiness even of the good works of the just. Above all there are those by which every Christian is taught to ask for the forgiveness of his sins, and he who says that he has no sin is judged to be a liar. Among the rest, these Scriptures are most closely bound up with our cause: Psalm 102.4, God is he who crowns us with mercy and compassion; and Matthew 5.7, Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. But the merit of condignity, which consists in an equality of justice with the crown of eternal life, so that a man could demand it from God on the day of coronation, has no need of God's acceptance and mercy. To loosen or cut through this knot, Bellarmine uses two wedges, as if borrowed from Augustine, from his book On Correction and Grace, chapter 13.

units.la: Primus est, Beatitudinem tribui misericordiæ, non quia non est merces vera Meritorum, sed quia ipsa Merita ex Misericordia sunt. Sic ille. Quem Augustini locus ipse, in eodem capite, convincit erroris & ineptitudinis: Cujus verba hæc sunt, Numerus Sanctorum per Dei gratiam Regno prædestinatus illuc perducetur; adhæret sibi misericordia Salvatoris sui, sive cùm convertitur, sive cùm præliatur, sive cùm coronatur: nam tunc ei misericordiam esse necessariam, Sancta Scriptura testatur, ubi Sanctus David de Domino Deo suo dicit anima sua, QVI CORONAT TE IN MISERATIONE ET MISERICORDIA. Ecce status ipsius gratiæ gradus tres: in quibus singulis Misericordia requiritur; Conversionis, Præalii [?], & Coronationis. Et postremus gradus adeò distinctus est ab aliis, ut expressiùs de coronatis tempore novissimo dixerit, Nam & tunc esse illis Dei misericordiam necessariam, &c. Quem non igitur misereat Jesuitæ jam tantis angustiis implicati?
units.tr: The first is this: blessedness is ascribed to mercy, not because the reward is not a true reward of merits, but because the merits themselves come from mercy. Thus he. Augustine's own passage, in the same chapter, refutes this as both erroneous and clumsy. His words are these: The number of the saints, predestined to the kingdom by the grace of God, will be brought there; the mercy of their Saviour cleaves to them, whether when they are converted, or when they fight, or when they are crowned. For that mercy is necessary to them then, as holy Scripture bears witness, where holy David says to the Lord his God, "my soul ... who crowns you in compassion and mercy." See here the three stages of grace, in each of which mercy is required: of conversion, of battle [?], and of coronation. And the last stage is so clearly distinguished from the others that he speaks more expressly of those crowned at the final time: For then also, God's mercy is necessary to them, etc. Who, then, does not pity the Jesuit, now entangled in such great difficulties?

units.la: Secundus cuneus est, Augustinum dicere, prater coronationem Meriti, necessariam esse misericordiam ad remissionem peccatorum venialium, & meritis Sanctorum misericordiam illam esse debitam. Sic ille, uno partu enixus geminum mendacium. Primum, Quòd dicit Augustinum meminisse Peccatorum venialium; quorum nulla est illic mentio. Secundum, Quòd ait dixisse Augustinum, Prater coronationem, necessariam esse misericordiam ad remissionem peccatorum venialium. Sed non dixit, PRÆTER coronationem, sed, CUM coronatione eam esse necessariam. Nam de loco Jacobi, JUDICIUM SINE MISERICORDIA ILLI, QUI NON FECERIT MISERICORDIAM; Ubi ostendit in illo etiam judicio, in quo justi coronantur, injustique damnantur, alios cum misericordia salvandos, alios sine misericordia damnandos. Et paulò post, QUIS GLORIABITUR SE MUNDUM ESSE A PECCATO? Ac per hoc etiam illi Dei misericordia necessaria est. Deinde Augustinus duntaxat ait, Et tunc pro bonorum operum Meritis (nempe improprie dictis, ut sæpe ex Augustino & aliis Patribus probavimus cap. 3.) in ipso judicio, etiam ipsa misericordia tribuetur. Contrà Cardinalis dicit,. Misericordiam debitam esse bonis operibus. Cùm tamen Deus, in judicio, sive damnet, sive parcat, justus est. Patres jam ipsi audiendi sunt. Quomodo verò Augustinus velit bona opera esse Merita, longè molliori sensu, alius erit differendi locus.
units.tr: The second wedge is this: Augustine says that, apart from the crowning of merit, mercy is necessary for the forgiveness of venial sins, and that this mercy is owed to the merits of the saints. Thus he, bringing forth two lies from one birth. The first is that he says Augustine mentioned venial sins, of which there is no mention there at all. The second is that he says Augustine said, apart from the crowning, mercy is necessary for the forgiveness of venial sins. But Augustine did not say APART FROM the crowning; he said WITH the crowning, mercy is necessary. For concerning the text of James, JUDGMENT WITHOUT MERCY TO HIM WHO HAS NOT SHOWN MERCY, he shows that in that very judgment, in which the just are crowned and the unjust condemned, some are to be saved with mercy and others condemned without mercy. And a little later: WHO WILL BOAST THAT HE IS CLEAN FROM SIN? And so God's mercy is necessary to him also. Then Augustine merely says: And then, for the merits of good works (namely, as improperly so called, as we have often proved from Augustine and the other Fathers, chapter 3) mercy itself will be given in the judgment. The Cardinal, on the contrary, says: Mercy is owed to good works. Yet God, in judgment, whether he condemns or spares, is just. The Fathers themselves must now be heard. But how Augustine wishes good works to be called merits, in a much milder sense, will be the subject of another place of discussion.
The ancient Fathers defend our cause carefully.
SECT. III.

units.la: TEstimonia ea duntaxat referemus, quæ necessitatem misericordiæ Divinæ, respeau[?] justorum, & suorum operum, aut ex-presse notant, aut æquipollenter inferunt. {e}Cyprianus: Non sunt condigna afflictiones hu-jus vitæ ad claritatem, cùm beati erimus, digna-tione Dei honorati. Sic ille. Ubi Primò vox Honorati idem atque Coronati sonat. Secundò, Altera illa, quâ dicitur hoc Dei Digna-tione fieri, perinde est ac Miseratione. Quas utraque voces contra Condignitatem Meriti pugnare, Vasquez in oppugnanda hac Protestantium doctrina jam supra palàm concessit, Sect. 2. {f}Hilarius, Non ipsa justitia nostra opera, inquit, sufficiunt ad perfectum beatitudi-nem meritum, sed ut misericordia Dei in hac justitia voluntate humanarum demutationum & motuum vitia non reputet.—Spes igitur in misericordia Dei in seculum. Ejusdem misericordiæ necessitatem supponebat {g}Hieronymus, cùm dixit, In die judicii nullum opus nostrum dignum reperietur. Sic ille, qui docuit, vitam æternam, ut donum, à Dei largitate donari. Augustinus, licèt hic ordine posterior, autoritate tamen nemini secundus: Is, in verba Psalmi, Psal. 102. CORONAT TE IN MISERICORDIA ET MISERATIONE, {h}Coronat dns sua, non Merita tua. Paulò post, EXPECTO CORONAM QUAM DABIT JUSTUS JUDEX: Sed quare? QUIA FIDEM SERVAVI. Unde forsitan[?] NON EGO, SED GRATIA DEI MECUM. Ergò quòd coro-naris, maris, misericordiâ ejus coronaris. Noli esse su-perbus, semper lauda Dominum, & noli obli-visci retributiones ejus. Ubi nullus erit locus alteri Pontificiorum diverticulo, quando respondent, Augustinum loqui de operibus extra gratiam factis. Loquitur enim de operibus, quæ vocantur Dona Gratia, quæque in novissimis Deus coronabit. Ut & alibi, {1}Maluit dicere ( nempe Paulus ad Rom. 6.) GRATIA DEI VITA ÆTERNA; ut intel-ligeremus Deum, non pro meritis nostris nos ad vitam æternam, sed pro sua miseratione perdu-cere. Sic ille. Quibus Merita tam præceden-[illegible, ~8 letters] tia Gratiam, quàm consequentia excludun-tur: Quia Perducere ad vitam aeternam, consummationem salutis significat. Uberiorem explanationem judicii Augustini in destinatum locum distulimus, viz. Cap. 17. Sect. 11.
units.tr: I will cite only those testimonies which either expressly state, or by clear implication involve, the necessity of God's mercy with respect to the righteous and their works. (e) Cyprian: The sufferings of this life are not worthy of the glory that will be revealed when we are blessed, honoured by the favour of God. So he. Here, first, the word Honorati means the same as Coronati (crowned). Secondly, the other phrase, by which it is said that this comes about by the favour of God, is the same as by mercy. Vasquez, in his attack on this Protestant doctrine, has already openly conceded above (Sect. 2) that both these expressions fight against the worthiness of merit. (f) Hilary: Our own works, he says, do not suffice to make up the perfect merit of blessedness, but it is so that the mercy of God in this righteousness does not count the faults of human wills and movements. Therefore: Hope in the mercy of God for ever. Jerome presupposed the necessity of this same mercy when he said (g): On the day of judgment no work of ours will be found worthy. So he, who taught that eternal life is given as a gift from the bounty of God. Augustine, though later in order here, is second to no one in authority. On the words of Psalm 102, He crowns you in mercy and compassion, (h) he says: The Lord crowns his own gifts, not your merits. A little later: I look for the crown which the righteous Judge will give. But why? Because I have kept the faith. Whence perhaps: not I, but the grace of God with me. Therefore, because you are crowned, you are crowned by his mercy. Do not be proud; always praise the Lord, and do not forget his rewards. Here there will be no room for the other escape route of the Papists, when they reply that Augustine is speaking of works done outside grace. For he speaks of works which are called gifts of grace, and which God will crown at the last. So also elsewhere: Paul preferred to say (namely in Romans 6) the grace of God is eternal life, so that we might understand that God leads us to eternal life not for our merits but by his mercy. So he. By these words both merits that precede grace and merits that follow it are excluded, since to lead to eternal life signifies the completion of salvation. I have deferred a fuller explanation of Augustine's judgment to its proper place, namely chapter 17, section 11.

units.la: Bellarminus per vitia intelligi vult peccata venialia. Quae (inquit) non faciunt hominem injustum. Et hoc est solenne ejus [?]κυριολεκτον[?]. Sed cujuscunque coloris vitia fuerint, Hilarius dixit, ea justitiae opera non sufficere ad beatitudinis Meritum. Quod autem non sufficit ad hoc beatitudinis Meritum, non potest esse beatitudinis opus Meritorium de Condigno.
units.tr: Bellarmine wants vices to be understood as venial sins, which (he says) do not make a man unrighteous. This is his usual proper term [κυριολεκτον]. But whatever kind of faults they were, Hilary said that they do not suffice as works of righteousness for the merit of blessedness. And what does not suffice for this merit of blessedness cannot be a meritorious work of blessedness of condign merit.

units.la: 1 Basilius: Manet sempiterna requies illos, qui in hac vita legitimè certarunt, non ob eorum merita merita factorum, sed de munificentissima Dei gratia. Respondet Cardinalis, in Graecis sic haberi, Reddendam sempiternam requiem, οὐ κατ' ὀφείλημα ἢ ἔργων, ἀλλὰ τῇ μεγαλοδωρίᾳ Θεοῦ [?]. Id est, Non secundum debitum operum, sed secundum Dei munificentissimi; ubi deest vox χάριν [?], Gratiam. Sic ille. Quasi vero verba haec, Secundum Dei munificentissimi, absque adjectione aliqua, non reddant hiulcam orationem: aut, ac si munificentissimo Deo non reſpondeat Gratia. Quanquam id quoque quod nos premimus & urgemus in verbis Basilii est, quod negat requiem aeternam concedi κατ' ὀφείλημα ἢ ἔργων [?], id est, Secundum debitum operum. Ubi Debitum operum atq; Meritum operum Synonyma esse quis dubitat? Ubi etiam de requie sempiterna, id est, beatitudine ipsa essentiali, non de gradu aliquo accidentali, aperte loquitur Basilius.
units.tr: (1) Basil: Eternal rest remains for those who have struggled lawfully in this life, not on account of the merits of their deeds, but from the most bountiful grace of God. The Cardinal replies that the Greek reads thus: to be rendered eternal rest, not according to debt of works, but by the great bounty of God [οὐ κατ' ὀφείλημα ἢ ἔργων, ἀλλὰ τῇ μεγαλοδωρίᾳ Θεοῦ]; that is, not according to the debt of works but according to the most bountiful God, where the word grace [χάριν] is lacking. So he. As if these words, according to the most bountiful God, without some addition, did not make an awkward sentence, or as if grace did not correspond to a most bountiful God! Yet the point we press and urge in Basil's words is this: he denies that eternal rest is granted according to debt of works [κατ' ὀφείλημα ἢ ἔργων]. Who doubts that debt of works and merit of works are synonyms? And Basil clearly speaks here of eternal rest, that is, of blessedness itself in its essence, not of some accidental degree of it.

units.la: {m}Autor operis imperfecti, sub nomine Chrysostomi, magnae antiquitatis; Quomodo sufficiat opus Sanctorum ad salutem aliorum, cum nec sufficiunt sibi solis ad gloriam illam justo judicio consequendam? Et {n}Gregorius Magnus, Pontifex; Si opus virtutis exercuero, ad vitam, non ex meritis, sed ex venia convalesco. Respondet {o}Bellarminus, Loquitur S. Gregorius de meritis, quae sunt in nobis ex nobis. Sic ille, pro more suo importune nimis; nam loquitur Gregorius de se, Si bonum opus opus exercuero, cùm jam se sentit esse in statu Gratiæ. Fac autem, ut itâ hunc unicum locum expediat Cardinalis; cur tamen alia, eáque apertissima prætervolat? Haud temere est; sensit proculdubio vir catus scilicet, Sanctum {P}Gregorium à nostris partibus athletam stare: Deus Sanctos coronat ex misericordia, & non remunerat justos propter opera, sed secundum opera.
units.tr: The author of the unfinished work, under the name of Chrysostom, of great antiquity: How can the work of the saints suffice for the salvation of others, when it does not suffice even for themselves to obtain that glory by the just judgment? And Gregory the Great, a Pope: If I exercise a work of virtue, I am strengthened for life not by merits but by pardon. Bellarmine replies: Gregory speaks of merits which are in us and from us. So he, as is his way, too importunately; for Gregory speaks of himself, if I exercise a good work, when he already feels himself to be in a state of grace. But suppose the Cardinal does manage to explain this single passage in this way; why does he slip past the others, which are so plain? It is not by chance: no doubt the shrewd man perceived that Saint Gregory stands as a champion on our side: God crowns the saints out of mercy, and does not reward the righteous on account of their works, but according to their works.

units.la: Bernardus in hoc Argumento, veluti in latissimo campo, exultat & expatiatur, & judicium suum orthodoxum satis explicat, tam quoad Thesin in genere, quàm quoad Hy-pothesin ergà seipsum. In Thesi sic, {q}Nequetu-lia sunt hominum merita, ut propter ea vita debeatur ex jure, aut Deus injuriam aliquam faceret, nisi eam donaret. Respondet {r}Cardinalis, Docet Bernardus vitam æternam non deberi meritis ex jure absolutè, non præsuppositâ Gratiâ & promissione. Sic ille, qui nunquam exuit Jesuitam, agens sophisticè, confundens ea quæ sunt distinguenda. Quasi vero quia Bernardus supponat nulla esse Merita sine Gratia præveniente, ergò non agat contra Merita post acceptam Gratiam, quibus debeatur vita æterna. Perversè omnino; nam quamvis vocet opera bona Merita; tamen esse ea Merita, quibus, ex Condignitate sua, debeatur vita æterna, nec dixit, nec sensit, nec unquam somniavit; sed contrà. Nam ibidem Bernardus addit, (Advertite) Necesse est primò omnium credere, quòd remissionem peccatorum habere non possis, nisi per indulgentiam Dei. Hæc est Prima & Præcedens Gratia, quam distinguit à proximo gradu Gratiæ: Sequitur enim, Deinde, quòd nihil prorsus habere queant operis boni, nisi & hoc dederit ipse. Hæc de gratia Adjuvante & Sanctificante: Tandem ad supremum Gratiæ gradum ascendens, dicit, Credendum esse postremò, quòd vitam æternam nullâ potes operiùs promereri, nisi gratiùs detur & illa. Sic ille, vir verè sanctus. Nisi detur ET illa: quæ particula, ET, non caret Emphasi, sed stimulum habet. Nec itâ multò post, ac si studio illi suisset sensum suum admodum luculenter exprimere, Ipse enim, inquit, peccata condonat, ipse donat merita (Hucusque constentur adversarii; sed adjungit) & præmia nihilominus ipse redonat. Sic ille. Quid autem est, Redonare, nisi Novo munere donare? Idéque nihilominus, id est, Non obstante quòd prius Merita donaverat. Ex quo clarissimè patet, per Merita se nihil minùs quàm Merita pontificia ex Condigno intellexisse, quibus (ut Adversarii adstruunt) vita æterna ex justitiæ æqualitate debeatur, & ab operantibus exigi possit.
units.tr: In this subject Bernard exults and ranges, as if in a very broad field, and sufficiently explains his orthodox judgment, both as to the thesis in general and as to the hypothesis concerning himself. In the thesis he says: Human merits are so insignificant that life is not owed to them as a matter of right, nor would God do any wrong unless he gave it as a gift. The Cardinal replies: Bernard teaches that eternal life is not owed to merits absolutely as a matter of right, without presupposing grace and promise. So he, who never laid aside the Jesuit, arguing sophistically and confusing what must be distinguished. As if, because Bernard supposes that there are no merits without preventing grace, he therefore does not argue against merits after grace has been received, by which eternal life is owed. Wholly perverse! For although he calls good works merits, yet that they are merits by which eternal life is owed, by their own condignity, he neither said, nor felt, nor ever dreamed; on the contrary. For in the same place Bernard adds: (Take note) It is necessary first of all to believe that you cannot have forgiveness of sins except through the indulgence of God. This is the first and preceding grace, which he distinguishes from the next degree of grace. For it follows: Then, that they can have no good work at all unless he himself gives this too. These things concern the assisting and sanctifying grace. Finally, ascending to the highest degree of grace, he says: Lastly, it must be believed that eternal life can be merited by no work, unless it is given also as a gift of grace. So he, a truly holy man. Unless it is given, AND that too: this particle AND is not without emphasis, but it has a sting. And not long after, as if he had set himself to express his meaning very clearly: For he himself, he says, forgives sins, he himself gives merits (so far the adversaries agree; but he adds) and nevertheless he himself rewards them again. So he. But what is to reward again, except to give again by a new gift? And indeed nevertheless, that is, notwithstanding that he had earlier given the merits. From this it is most clearly evident that by merits he understood nothing less than the Papists' merits of condign worth, by which (as the adversaries maintain) eternal life is owed from the equity of justice and can be demanded from those who work.

units.la: {t}Bernardus ad Hypothesin, id est, ad seipsum venit: Meritum meum (inquit) miseratio tio Domini. Respondet Cardinalis, intelligi, Merita nostra non esse ex nobis, sed ex Deo; ut ipse explicat, Serm. 68. in Cant. MERITA HABERE CURES: HABITA, DATA NO. VERIS. Sic ille. Nos vero potius ipsi Bernardo credimus: ‘Majorem miserationem ne-mo habet, quàm ut animam suam ponat quis pro addictis morti & damnatis: meum proinde meritum miseratio Domini. Non planè sum meriti inops, quamdiu ille miserationum non su-erit: quòd si misericordia Domini multa, multus nihilominus ego in meritis sum. Quid si multorum mihi conscius sim delictorum? Nempe UBI ABUNDAVIT DELICTUM, IBI SUPERABUNDAVIT GRATIA.’ Sic Bernardus, tantum de Meritis Christi erga se, in quae totus recumbit: quae tamen ausus est Bellarminus interpretari pro defensione etiam Meriti de Condigno ex æqualitate iustitiæ apud Deum; qui eâdem operâ lucem trans-mutet in tenebras.
units.tr: Bernard comes to the hypothesis, that is, to himself: My merit (he says) is the Lord's mercy. The Cardinal replies that this is to be understood as: Our merits are not from ourselves but from God; as he himself explains in Sermon 68 on the Song of Songs: to have merits is a care: having been given, not true (?). So he. But we rather believe Bernard himself: No one has greater mercy than that someone should lay down his soul for those given over to death and condemned. My merit, therefore, is the Lord's mercy. I am not altogether lacking in merit so long as he has not ceased to be merciful; but if the mercy of the Lord is great, I nevertheless am great in merits. What if I am conscious of many offences? Surely, where sin abounded, there grace did much more abound. So Bernard, speaking only of Christ's merits towards himself, on which he wholly leans. Yet Bellarmine has dared to interpret these as a defence even of merit of condign worth, by equity of justice before God; who by the same work turns light into darkness.
Confirmation of the same argument, from the consensus of the Papists.
SECT. IV.

units.la: AUtores Pontificios bene multos antea{*} produximus, qui nobis astipulantes, remunerationem operum bonorum, ex Divina benignitate, acceptatione, dignatione, ac misericordia
units.tr: We have already produced very many Papist authors who, agreeing with us, have copiously and stoutly defended that the reward of good works is to be obtained from divine goodness, acceptance, favour and mercy{*}

units.la: {*} Cap. 7. Sect. 1.&c. fericordia obtinendam esse, copiosè & per-pugnaciter defenderunt: quem locum, nè sim longus, Lector potest consulere. Jam postquam probavimus bonum omne opus nostrum (modò Divinæ legis trutinâ appendatur) quamvis Deo indignum, ta-men debitum ei esse; instamus porrò atque urgemus, ex operibus nostris bonis Deum non fieri nobis debitorem.
units.tr: {*} Chap. 7, Sect. 1, etc. ...to be obtained. The reader may consult that passage, lest I be too long. Now that we have proved that every good work of ours (provided it is weighed in the balance of the divine law), although unworthy before God, is nevertheless owed to him, we press further and insist that God does not become our debtor because of our good works.
CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Quartum nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, ex parte Dei remunerantis. Argumentatio.
units.tr: Our fourth argument against the Merit of Condignity, on the part of God as rewarder. Argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: OMne opus proprie meritorium apud Deum, Deum ipsum con-stituit operanti proprie debi-torem: Sed nullum opus bo-num constituit Deum operanti proprie debitorem: Propterea nullum opus bonum est proprie meritorium apud Deum. Major est in confesso apud Adversariorum nostrorum Doctores primarios; qui ad Mi-norem nocem expugnandam, ingeniorum suorum nervos omnes intendunt. Nam cùm duplex sit debitum: unum fidelitatis, ut quis constet promissis suis; alterum obligationis ex rigore justitiæ ad alium: quorum primum Deo competere Christiani omnes credunt, Pontificii posterius nunc adstruunt atque affirmant. Utpote {u}Suarez Jesuita: Debitum fidelitatis (inquit) nititur promissionis veritate: at debitum, de quo modò agimus, quamvis requirat promissionem, & in ea potissimum fundatur; tamen operibus commensuratur & proportionatur. Sic ille. Postea exigens ex hoc merito æqualitatem justitiæ apud Deum, {x}Debitum justitiæ, inquit, est cùm facta est promissio per modum stipendii & mercedis laboris debita, ut laborantibus in vinea, Matth. 20. aut per modum bravii & præmii in certamine, ut 1. Cor. 9. & Phil. 3. Cùm igitur conditio in promissione proponitur, jus sibi acquirit justitia, ne quis nobis objiciat, præmium reddi ex debito Fidelitatis salvis, contra proprietates verborum justitiæ & Mercedis, quæ in rigore debitum justitiæ requirunt. Hæc ille, qui præterea doctrinam hanc à Conc. Tridentino approbari autumat.
units.tr: Every work that is properly meritorious before God makes God himself the proper debtor to the one who performs it. But no good work makes God the proper debtor to the one who performs it. Therefore no good work is properly meritorious before God. This minor premise is conceded among the chief teachers of our opponents, who strain every sinew of their wits to storm this lesser fort. For since debt is twofold, one of fidelity, so that a person keeps his promises, and the other of obligation arising from the strictness of justice toward another, all Christians believe that the first belongs to God, while the Papists now assert and affirm the second. Thus Suarez the Jesuit: "The debt of fidelity rests on the truth of the promise; but the debt of which we are now speaking, although it requires a promise and is chiefly founded upon it, is nevertheless commensurated and proportioned to works." So he. Afterwards, demanding from this merit an equality of justice before God, he says: "The debt of justice is when a promise has been made, by way of a wage and reward owed for labour, as to the labourers in the vineyard, Matt. 20; or by way of a prize and reward in a contest, as in 1 Cor. 9 and Phil. 3. Since, therefore, a condition is proposed in the promise, justice acquires a right for itself, lest anyone object to us that the reward is repaid from a debt of fidelity, with the proper meanings of the words justice and reward being set aside, which in strict sense require a debt of justice." So he, who moreover thinks this doctrine is approved by the Council of Trent.

units.la: Et suppositâ eâdem Dei promissione, eandem justitiæ obligationem urget Bellarminus: {y}Respondeo, (inquit) omnem veram promissionem ferre secum obligationem, & à Deo implendam atque servandam. Hæc ille, nempe idem ille, qui non dubitavit dicere, {*}Debet Deus vitam aeternam meritis nostris secundum justitiam commutativam. Eamque vocat alibi justi-tiam absolutam, quae praeterea exigere potest a Deo mercedem. (viz. supra, cap. 2. sect. 1.) Item {*}Vasquez: Meritum est comparatione alicujus praemii obsequium, quod natura sua exigit praemium hujusmodi, tanquam parem gratiam, sibi referri ex grati animi lege, & cui illud praemium, veluti aequalis remuneratio & legitima compensatio, respondet secundum rectam obsequii & mercedis aestimationem. Istis igitur Doctoribus, modo in disciplinam nos illis tradere velimus, discamus necesse est, Deum ita Meritis hominum obligatum esse, ut debeat in summo rigore justitia absoluta operâ illa remuneratione vita aeterna compensare. Et illud sane proprie dictum Meritum requirit & exigit. Nos contrarium evincemus, illis praesidiis nixi, quibus absque Scripturarum violatione, venerandae Antiquitatis despectu, & melioris notae Pontificiorum Doctorum irrisione, renitendum non sit.
units.tr: And with the same promise of God supposed, Bellarmine presses the same obligation of justice: "I answer," he says, "that every true promise carries with it an obligation to be fulfilled and kept by God." So he, namely the same man who did not hesitate to say: "God owes eternal life to our merits according to commutative justice." He elsewhere calls this "absolute justice, which can moreover demand a reward from God" (see above, ch. 2, sect. 1). Likewise Vasquez: "Merit is a service which, in comparison with some reward, by its nature demands such a reward, as a like grace to be returned to it by the law of a grateful mind, and to which that reward corresponds as an equal remuneration and lawful compensation, according to the right estimation of service and wage." Therefore, if we are willing to submit ourselves to these teachers' discipline, we must learn that God is so bound by the merits of men that he ought, in the highest rigour of absolute justice, to repay that work with the reward of eternal life. And that is certainly what the properly so-called merit requires and demands. We shall prove the contrary, relying on those defences by which, without violating Scripture, disparaging venerable antiquity, or mocking the more reputable Papist teachers, we need not shrink from resisting.
Scripture, which is opposed to the dogma of the Papists.
SECT. II.

units.la: Illæ Scripturæ quas præmisimus, ad has tenebras depellendas satis esse possunt: qui-bus bus hactenus probavimus, vel omne opus bo-num esse Dei Donum, (cap. 8.) vel quibus evicimus, omne opus bonum, quamvis ex se non dignum, (cap. 10.) esse tamen Deo debi-tum. Quantò magis hoc constabit, cùm ostenderimus nullùm opus bonum esse remuneratione coelesti condignum? Ab illarum repetitione abstineo, & an Patres in sententiam nostram inclinent periculum faciemus.
units.tr: The Scriptures which we have already cited may be enough to dispel these shadows: by them we have hitherto proved either that every good work is the gift of God (chap. 8), or that, although in itself no good work is worthy (chap. 10), every good work is nevertheless owed to God. How much more will this be established when we show that no good work is worthy of heavenly reward? I refrain from repeating those passages, and we shall test whether the Fathers incline to our opinion.

units.la: Sanctorum Patrum patrocinium, quo Argu- mentum superius confirmatur.
units.tr: The defence of the holy Fathers, by which the preceding argument is confirmed.
SECTION III.

units.la: SCriptura una (fateor enim) videtur nobis Obesse, sed duntaxat videtur; cui, primo in loco, satisfaciendum est, ut facilior & expeditior in reliquis differtatio nostra reperiatur. 2. Tim. 4. 8. Relicta est mihi corona justitia, quam reddet mihi justus Judex. Quem locum objecit Bellarminus, (supra, cap. 7. sect. 7.) indéque conclusit, Operibus bonis premium ex absoluta aequalitate justitiae esse red-dendum. Ubi accepit responsum ab Espencaeo; Deum quodammodo Debitorem dici, etsi non ob nostra merita, tamen ob promissa sua. Quam ille expositionem Scholasticam vocat. Deinde Augustini dicta refert; Justum est ut Deus reddat, quia debet: debet autem, quia promisit; ex gratia, licet non ex debito. Hæc singula concludunt pro justitia Promissionis; justitiam vero Condignitatis operum penitus excludunt. Et quasi doctrina haec non satis edoceri discive possit, alibi primo monitorem agit:{b} Nemo de operibus gloriatur, quia pro nostra conditione debemus obsequia, ut servi Domino, ut famuli Deo, ut subditi Potenti, ut mancipia Redemptori, &c. Hic homo debitor esse monstratur, non Deus; nisi ut promissor, debito fidelitatis duntaxat. Alibi etiam contra superiorem Pontificiorum assertionem arguit:{c} Tibi (inquit) tanquam debita redderetur corona, si ex te esset justitia cui deberetur. Denique expressissime contra eam concludit;{d} Fidelis Deus, qui se nobis debitorem fecit. Quo vero tandem modo? Dicito, obsecro, Sancte Pater. Non aliquid a nobis accipiendo, sed tanta nobis promittendo. Sic ille.
units.tr: I confess that one passage of Scripture seems to stand against us, but it only seems to. This must be answered first, so that the rest of my discussion may be easier and quicker. 2 Tim. 4. 8. A crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the righteous Judge shall give me. Bellarmine objected to this text (above, ch. 7, sect. 7) and concluded from it that good works must be rewarded from the absolute equality of justice. He received an answer from Espencaeus: God may in some sense be called a debtor, not on account of our merits, but on account of his promises. He calls this a Scholastic exposition. Then he cites the words of Augustine: It is just that God should render, because he owes; but he owes because he promised; it is from grace, though not from debt. All these statements argue for the justice of promise, and wholly exclude the justice of the condignity of works. As if this doctrine could not be taught or learned well enough, he elsewhere warns first: No one boasts of works, because by our condition we owe obedience, as servants to the Lord, as household servants to God, as subjects to a mighty one, as slaves to a Redeemer, etc. Here man is shown to be the debtor, not God, except as promiser, and only by the debt of fidelity. Elsewhere too he argues against the earlier assertion of the Papists: To you, he says, the crown would be rendered as something owed, if justice were from you, to which it would be owed. Finally he concludes most expressly against that view: Faithful is God, who has made himself a debtor to us. But in what way, pray? Tell me, I beg you, holy Father: Not by receiving anything from us, but by promising us such great things. Thus he.

units.la: Hactenus ex Patribus, non quòd non interdum dicant Deum debitorem esse, sed sensu minimè Papistico illo, quem Pontificii alii sunt commenti; sed nostro, id est, plane Orthodoxo & Catholico, quem nunc defendimus. dimus. Id quod ex Adversariis nostris, per-celebris notæ apud suos,{k} Stapletonus inge-nuè fatetur: Quotiescunque, inquit, legitur apud Patres, Deum esse debitorem vitæ æter-næ; intelligendum est, sibi, & quoad sua promis-sa; non autem nobis debitorem esse. A Patrum antiquorum consensu, quasi ἀ̓ [illegible, ~6 letters], ad Pontificiorum quorundam confessiones, ve-luti inferius conclave, descendamus.
units.tr: So far from the Fathers, not that they never sometimes call God a debtor, but in a sense by no means that Papistic one which some Papists have invented, and rather in our sense, that is, plainly Orthodox and Catholic, which we now defend. Stapleton, a writer very well known among his own people, frankly admits this against us: whenever it is read in the Fathers that God is a debtor of eternal life, it must be understood as to himself and with respect to his promises, and not that he is a debtor to us. From the consensus of the ancient Fathers, as it were [illegible], let us go down to the confessions of certain Papists, as to a room below.

units.la: Pontificiorum nonnullorum confessiones contra dogma de Deo debitore.
units.tr: Confessions of some Papists against the doctrine of God as debtor.
SECT. IV.

units.la: Stapletoni de Patrum dictis judicium opportunum & accommodum accepimus: ejus porrò sententiam propriam expectamus, in qua petimus, ut se verum Theologum præstet, & ex Divinis eloquiis sensum suum proferat. {1}Hunc sen-sum, inquit, Apostolus expressit.
units.tr: We have received Stapleton's judgment on the sayings of the Fathers as opportune and suitable; we look, moreover, for his own opinion, in which we ask that he show himself a true theologian and set forth his sense from the divine oracles. "This sense," he says, "the Apostle has expressed."

units.la: 2. Tim. 2. 12. SI SUSTINEBIMUS, ET CONRE-GNABIMUS: postea subdit, ILLE (Deus) FIDELIS EST, SEIPSUM NEGARE NON POTEST. Et ad Heb. 10. 23. TENEAMUS SPEI NOSTRÆ CONFESSIONEM INDECLINABILEM; FIDELIS ENIM EST QUI REPROMISIT. Hoc enim sensu Deus debitor est, sed sibi, non nobis; propter promissa sua, non propter dignitatem nostram aut operum nostrorum; quæ quamvis magna sit, tamen quanta quanta est, gratia est, à Deo est. Neque verò in idem recidunt hæc duo, DEUM ESSE SIBI DEBITOREM sensu prædicto, & DEUM NOBIS DEBITOREM ESSE: quia posterior hic sensus videtur ponere debitum meriti sine gratia, vel certè sine gratuita retri-butione; quod prior sensus non facit. Sic ille. Quâ quidem non poterat graviorem plagam causæ Pontificiæ infligere. Nam definitioni Meriti de condigno nihil esse potest repugnantius, quàm negare opera bona remunerationem consequi ex dignitate operum, in qua formalis ratio meriti de condigno omni-no consistit, ut ut Stapletonus sensum illum su-um novo glossemate molliat. Imò verò etiam de operibus, quatenus ex Gratia proficiscun-tur, Absit (inquit Faber Stapulensis) ut cogitemus ullum nobis à Deo esse debitum, qui servi inutiles sumus, faciendo quod debuimus: imò supra quàm inutiles, non faciendo etiam quod debuimus. (supra, cap. 8. sect. 6.) Quidni Lutheromastix ille {m}Pighius suum hîc interponat judicium? Hoc meriti genus, inquit, locum non habet inter Deum & homines, cùm illum nobis debitorem nullâ ratione possimus constituere: ut cujus est universum, & quod sumus, & quod facimus, & quod possumus. Sic ille. Objectionem hanc olim Schola urgebat, viz. Debitum esse ut merces rependa-tur. tur. Cui occurrebat Aquinas, afferens, Deum non effici nobis debitorem simpliciter, sed sibi ipsi, in quantum debitum est ut sua ordinatio impleatur. Deinde (teste {a} Vasque) Themistae recentiores concedere nolunt Deum esse nobis debitorem, sed sibi; quia debitum est obligatio quadam ad alterum, obligatio autem semper respicit eum ut superiorem cui quis est obligatus. Imò & {b} Cofterus Jesuita, ac si jam resipisceret, & ad mentem rediret saniorem, Non est, inquit, exacta ratio inter Deum & homines: & haec ratio est cur Deus nequeat proprie esse debitor. Idcirco {c} Andreas Vega in hac quaestione exigit à suis sobrietatem: Oportet, inquit, sobrie & religiose temperare sermones nostros, ut dicentes Deum debere nobis beatitudinem, indicemus hoc non esse ex dignitate operum nostrorum, sed ex Dei nimia misericordia. Ex his cuivis promptum & proclive erit à definitione Meriti de Condigno irrefragabiliter argumentari: quia Meritum de Condigno est opus, quod Condignitate suâ exigat à remunerante praemium, tanquam debitum. Quod quia non potest absque impietate de Deo affirmari, propterea nullum potest esse hominis Meritum de Condigno apud Deum.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 2. 12. IF WE ENDURE, WE SHALL ALSO REIGN; afterwards he adds, HE (God) IS FAITHFUL; HE CANNOT DENY HIMSELF. And Heb. 10. 23: LET US HOLD FAST THE CONFESSION OF OUR HOPE WITHOUT WAVERING; FOR HE IS FAITHFUL WHO PROMISED. In this sense God is a debtor, but to himself and not to us, on account of his promises, not on account of our worth or our works. Although these works are great, however great they are, they are grace and come from God. Nor do these two senses coincide: that God is a debtor to himself in the sense stated, and that God is a debtor to us. For the latter seems to posit a debt of merit without grace, or at least without gratuitous recompense, which the former sense does not do. Thus he. Yet he could not have inflicted a heavier blow on the Papist cause. For nothing can be more contrary to the definition of merit de condigno than to deny that good works obtain a reward from the worth of the works, which is wholly what the formal ground of merit de condigno consists in, however much Stapleton softens that sense with a new gloss. Indeed, even of works insofar as they proceed from Grace, Faber Stapulensis says: Far be it that we should think any debt is owed us by God, we who are unprofitable servants, doing what we ought; nay, more than unprofitable, not even doing what we ought. (above, ch. 8, sect. 6.) Why should that Luther-scourge Pighius not add his own judgement here? This kind of merit, he says, has no place between God and men, since we can in no way make him our debtor, as all things are his, both what we are, what we do, and what we are able to do. Thus he. The Schools once pressed this objection, namely: It is owed that the reward be repaid. Aquinas met it, asserting that God is not made our debtor simply, but to himself, insofar as it is owed that his own ordinance be fulfilled. Then (according to Vasquez) the more recent Thomists are unwilling to grant that God is our debtor, but his own, because a debt is a certain obligation to another, and an obligation always regards the one to whom one is bound as superior. Indeed Coster the Jesuit, as if he were now coming to his senses and returning to a saner mind, says: There is no exact reckoning between God and men, and this is why God cannot properly be a debtor. Therefore Andreas Vega in this question requires sobriety of his own people: We must temper our words soberly and reverently, so that in saying God owes us blessedness, we show that this is not from the worth of our works, but from God's great mercy. From these things it will be easy for anyone to argue irrefutably from the definition of merit de condigno: for merit de condigno is a work which by its own worth demands a reward from the rewarder as something owed. Since this cannot be affirmed of God without impiety, there can therefore be no merit of man de condigno before God.

units.la: Denique Scripturarum sensum supra ab Adversariis objectum, ex Scripturis aliis labefactari docebant Pontificii alii: exempli gratiâ; 1. Joan. 1. Si quis confitetur peccata sua, justus est Deus ut remittat peccata. Quæ-nam isthæc justitia est? Condignitatis in con-sitente? An fidelitatis in promittente? Effi-us Jesuita expediet: Justus hic Deus dicitur, inquit, non quòd pœnitenti, lege justitiâ, debe-atur peccati veniâ; sed quia servare fidem pars quædam justitia est. Sic ille. (supra, cap. 2. sect. 8.) Quæ est Pontificiorum omnium sen-tentia, æquè ac {q}Vegæ vestri: Non enim Deus, inquit, promisit pœnitentibus veniam, ut mer-cedem & præmium pœnitentiæ; noverat enim pœnitentiam non esse meritoriam tanti & tam excellentis beneficii: sed pollicitus est veniam, ut donum quoddam eximium & superexcedens omne omnium nostrorum operum pretium. Hæc Vega. Nec igitur dubium est, quin Bellar-mini, Suaris, & aliorum assertiones incum-bant in spongiam Borgiæ Jesuitæ, qui nu-meratur inter societatis Jesuiticæ primos decem: {r}Est (inquit ille) alius error in-signis, qui spirituales detinet viros; qui cùm sentiant in se paupertatis, obedientia, & caeterarum virtutum desiderium, in eo sibi placent, & quasi à debitore Deo petunt, ut sibi faveat; nec advertunt quanta Deo debeant, à quo hujusmodi desideria habuerant; nec intelligunt non sibi nova debere beneficia, sed pro acceptis nova se debere officia. Hæc ille. Sed quàm minimè spirituales dicendi sunt ii, quos error tam in-signis signis occupat, velut morbus Lymphaticus; quamquè sit hic morbus Meriti propriè dicti de Condigno apud Pontificios Doctores Epidemicus, & planè Sonticus, difficile dictu est.
units.tr: Finally, other Papists taught that the sense of Scripture objected by our opponents above is weakened by other Scriptures. For example, 1 John 1: If anyone confesses his sins, God is just to forgive them. What justice is this? Justice of worth in the one who confesses? Or justice of fidelity in the one who promises? The Jesuit Effius will explain: God is called just here, he says, not because forgiveness of sin is owed to the penitent by the justice of law, but because keeping faith is a certain part of justice. Thus he. (above, ch. 2, sect. 8.) This is the opinion of all the Papists, and equally of your Vega: For God did not promise forgiveness to the penitent as the wages and reward of repentance; for he knew that repentance is not meritorious of so great and so excellent a benefit; but he promised forgiveness as a certain singular gift, exceeding every price of all our works. Thus Vega. There is therefore no doubt that the assertions of Bellarmine, Suárez and others fall into the sponge of Borgia the Jesuit, who is counted among the first ten of the Jesuit Society: There is another notable error, he says, which holds spiritual men; who, since they feel in themselves a desire for poverty, obedience and the other virtues, take pleasure in this, and as if God were a debtor they ask him to favour them; nor do they notice how much they owe God, from whom they had such desires; nor do they understand that they do not owe new benefits to themselves, but that for benefits received they owe him new services. Thus he. But how far from spiritual those men are to be called whom so notable an error occupies, like a lymphatic disease, is hard to say, though this disease of merit properly so called, de condigno, is epidemic and plainly sickly among the Papist teachers.
CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Quintum nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno,ex parte Finis Secundarii, viz. vitæ æternæ, quatenus est Dei donum. Argumentatio.
units.tr: Our fifth argument against merit of condignity, taken from the side of the secondary end, namely eternal life, insofar as it is a gift of God. An argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: Nullum donum propriè est ex Merito de Condigno: sed æterna vita est Dei donum: ergò vita æterna non est ex Merito de Condigno.
units.tr: No gift comes properly from merit of condignity; but eternal life is a gift of God; therefore eternal life does not come from merit of condignity.

units.la: Major per se patet, quia donare est tantum liberalitatis. De Minore contenditur.
units.tr: The major premise is evident in itself, since to give belongs only to liberality. The minor is disputed.
From the Scriptures.
SECT. II.

units.la: Rom. 6. vers. ult. Stipendium peccati mors; gratia autem Dei est vita æterna, per Chrisitum[?] Dominum nostrum. Ratio nostra haec est: Si eadem essent ratio Meriti de Condigno bonorum ad [illegible, ~10 letters], quae est [?] ad aeternam mortem; Apostolus non ex destinato mutasset formulam loquendi, vocando mortem aeternam, stipendium peccati, vitam autem aeternam χάρισμα[?], Gratiam, vel Donum gratia. Hic pugio[?] in causa ipsius visceribus inhaeret. Interpretationem hujus loci Antiquitatis patrocinio permittamus.
units.tr: Rom. 6, last verse: The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life, through Christ Jesus our Lord. Our reasoning is this: if the reason of merit of condignity for good works were the same as for eternal death, the Apostle would not, by design, have changed the form of speech, calling death eternal wages of sin, but calling eternal life a gift [χάρισμα], grace, or a gift of grace. Here the dagger sticks in the very vitals of their cause. Let us allow the interpretation of this passage to rest on the support of antiquity.

units.la: Patrum antiquorum communis interpretatio Pontificiorum glossematis repugnans.
units.tr: The common interpretation of the ancient Fathers, opposed to the Papists' gloss.
SECTION III[?].

units.la: Sed dum hoc ostendere conamur, Adversarii nos interpellant interturbantque objectione illa[?] ex Augustino, qui, ne nobis nimis sit mora, audiendus primum, dein[?] concedendus[?] est nobis. Locus quem saepe ipsi piusque inculcant{1}, hic est: Vide (inquit) quam vigilanter Apostolus verba posuerit, STIPENDIUM PECCATI MORS. Quis non consequentum[?] & congruentissime addere iudicaret, STIPENDIUM JUSTITIÆ VITA ÆTERNA. Et verum est, sicut peccati merito redditur mors, ita merito justitia tanquam stipendium redditur vita aeterna. Haec ille. Ita, inquiet[?], & quidem verissime. Nam si eventum spectemus, aeque Deus bonos ac malos remuneremuneratur, non verò si causam adæquatam utrumque pœnitemus. De quâ paulò post.
units.tr: But while we try to show this, our opponents interrupt us and disturb us with that objection from Augustine. So that we are not delayed too long, let him be heard first and then granted to us. The passage they and their devotees often press is this: "See," he says, "how carefully the Apostle chose his words: THE WAGES OF SIN IS DEATH. Who would not judge it the consequent and most fitting thing to add, THE WAGES OF RIGHTEOUSNESS IS ETERNAL LIFE? And it is true: just as death is paid as the due reward of sin, so eternal life is paid as the wage of righteousness by merit." So far he. "Yes," they will say, and most truly. For if we look at the outcome, God rewards good and bad alike; but we do not weigh the adequate cause of each. We shall come to this a little later.

units.la: Pergit interim Augustinus, enarrans rationem cur Apostolus eandem formam non utrique adhibeat. Adversùs elationis[?] pestem, inquit Apostolus, STIPENDIUM PECCATI MORS. Recte STIPENDIUM, quia debetur, quia digne retribuitur, quia merito redditur. Deinde, ne justitia de humano se extolleret bono merito, sicut humanum meritum malum non dubitatur esse peccatum, non è contrario retulit[?], dicens, STIPENDIUM JUSTITIÆ VITA ÆTERNA: sed, GRATIA, inquit, DEI EST VITA ÆTERNA: & hoc, ne præter Mediatorem aliqua alia via quæreretur, adjecit, IN CHRISTO JESU DOMINO NOSTRO.—O humana non Justitia, sed nomine Justitia planè superbia!—Cui debetur vita æterna, vera justitia est; si autem vera, non ex te est, DESURSUM EST, A PATRE LUMINUM.—QUID ENIM HABES QUOD NON ACCEPISTI? Quapropter, ô homo, si accepturus es vitam æternam, justitia quidem stipendium est, sed tibi gratia est, cui gratia est: & ipsa justitia tibi autem tanquam debita redderetur, si ex te esset justitia cui deberetur. Hæc Sanctus Pa-ter. Sed verborum ejus cohærentiam quisquis accuratè expenderit, seniet[?] profectò Papisticum illud Meritum de Condigno protinus du-abus rationibus profligari.
units.tr: Augustine goes on, explaining why the Apostle does not use the same form for both. "Against the plague of pride," says the Apostle, "THE WAGES OF SIN IS DEATH." He rightly says WAGES, because it is owed, because it is justly repaid, because it is rendered as a due. Then, lest righteousness should exalt itself over a human good merit, since it is not doubted that human merit is evil sin, he did not answer in the opposite way, saying THE WAGES OF RIGHTEOUSNESS IS ETERNAL LIFE. Instead he said, "THE GRACE OF GOD IS ETERNAL LIFE, THROUGH CHRIST JESUS OUR LORD." He added this so that no other way apart from the Mediator should be sought. O human righteousness, which is not righteousness but, in name only, plainly pride! Whoever has eternal life due to him possesses true righteousness; but if it is true, it is not from you: IT IS FROM ABOVE, FROM THE FATHER OF LIGHTS. FOR WHAT HAVE YOU THAT YOU HAVE NOT RECEIVED? Therefore, O man, if you are to receive eternal life, righteousness is indeed the wage, but to you it is grace, to whom grace is given; and righteousness itself would be rendered to you as if it were owed, if righteousness were from you, to which eternal life would be due. So the Holy Father. But whoever weighs carefully the coherence of his words will surely see that the Papist doctrine of merit de condigno is at once overthrown on two grounds.

units.la: Agedum igitur, prodeat in medium portentum illud vestrum, scilicet Meritum de Condigno. Est (inquiunt, supra, cap. 2.) libera actio in aequalitate justitiæ consistens, cui ex condignitate operis vita æterna debetur apud Deum. Nunc S. Augustinum arbitrum ad-vocamus. I. Vocat ille quidem opera-tionem bonorum justitiam; sed justitiam quæ est Gratia Dei, quia non ex te. Secunda ex priori consequitur in hunc modum: Quam-vis vita æterna sit Stipendium, sed tibi Gratia est, inquit, cui tanquam debita redderetur, si ex te esset justitia cui deberetur. Tale igitur sti-pendium vocat vitam æternam, quam concludit non reddi operantibus ex debito; δὶς διὰ ταῦτ[?] diffidens à Merito de Condigno, cui (ex Pontificiorum definitione) vita æterna debetur, idque ex æqualitate justitia; à quo sensu Augustinus totus abhorruit. Propterea sub Sacramento juramenti liceret pio Lectori pronunciare, Augustinianum stipendium non red-di ex Merito de Condigno: Sed præcipuè, quòd alibi {*}Augustinus sese explicans ait, Cùm pos-sit [Apostolus] rectè dicere, STIPENDIUM AUTEM JUSTITIÆ EST VITA ÆTERNA, maluit dicere, GRATIA AUTEM DEI EST VITA ÆTERNA: ut intelligeremus Deum non pro meritis nostris nos ad vi-tam æternam, sed pro sua miseratione perducere. Cùm Pontificii, si suæ definitioni constare velint[?], Augustino ex diametro repugnantes, dicerent, Ut intelligeremus, Deum pro meritis nostris nos ad vitam aeternam, & non pro sua misericordia perducere. Quid multa? Nunquam negasset Augustinus ex justitia debere vitam aeternam, si cum Pontificiis credidisset, justum aeque mereri vitam aeternam, atque impius & sceleratus meretur, ut stipendium, aeternam mortem. Quanquam nec vox stipendium, si esset, necessario inferret Meri-tum de Congruo. Parum alii absque ulla tam de Condigno. Patres alii abique illa hæsitatione nobiscum iisdem ferè syllabis consonant, non modò mente consentiunt.
units.tr: Come now, let that monster of yours, the merit de condigno, step forward. "It is" (they say, above, chapter 2) "a free action consisting in equality of justice, to which eternal life is owed before God from the condignity of the work." Now let us call Augustine as arbiter. First, he indeed calls the operation of good works "righteousness," but a righteousness which is the grace of God, because it is not from you. The second point follows from the first in this way: although eternal life is a wage, yet, he says, it is grace to you, to whom it would be rendered as owed, if righteousness were from you and eternal life were due to it. So he calls eternal life a wage of such a kind, which he concludes is not given to those working as a debt; and for this reason he is at odds with the merit de condigno, to which (by the Papists' own definition) eternal life is owed, and that from equality of justice; from which sense Augustine wholly shrinks. Therefore a pious reader could swear, under the sanction of an oath, that Augustine's wage is not paid from merit de condigno. Above all, because elsewhere Augustine, explaining himself, says: "Although [the Apostle] could rightly say, BUT THE WAGES OF RIGHTEOUSNESS IS ETERNAL LIFE, he preferred to say, BUT THE GRACE OF GOD IS ETERNAL LIFE, so that we might understand that God leads us to eternal life not for our merits, but by his own mercy." If the Papists, to be consistent with their definition, were to say, diametrically opposed to Augustine, "so that we might understand that God leads us to eternal life for our merits and not by his mercy," what more is there to say? Augustine would never have denied that eternal life is owed from righteousness, if he had believed with the Papists that the just man merits eternal life as the wicked and criminal merits eternal death as his wage. Yet even the word "wage," if it were used, would not necessarily imply merit de congruo. The other Fathers, without that hesitation, agree with us in nearly the same words, and not merely in sense.

units.la: Quorum primus est {*}Origenes, qui indè intelligi docet, mortem æternam dici stipendium peccati, quia debitum; & vitam æternam non dici stipendium, sed donum, quia non debitum. Bene, inquit, Apostolus Metaphoram propositam servat, ut militantibus sub peccati Rege mortem dicat stipendium exolvi: Deum autem non erat dignum suis militibus stipendium, quasi debitum aliquod dare; sed donum & gratiam, quæ est vita æterna.
units.tr: The first of these is Origen, who teaches that from this it is to be understood that eternal death is called the wage of sin because it is owed, and eternal life is not called a wage but a gift, because it is not owed. "Well," he says, "the Apostle keeps the metaphor he has proposed, so that he says the wage is paid as death to those who serve under the king of sin. But it was not fitting for God to give his soldiers a wage, as if it were some debt; but a gift and grace, which is eternal life."

units.la: Secundus erit Chrysostomus, qui ex ratione mutati ordinis verborum observat, ideo vitam æternam non dici MERCEDEM, sed DONUM, quia DATA est, non DEBITA; sive hominis liberationem ante justificationem, sive, post illam, operum bonorum functionem consideremus: Apostolus de bonis verba faciens, non eundem ordinem servavit. Non enim dicit, MERCES BENEFA-CTORUM VESTRORUM VITA ÆTERNA, sed, DONUM DEI VITA ÆTERNA; ut ostenderet quod non propriis viribus liberati sitis, neque debitum, aut merces, aut laborum retributio; sed omnia illa ex Divino munere gratuito acceperitis.
units.tr: The second will be Chrysostom, who, from the reason for the changed order of the words, observes that eternal life is not called a REWARD but a GIFT, because it is GIVEN, not OWED. Whether we consider man's deliverance before justification, or, after it, the performance of good works: the Apostle, speaking of good things, did not keep the same order. For he does not say, THE REWARD OF YOUR BENEFACTIONS IS ETERNAL LIFE, but THE GIFT OF GOD IS ETERNAL LIFE; to show that you were freed not by your own strength, and that it is not a debt, nor a reward, nor a repayment of labours; but that you received all those things from the free gift of God.

units.la: Tertius est Hieronymus, qui mortem, ut stipendium peccati, opponi ita vult vitæ æternæ, ut dono Dei. Atque justitia Dei in improbis opponitur largitati & bonitati ejus erga pios. Peccatoribus dabit Deus juxta vias ipsorum, ut ille teneat judicii veritatem: caeterum in Sanctos excedit modum clementiæ. STIPENDIUM PECCATI MORS; quam recipit peccator juxta vias & opera sua: at justorum virtus fruitur Domini largitate, de qua Paulus loquitur, DONUM DEI EST VITA ÆTERNA.
units.tr: The third is Jerome, who wishes death, as the wage of sin, to be set against eternal life as the gift of God. And the justice of God toward the wicked is set against his largesse and goodness toward the godly. God will give to sinners according to their ways, so that he may hold to the truth of judgment; but toward the saints he exceeds the measure of clemency. THE WAGES OF SIN IS DEATH, which the sinner receives according to his ways and works; but the virtue of the just enjoys the Lord's largesse, of which Paul speaks: THE GIFT OF GOD IS ETERNAL LIFE.

units.la: Quartus est Theodoretus, qui antithesin supponit esse inter mortem, ut mercedem impiorum, & vitam æternam erga pios, ut donum: Quia peccatum olim regnavit, nunc autem tyrannidem exercet, Apostolus appellat STIPENDIA, [MERCEDEM] quæ est TESSERA MILITARIS, 1.Cor.9.7. Cum vero loquitur de vita æterna, quæ redditur justitiæ operibus, non dixit eam esse MERCEDEM, sed GRATIAM; est enim Dei donum vita æterna.
units.tr: The fourth is Theodoret, who supposes there is an antithesis between death, as the wage of the impious, and eternal life toward the godly, as a gift. "Because sin once reigned but now exercises tyranny, the Apostle calls [them] WAGES [MERCEDEM], which is the soldier's pay (1 Cor. 9.7). But when he speaks of eternal life, which is rendered to the works of righteousness, he did not call it a WAGE, but GRACE; for eternal life is the gift of God."

units.la: Quintus est Theophylactus: GRATIAM autem, non MERCEDEM, dixit à Deo futurum; perinde ac si dicat, Non enim laborum accipitis mercedem, sed per gratiam haec fiunt omnia, in Christo Iesu, qui haec operatur & factitas[?].
units.tr: The fifth is Theophylact: he said that GRACE, not WAGES, would come from God; as if he were saying, "For you do not receive the wage of your labours, but all these things are done through grace, in Christ Jesus, who works and effects these things."

units.la: Sextus, qui agmen claudit, Fulgentius: Cur verò mors STIPENDIUM, vita aeterna GRATIA DEI dicitur: nisi quia illa REDDITUR, haec DONATUR? Sic hi antiqui Patres; nec iis ex tota Antiquitate, quod sciam, Pater ullus adversatur, nè unus quidem. Qui si causam Protestantium consulto dissendere voluissent, non potuissent clarius aut distinctius sensum nostrum exprimere.
units.tr: The sixth, who closes the line, is Fulgentius: "Why then is death called the WAGES, and eternal life the GRACE OF GOD, unless because the former is PAID BACK and the latter is GIVEN?" Thus these ancient Fathers; and, so far as I know, no Father from the whole of antiquity opposes them, not even one. If the defenders of the Protestant cause had wished to deliberately agree, they could not have expressed our sense more clearly or distinctly.

units.la: Illustrissimus pro Ecclesia Romana, Co[illegible, ~45 letters]
units.tr: The most illustrious [defender] for the Roman Church, Co[illegible, ~45 letters]
Chapter XIII.

units.la: Sextum nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, rursus ex parte Finis Secundarii, nempe vitæ æternæ, quatenus est hæreditarium donum. Argumentatio. SECT. I.
units.tr: Sixth argument of ours against merit of condignity, again from the side of the secondary end, namely eternal life, as an inherited gift. Argument. SECT. I.

units.la: Cujus operis finis non est proprie merces, sed hæreditas, illud non est proprie Meritorium de Condigno apud Deum: sed boni operis finis (scilicet vita æterna) non est proprie merces, sed hæreditas: idcirco ipsum opus bonum non est proprie Meritorium de Condigno apud Deum. Adversarii, concessa Majore, ad Minorem respondent.
units.tr: Whose work's end is not properly reward, but inheritance, therefore it is not properly meritorious of condignity before God. But the end of a good work (namely eternal life) is not properly reward, but inheritance; hence the good work itself is not properly meritorious of condignity before God. The opponents, granting the major premise, reply to the minor.
State of the Question.

units.la: Bellarminus pro Ecclesia Romana, Certum est, inquit, Concil. Trident. sess. 6. cap. 16. docere vitam æternam filiis dari, per Christum misericorditer promissam, & simul mercedem bonis operibus fideliter ex Dei promissione missiem[?] missione reddendam. Et Can. 32. Opera illa Meritoria esse declarat, quae fiunt à justificatis per gratiam Dei, ut sunt viva Christi membra. Et alibi, Vita aeterna in Scripturis tam sepe, & fortasis sapius, dicitur MERCES, quàm HÆREDITAS. {4}Maldonatus verò plùs satis incalescens, in Protestantes invehitur: Nisi errore suo caeci essent, inquit, sanè intelligerent vitam aeternam dici MERCEDEM, quia Servis; HÆREDITATEM, quia Filiis data est. Sic ille; cui Jesuitae nimis familiaris est [illegible, ~4 letters] Sed ad rem. Nos dicimus vitam aeternam, respectu justorum, haereditatem proprie dici: mercedem verò non nisi impropriè & latè sumptam. Atque itâ mercedem dicimus, quatenus est tantùm praemium munificentiae, & remuneratio ex pacto, quae remuneratio est supra condignum: proprie verò & strictè ea Merces est, quae est condignitatis, & respondet definitioni Meriti de condigno, quam verè sentiunt Adversarii consistere in aequalitate justitiae & condignitate ad vitam aeternam. Secundùm priorem acceptionem nos admittimus & approbamus: alteram detestamur, quia tum Scripturarum autoritati, tum etiam doctrinae Antiquitatis Catholicae repugnat. Haec distinctio, si verè pateat, posset esse totius hujus controversiae absoluta decisio: patere verò eam vel maximè, subsequentes sectiones demonstrant.
units.tr: Bellarmine, for the Roman Church, says: "It is certain that the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 16, teaches that eternal life is mercifully promised to the children of God through Christ, and is also to be faithfully rendered as a reward for good works from God's promise." And canon 32 declares: "Those works are meritorious which are done by the justified through the grace of God, as they are living members of Christ." And elsewhere: "Eternal life is called in Scripture as often, and perhaps more often, REWARD than INHERITANCE." Maldonatus, however, grows rather heated and rails against the Protestants: "Unless they were blind through their own error," he says, "they would surely understand that eternal life is called REWARD, because it is given to servants; INHERITANCE, because it is given to sons." So he writes; the Jesuits are far too familiar with this sort of thing. But to the point. We say that eternal life, with respect to the just, is properly called inheritance, but reward only improperly and in a broad sense. And so we call it reward insofar as it is merely the prize of munificence and a remuneration arising from a covenant (a remuneration which is above condignity); but properly and strictly that is reward which is of condignity, and corresponds to the definition of merit of condignity, which our opponents truly hold consists in equality of justice and condignity to eternal life. In the former sense we admit and approve; the latter we detest, because it contradicts both the authority of Scripture and the doctrine of Catholic antiquity. This distinction, if it were truly evident, could be the absolute decision of this whole controversy; and that it is indeed evident, the following sections demonstrate.

units.la: Vitam aeternam esse Iustis absolutè hære- ditatem, probatur ex Scripturis.
units.tr: That eternal life is absolutely an inheritance to the just is proved from Scripture.
SECT. II.

units.la: Esse vitam æternam propriè hæreditatem pleno & unanimi consensu Adversarii nostri liberè largiuntur. Quid igitur nos in eo probando tempus & chartam frustra terimus[?] At nos eam absolutè hæreditatem esse statuimus: id est, ita, ut Christianismus ipse adoptionis filiatione totus nitatur. De qua filiatione si quæratur, Unde est: 1. Pet. 1. 3,4. Deus Pater nos regeneravit in hæreditatem. Si, Quomodo hæres fieri potest, cùm sit adhuc infans? Gal. 4. 1. Etiam[?], infans licèt, tamen Hæres. Si, quoad statum Gratiæ, Quatenus? Gal. 4. 1, 2. Quamvis sub tutoribus, tamen Dominus est omnium. Si, Quorsum?
units.tr: Our opponents freely grant, with full and unanimous consent, that eternal life is properly an inheritance. Why then do we waste time and paper in proving what is already conceded? We maintain, however, that it is an inheritance absolutely: that is, in such a way that Christianity itself rests wholly upon adoptive sonship. If someone asks about this sonship, Where is it found? 1 Pet. 1.3, 4: God the Father has begotten us again to an inheritance. If he asks, How can one be an heir while still an infant? Gal. 4.1: Though an infant, yet an heir. If he asks, In what respect, as to the state of grace? Gal. 4.1, 2: Although under guardians, yet he is lord of all. If he asks, To what end?

units.la: 1. Pet. 1. 14, & 15. Sicut filii obedientiæ, & in omni conversatione Sancti: & (si modò causa postulet) non solùm faciendo, sed & pariter patiendo; Rom. 8. 17. Si filii, etiam hæredes, & cohæredes cum Christo, si modò compatimur cum eo. Si denique quoad statum Gloriæ; Matth. 25. 34. Venite benedicti Patris mei, κληρονομήσατε[?], quod non est nudè Possidete, (ut Vulgata habet) sed Possidete hæreditatem. Quæ hæreditatis acceptatio quamvis cohærere possit cum mercede Munificentiæ, at cum mercede Commensurationis & Condignitatis nunquam potest profectò consistere.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1.14, 15: As obedient children, and holy in all conversation; and (if the cause should require it) not only by doing but equally by suffering. Rom. 8.17: If children, then heirs also, and joint-heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him. Finally, as to the state of glory: Matt. 25.34: Come, blessed of my Father, inherit (κληρονομήσατε), which does not simply mean Possess (as the Vulgate has it), but Possess the inheritance. Although this acceptance of an inheritance can cohere with a reward of bounty, it can certainly never agree with a reward of commensuration and condignity.

units.la: Vitam aeternam non proprie Mercedem posse dici simul & Haereditatem, ex Scripturis probatur.
units.tr: Eternal life cannot properly be called both a reward and an inheritance at the same time, as is proved from the Scriptures.
SECT. III.

units.la: NOn possumus non hanc {•}Bellarmini sententiam avidis, quod dicitur, ulnis amplectì: In Scripturis, inquit, Epist. ad Ephes. Coloss. & alibi, aeterna vita dicitur haereditas, quae proprie ad filios pertinet; non igitur est merces servorum, etiamsi annis mille servirent, sed propria portio filiorum. Haec ille; sed tamen respectu operum extra Gratiam, idcirco addit, quòd Necessaria est conditio ad Meritum vitae aeternae Regeneratio, & Adoptio filiorum. Cæterùm nos magis Scripturae credimus, quae hos duos titulos Filii & Servi distinguit, & plane distrahit atque dissolvit: Gal. 4. 7. Itaque jam non amplius es servus, sed filius: Ità ut nomen haereditatis Nativum sit, cùm aeternae vitae tribuitur, nomen autem mercedis, respectu prioris, Adventitium: ut in sectione praecedente ipsa Scripturarum loca declarant.
units.tr: We cannot but embrace, with eager arms, this opinion of Bellarmine, as the saying goes: "In the Scriptures," he says, "in the Epistle to the Ephesians, the Colossians and elsewhere, eternal life is called an inheritance, which properly belongs to sons; therefore it is not the wages of servants, even if they should serve for a thousand years, but the proper portion of sons." So he says. Yet he adds, with respect to works apart from grace, that "regeneration and the adoption of sons are a necessary condition for the merit of eternal life." But we rather believe Scripture, which distinguishes the two titles, sons and servants, and plainly separates and dissolves them: "Gal. 4. 7. So you are no longer a servant, but a son." Thus the name inheritance is native when eternal life is given, but the name wages, with respect to the former state, is adventitious, as the passages of Scripture themselves show in the preceding section.

units.la: Sancti Patres antiqui mercedis nomen improprie, hæreditatis verò, in statu Gratiæ, proprie sumptum esse crediderunt.
units.tr: The ancient Fathers believed that the name wages was used improperly, but the name inheritance, in the state of grace, was used properly.
SECT. IIII.

units.la: EX Apostolo, ad Rom. 6. 23. Stipendium peccati mors, vita autem æterna Gratia Dei est, Sancti Patres, Catholicæ veritatis Patroni, summo cum consensu affirmarunt, In hac comparatione vitam æternam Gratiam, & non Stipendium dici, ut nobis innotescat ingens esse discrimen inter remunerationem bonorum operum, ut χάρισμα[?], id est, donum gratiæ, & supplicium impiorum, ut est justum eorum stipendium: nec igitur hanc vocem æternæ vitæ proprie competere. Patres nec pauciores, nec inferiores fuerunt quàm hi quos designamus, Origenes, Chryso-stomus, Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, contra sensum Papisticum omnino: (de quo supra.) nunc alia Patrum suffragia adjungimus. Basilii: Vita æterna non secundùm debitum operum, sed juxta Dei munificentiam datur. Sic ille. (supra, cap. 11. sect. 3.) Quæ verba nostram superiorem distinctionem de mercede Liberalitatis seu Munificentia, & Condignitatis atque Æqualitatis manifestè confirmant. Pariter {r}Hilarii: Sed ad spem omne tempus est liberum, ut mercedem tedem non operis, sed misericordia, vindemia operarii consequerentur. Et rursus; {g}Merces quidem ex dono nulla est, quia debetur ex opere. {h}Marci Eremitæ Græcorum Patrum suorum vestigia prementis, cujus est hæc conclusio, Διὰ τοῦτο οὐχ ὡς μισθὸς ἔργων ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς χάρις δωρεὰ τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἡτοιμασμένη[?], id est, Idcirco Regnum cœlorum non est merces operum, sed gratia Domini servis fidelibus parata. {i}S. Bernardi: Dei sunt universa: Gratia gra-tis datur: etiam cùm emitur, gratis emitur; quia quod datur pro ea, nobis melius retinetur. Hactenus partem negativam absolvimus; viz. vitam æternam non dici proprie Mercedem: Ad affirmativam accingimur, de Hæreditate, ut intelligamus an hic Titulus illis arriserit magis.
units.tr: From the Apostle, Rom. 6. 23: The wages of sin is death, but eternal life is the grace of God. The holy Fathers, patrons of Catholic truth, affirmed with the greatest agreement that in this comparison eternal life is called grace and not wages. This makes it plain to us that there is a vast difference between the reward of good works, which is a gift (χάρισμα), that is, a gift of grace, and the punishment of the wicked, which is their just wages. Therefore this word "eternal life" does not properly belong to the reward. The Fathers were neither fewer nor lesser than those we name: Origen, Chrysostom, Jerome, Theodoret, and Theophylact, who are wholly against the Papist sense (of which above). Now we add other testimonies of the Fathers. Basil: Eternal life is given not according to the debt of works, but according to God's bounty. So he; see above, chap. 11, sect. 3. These words clearly confirm our earlier distinction between wages of liberality or bounty, and condignity and equality. Likewise Hilary: But for hope every time is free, so that they might obtain the reward not of work but of mercy, the vintage of the labourer. And again: Truly there is no wage from a gift, because it is owed from work. Mark the Hermit, following the footsteps of his Greek Fathers, whose conclusion is this: "Therefore the kingdom of heaven is not a wage of works, but a grace, a gift prepared for those who love" (Διὰ τοῦτο οὐχ ὡς μισθὸς ἔργων ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς χάρις δωρεὰ τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἡτοιμασμένη), that is, Therefore the kingdom of heaven is not the wage of works, but the grace of the Lord prepared for faithful servants. St. Bernard: All things are God's. Grace is given freely; even when it is bought, it is bought freely, because what is given for it is kept better for us. Thus far we have finished the negative part, namely that eternal life is not properly called a wage. We now turn to the affirmative, concerning inheritance, so that we may see whether this title has pleased them more.

units.la: Inter antiquissimos omnium Patrum Origenes ferè primum locum obtinuit: {k}Is, Posteaquam à spiritu servitutis, inquit, in spiritum adoptionis venerimus, nihil est timoris, id est, nihil propter pænam gerimus, sed propter amorem Patris. Et paulò pòst, Mercedem Servus expectat, hæreditatem Filius. Sic ille; opponens Servum & Filium invicem, tanquam quæ sint, si strictè sumantur, ἀσύνδετα[?]. Ejusdem hereditariæ proprietatis ἰδιότητος[?] ex eadem oppositione observavit {l}Ambrosius: Deus, inquit, ut promptiores nos faceret ad obediendum ei, ideo nos vocat Filios & Haredes futuros. Quam rursus proprietatem Theophylactus discerni docet, in istis Christi verbis, VENITE BENEDICTI PATRIS MEI, POSSIDETE REGNUM: Christus Sanctus vocat (inquit) BENEDICTOS, ut à Patre susceptos: haredes autem ipsos facit regni, ostendens quòd Deus eos participes faciet regni, ut filios suos. Non enim dixit ACCIPITE, sed POSSIDETE, ut paternam substantiam. Sic ille de filiis regni, id quod de proprié servis proprié affirmari posse sentiet opinor nemo. Quippe distinguit Theophylactus ius hereditarium possidendi, ab omni iure merito acquirendi illam paternam substantiam. Gregorium Nazianzenum ad hunc locum postremum distulimus, non quòd huic admirabili Theologo quicquam detractum velimus, sed ad autoritatem eius usquè adeò praeferendam, ut propter sententiae suae exquisitam & enucleatam expositionem, causae huius Moderatorem merito eum designare possimus. Hic distinguens eos, qui salutem consequuntur, in tres classes, viz. Δουλῶν[?], Μισθωτῶν[?], Υἱῶν[?], id est, Servorum, Mercenariorum, & Filiorum; Servos vocat Μικροψύχους[?], abiectis animis praditos; οἱ μόνον τὸ φυγεῖν[?] βάσανον[?], quibus praeclarum videtur poenam tantùm vitare: Mercenarios verò appellat μεγαλοψύχους[?], magnanimos, quibus propositum est ἡ τυχεῖν[?] ἀποδοῦναι[?] etiam ad mercedem aspirare: Filios denique dicit esse ὡς τέκνα[?], super utrosque. Deinde singulos ordines sigillatim monet: Si servus es, plagas metue: si mercenarius, mercedem damnaxat[?] expectas: si denique filius, patrem reverere, ac bonis operibus stude; quia bonum est Patri obtemperare, [illegible, ~18 letters] Etiamsi ex eo re nihil tibi quaestus redituram sit: quia hoc ipsum merces est, nempe, Patri obsequi. Sic ille, docens has classes distingui debere, non confundi. Adversarii vero, ne omni Patrum antiquorum praesidio destituti esse videantur, tanquam homines aquis submersi, scirpos, & quidvis vel umbratile arripiunt; sed frustra, nisi quòd hoc modo nobis molestiam creare satagunt.
units.tr: Among all the most ancient Fathers, Origen holds almost the first place. He says: After we have come from the spirit of bondage into the spirit of adoption, there is no fear; that is, we do not act out of punishment, but out of love for the Father. And a little later: The servant expects a wage, the son an inheritance. So he, setting servant and son against each other, as things which, if taken strictly, are not joined together (ἀσύνδετα). Ambrose, from the same opposition, observed the same property of inheritance (ἰδιότης): "God, he says, in order to make us more ready to obey him, therefore calls us sons and future heirs." Theophylact teaches that this same property is to be distinguished in Christ's words, COME, YE BLESSED OF MY FATHER, POSSESS THE KINGDOM: "Christ the Holy One calls them blessed," he says, "as received by the Father; but he makes them heirs of the kingdom, showing that God will make them partakers of the kingdom as his sons. For he did not say RECEIVE, but POSSESS, as the paternal substance." So he speaks of the sons of the kingdom; and I think no one will feel that what is said of sons can properly be said of servants. Indeed, Theophylact distinguishes the hereditary right of possessing from every right of acquiring that paternal substance by merit. We have deferred Gregory Nazianzen to the end of this passage, not because we wish to take anything from this admirable theologian, but to set his authority so high that, on account of the careful and clear exposition of his view, we may rightly name him the moderator of this cause. Dividing those who obtain salvation into three classes, namely servants (Δοῦλοι), hired men (Μισθωτοί), and sons (Υἱοί), that is, of servants, of hired men, and of sons, he calls the servants Μικροψύχους, of abject spirits, who think it an excellent thing only to flee punishment (οἱ μόνον τὸ φυγεῖν βάσανον). He calls the hired men μεγαλοψύχους, magnanimous, whose purpose is to attain even the reward (ἡ τυχεῖν ἀποδοῦναι). Finally he says the sons are as children (ὡς τέκνα), above both. Then he admonishes each order separately: If you are a servant, fear the blows; if a hired man, you look only for the wage; if finally a son, revere the Father and apply yourself to good works, because it is good to obey the Father [illegible]. Even if nothing of gain will come to you from it, because this very thing is the wage, namely, to obey the Father. So he teaches that these classes must be distinguished and not confused. As for the adversaries, lest they seem to be destitute of all the protection of the ancient Fathers, they snatch at reeds and at anything however shadowy, like men drowning in water; but in vain, except that in this way they labour to create trouble for us.

units.la: Objectio Adversariorum ex Patribus, Regnum coelorum ab iis dici VENALE, vehemens admodum, sed evanida. Sect. V.
units.tr: Objection of the adversaries from the Fathers, that the kingdom of heaven is called VENAL by them: very vehement, but vanishing. Sect. V.
