units.la: NON desistit Jesuita Vasquez nos quibusdam Patrum testimoniis premere, in quibus dicitur Coelum nobis proponi Venale: {•}Optimè (inquit) Jesuitae nostri Coloniensis docuerunt Coelum nobis proponi Venale, ea quòd meritis condigniis, tanquam pretio aequali, comparandum sit. Quam sententiam Kemnitius (hic unus ex Protestantibus) indignè tulit & refutavit, ut dignitatem meritorum nostrorum tolleret.—Caeterùm Jacobus Paiva nostrorum Jesuitarum sententiam confirmavit, & Kemnitii calumniam contudit ex Patribus: nam Clemens Alexandrinus in Paraenetico inquit, Pretiosissimam salutem emi pro thesauro, charitate & fide, ut justo pretio. Et Basilius, in Proverbiorum initium, Mercatores nos esse, ait, operibus possessionem cœlestem comparantes. Etiam Augustinus (Serm. 22. de verbis Apostoli) de Juda Iscariota ait, Avaritia te ad Indos misit ad deportandum aurum; ego tibi ante ostium posui Christum, à quo emeres Regnum cœlorum. Hæc ille; sed parciùs. Ergò Cardinalis Hosius intromittendus est; habet enim ille quod det, & quidem largiter; {†}Augustinus (inquit) in Psal. 93. Venale est Regnum cœlorum. Sed dices, Quantum valet? Pretium ipsius labor est.—Ambrosius de Helia & jejunio, cap. 20. Subsidia habemus, quibus peccata nostra redimamus: pecuniam habes, redime peccatum tuum: non venalis est Dominus, sed tu ipse venalis es.—Chrysost. in Epist. ad Philip. Serm. 15. Non dicimus pecuniâ emi Regnum cœlorum, sed voluntate:—Illam si habueris, potes per ara minuta duo emere Cœlum.—Gregorius Nazianzenus in orat. 18. ad cives; Pauco sanguine Regnum emitur cœlorum, & gloria sempiterna rebus temporariis.—Petrus Chrysologus, hom. 41. Amore pauperis Deus Deo regnum suum vendit.—Gregorius Pontisex, lib. Moral. 20. cap. 16. Apostoli relinquentes temporalia, gloriam potestatis aeterna mercati sunt.—Clemens Alexandrinus, in orat. hortatoria ad Gentes, Pretiosissima salus numismate charitatis emitur. Non dissimilia reperiuntur apud Ambrosium, Ephraem, & Caesarium. Has phrases Adversarii a Patribus operose coraferunt in defensionem sui Meriti de Condigno: Et sane nos, si quidem Regnum coeleste proprie meritis nostris venale sit, illud minime hereditarium esse fateri oportet. Huic objectioni solutionem triplicem adaptabimus.
units.tr: Jesuit Vasquez does not cease to press us with certain testimonies of the Fathers, in which the kingdom of heaven is said to be offered to us as something for sale. Our Jesuits of Cologne have taught very well, he says, that heaven is offered to us for sale, because it is to be bought by merits worthy of it, as by an equal price. Kemnitz (one of the Protestants) took this opinion badly, and refuted it, so that he might remove the dignity of our merits. Moreover, James Paiva, one of our Jesuits, confirmed this opinion and crushed Kemnitz's calumny from the Fathers: for Clement of Alexandria says in his Exhortation, that the most precious salvation is bought for the treasure of charity and faith, as at a just price. And Basil, at the beginning of his Proverbs, says that we are merchants, acquiring the heavenly possession by works. Augustine too (Sermon 22 on the words of the Apostle) says of Judas Iscariot: Avarice sent you to the Indies to carry gold; I have set Christ before your door, from whom you might have bought the kingdom of heaven. So he; but more sparingly. Therefore Cardinal Hosius must be brought in, for he has something to give, and that abundantly. Augustine (he says) on Psalm 93: The kingdom of heaven is for sale. But you will say, How much is it worth? Its price is labour. Ambrose, On Elijah and Fasting, chap. 20: We have helps by which we may redeem our sins: you have money, redeem your sin; the Lord is not for sale, but you yourself are for sale. Chrysostom, on the Epistle to the Philippians, Sermon 15: We do not say that the kingdom of heaven is bought with money, but with the will. If you have it, you can buy heaven with two small coins. Gregory Nazianzen, in his Oration 18 to the citizens: The kingdom of heaven is bought with a little blood, and eternal glory with temporal things. Peter Chrysologus, Homily 41: Through love for the poor, God sells his kingdom to God. Pope Gregory, Morals, book 20, chap. 16: The apostles, leaving temporal things, bought the glory of eternal power. Clement of Alexandria, in his Exhortation to the Gentiles: The most precious salvation is bought with the coin of charity. Not dissimilar phrases are found in Ambrose, Ephraem, and Caesarius. The adversaries laboriously gather these phrases from the Fathers in defence of their merit of condignity. Indeed, if the heavenly kingdom were really for sale to our merits, we must confess that it is by no means an inheritance. To this objection we shall fit a threefold solution.
SOLUTION I.

units.la: Explicando Adversariorum technam sophisticam, qua Lectores suos quasi pro ludibrio & deridiculo habent.
units.tr: Explaining the sophistical trickery of the Adversaries, by which they treat their readers as if for mockery and derision.
SECT. VI.

units.la: Mira haec est & misera Adversariorum sophisticario, quae res diversissimas confundit. Nam duo sunt genera Comparatorum: unum qualitatis, seu similitudinis: alterum quantitatis, sive aequalitatis, ut omnes norunt. Exemplum petam ab Evangelio, ut nobis quidem videtur, luculentissimum: Matth. 13. 45, 46. Regnum coelorum simile est homini negotiatori quaerenti pulchras margaritas; qui, inventa inventâ quâdam magni pretii margaritâ, abiens vendidit omnia quae habuit, & emit eam. Quae Parabola quid sibi velit, vestris Interpretibus explicandum permittemus: in primis vero Jesuitæ {*} Salmeroni in hunc Textum; Sensus ex Augustino est, Nos Christianos esse mercatores, & Christum margaritam: Margarita est Christus, Verbum caro factum; nos ipsos pro illa margarita damus, non quia tanti valeamus, sed quia plus dare non possumus. Hactenus Augustinus. Ergo, inquimus nos, Nihil minus intelligitur, quam pretium ex condigno collatum. Et {r} Am-brosius; Christianus negotiator maluit omnes quas habet seculi gemmas amittere, ut hanc unam emeret margaritam. Sic ille. Haec quoq; mercatura est ultra condignum, ni forte eo venerint vecordiae Adversarii, ut putent ex aequalitate justitiae se posse Christum ipsum promereri, qui est (ut praeterea Salmeron ibidem recte notat) Margarita, quae omnium lapidum pretiosorum proprietates in se habet. Nihil igitur planius esse potest, quam, Comparationem hanc de emptione, in se, qualitatis & similitudinis rationem continere: non autem quantitatis, condignitatis, commensurationis, & aequalitatis ullam.
units.tr: This is a strange and wretched sophistry of our opponents, which confuses things that are wholly different. There are two kinds of comparison: one of quality, or likeness, and the other of quantity, or equality, as everyone knows. Let me take an example from the Gospel, which seems to us most clear: Matt. 13:45, 46. The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls, who, having found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Let your interpreters explain what this parable means. Above all, let the Jesuit Salmeron be heard on this text: the sense, from Augustine, is that we Christians are the merchants and Christ is the pearl: "Christ is the pearl, the Word made flesh; we give ourselves for that pearl, not because we are worth so much, but because we cannot give more." So far Augustine. Therefore, we say, nothing is less understood than a price agreed on the basis of merit. And Ambrose: "The Christian merchant preferred to lose all the jewels of this world that he had, so that he might buy this one pearl." Thus he. This purchase, too, goes beyond merit, unless our opponents have reached such madness that they think they can merit Christ himself by an equal righteousness. Christ is (as Salmeron rightly notes in the same place) the Pearl, which has in itself the qualities of all precious stones. Nothing, therefore, can be plainer than that this comparison of buying contains a comparison of quality and likeness, and not at all of quantity, worthiness, commensurability and equality.

units.la: SOLUTIO II. Adversariorum Argumentum pro Condigno ex eadem similitudine emptionis, à Patribus ipsis confutari.
units.tr: SOLUTIO II. The opponents' argument for merit of condignity from the same likeness of buying, refuted by the Fathers themselves.
SECT. VII.

units.la: CHryfostomum Adversarii jam suprà ur-ferunt strenuè ex Serm. 15. in Epist. ad Philip. Sanctus ille Pater in loco allegato, in hunc modum animi sui sensum exprimens, Pretii, inquit, nè objicias inopiam: quanti potes, tanti eme. Habes denarium? eme cælum; non quòd venale sit cælum, sed quòd clemens est Dominus. Non habes denarium? da calicem aquæ frigidæ. Hæc ille. Ergò, Chrysostomo Moderatore, cælum non est venale: Sic enim ait, nempe proprie ex commensuratione æqualitatis, propter denarium, aut calicem aquæ frigidæ, sed ex gratia & acceptatione clementis Domini. Quid clarius? nec tamen puduit Adversarios hoc ejus testimonium, tam eorum placitis omnino repugnans, nobis objectare.
units.tr: Our opponents have already earlier pressed hard with Chrysostom, from his fifteenth sermon on the Epistle to the Philippians. That holy Father, in the place cited, expressing his mind in this way, says: Do not object to the price, saying that you are poor: buy it for as much as you can. Do you have a penny? Buy heaven; not because heaven is for sale, but because the Lord is merciful. Do you not have a penny? Give a cup of cold water. So he. Therefore, with Chrysostom as our guide, heaven is not for sale. For he says this, namely, that it is not bought by a commensurate equality, for a penny or a cup of cold water, but by the grace and acceptance of the merciful Lord. What could be clearer? Yet our opponents were not ashamed to throw this testimony at us, although it wholly contradicts their tenets.

units.la: Eodem planè ingenio, distorto omnino, nobis Ambrosium obtruserunt. Is vult poenitentem elecmosynâ peccata sua redimere, quæ est etiam phrasis vulgatæ editionis: quod ejus dictum pro Merito de Condigno adferunt, cum tamen ex Condigno nos posse veniam peccatorum mereri negent universi. Imò & Augustinum etiam sibi vendicant, qui, si viveret, religiosè juraret, hunc sibi sensum in mentem venisse nunquam. Dicit quidem, Venale est Regnum pretio laboris. An verò pretio æqualitatis & condignitatis? Ille ( capite sequente, sect. 3.) planè contrarium docebit, ubi, ut æquale sit præmium laboris, dicit, Vitam æternam (quod impossibile est) labore æterno esse comparandam.
units.tr: In exactly the same way, and with the same wholly distorted cleverness, they have thrust Ambrose upon us. He says that the penitent redeems his sins by almsgiving, which is also a phrase of the Vulgate edition. They bring this saying forward as support for merit of condignity, though all of us deny that by condign merit we can earn forgiveness of sins. Indeed they claim Augustine too for their side, though if he were alive he would solemnly swear that this sense never came into his mind. He does indeed say, The kingdom is for sale for the price of labour. But is it for the price of equality and condignity? In the following chapter (sect. 3) he will teach the very opposite, where, so that the reward may be equal to the labour, he says that eternal life (which is impossible) is to be obtained by eternal labour.

units.la: Si rursus de labore possibili quæstio sit, Quis potissimùm Regnum cœlorum promereatur; omnes uno ore opus martyrii præferent laboribus cæteris omnibus: quo tamen, tantùm abest, ut proprie empturi sint Regnum cœlorum, ex sententia Augustini; ut ipse affirmet, Martyris mortem pro Christo, priùs per Christi mortem emptam fuisse. (infrà cap. 15. sect.3.) Denique, de omni gratia, Bernardus: Gratia omnis, cùm emitur, gratis emitur. (supra, sect.4. hujus capitis.) Hactenus Patres. Optandum est igitur ut Adversarii ad mentem tandem redeant saniorem, & desinant Patrum ingeniosis elegantiis abuti, & eorum [illegible, ~8 letters], quasi [illegible, ~8 letters], obtrudere; ut lectoribus suis perniciosè imponant. Quod Solutio proxima clariùs ostendet. Interea constat, Adversarios adhuc, in objectandis Patribus, piscatos esse in aëre; & venatos in medio maris.
units.tr: If again the question concerns possible labour, namely, which labour above all earns the kingdom of heaven, all with one voice will put the work of martyrdom before all other labours. Yet they are so far from actually buying the kingdom of heaven by it, according to Augustine's view, that he himself affirms that the death of a martyr for Christ was itself first bought by the death of Christ (below, ch. 15, sect. 3). Finally, concerning all grace, Bernard says: All grace, when it is bought, is bought freely. (Above, sect. 4 of this chapter.) So far the Fathers. It is therefore to be wished that our opponents would at last come to a saner mind, and stop abusing the clever elegancies of the Fathers, and thrust upon us their [illegible, ~8 letters], as if [illegible, ~8 letters], so that they may wickedly deceive their readers. The following solution will show this more clearly. Meanwhile it is plain that our opponents, in bringing forward the Fathers, are still fishing in the air and hunting in the middle of the sea.

units.la: SOLUTIO III. Adversarios ipsos objectionem hanc, de Coelo venali, laevâ ac lasâ conscientiâ blaterâsse.
units.tr: SOLUTIO III. The adversaries themselves have babbled this objection about a purchasable heaven, with a corrupt and defiled conscience.
SECT. VIII.

units.la: Pontificii Doctores, quoties in has Patrum phrases incidunt, de emptione caeli, & Caelum venale esse, &c. statim eas urgent atque inculcant, tanquam luculentum Argumentum pro Merito de Condigno. In quo sese ostendunt esse versipelles egregios; quia saepe contrarium coguntur agnoscere. Nam cùm emptio & venditio, & omnis hujusmodi contractus, ex omnium confessione, pertinent ad justitiam Commutativam, quam ipsi negârunt intercedere inter nos & Deum; audent tamen has emptiones & venditiones nobis ex Patribus objicere.
units.tr: The Papist doctors, whenever they come upon these phrases of the Fathers about the purchase of heaven and heaven being for sale, etc., at once press them and drive them home as a striking argument for merit of condignity. In doing so they show themselves to be clever dodgers, because they are often forced to admit the opposite. For since buying and selling, and every contract of this kind, by the common agreement of all, belong to commutative justice, which they deny exists between us and God, they nevertheless dare to throw these purchases and sales in our faces from the Fathers.

units.la: Inter eos qui rei deprehenduntur extat Cardinalis {r}Hosius: Justitia inter contrahentes, id est, emptorem & venditorem, est Commutativa, quae respicit aequalitatem Arithmeticam, quae est quantitatis: quam si quis spectet, certum est, neque justum vel dignum esse, ut pro passionibus hujus temporis detur gloria aeterna; cùm inter passiones hujus temporis & praemium aeternum nulla sit aequalitas. Sic nunc ille contra Commutativam justitiam, qui tamen modò tot congessit Patrum testimonia, ad probandum, ex Merito de Condigno Cœlum venale esse, & vendibile, quod peculiare est justitia Commutativa.
units.tr: Among those who are caught in this fault stands Cardinal Hosius: Justice between contracting parties, that is buyer and seller, is commutative, which regards arithmetical equality, which belongs to quantity: if one considers this, it is certain that it is neither just nor fitting that eternal glory be given for the sufferings of this time, since between the sufferings of this time and the eternal reward there is no equality. So now he speaks against commutative justice, though he has just heaped up so many testimonies of the Fathers to prove from the merit of condignity that heaven is for sale and saleable, which is peculiar to commutative justice.

units.la: Huic Cardinali succedit & succinit Vasquez Jesuita; testimonia Patrum de emptione cœli urgit gnaviter, cum tamen sit hæc Commutativa justitia propria, quam ille pariter oppugnavit: dixit enim eam doctrinam a nullo hactenus ex antiquis Scholasticis traditam esse. (supra, cap. 5. sect. 2.) Libet hic aliam Adversariorum contradictionem notare.
units.tr: To this cardinal succeeds and echoes the Jesuit Vasquez, who presses the testimonies of the Fathers about the purchase of heaven vigorously, although this is commutative justice properly so called, which he likewise attacked. For he said that this doctrine has not hitherto been handed down by any of the ancient Schoolmen (above, chap. 5, sect. 2). It is worth noting here another contradiction among the adversaries.

units.la: Costerus Jesuita præclarè rem expedire se putamat[?], cum dicit, Cui hereditas datur in mercedem, est mercenarius & filius. Sic ille: Ubi utrumque vocabulum acceptione propriâ urget: quem ad Stapletonum mittimus, à quo rationem deposcat[?], cur ille Meritum juxta justitiam Commutativam obvenire negaverit. Ne bona opera servilia esse videantur. At nunc Adversarios suis propriis Argumentis (veluti laqueis) constrictos relinquemus. Properamus ad Argumentum, quod (prout nobis videtur) quasi terminis terminantibus causam concludat.
units.tr: The Jesuit Costerus thinks he has settled the matter neatly when he says: He to whom an inheritance is given as wages is a hired servant and a son. Thus he; where he presses each term in its proper sense. We send him to Stapleton, from whom he may demand a reason why Stapleton denied that merit comes by commutative justice, lest good works should appear to be servile. But now we shall leave the adversaries bound by their own arguments, as by snares. We hasten to the argument which (as it seems to us) concludes the cause, as with decisive terms.
CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Septimum nostrum Argumentum adversus Pontificiorum Meritum de Condigno, ex parte Præmii bonorum operum, quatenus est supra condignita- tem operis. Argumentatio.
units.tr: Our seventh argument against the Papists' Merit of Condignity, from the side of the reward of good works, in so far as it exceeds the condignity of the work. The argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: Cujus operis præmium est supra Condignum, illud opus non est proprie Meritorium de Condigno apud Deum: Sed cujuslibet operis boni præmium (quæ est vita æterna) est supra illius Condignum, seu Condignitatem: Idcirco nullum opus bonum est vitæ æternæ proprie Meritorium de Condigno apud Deum.
units.tr: Whatever work has a reward that is above its condign value is not properly meritorious of condign before God. But the reward of any good work, which is eternal life, is above that work's condign value or condignity. Therefore no good work merits eternal life properly, of condign, before God.

units.la: Propositio Major desumitur à loco oppositorum absolutorum: quia præmium esse Ex Condigno, & esse Supra Condignum (quod est Non ex Condigno) sunt ἀντίθετα[?] & contradictoria: Itâ ut Majoris consequentiam Vasquez Jesuita ingenuè concedat: Etenim si concedamus (inquit) nostra opera à Deo remunerari ultra ipsorum dignitatem, planè consequitur illam accessiaccessionem remunerationis nobis donari intuitu meritorum Christi, non autem intuitu solùm no-strorum operum. Scripturarum loca duo sunt, luculentissimis Patrum expositionibus illu-strata, in quibus insistemus.
units.tr: The major premise is drawn from the place of absolute opposites, because to be of condign and to be above condign (which is not of condign) are opposites [ἀντίθετα] and contradictories. Hence the Jesuit Vasquez freely concedes the consequence of the major premise: For if we grant, he says, that our works are rewarded by God beyond their own worth, it plainly follows that this additional reward is given to us on account of the merits of Christ, and not on account of our works alone. There are two passages of Scripture, illustrated by the clearest expositions of the Fathers, on which we will dwell.

units.la: Primus Scripturæ locus convincens Pontificiorum dogma falsitatis.
units.tr: The first passage of Scripture, which convicts the Papists' doctrine of falsehood.
SECT. II.

units.la: Rom. 8. 18. Non sunt condigne passiones hu-jus temporis gloriâ futurâ, quæ revelabitur in nobis. Hunc locum, quem nos planè Achil-leum esse duximus, {b}Bellarminus, levi quasi corporis sui declinatione, vitare se posse putat: Loquitur Apostolus, inquit, de substantia operum, non de proportione absoluta: nam passiones hujus temporis breves sunt, gloria autem æterna: tamen proportio est inter istas passiones & illam gloriam, propter charitatis dignitatem unde procedunt. Sic ille, adhuc crepans operum bonorum absolutam æqualitatem justitiæ apud Deum. De cujus objectionibus postea, sect. 4.
units.tr: Rom. 8. 18. "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." This passage, which we have judged to be truly our Achilles' heel, Bellarminus thinks he can avoid by a slight dodge of his body: "The Apostle speaks, he says, of the substance of works, not of absolute proportion. For the sufferings of this time are brief, but the glory is eternal. Yet there is a proportion between those sufferings and that glory, on account of the dignity of the charity from which they proceed." Thus he, still clamouring for an absolute equality of good works before God. I shall deal with his objections later, in section 4.

units.la: Nos verò tenemus atque defendimus ex hac Scriptura, Comparationem bonorum operum esse, non modò quoad substantiam actum, respectu brevitatis passionum, & vitæ æternitatis; sed etiam respectu cujuscunque proportionis quæ esse potest dignitatis operem ad excellentiam beatitudinis vitæ æter-næ, ut ex verbis immediatè præcedentibus li-quet: Non enim accepistis (inquit) spiritum servitutis, ad metum; sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba Pater. Quia ipse Spiritus testatur unà cum spiritibus nostris, quod esse filios Dei. Quòd si filii, etiam hæredes; hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes autem Christi; si modò simul cum eo compatimur, ut simul cum eo etiam conglorificemur: Nam statim addit, Non esse condignas passiones, &c. In quibus verbis habetis quicquid requiri potest ad operis boni dignitatem. 1. Vox est ἀξία, digna. 2. Quia agitur de operibus factis in statu Gratiæ, & ab iis in quibus Spiritus Sanctus est inhabitans, Accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, inquit. 3. Exprimitur etiam pa-ctum Dei: Si (inquit) compatimur, ut conglorificemur. Fatendum est igitur, illud, Non Condigna, &c. referri debere tam ad perso-narum quamlibet dignitatem, quàm ad operum sive actuum substantiam. In quo nos tamen nullam fidem nobis adhiberi cupimus, quam non sanctorum Patrum autoritas exigere & quasi imperare videatur.
units.tr: But from this Scripture we hold and maintain that there is a comparison of good works, not only as to the substance of the acts, in respect of the brevity of the sufferings and the eternity of life, but also in respect of whatever proportion of worthiness there can be between works and the excellence of the blessedness of eternal life. This is clear from the words immediately preceding: "For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit himself beareth witness with our spirits that we are the children of God. And if children, then heirs; heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ, if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together with him." For he immediately adds that "the sufferings are not worthy," and so on. In these words you have whatever can be required for the worthiness of a good work. (1) The word is ἀξία [axia], "worthy." (2) Because the matter concerns works done in the state of grace, and by those in whom the Holy Spirit dwells: "you have received the Spirit of adoption," he says. (3) The covenant of God is also expressed: "if we suffer, that we may be glorified together." It must therefore be granted that "not worthy," and so on, ought to be referred both to the worthiness of any persons and to the substance of the works or acts. In this we do not wish any faith to be placed in us that the authority of the holy Fathers does not seem to demand, or almost to command.

units.la: Sanctorum Patrum disertissima testimonia, quibus docent, opera insignissima (qua sunt passiones Sanctorum) non esse omnino condigna vitâ æternâ.
units.tr: The most explicit testimonies of the holy Fathers, in which they teach that the most remarkable works (which are the sufferings of the saints) are by no means worthy of eternal life.
SECT. III.

units.la: Disertissima ea esse diximus, quia non nisi de essentiali beatitudine loquuntur, & non tantùm Passionum, sed & Patientium di-gnitatem pensitant.
units.tr: We said they are most eloquent because they speak only of essential blessedness, and they weigh the worth not only of the sufferings but also of the sufferers.

units.la: Primus erit {*}Cyprianus: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES,&c. Cùm (nempe) beati erimus, dignatione Domini honorati. Sic ille. Ubi Dignatio Dei certissimè Patientium ipsorum dignitatem qualemcunque sub-indicat.
units.tr: The first will be Cyprian: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. For when we shall be blessed, we shall be honoured by the Lord's condescension. Thus he. Here the Lord's condescension certainly hints at some kind of worth in the sufferers themselves.

units.la: Secundus, {d}Athanasius: Nec universo orbi renunciantes, dignum aliquid habita-culis possu-mus[?] compensare cœlestibus. Loquitur generaliter de optimis omnibus operibus, & de quovis cœlesti habitaculo.
units.tr: The second, Athanasius: Nor, renouncing the whole world, can we offer anything worthy to the heavenly dwellings in return. He speaks generally of all the best works, and of any heavenly dwelling.

units.la: Tertius, {e}Ambrosius: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Pro Christo dicimur pati, cùm non illi, sed nobis proficiat, quod patimur: sed ille [Christus] quia quærit occasionem remunerandi nos, hoc præcipit. Ut profusus enim largitor, causam quærit quomodo donet indigno aut verecundus. Denique, ut ipsa exitia tolerari possint, ipse vires suggerit. Rursus idem
units.tr: The third, Ambrose: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. We are said to suffer for Christ, though what we suffer profits not him but us. But he [Christ], because he seeks an occasion to reward us, commands this. For a lavish giver seeks a reason how to give to the unworthy or the shameless. Finally, that they may be able to endure the very destructions, he himself supplies the strength. Again the same Ambrose:

units.la: {f}Ambrosius: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c: Non ergò secundùm merita nostra, sed secundùm misericordiam Dei cælestium decretorum in homines forma procedit. Hìc sanctus Pater Conclusionem nostram adstruit, Non secundùm merita nostra vitam æternam obtineri: quibus condignitatem nostram merendi ex æqualitate justitiæ (idque argumentis sex) pedibus quasi conterit atque conculcat. Primum est indignitas patientis, Quòd non Christo, sed sibi soli proficiat. Secundum, Quòd {n}[?]Pati illi præcipiatur, itâ ut sit opus Christo debitum. Tertium, Quòd remuneratio non ex debito, sed ex profusa largitione reddatur. Quartum, Quòd præmium conferatur, si strictè examinentur Sancti, in indignos. Quintum, Quòd in patiendo, non suâ, sed Dei virtute sustententur. Sextum, Quòd Deus, in dispensatione suâ judiciali, secundùm misericordiam agat.
units.tr: Ambrose: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc.: Therefore not according to our merits, but according to the mercy of God, the form of the heavenly decrees proceeds towards men. Here the holy Father establishes our conclusion, that eternal life is not obtained according to our merits. By these arguments (six of them) he, as it were, crushes and tramples underfoot our claim to a worthiness of merit arising from equality of justice. (1) The first is the unworthiness of the sufferer, that it benefits not Christ, but only himself. (2) The second, that he is commanded to suffer, so that the suffering becomes a work owed to Christ. (3) The third, that the reward is paid not as a debt but from lavish generosity. (4) The fourth, that the prize is conferred on the unworthy if the saints are strictly examined. (5) The fifth, that in suffering they are sustained not by their own, but by God's power. (6) The sixth, that God in his judicial dispensation acts according to mercy.

units.la: {s}Quartus, Hieronymus: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Nam revera nihil potest homo pati condignum gloriâ cælesti, etiamsi talis esset illa, qualis est modò vita. Quicquid enim passus fuerit à morte, plus non est, quàm etiam pro peccatis suis antea merebatur; nunc autem & peccata condonantur, & tunc vita æterna præstabitur. Duplici modo pungit & expurgat meritoriæ condignitatis vomicam, dum negat nos posse, per passiones martyrii, vel hujus vitæ beneficia promereri: nec hoc solùm, sed etiam monet, Martyres, dum patiuntur pro Christo, potiùs de demeritis suis cogitare; quasi qui passiones istas ipsi meruerint.
units.tr: The fourth, Jerome: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. For in truth man can suffer nothing worthy of heavenly glory, even if that glory were of the kind that life now is. For whatever he has suffered from death is no more than what he had already deserved for his sins; but now sins are forgiven, and then eternal life will be bestowed. In a twofold way he pricks and cleanses the abscess of meritorious worthiness, while he denies that we can earn, through the sufferings of martyrdom or the benefits of this life, anything at all. And not only this, but he also warns martyrs, while they suffer for Christ, to think rather about their own demerits, as if they had themselves merited these sufferings.

units.la: Sequitur quinto in loco {h}Chryfostomus: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ &c. subjunxit, SI QUIDEM SIMUL CUM EO COMPATIMUR, UT SIMUL CUM EO ETIAM CONGLORIFICEMUR. Quomodo enim non retribuet, cum viderit laborantes, taliaque patientes, qui tantis nos donis, dum nihil boni secisemus, cumulavit? Et paulò post; Vide quomodo certantium sensum deprimat, & erigat; quando enim ostendit laboribus præmia esse majora, & hortatur magis, & non permittit ut superbiendo sapiant; utpote qui vincantur coronarum retributione. Sic ille. At in patiendo pro Christo, superbia non oritur ab excellentia præmii; sed ex patientis opinione de condignitate sua. Rursus idem Chryfostomus aliam machinam adhibet, ad hanc Meriti condignitatem expugnandam. {i}Qui primum temporalia Dei beneficia, tam creationis, quàm conservationis perpendens, Etsi millies moriamur, inquit, etsi omnes virtutes animi expleamus, nihil dignum gerimus ad ea, quæ percepimus ab eo. Vide enim quomodo, cum in nullo ipse nostri indigeat, tamen cum non essemus esse nos fecit, &c. Deinde, spiritualia Dei beneficia pensitans, Multò magis, inquit, justus, qua per Christum futu-
units.tr: Fifth in order comes Chrysostom: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. He added, IF INDEED WE SUFFER WITH HIM, THAT WE MAY ALSO BE GLORIFIED WITH HIM. For how will he not repay, when he sees us labouring and enduring such things, he who heaped such gifts upon us when we had done nothing good? And a little after: See how he both lowers and raises the spirit of the contenders; for when he shows that the rewards are greater than the labours, he encourages more, and does not allow them to become wise in their own pride, since they are overcome by the reward of crowns. Thus he. But in suffering for Christ, pride does not arise from the excellence of the reward, but from the sufferer's opinion of his own worthiness. Again the same Chrysostom brings in another engine to overthrow this worthiness of merit. First, weighing God's temporal benefits, both of creation and of preservation, he says: Even if we die a thousand times, even if we fulfil all the virtues of the soul, we do nothing worthy in return for what we have received from him. For see how, though he has no need of us in anything, yet when we were not, he made us to be, etc. Then, weighing God's spiritual benefits, he says: Much more the just man, [in the] good things promised through Christ for the future
In Rom. 8. hom. 14.

units.la: {i} Chryfost. de compunctione cordis, circa medium lib.2. tura promittuntur bona, per horas singulas & momenta considerans, & immensum Dei beneficiorum pelagus attendens, dicebat, QVID RETRIBVAM DOMINO PRO OMNIBVS, &c. Sic ille. Observate, obsecro, Patris hujus sanctissimi, juxtà & doctissimi, Dialecticam. Si millies moriendo pro Christo, nullâ tamen virtute nostrâ beneficiis praeteritis nos digni judicandi simus; multò minùs digni censendi sumus futuris illis, quæ præterita excellunt non minùs, quàm immensorum bonorum pelagus vilium pugillum donorum, non obstante quantacunque virtutis nostræ æstimatione. Sic enim ait, Etsi omnes virtutes animi expleamus.
units.tr: Chrysostom, On compunction of heart, around the middle of book 2: ...considering the blessings hour by hour and moment by moment, and attending to the immense sea of God's benefits, he said, WHAT SHALL I RENDER TO THE LORD FOR ALL THINGS?, etc. Thus he. Observe, I beg you, the dialectic of this most holy and most learned Father. If, though we die a thousand times for Christ, we could nevertheless not be judged worthy, by any virtue of ours, for past benefits, much less are we to be judged worthy of those future things, which surpass the past no less than the immense sea of good things surpasses a handful of small gifts, however high an estimate of our virtue is made. For he says, Even if we fulfil all the virtues of the soul.

units.la: Sextus est{k} Autor operis imperfecti, scriptor sanè perantiquus: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Si ergò major erit gloria, quàm quod Sanctorum unusquisque meretur; quomodo aliis sufficiat ad salutem opus illorum, cùm nec sibi solis sufficiat ad gloriam justo juditio[?] consequendam? — Quid ergò dignum faciemus in hoc sæculo, ut participes Domini nostri in regnis cælestibus facti simus? Ideo dixit Apostolus, NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES, &c. Sic ille. Cujus consequentia est nostra conclusio, Non esse condignas passiones, &c. At est ejus ratio una ex nostris præmissis: non solùm quia remuneratio passionem excellat, sed quia nemo sufficiat sibi ad gloriam consequendam.
units.tr: The sixth is the author of the Opus Imperfectum, a writer certainly very ancient: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. If therefore the glory will be greater than what each of the saints merits, how will their work suffice for others' salvation, since it does not even suffice for themselves to obtain glory by the just judgment? — What then shall we do that is worthy in this age, that we may be made partakers of our Lord in the heavenly kingdoms? Therefore the Apostle said, THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. Thus he. His conclusion is our own conclusion, that the sufferings are not worthy. But his reason is one of our premises: not only because the reward exceeds the suffering, but because no one is sufficient for himself to obtain glory.

units.la: Septimus, {1}Eusebius Emissenus: Totis licet anima & corporis viribus desudemus, totis licet obedientia viribus exerceamur; nihil tamen condignum merito pro caelestibus bonis compensare & offerre valebimus. Sic ille. His verbis, ani-ma viribus, & obedientia, omne charitatis & fidei officium, & quicquid esse potest spiritualis dignitatis, comprehendit; & tamen Nihil condignum, &c.
units.tr: The seventh, Eusebius of Emesa: Though we labour with all the strength of soul and body, though we are exercised with all the strength of obedience, we shall nevertheless be unable to offer anything worthy as a recompense for heavenly goods. Thus he. By these words, strength of soul and obedience, he comprehends every office of love and faith, and whatever spiritual dignity there can be; and yet nothing worthy, etc.

units.la: Octavus, {m}Augustinus: Attendite: (inquit) quodammodo Deus proposuit venale regnum caelorum. Dicis illi, Quantum valet? Pretium ipsius labor est. Quantus labor est? Ego ostendo quanta sit illa requies, tu judica quanto labore emenda sit. Vitam aeternam habebis, requiem quae non habet finem. Quanto labore digna est requies, quae non habet finem? Si verum vis comparare, & verum judicare, aeterna requies aeterno labore recte emitur. Quia sempiterna requies est, aequa pretium: aeterno certe labore digna est aeterna requies comparari. Verum hoc est, sed noli timere, misericors Deus est. Hic pugio acutior est quam qui obtundi possit. Reperimus Vasquem & Jesuitas Colonienses serio jactitantes, Caelum esse venale; ut ostendant veram & propriam esse Condignitatis commensurationem meriti patientium cum praemio vitae aeternae: Noster tamen Patronus insignissimus Augustinus asserit, Si vita aeterna venalis esset, deberet aeterno aliquo labore labore emi. Cui cùm nos prorsus impares simus, propterea suadet, ut nos conjiciamus in sinum Divinæ misericordiæ. Item idem {n}Augustinus, Si per totam vitam, inquit, homo in laboribus, ærumnis, & tormentis esset; pauci sunt dies hujus vitæ ad regnum cœleste. Item alibi, {o}Si quotidie, inquit, oporteret tormenta perferre, si ipsam gehennam pro tempore tolerare, ut Christum videre digni essemus in gloria venientem; non erit dignum tanta pati, ut tanti boni participes habeamur. In hoc argumento singit apud se vir undiquaque sanctissimus, passionem extremorum malorum, Gehennam pro tempore tolerare, & hoc homini imponi sub pacto & conditione obtinendi gloriam futuram: Nihilominus aperte disertéque concludit, tam de patiente, quòd non dignus, quàm de patientis opere, quòd non sit dignum tanto bono.
units.tr: The eighth, Augustine: Attend, he says, God has, in a manner, put the kingdom of heaven up for sale. You say to him, How much is it worth? Its price is your labour. How great is the labour? I show you how great that rest is; you judge with how much labour it is to be bought. You will have eternal life, a rest that has no end. With how much labour is a rest that has no end worth purchasing? If you want to buy truly and judge truly, eternal rest is rightly bought with eternal labour. Because eternal rest is everlasting, its price is equal: eternal rest is surely worth acquiring with eternal labour. This is true, but do not be afraid; God is merciful. Here the dagger is too sharp to be blunted. We find Vasquez and the Jesuits of Cologne seriously boasting that heaven is for sale, in order to show that there is a true and proper commensurability of the worth of the sufferers' merit with the reward of eternal life. Yet our most distinguished Patron, Augustine, asserts: If eternal life were for sale, it would have to be bought with some eternal labour. Since we are wholly unequal to this, he therefore urges us to cast ourselves into the bosom of Divine mercy. Likewise the same Augustine: If, he says, through the whole of life a man were in labours, hardships, and torments, the days of this life would be few for the heavenly kingdom. Likewise elsewhere: If, he says, we ought to bear torments every day, if we ought to endure Gehenna itself for a time, that we might be worthy to see Christ coming in glory, it will not be worthy to suffer so much, that we might be partakers of so great a good. In this argument this man, most holy in every way, imagines to himself the suffering of extreme evils, enduring Gehenna for a time, and this imposed on man under a pact and condition of obtaining future glory. Nevertheless he openly and clearly concludes both that the sufferer is not worthy, and that the sufferer's work is not worthy of so great a good.

units.la: Nonus & decimus, (ut duos simul conjungam, præsertim tam [?]) Primasius & Isidorus Hispalensis. {p}Primasius : NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Quicquid enim pati sumus à morte, non plus est, quàm quod à peccatis nostris merebamur. Similiter & {q}Isidorus: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Non murmures, non dicas, Quare ista sustineo? sed, Non sum dignus; me minus percussum esse quàm merebar agnosco. Utrique penè verbatim superiori Hieronymi suffragio (suprà in hac sectione) consentientes. Quorum Pa-
units.tr: The ninth and tenth (I will join two together at once, especially since they are so alike): Primasius and Isidore of Seville. Primasius: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. For whatever we suffer from death is no more than what we merited from our sins. Likewise Isidore: THE SUFFERINGS ARE NOT WORTHY, etc. Do not murmur, do not say, Why do I bear these things? but say, I am not worthy; I recognise that I have been struck less than I deserved. Both agree almost word for word with the earlier testimony of Jerome (above in this section). Of these, the Fa-

units.la: {n} ... trum verba commentario nostro non egent. Nihil enim dici potuit adversus Meritum de Condigno vitæ æternæ ex æqualitate justitiæ, efficacius, nervosius, repugnantius.
units.tr: ...the words of these Fathers need no commentary from us. For nothing could be said against the merit of condignity of eternal life, from the equality of justice, more effectively, more forcefully, or more opposed to it.

units.la: Undecimus, {r}Fulgentius: Vita æterna non injustè GRATIA dicitur; quia non solum donis suis Deus dona sua reddit, sed quia tantum Gratia Divina retributionis exuberat, ut incomparabiliter atque ineffabiliter omne meritum, quamvis bona, & à Deo data, humana voluntatis atq;[?] operationis excedat. Sic ille, non tantum de actu bonorum operum, sed etiam expresse de merito & qualicunque eorum dignitate, responsis Papistarum repugnat.
units.tr: The eleventh is Fulgentius: Eternal life is not unjustly called grace; because God does not only repay his gifts with his gifts, but because divine grace so abounds in reward that it incomparably and inexpressibly exceeds every merit of human will and work, even though those works are good and given by God. Thus he writes, and he opposes the answers of the Papists not only regarding the act of good works, but also expressly regarding the merit and whatever worth they have.

units.la: Duodecimus, {s}Remigius: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Si quilibet hominum omnia præcepta Veteris & Novi Testamenti potuisset implere, (en utrumque pactum!) et omnia genera tormentorum perferre, (en nobilissimum Christianorum opus!) nequaquam esset dignus gloriâ futurâ, quam percepturi sunt electi. En! Patiens ipse, Martyr licet, vitâ tamen æternâ indignus judicatur.
units.tr: The twelfth is Remigius: NOT WORTHY TO BE COMPARED, &c. If any man could have fulfilled all the precepts of the Old and New Testaments (see, both covenants!) and endured every kind of torment (see, the most noble work of Christians!), he would by no means be worthy of the future glory which the elect are to receive. See! Even the one who suffers, though a martyr, is judged unworthy of eternal life.

units.la: Decimus tertius, {t}Bernardus: Quid sunt merita omnia ad tantam gloriam? Hem vobis vocabulum ipsum Merita, & quidem omnia, nullo excepto; in qua tamen voce operum vestrorum dignissimam dignitatem collocatis.
units.tr: The thirteenth is Bernard: What are all merits compared with so great a glory? Here you have the very word merits, and indeed all of them, with none excepted; yet in this word you place the most worthy dignity of your works.

units.la: Decimus quartus, {u}Anselmus: NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ, &c. Si quis pateretur (inquit)
units.tr: The fourteenth is Anselm: NOT WORTHY TO BE COMPARED, &c. If anyone should suffer (he says)

units.la: {r} Lib. 1. ad Monim. pag.19. omnes acerbitates hujus vitæ, non essent omnes passiones dignum meritû ad consecutionem gloriæ.
units.tr: Lib. 1. ad Monim. pag. 19. all the bitternesses of this life, they would not all be a passion worthy as merit for the attainment of glory.

units.la: Hæc sancti Patres exactè admodum. Eandem veritatem persequemur fusiùs, &c, quoad fieri potest, clarius, ubi de martyrio disseremus, infrà, cap. 18.
units.tr: These holy Fathers speak very exactly. We shall pursue this same truth more fully, &c., and as clearly as possible, when we discuss martyrdom, below, chapter 18.
Refutation of the adversaries' objections.
SECT. IV.

units.la: Prima obiectio. Cardinalis (ut probet Christianos, quamvis non ex suis operis, tamen ex ipsarum personarum dignitate, mereri vitam æternam) sic arguit; {*}Alioqui Christi passiones, quæ breviores erant pœnis damnatorum, quæ sunt æternæ, non propter personam suam dignitatem satisfecissent. Sic ille. Quo nihil concludi potest obtusius, aut fidei Christianæ, imò vel Bellarmino ipsi repugnantius. Primò enim immane quantum (quod ad merendi & satisfaciendi virtutem spectat) persona Christi à cujuslibet Christiani persona distat! Nam cùm Christi persona erat θεάνθρωπος[?], propter hypostaticam unionem Deitatis, ut & passio ejus θεανδρικὴ[?], non potuit ulla sanguinis ejus pretiosi vel guttula, per se, etiamsi ex justitiæ rigore, non sufficiens esse ad mille mundos redimendos; quia in eo habitat Deitas ipsa corporaliter. De Christianis verò, vel sanctissimis, (si cum Christo comparentur) Apostolus Joannes pronunciat, {*}De plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes gratiam pro gratia. Quid vero nostra guttula ad summam istam plenitudinem? Ne nimius sim; ad satisfaciendum objectioni Bellarmini,unicus sufficiet{7} Bellarminus. Verba ejus haec sunt, Non acceptat quidem Deus in veram satisfactionem pro peccato, nisi justitiam infinitam; quoniam peccatum ofsensa est infinita: sed satis est ad hoc, ut sit justitia persona infinita, qualis est Christus, Deus & homo; quo respectu infinita est, & in vera justitia rigore propitiatio fuit pro peccatis totius mundi. Sic ille. Jam vero Meritum semper est satisfactionis fundamentum, & non minus respicit infinitam Dei justitiam, quae infinitam justitiam nostram exigit. Fingant igitur Adversarii oportet novum Christum, & supositum aliud hypostaticę unionis, priusquam probare possint meri hominis cujusquam actum de condigno praemium ullum infinitum promereri.
units.tr: The first objection. The Cardinal, to prove that Christians merit eternal life, though not by their own works, yet by the dignity of their persons, argues thus: Otherwise Christ's sufferings, which were briefer than the punishments of the damned, which are eternal, would not have satisfied on account of his personal dignity. Thus he. Nothing can be concluded more dully, or more opposed to the Christian faith, even to Bellarmine himself. For first, how immensely the person of Christ differs from the person of any Christian, as far as the power of merit and satisfaction is concerned! For since the person of Christ was theanthropos [θεάνθρωπος], by reason of the hypostatic union with the Deity, and his passion was likewise theandric [θεανδρικὴ], not even a single drop of his precious blood could by itself be insufficient to redeem a thousand worlds, even by the strict rigour of justice, because in him dwells the Deity itself bodily. But concerning Christians, even the most holy, when they are compared with Christ, the Apostle John declares: Of his fulness have we all received, and grace for grace. But what is our little drop compared with that fulness? Not to be excessive: one witness, Bellarmine, will suffice to answer Bellarmine's objection. His words are these: "God does not accept as true satisfaction for sin anything but infinite justice, since the offence is infinite; but it is enough for this that the justice be of an infinite person, such as Christ, God and man; with respect to which it is infinite, and by the strict rigour of true justice it was a propitiation for the sins of the whole world." Thus he. Now merit is always the foundation of satisfaction, and it looks no less to the infinite justice of God, which demands infinite justice from us. Let our opponents therefore first invent a new Christ, and another subject of the hypostatic union, before they can prove that the act of any mere man de condigno merits any infinite reward.

units.la: Secunda objectio. Jesuitae duo (viz. {*}Vasquez & Eftius) aliter nobis, animo eodem, Argumento tamen diverso, ogganniunt: Inter impiorum peccatum & stipendium nemo (inquiunt) negabit esse condignitatem: At impiorum voluptates sunt momentanea & temporales; pœna tamen, & dolor, qui eis infligitur, est aeternus. Sic illi. Sophismatis hujus futilitas jam{*}supra explosa est:quia ingens est inter hosce discrimen: quandoquidem opera impiorum propriissimè sua sunt; at opera sanctorum charismata & dona Dei, quæ, ex gratia adoptionis, per Christi meritum Deo grata fiunt. Latam differentiam hanc enucleatè tradidit Apostolus Jacobus, cap.2.verf.13. ubi primò adversus impios, Iudicium, inquit, sine misericordia ei qui non fecerit misericordiam. Erga pios verò quid? Superexaltat misericordia judicium. Interpretem quæritis? En præsto vobis {a}Eftius: Impius non faciens misericordiam, inquit, experietur Deum justum judicem, secundum exactum rigorem justitia, eum punientem: At quoad electos misericordia dicitur [illegible, ~9 letters] exaltare & gloriari supra judicium, quia justi cum misericordia judicandi sunt. Hæc ille. Quid clarius? Quis igitur Adversariorum nostrorum pertinaciam pervicaciámque non merito fastidiat, pro Merito de Condigno tam importunè támque pertinaciter certantium?
units.tr: The second objection. Two Jesuits, Vasquez and Estius, viz. make the same point to us, with the same aim but a different argument: No one, they say, will deny that there is condignity between the sin and the wages of the wicked. But the pleasures of the wicked are momentary and temporal; the punishment, however, and the pain inflicted on them, is eternal. Thus they. The futility of this sophism has already been exploded above, because the difference between these is great. The works of the wicked are most properly their own, but the works of the saints are charismata and gifts of God, which, by the grace of adoption, become pleasing to God through the merit of Christ. The Apostle James set out this wide difference clearly, ch. 2, verse 13, where first he speaks against the wicked: Judgment without mercy to him who has not shown mercy. But what does he say of the godly? Mercy exalts itself above judgment. Do you want an interpreter? Here is Estius ready for you: The impious man who does not show mercy, he says, will experience God as a just judge, punishing him according to the exact rigour of justice. But as regards the elect, mercy is said [illegible] to exalt itself and glory over judgment, because the righteous are to be judged with mercy. Thus he. What could be clearer? Who, then, would not rightly loathe the obstinacy and stubbornness of our opponents, who contend so importunately and so persistently for merit de condigno?
CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Octavum nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, ex parte Dei remuneratis, quatenus bonum opus nihil ei prodest. Argumentatio. SECT. I.
units.tr: Our eighth argument against condign merit, taken from God's side as the rewarder, insofar as a good work profits him nothing. Argument. SECT. I.

units.la: Quicunque proprie meretur de Condigno, prodest aliquo modo etiam remuneratori ipsi: Sed nemo omnium, bonis su-is operibus, prodest ullo modo Deo remuneratori: Ergò nemo suis bonis operibus meretur aliquid de Condigno apud Deum.
units.tr: Whoever merits properly by condign merit benefits the rewarder himself in some way. But no one at all benefits God the rewarder in any way by his good works. Therefore no one merits anything by condign merit before God by his own good works.
The witness of the Scriptures.
SECT. II.

units.la: Scripturæ docent [?], neminem [?] benefaciendo Deum prævenire. Rom. 11. 35. Quis prior dedit, & retribuetur ei? Quem in locum {b}Toletus Jesuita eruditè admodum: Deus est qui prior benefecit: quicquid autem boni fecerit homo. homo erga Deum, posterius est;prius enim id boni acceperat à Deo, quàm aliquid boni exhiberet, qui dedit ut homines essemus: Deus ergò tribuit homini, non retribuit. Hæc ille. Ergò à priore nil Deo confert: An verò à posteriore? Tantundem: certè nè pilum quidem. Mi-ræ antiquitatis est hæc veritas. In libro Job, cap. 22. verf. 3. Quid prodest Deo, quòd justus es? & 35. 7. Si justè egeris, quid donabis ei, aut quid de manu tua accipiet? Uno verbo dicam. In Scripturis homo Deo gratias agere & benedicere millies dicitur, benefacere verò nunquam. Scholasticorum confessiones nihil moramur. Testimonia superiora sparsim disseminata hunc sensum præ se ferunt. An verò antiqui Patres præmissas nostras comprobent experiemur.
units.tr: The Scriptures teach [?] that no one [?] anticipates God by doing him a good turn. Rom. 11. 35. Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? On this passage Toletus the Jesuit writes quite learnedly: It is God who first does good; whatever good man does toward God comes afterward. For before man could offer any good, he had already received good from God, who gave that we should be men. God therefore bestows on man; he does not repay him. So he writes. Then nothing is conferred on God by the first, but is it by the second? Just as little: not even a hair. This truth is of very ancient standing. In the book of Job, ch. 22, v. 3: What profit is it to God that you are righteous? And 35. 7: If you act justly, what will you give him, or what will he receive from your hand? To put it in one word: in the Scriptures man is said a thousand times to give thanks and bless God, but never to do him a good turn. We need not linger over the confessions of the Schoolmen. The passages above, scattered here and there, show this sense on their face. Whether the ancient Fathers confirm what we have premised, we shall now see.
Judgments of the ancient Fathers.
SECT. III.

units.la: {c}TErtullianus, ut exprimeret illud minus nihilo esse, quod Deo conferimus, Precamur, inquit, SANCTIFICETUR NOMEN TUUM, non quòd deceat homines bene Deo optare, quasi sit & aliud de quo ei possit optari, aut laboret nisi optemus. Planè benedici Deum omni in loco & tempore condecet, ob debitam semper memoriam beneficiorum ejus: Sed & hoc be-nedictionis vice fungitur. Per Antonomasiam
units.tr: {c}Tertullian, to express that what we give to God is less than nothing, says: "We pray, he says, 'Hallowed be thy name', not because it befits men to wish well to God, as though there were something else that could be wished for him, or as though he labored unless we wished it. Certainly it is fitting that God be blessed in every place and time, on account of the constant remembrance of his benefits. But this also serves in place of a blessing." By antonomasia.

units.la: {d}Theologus dictus Gregorius Nazianzenus, Quamvis omnium facultatum tuarum, inquit, iacturam [largiendo] feceris, quamvis teipsum facultatibus adjunxeris, [nempe mortem pro Christo sustinendo] nunquam tamen Dei liberalitatem vinces. Rationem attexit, Τῶν γὰρ ὧν λα- [?] ζεῖν, τὸ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν δοῦναι[?] Quia donari Deo, est [à Deo] accipere. Sic ille. Tantum igitur abest, ut addamus aliquid Deo, ut potius ei debeamus ipsam donationem nostram, eámque tanquam acceptationem gratiæ interpretari.
units.tr: {d}Gregory Nazianzen, called the Theologian, says: "Although you have made a loss of all your possessions [by giving], although you have added yourself to your goods [namely by undergoing death for Christ], yet you will never outdo the liberality of God." He adds the reason: "Τῶν γὰρ ὧν λαμβάνειν, τὸ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν δοῦναι" ["For to give to God is to receive"], that is, to be given to God is to receive from God. Thus he. So far is it from the case that we add anything to God, that rather we owe him our very giving, and must interpret it as the acceptance of grace.

units.la: {e}Chryfostomus paulò expressiùs: Si aliquid offerre Deo volumus, quid amplius quàm gratias possumus? — Nullâ nostrarum rerum indiget, praeterquam verbis; hanc tamen ipsam in sermonibus gratiarum actionem exigit, non quòd ea ipse opus habeat, sed ut nos doceat gratos esse, & agnoscere tantorum bonorum suppeditatorem. Sic ille. Qui jam * suprà dixit, Cùm damus eleemosynam, Deus nos sibi obnoxios & obstrictos facit. Hominem autem ab homine, tantùm gratias agendo pro beneficiis, vel bonum quod agit accipiendo, nihilque quicquam benefactori conferendo, bene mereri, vix fando auditum est unquam.
units.tr: {e}Chrysostom says it more expressly: "If we wish to offer anything to God, what can we offer beyond thanks? He has need of none of our things, except words; yet he requires this very thanksgiving in our speeches, not because he has any need of it, but so that he may teach us to be grateful and to acknowledge the giver of such great goods." Thus he. The same man, who said above, "When we give alms, God makes us his debtors and bound to him." But that a man can merit well from a man merely by giving thanks for benefits, or by receiving the good that he does, and by conferring nothing at all on his benefactor, has scarcely ever been heard of.

units.la: His accedat (de quo diximus) aliorum Patrum consensus. {f}Basilii: Non debitor nobis Deus aliquid accipiendo. {g}Augustini: PRETIOSA IN CONSPECTU DOMINI MORS SANCTORUM: Emit eam sanguine, [Christus] quem prior effudit pro salute servorum, nè pro nomine Domini servi fundere dubitarent: quod tamen eorum, non Domini, utilitati proficeret. Hæc Augustinus de ipso martyrio, quod Ecclesia inter opera consummatissimæ virtutis semper habuit. Quod & {h}Prosper, Augustini quasi discipulus, non minùs religiosè notavit: Cum tamen servorum mors (inquit) servis prosit, non Domino. Ipsissima planè ratio, quâ usus est {i}Ambrosius, ubi exponit verba Apostoli, NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES HUJUS VITÆ GLORIA QUÆ REVELABITUR IN NOBIS: Quia pro parvis magnifica, pro temporalibus perpetua pramia pollicitus est. Pro Christo dicitur pati, cum non illi, sed sibi [martyr ]proficiat. Venerabilis {k}Bedæ, cum sæpe alibi, tum maximè in hoc Argumento veneranda est autoritas, qui in illa verba Christi, CUM OMNIA FECERITIS QUÆ PRÆCEPTA SUNT VOBIS, DICITE, SERVI INUTILES SUMUS; QUOD DEBUIMUS FACERE, FECIMUS, Inuti-les, inquit, quia Dominus bonorum vestrorum non indiget: si autem inutilis est qui fecit omnia, quid de eo dicendum, qui explere quæ præcepta sunt, aut infirmitate non potuit, vel, quod pejus est, superbiâ despexit?
units.tr: To these let there be added (as we have said) the agreement of the other Fathers. "Of Basil: God is not made our debtor by receiving anything." {g}"Of Augustine: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.' He bought it with the blood which he [Christ] first poured out for the salvation of his servants, lest they should hesitate to shed their blood for the name of the Lord; which, however, profited their advantage, not the Lord's." Augustine says this of martyrdom itself, which the Church has always counted among the works of the most perfect virtue. Prosper, as a kind of disciple of Augustine, noted this no less devoutly: "Yet the death of servants (he says) profits servants, not the Lord." Ambrose used exactly the same reasoning when he expounded the words of the Apostle, "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us": "Because for small things he has promised great rewards, and for temporal things eternal ones. A man is said to suffer for Christ, when it profits not him but the martyr himself." The venerable Bede, both often elsewhere and especially in this argument, is worthy of reverence. On those words of Christ, "When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do," he says: "Unprofitable, he says, because the Lord does not need your goods. But if he is unprofitable who has done all things, what is to be said of him who could not, through weakness, fulfil what is commanded, or, what is worse, despised it through pride?"

units.la: Utræque præmissæ nostræ ex hisce Patrum sententiis satis corroboratæ & stabilitæ sunt. Nosce teipsum, etiam apud Ethnicos habebatur vox oraculo digna. Discamus igitur & nos tandem sapere. Quid enim est, Conferre aliquid in gloriam Dei? Nempe id quod est, Candelæ splendorem soli fœnerari. Nè quis vestrûm me hoc fingere dicat, {1}Toletum ve-strum consulat, oro: Deus (inquit) hominem, & homo Deum clarificat, seu glorificat; at multo aliter: nam Deus glorificat hominem ei beneficia conferendo, & bona, quibus efficitur homo gloriosus: at homo nihil potest offerre Deo boni; sed glorificat Deum, cùm præclaram habeat notitiam Dei, & manifestum facit eis qui ignorant. Hæc ille. Addo: In eo quòd istæc no-stra glorificatio grata sit Deo, ejus solius gratiæ debetur. Quid porrò? Nostrum quod di-citur Meritum de Congruo, quandoquidem non proficit Deo, non potest non esse ei contumeliosum: id quod nunc exactius confirmare conamur.
units.tr: Both of our premises are sufficiently confirmed and established by these sentiments of the Fathers. "Know yourself" was regarded as a saying worthy of an oracle even among the heathen. Let us therefore learn at last to be wise. For what is it to confer something to the glory of God? Namely, it is to lend the light of a candle to the sun. Lest any of you say that I am making this up, I beg you consult your Toletus: "God glorifies man, and man glorifies God, but in a very different way: for God glorifies man by conferring benefits on him and goods by which man is made glorious; but man can offer God nothing good, yet glorifies God when he has a clear knowledge of God and makes it manifest to those who are ignorant." Thus he. I add: that this our glorifying is pleasing to God is owed to his grace alone. What then? "Our so-called merit of congruity, since it does not profit God, cannot but be offensive to him": which we now try to confirm more exactly.

units.la: CAP. XVI. Nonum nostrum Argumentum adversus Me- ritum de Condigno, ex comparatione Meritorum inter homines invicem.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI. Our ninth argument against the merit of condignity, drawn from the comparison of merits among men with one another.
The argument. SECT. I.

units.la: QUod, cùm homini offertur, necessariò contumeliosum est, id si Deo offeratur non potest non esse profanum: Sed apud hominem amplissimè de nobis merentem, Meritum nostrum de Condigno venditare, non potest non esse ei contumeliosum: Ergò, id apud Deum facere, profanum sit, necesse est. Argumentum hoc Divinum, Catholicum, Ethicum seu Morale, nec non lumine naturali Ethnicum, & tandem omnino convincens esse facilè probabimus.
units.tr: Whatever is necessarily insulting when offered to a man, cannot fail to be profane if it is offered to God. But to boast of our merit of condignity before a man who has deserved most highly of us cannot fail to be insulting to him. Therefore it must be profane to do this before God. We shall easily prove that this argument is divine, catholic, ethical or moral, and also heathen by the light of nature, and finally wholly convincing.

units.la: I. Argumentum superius Divinum esse Scriptura sacra demonstrant.
units.tr: I. That the foregoing argument is divine the holy Scriptures demonstrate.
SECT. II.

units.la: LOca Scripturarum plurima sunt: nos delectum fecimus, duobus duntaxat contenti: quorum unus ex Vetere Testamento, alter est ex Novo depromptus.
units.tr: There are very many passages of Scripture. We have made a selection, content with only two, one taken from the Old Testament and the other from the New.

units.la: In Veteri, scil. Malach. 1. postquam Propheta acriter invectus esset in nefariam eorum profanationem, qui, retentis apud se animalibus sanis & integris, non nisi languida, marcida, & maculosa in sacrificium Deo offerebant, illos Dei nomine exprobrat, Nónne hoc malum? Offer illud duci tuo, si placuerit ei, aut si susceperit faciem tuam, dicit Dominus exercituum. Si quis Pontificiorum fortasse hujus Argumenti vim non satis assequitur, consulat Jesuitam {m}Riberam: Propheta argumentum est (inquit) à majori ad minus; quasi dixerit, Non audebis tu hac offerre duci tuo, & tamen mihi [Deo tuo] offerre audebis? Sic ille. Summa itaque impietas est, non exhorrescere tantum contemptum & contumeliam Deo immortali inferre, quantum mortali duci imponere virum probum & modestum prorsus dispuderet.
units.tr: In the Old, namely Malachi 1, after the prophet had sharply inveighed against the wicked profanation of those who, keeping back sound and whole animals for themselves, offered to God only lame, sickly and blemished ones for sacrifice, he rebukes them in God's name: Is it not evil? Offer it to your governor; will he be pleased with you, or will he accept your person? says the LORD of hosts. If any of the Papists perhaps does not sufficiently grasp the force of this argument, let him consult the Jesuit Ribera: The prophet's argument (he says) is from the greater to the less; as if he had said, Would you not dare to offer this to your prince, and yet will you dare to offer it to me [your God]? Thus he. It is therefore the height of impiety not to shudder at bringing as much contempt and insult upon the immortal God as an honest and modest man would be utterly ashamed to impose on a mortal prince.

units.la: Alterum ex Evangelio exhausimus, viz. Luc. 17. 7. Quis vestrum habens servum arantem, cui regresso ex agro dicat statim, Prodi & recumbet[?] imò nonne dicet, Ministra mihi usque dum edero & bibero, & postea edito tu & bibe? Num gratiam habet servo illi, quia fecit quae ipse praecepit facere? Non puto. Sic vos, cum omnia feceritis, dicite, Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Ubi Christus (ut & nos) Argumentum sumit, quod Ad hominem dicitur in Scholis: quasi constituere velle homines ipsos sibi judices, Quis, inquit, vestrum? Deinde, servi cujuslibet ingenium quale esse debeat (si verum fateri velit) innuit, dicens, Quod debui feci, scilicet, arando, ministrando, & alia servi munera obeundo, prout Dominus mihi in mandatis dederit: quae officia licet grata sint Domino, ego tamen ingratus, si mihi ab eo hanc vel gratitudinis gratiam deberi existimem. Nunquid (inquit) gratiam servo illi habebit? Non puto.
units.tr: We have drawn the other from the Gospel, namely Luke 17:7. Which of you, having a servant plowing or keeping sheep, will say to him by and by, when he is come from the field, Go and sit down to meat? And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me, till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink? Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I trow not. So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do. Here Christ (as we also do) takes up an argument which in the schools is called ad hominem, as if he wished men themselves to be their own judges: Which of you, he says? Then he hints at what the disposition of any servant ought to be, if he is willing to speak the truth, saying, I have done what I ought to do, namely, by plowing, serving, and performing the other duties of a servant, as the Lord has commanded me. Although these services may be pleasing to the Lord, I would still be ungrateful if I thought that any thanks or gratitude were owed to me from him. Will he (says he) have thanks of that servant? I trow not.
2. That the same argument is plainly catholic, the Fathers will show.
SECT. III.

units.la: Quanquam quid Patres dixi; quasi in re tam explorata operae pretium sit in multorum Patrum testimonia operosius inquirere, cum unus Chrysostomus instar universorum esse possit, praesertim in ea sententia, cui nemo refragari velit? Ille igitur in illa verba Christi, Matth. 7. 11. Si vos, cum sitis mali, nostis[?] bona dare filiis vestris, &c. filiorum officium erga parentes suaviter edocens, {n}Gratias[?] agamus Deo, inquit: plus enim nos, quam liberi a parentibus amantur, amat. Quantum enim dissimilitudinis est inter malitiam & bonitatem, tantum est inter dilectionem Dei & parentum nostrorum. quorum unus ex Veteri Testamento, alter est ex Novo depromptus.
units.tr: Yet why do I speak of the Fathers? As if, in a matter so well established, it were worth the trouble to search out at great length the testimonies of many Fathers, since Chrysostom alone may stand for all of them, especially on a point which no one would wish to gainsay. He, then, on those words of Christ, Matth. 7. 11, "If you, being evil, know how to give good things to your children," etc., gently teaching the duty of children towards their parents, says: "Let us give thanks to God; for he loves us more than children are loved by their parents. For as great as the difference is between malice and goodness, so great is the difference between the love of God and of our parents." Of these, one is drawn from the Old Testament, the other from the New.

units.la: In Veteri, scil. Malach. 1. postquam Propheta acriter invectus effet in nefariam eorum profanationem, qui, retentis apud se animali-bus sanis & integris, non nisi languida, marci-da, & maculosa in sacrificium Deo offerebant, illos Dei nomine exprobrat, Nonne hoc malum? Offer illud duci tuo, si placuerit ei, aut si susceperit faciem tuam, dicit Dominus exercituum. Si quis Pontificiorum fortasse hujus Argumenti vim non satis assequitur, consu-lat Jesuitam {m}Riberam: Propheta argumentum est (inquit) a majori ad minus; quasi dixerit, Non audebis tu hac[?] offerre duci tuo, & tamen mihi [Deo tuo] offerre audebis? Sic ille. Summa itaque impietas est, non exhorrescere tantum contemptum & contumeliam Deo immortali inferre, quantum mortali duci imponere virum probum & modestum prorsus dispuderet.
units.tr: In the Old, namely Malachi 1, after the prophet had sharply inveighed against the wicked profanation of those who, keeping back what was sound and whole for themselves, offered to God only the sick, wasted and blemished animals in sacrifice, he rebukes them in God's name: "Is not this evil? Offer it to your governor; will he be pleased with you, or will he accept your face? says the Lord of hosts." If any of the Papists perhaps does not sufficiently grasp the force of this argument, let him consult the Jesuit Ribera: "The prophet's argument is (he says) from the greater to the less; as if he had said, Would you not dare to offer this to your prince, and yet you will dare to offer it to me, your God?" Thus he. The greatest impiety, therefore, is not to shudder at heaping such contempt and insult upon the immortal God, when an honest and modest man would utterly disdain to put it upon a mortal prince.

units.la: Alterum ex Evangelio exhausimus, viz. Luc. 17. 7. Quis vestrum habens servum arantem, cui regresso ex agro dicat statim, Prodi & recumbe[?] imò nonne dicet, Ministra mihi, dum edero & bibero; & postea edito tu & bibe? Num gratiam habet servo illi, quia fecit quae ipse praecepit facere? Non puto. Sic vos, cùm omnia feceritis, dicite, Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Ubi Christus (ut & nos) Argumentum sumit, quod Ad hominem dicitur in Scholis: quasi constituere vellet homines ipsos sibi judices, Quis, inquit, vestrum? Deinde, servi cujuslibet ingenium quale esse debeat (si verum fateri velit) innuit, dicens, Quod debui feci, scilicet, arando, ministrando [?], & alia servi munera obeundo, prout Dominus mihi in mandatis dederit: quæ officia licèt grata sint Domino, ego tamen ingratus, si mihi ab eo hanc vel gratitudinis gratiam deberi existimem. Nunquid (inquit) gratiam servo illi habebit? Non puto.
units.tr: The other we have drawn from the Gospel, namely Luke 17. 7: "Which of you, having a servant ploughing, or tending sheep, will say to him when he comes in from the field, 'Come at once and sit down to eat'? Will he not rather say to him, 'Prepare my supper, and gird yourself and serve me while I eat and drink; afterwards you shall eat and drink'? Does he thank that servant because he did what he was commanded? I think not. So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, 'We are unprofitable servants; we have done only what we ought to do.'" Here Christ (as we also do) uses the argument which in the schools is called ad hominem, as if he wished to make men themselves the judges: "Which of you," he says. Then he indicates what the disposition of any servant ought to be, if he is willing to speak the truth: "I did what I ought, namely plough, serve and perform the other duties of a servant, as the Lord has commanded me. Although these duties are pleasing to the Lord, I would be ungrateful if I thought that he owed me any thanks or favour for them." "Will he have thanks for that servant? (he says.) I think not."
2. That the same argument is plainly Catholic, the Fathers will teach.
SECT. III.

units.la: QUanquam quid Patres dixi; quasi in re tam explorata operæ pretium sit in multorum Patrum testimonia operosius inquirere, cùm unus Chrysostomus instar universorum esse possit, præsertim in ea sententia, cui nemo refragari velit? Ille igitur in illa verba Christi, Matth. 7. II. Si vos, cùm sitis mali, nostis [?] bona dare filiis vestris, &c. filiorum officium erga parentes suaviter edocens, {n}Gratias agamus Deo, inquit; plus enim nos, quàm liberi à parentibus amantur, amat. Quantum enim distantia [?] est inter malitiam & bonitatem, tantum est inter dilectionem Dei & parentum nostrorum. nostrorum. Sic ille. Quisquámne verò filius bonæ indolis, paternam hæreditatem ob aliquod officium suum præstitum promeruisse jactitet? Utut verò hoc possibile fuerit, obtendere tamen Meritum de Condigno ex æqualitate justitiæ apud Deum, inter quem & parentes nostros Christianissimos nulla major esse potest proportio amoris & lenitatis, quàm est (ut Chrysostomus loquitur) inter malitiam & bonitatem; non sani esse hominis, nemo sanus dubitabit.
units.tr: Yet why speak of the Fathers? As if, in a matter so well established, it were worth the trouble to search out at great length the testimonies of many Fathers, when Chrysostom alone may stand for all of them, especially on a point which no one would wish to contradict? He, teaching sweetly the duty of children towards their parents, comments on those words of Christ, If you, being evil, know how to give good things to your children, etc. (Matth. 7. 11), and says: Let us give thanks to God; for he loves us more than children are loved by their parents. For as great as the distance is between wickedness and goodness, so great is the distance between the love of God and that of our parents. Thus he. But what son of good disposition would boast that he had earned his paternal inheritance by some service of his own? Yet however that may be possible, to put forward merit of condignity from equality of justice before God, between whom and our most Christian parents there can be no greater proportion of love and kindness than there is (as Chrysostom puts it) between wickedness and goodness, is the mark of no sound mind, as no sane person will doubt.
3. The same argument holds good altogether in Ethics and Morals as well.
SECT. IIII.

units.la: CUm fictæ similitudines parem vim habeant cum realibus, ut Logici tenent, ut etiam in Evangelicis Parabolis videre est; fingamus servum merita sua erga Regem venditantem, tanquam qui insignissimum honoris gradum ex æqualitate justitiæ à Rege velit exigere, quæ est Meriti de Condigno vera & propria definitio. Rex, prout id intellexerit, servum ad se advocari jubet, quem, ut primum conspicit, sic exagitat: Tu verò, quem olim læsæ Majestatis reum, à morte ad vitam restitui; quem, infimæ sortis homuncionem, ad dignitatem provexi, quémque, licèt præclaris facinoribus (meis tamen impensis, subfidiis, viribúsque) perfunctum, amplissimis possessionibus locupletavi; ita tamen, ut nisi praestitisses, actum esset de salute tua; Tune, inquam, ut tantum beneficium, ex æquali-tate iustitiæ, condignitate tua, tibi deberi sententias? Sic Rex subdito os occlusit: Quantò magis Deus immortalis homini de Meritis suis nimis sibi blandienti; ubi constiterit nihil eum habere, quod non acceperit; nec accepisse, nisi ex suppeditata accipiendi facultate; imò nè voluisse quidem accipere, nisi per gratiam eam quæ ex nolente facit hominem volentem; nec, cùm voluerit aut potuerit, maluisse tamen Deo inservire, quàm propriæ saluti consulere; aut, si id maluerit, nil Deum adjuvàsse tamen! Fac denique ex pacto eum bonum fecisse, at hoc bonum erat nihilominus ex iure debitum: atque propter remunerationem quoque, sed longè ultra condignum. Unde factum erit, ut præclara opera tanto arrogantiæ veneno infecta, non facta censeantur omnino.
units.tr: Since fictional likenesses have the same force as real ones, as the logicians hold, and as can be seen in the Gospel parables, let us imagine a servant who boasts of his merits toward the King, as though he wished to demand from the King the highest degree of honour by equality of justice. This is the true and proper definition of merit of condignity. The King, understanding it so, orders the servant to be called before him, and as soon as he sees him, he rebukes him thus: "You, whom I once restored from death to life, though you were a guilty party of treason; you, a little man of the lowest rank, whom I raised to dignity, and whom I enriched with the most ample possessions, though you have performed brilliant deeds (yet at my expense, with my help and my strength), and so much so that, unless you had done so, your safety would have been lost; do you, I say, think that such a great benefit is owed to you by equality of justice, by your condignity?" Thus the King silenced the subject: "How much more, then, [should we say this of] the immortal God toward man, who flatters himself too much on his merits; when it is clear that he has nothing that he has not received, and that he received only from the ability to receive that was supplied to him; nay, that he did not even wish to receive except through that grace which makes a man willing out of one unwilling; and that, when he was willing or able, he did not prefer to serve God rather than to look after his own salvation; or, if he did prefer that, that he nevertheless did not help God at all! Finally, suppose that by agreement he did something good; yet this good was nonetheless owed by right, and was rewarded beyond what was condign." Hence it will come about that brilliant works, tainted with such a poison of arrogance, are not reckoned as works at all.
Ejusdem [?]Argumenti ex Ethnicorum Scholis Philosophicis adum- bratio.
SECT. V.

units.la: ARgumentum [illegible, ~12 letters] ad minus (vizprobabili) ad magis, Aristoteles discipulis
units.tr: The argument from the less to the greater (that is, from the probable to the more probable), which Aristotle handed down to his disciples.

units.la: [?] The Greek words in the opening line of the section are only partly legible on the scan. pulis[?] suis tradidit: Hoc ad nostrum propositum Seneca accommodavit, qui cùm in cæteris Tractatibus suis alios omnes disciplinæ Ethicæ Profeffores, tum in hoc de beneficiis seipsum excelluit. Ubi de sole & luna, inter Ethnicorum deos numeratis, ut quid inter homines & deos illos interesset doceret, Nostra, inquit, & horum conditio dissimilis: nam qui mihi prodest, ut prosit & sibi, non dedit be-neficium; quia instrumentum utilitatis suæ fuit. Sol tamen & luna etiamsi nobis prosint, non tamen in hoc prosunt, ut per nos prosint & sibi: quid enim nos illis conferre possumus? Hanc rationem quam Doctor hic Ethnicus in patrocinium falsorum deorum profert, eandem ex parte Dei veri, adversus fastidiosam de Meri-tis hominum superbiam, antiqui Patres sæpius inculcârunt, ut supra videre est.
