units.tr: Seneca adapted this to our purpose. In his other treatises he surpassed all the other teachers of ethical doctrine, and in this one, On Benefits, he surpassed himself. Where he speaks of the sun and moon, which are counted among the gods of the Gentiles, he teaches what the difference is between men and those gods: Their condition and ours, he says, is unlike. For he who does me good so that he may benefit himself too has not bestowed a benefit, because he was an instrument of his own usefulness. The sun and moon, however, even if they benefit us, do not benefit us in this, that through us they may benefit themselves too: for what can we confer on them? The ancient Fathers often pressed this same argument against the disdainful pride in human merits, on the side of the true God, as may be seen above. The heathen teacher brought it forward in defence of false gods.

units.la: Deinde beneficiorum exquisitus æstimator eadem Seneca, benefaciendi proprietates describens, Beneficiorum maxima sunt, inquit, quæ in nescientes, & interdum nolentes conferuntur. Et rursus, Dii sua munera, sine intercessione nostra, diebus & noctibus fundunt. Denique in præcipuis beneficiis requirit, ut ea accipienti necessaria, utilia, jucunda, & mansura sint. Sic ille de beneficiis sublunaribus duntaxat, qui, si per Dei gratiam in Schola Christianorum institutus fuisset, & intellexisset gratias infinitas per Christum Jesum in nos collatas, beneficia, inquam, ex mero Dei beneplaci-to gratuita, primò, ut ad animæ & cor-poris redemptionem ex gehenna, tam ne-cessaria; secundò, ut ad utriusque etiam in statu Gratiæ conservationem, tam utilis; ter-tiò, ut ad beatitudinem nostram conducenria, tam jucunda; & denique, ut ad aeternita- tem ipsam spectantia, tam mansura; hanc, in- quam, Theologiam vir ille eruditus si un- quam imbibisset, istam Pontificiorum de su- orum Meritorum condignitate opinionem diris utique devovisset. Utinam non de Deo vero liceret nobis eandem querelam in Pontificios, hodiernos praesertim, suscipere, quam {°}Seneca pro diis falsis intorquebat in Ethni- cos suos; Multos aequos inveni erga homines, adversus Deum neminem. Colophonem ex Cicerone artexam, ex quo colligere liceat quomodo animati Ethnici fuissent, si qui- dem doctrinam de gratuitis Dei donis erga nos spiritualiter gustum aliquem hausissent: Hoc quidem (inquit {P}Cicero) omnes mortales se habent, Externas commoditates, prosperitatemque vitae à diis se habere: virtutem autem nemo unquam acceptam Deo retulit. Nimirum recte. Propter virtutem enim jure laudamur, & in virtute recte gloriamur. Quod non contingeret, si id donum à Deo, & non à nobis haberemus. At verò, aut honoribus auctì, aut aliquid multi fortuiti boni, aut si malum depulimus, cùm-
units.tr: Seneca, the most exacting appraiser of benefits, likewise describes the qualities of doing good: The greatest benefits, he says, are those conferred on those who do not know, and sometimes on those who are unwilling. And again: The gods pour out their gifts day and night, without any intercession of ours. Finally, he requires of the chief benefits that they be necessary, useful, pleasant, and lasting for the one who receives them. So he speaks of earthly benefits only. But if he had been trained in the school of Christians by the grace of God, and had understood the infinite graces conferred upon us through Jesus Christ, then, I say, benefits freely given by the mere good pleasure of God, first, as necessary for the redemption of soul and body from hell; second, as useful for the preservation of both in the state of grace; third, as pleasant and conducive to our blessedness; and finally, as pertaining to eternity itself, as lasting — if that learned man had ever drunk in this theology, he would certainly have cursed that opinion of the Papists about the worthiness of their own merits. Would that we might not be allowed to bring against the Papists, especially those of today, the same complaint about the true God that Seneca turned against his heathen about their false gods: I have found many fair toward men, and no one toward God. I will add a closing remark from Cicero, from which we may gather what the heathen would have been like if they had tasted at all, spiritually, the doctrine of God's free gifts toward us. This, indeed, (says Cicero) is how all mortals are: they hold that external advantages and prosperity of life come from the gods, but no one has ever ascribed virtue to God as its source. Rightly so. For we are justly praised on account of virtue, and rightly glory in virtue. This would not be the case if we had this gift from God and not from ourselves. But when we are enriched with honours, or with some chance good, or when we have repelled an evil, although we give thanks to the gods, we still think that nothing of this is added to our praise. Did anyone ever thank the gods for being a good man? But for being rich, honoured, or unharmed. So he. Do you see, O Romanists, the disposition of the Roman heathen, who claimed nothing of merit or glory for themselves from any gift conferred on them by God?

units.la: {°} Seneca: In epist. (note in the right margin)
units.tr: Seneca: In epist.

units.la: {P} Lib. 3. de Natura deorum, pag. 160. pulis suis tradidit: Hoc ad nostrum propositum Seneca accommodavit, qui cùm in cæteris Tractatibus suis alios omnes disciplinæ Ethicæ Professores, tum in hoc de beneficiis ipsum excelluit. Ubi de sole & luna, inter Ethnicorum deos numeratis, ut quid inter homines & deos istos intersit doceret, Ne-stra, inquit, & horum conditio dissimilis: nam qui mihi prodest, ut prosit & sibi, non dedit beneficium; quia instrumentum utilitatis suæ fuit. Sol itaque & luna etiamsi nobis prosint, non tamen in hoc prosunt, ut per nos prosint & sibi: quid enim nos illis conferre possumus? Hanc rationem quam Doctor hic Ethnicus in patrocinium falsorum deorum profert, eandem ex parte Dei veri, adversus fastidiosam de Meritis hominum superbiam, antiqui Patres sæpius inculcârunt; ut supra videre est.
units.tr: Book 3, On the Nature of the Gods, p. 160. Seneca adapted this to our purpose. In his other treatises he surpassed all the other teachers of ethical doctrine, and in this one, On Benefits, he surpassed himself. Where he speaks of the sun and moon, which are counted among the gods of the Gentiles, he teaches what the difference is between men and those gods: Their condition and ours, he says, is unlike. For he who does me good so that he may benefit himself too has not bestowed a benefit, because he was an instrument of his own usefulness. The sun and moon, therefore, even if they benefit us, do not benefit us in this, that through us they may benefit themselves too: for what can we confer on them? This argument, which this heathen teacher brings forward in defence of false gods, the ancient Fathers often pressed, from the side of the true God, against the disdainful pride in human merits, as may be seen above.

units.la: Deinde beneficiorum exquisitus æstimator idem Seneca, benefaciendi proprietates describens, Beneficiorum maxima sunt, inquit, quæ in nescientes, & interdum nolentes conferuntur. Et rursus, Dii sua munera, sine intercessione nostra, diebus & noctibus sundunt. Denique in præcipuis beneficiis requirit, ut ea accipienti necessaria, utilia, jucunda, & mansura sint. Sic ille de beneficiis sublunaribus duntaxat, qui, si per Dei gratiam in Schola Christianorum institutus fuisset, & intellexisset gratias infinitas per Christum Jesum in nos collatas, beneficia, neficia[?], inquam, ex mero Dei beneplaci-to gratuita, primò, ut ad animæ & corporis redemptionem ex gehenna, tam ne-cessaria; secundò, ut ad utriusque etiam in statu Gratiæ conservationem, tam utilia[?]; tertiò, ut ad beatitudinem nostram conducentia, tam iucunda; & denique, ut ad æternitatem ipsam spectantia, tam mansura; hanc, inquam, Theologiam vir ille eruditus si unquam imbibisset, istam Pontificiorum de suorum Meritorum condignitate opinionem diris utique devovisset. Utinam non de Deo vero liceret nobis eandem querelam in Pontificios, hodiernos præsertim, suscipere, quam {o}Seneca pro diis falsis intorquebat in Ethni-cos suos; Multos aquas inveni erga homines, adversus Deum neminem. Colophonem ex Cicerone artexam[?], ex quo colligere liceat quomodo animati Ethnici fuissent, si quidem doctrinam de gratuitis Dei donis erga nos spiritualiter gustum aliquem hausissent: Hoc quidem (inquit {p}Cicero) omnes mortalessic habent, Externas commoditates, prosperitatemque vita à diis se habere: virtutem autem nemo unquam acceptam Deo retulit. Nimirum rectè[?]. Propter virtutem enim jure laudamur, & in virtute rectè gloriamur. Quod non contingeret, si id donum à Deo, & non à nobis habere-mus. At verò, aut honoribus auctì, aut aliquid nulli fortuiti boni, aut si malum depulimus, cùmdiis gratias agimus, tum nihil laudi nostrae assumptum arbitramur. Num quis, quòd bonus vir esset, gratias diis egit unquam? At quòd dives, quòd honoratus, quòd incolumis. Hæc ille. Videtisne, ô Romanenses, Ethnicorum Romanorum indolem, nihil ut meriti gloriolæve sibi arrogent de ullo dono sibi à Deo collato?
units.tr: Seneca, the same most exacting appraiser of benefits, describes the qualities of doing good: The greatest benefits, he says, are those conferred on those who do not know, and sometimes on those who are unwilling. And again: The gods pour out their gifts day and night, without any intercession of ours. Finally, he requires of the chief benefits that they be necessary, useful, pleasant, and lasting for the one who receives them. So he speaks of earthly benefits only. But if he had been trained in the school of Christians by the grace of God, and had understood the infinite graces conferred upon us through Jesus Christ, then, I say, benefits freely given by the mere good pleasure of God: first, necessary for the redemption of soul and body from hell; second, useful for the preservation of both in the state of grace; third, pleasant and conducive to our blessedness; and finally, pertaining to eternity itself, and so lasting. If that learned man had ever imbibed this theology, he would certainly have cursed that opinion of the Papists about the worthiness of their own merits. Would that we might not be allowed to bring against the Papists, especially those of today, the same complaint about the true God that Seneca turned against his heathen about their false gods: I have found many fair toward men, and no one toward God. I will add a closing remark from Cicero, from which we may gather what the heathen would have been like if they had tasted at all, spiritually, the doctrine of God's free gifts toward us. This, indeed, (says Cicero) is how all mortals are: they hold that external advantages and prosperity of life come from the gods, but no one has ever ascribed virtue to God as its source. Rightly so. For we are justly praised on account of virtue, and rightly glory in virtue. This would not be the case if we had this gift from God and not from ourselves. But when we are enriched with honours, or with some chance good, or when we have repelled an evil, although we give thanks to the gods, we still think that nothing of this is added to our praise. Did anyone ever thank the gods for being a good man? But for being rich, honoured, or unharmed. So he. Do you see, O Romanists, the disposition of the Roman heathen, who claimed nothing of merit or glory for themselves from any gift conferred on them by God?

units.la: Ejusdem veritatis ex Jesuitarum non- nulla confessione evictio.
units.tr: The same truth, proved from a certain confession of the Jesuits.
SECT. VI.

units.la: {p}COsterus Jesuita, cujus nomen inter Jesuitarum primarios claruit, Papisticam condignitatem totis propugnat viribus, & quæstione hùc illùc agitatâ ac vexatâ, postquam definiebat Meritum de Condigno niti æqualitate justitiæ, quæ Commutativa vel Distributiva sit, & revera {¶}ad utramque justitiæ partem aliquo modo pertinere; tandem eò est redactus angustiarum, ut coactus sit profiteri in verba sequentia, Propositio tertia est, Inter Deum & homines non potest, qualis inter homines, exacta justitia intercedere. 1. Quia non potest Deus eo modo debere nobis, ut, misericordi gratiâ suâ sepositâ, ex re aliqua remaneat nobis obligatus. Cujus tres rationes reddit. Prima, Quia factura ejus sumus, qui omni ex parte nos fecit & possidet, & cujus sunt omnia nostra. Hæc ratio de creatione & præservatione loquitur.
units.tr: Costerus the Jesuit, whose name shone among the leading Jesuits, defends Papist condign merit with all his strength. After the question has been tossed back and forth and worried over, he defines merit of condignity as resting on an equality of justice, which is either commutative or distributive and which in some way pertains to both parts of justice. At last he was driven into such straits that he was compelled to profess in these words: "The third proposition is: between God and men there cannot be, as there is between men, exact justice." 1. "Because God cannot be indebted to us in such a way that, his mercy and grace being set aside, he remains bound to us by some thing." He gives three reasons for this. The first: "Because we are his workmanship, who made us and wholly possesses us, and to whom all our things belong." This reason concerns creation and preservation.

units.la: Secunda, Quia cum aliis innumeris beneficiis nos sibi devinxerit, tum pretio sanguinis vitæ suæ nos emit. Hæc ejus ratio beneficium redemptionis commonstrat. Tertia, Quia & Gratiam quâ operemur, & ipsum Cœlum mereri datur[?], accepimus à Deo, QUI OPERATUR IN NOBIS ET VELLE ET PERFICERE, PRO BONA SUA VOLUNTATE, Phil.2.13. Hæc ille. Quid autem magis facere potest ad prodendum horum hominum stuporem egregium, suámq; meritoriam condignitatem jugulandam; quàm cùm confitentur non exactam justitiam intervenire inter Deum & homines, qualis inter homines ipsos intercedit, & nihilominus Meritum De Condigno ex absoluta æqualitate justitiæ definiunt, quale homines ipsi inter se, hujusmodi casibus, abhorrerent agnoscere?
units.tr: "The second: because, though he has bound us to himself by countless other benefits, he has also bought us with the price of the blood of his life." This reason points to the benefit of redemption. The third: "Because we have received from God both the grace by which we work and heaven itself to be merited, WHO WORKS IN US BOTH TO WILL AND TO DO, ACCORDING TO HIS GOOD PLEASURE, Phil. 2.13." Thus he. But what could do more to expose the remarkable stupidity of these men, and to slay their own meritorious condign worth, than when they confess that "no exact justice intervenes between God and men, such as intervenes between men themselves," and yet define "merit of condignity from absolute equality of justice," which men themselves, in such cases, would be ashamed to acknowledge between one another?

units.la: Deinde, rem hanc similitudo alia, quæ apud eundem Jesuitam in eadem sectione habetur, illustrat: Pecunia Dei est (inquit) quâ quippiam ab ipso mercamur, hoc est, Gratia Dei, in quâ tota meriti nostri ratio consistit. Quamobrem sicut non est perfectam justitiam statuere inter mendicum à divite quopiam ementem domum, & divitem ipsum; quia mendico quidem vendit ædes justo pretio, sed pecuniam interim gratis dat, quâ mercetur eam: Itâ nec inter Deum & nos; quia & Gratiam quâ operemur, & ipsa opera quibus cælum mercari & mereri dicamur, accepimus à Deo. Hæc ille, ubi agitur de Merito de Condigno, secundùm justitiæ æqualitatem. In qua similitudine, qui ex pecunia emptoris sibi à venditore gratis datâ proprie dictum Meritum de Condigno elicere conabi-tur, cur non febricitantis insomnium somni-âsse existimetur, equidem non video.
units.tr: Next, another comparison, which the same Jesuit gives in the same section, illustrates the matter: "The money of God is (he says) that by which we purchase anything from him, that is, the grace of God, in which the whole reckoning of our merit consists. Wherefore, just as it is not right to set up perfect justice between a beggar buying a house from some rich man and the rich man himself, because to the beggar he indeed sells the house at a just price, but meanwhile gives him the money gratis, with which he buys it: so neither is it between God and us, because we have received from God both the grace by which we work and the works themselves by which we are said to purchase and merit heaven." Thus he, where he treats of condign merit according to the equality of justice. In this comparison, I do not see why one who tries to draw from the money freely given by the seller to the buyer "merit of condignity, properly so called," should not be thought to have dreamed the dream of a feverish man.

units.la: Altera erit conclusio Jesuitæ {*}Vasquezii: Is qui æquum promittit (inquit) pro pecunia exi-gi valeris, non[?] propterea auget pretium & valorem pecuniæ, pro qua illum est pollicitus: sed eodem modo excederet illud, quod ex promisso daretur, illud minimum pretium, ac si pactum nullum intercessisset. Et propterea excessus illius rei, quæ redditur ex promissione pro parvo pretio, potiùs donatio judicatur, quàm pretii compensatio & venditio. Sic ille. Qua confessione Pontificiorum munimentum maximum Meriti de Condigno, quod pactum dicitur, dejectum corruit. Qui in his similitudinibus causæ nostræ firmamentum non videt, nihil illi aliud dicam, quàm illud proverbiale, [illegible, ~10 letters]. Sed majora molimur.
units.tr: Another conclusion is from the Jesuit Vasquez: "He who promises a fair price (he says) can be exacted for money does not on that account increase the price and value of the money for which he has promised it; but in the same way it would exceed that minimal price, which is given from the promise, as if no agreement had intervened. And therefore the excess of that thing which is given from a promise for a small price is judged to be a gift rather than a compensation and sale of a price." Thus he. By this confession the greatest bulwark of the Papists' merit of condignity, which is called a "covenant," is thrown down and collapses. If anyone does not see the firm support of our cause in these comparisons, I would say nothing to him but that proverb, [illegible in the scan]. But we are undertaking greater things.
CAP. XVII.

units.la: Decimum nostrum Argumentum, ex parte Christi meritis, adversus Pontificiorum ultimum propugnaculum, seu potius latibulum defensionis suae: viz. Christum meruisse nobis virtutem merendi vitam aeternam.
units.tr: The tenth argument of ours, from the merits of Christ, against the last bulwark of the Papists' defence, or rather their hiding-place: namely, that Christ merited for us the power of meriting eternal life.

units.la: Quaestionis status de nostra virtute me- rendi ex Meritis Christi.
units.tr: The state of the question concerning our power of merit from the merits of Christ.
SECT. I.

units.la: PRotestantes ex Meritis Christi propriis opera nostra bona grata & accepta Deo reddi fideli-ter credunt, & palam constan-ter profitentur: Pontificii vero, propriis Meritis Christi diffisi, (ut statim patebit) suam peculiarem merendi virtutem, tanquam ex ejus Meritis sibi indultam, commini-scuntur. Adversarios ipsos audiamus aequam est. {f} Stapletonus, Christus, inquit, nobis meruit virtutem merendi. A qua cantilena {t} Bellarmi-nus didicit illam suam, Merita nostra innituntur [?] Meritis Christi, qui nobis meruit virtutem merendi. Hos, velut assecla, comitatur Costerus. Redit denuo Bellarminus, & recoctam cramben apportat: Meruerunt (inquit) Christi opera apud Deum, non solum ut salutem consequeremur, sed etiam ut eam per merita propria consequeremur. Sed ut omnes intelligant, eos hunc speciosum praetextum Meriti Christi, veluti larvam, sibi induere, qua pueris sucum faciant, & ex hoc titulo, tanquam ex poculo aureo, exitiale venenum condignitatis suae meritoria lectoribus propinent; nos hoc erroris mysterium, Deo adjuvante, discutiemus & detegemus.
units.tr: Protestants faithfully believe, and openly and constantly profess, that our good works are rendered pleasing and acceptable to God through the merits of Christ. The Papists, however, distrustful of the merits of Christ (as will shortly be made plain), invent for themselves a peculiar power of merit, as though it had been granted to them from his merits. It is fair that we hear the adversaries themselves. Stapleton: Christ, he says, merited for us the power of merit. From this refrain Bellarmine learned his own: Our merits rest [?] on the merits of Christ, who merited for us the power of merit. Costerus follows these men like a servant. Bellarmine returns again and brings up the reheated cabbage: The works of Christ merited before God (he says) not only that we should obtain salvation, but also that we should obtain it through our own merits. But so that everyone may understand that they put on this specious pretext of the merit of Christ as a mask, by which they may beguile the simple, and from this title, as from a golden cup, offer their readers the deadly poison of the meritorious character of their own worthiness; we, God helping, will uncover and expose this mystery of error.

units.la: Argumentatio adversus Pontificiorum commentitiam virtutem me- rendi.
units.tr: Argument against the Papists' fictitious power of merit.
SECT. II.

units.la: OMne dogma sacrilegum, & propriis Christi Meritis derogatorium, est execrabile: At haec Pontificiorum opinio de sua virtute Merendi, ex praetextu quod eam Christus illis meruerit, est dogma propriis Christi Meritis derogatorium: Est ergo execrabile.
units.tr: Every sacrilegious doctrine, which detracts from the proper merits of Christ, is detestable. But this opinion of the Papists concerning their own power of merit, on the pretext that Christ merited it for them, is a doctrine which detracts from the proper merits of Christ. Therefore it is detestable.

units.la: Minor (nam de Majori nulla lis erit) per Theologicas rationes, per Patrum antiquorum sententias difertissimas, per ipsius deniq; Romanae Ecclesiae judicium & praxin muni-etur etur & confirmabitur. Institutum nostrum per Theses prosequemur, quarum aliæ directè, aliæ oblique & ex consequente, istud Pontificiorum portentum impugnant.
units.tr: The minor premise (for no dispute will arise over the major) will be secured and confirmed by theological arguments, by the most explicit opinions of the ancient Fathers, and finally by the judgment and practice of the Roman Church itself. We shall pursue our purpose through theses, some of which attack this monstrosity of the Papists directly, and others indirectly and by way of consequence.
Against the doctrine of the Papists
I. THESIS.

units.la: Sunt varia Christi virtutes Excellentiæ, quas mero homini tribuere, est sacrilega præsumptio.
units.tr: There are various excellences of Christ which it is sacrilegious presumption to ascribe to mere man.
SECT. III.

units.la: Recensebimus varias species earum, quæ dicuntur Virtutes Excellentiæ Christo propriæ, ex Pontificiorum ipsorum confessionibus. Primò, (ut in Tractatibus suis Suarez) Ad virtutem Excellentiæ Christo propriæ pertinet, habere potestatem ad redimendos homines, & animos illuminandos: Secundò, miracula per se facere. Hujus specimen habemus, ubi de miraculo à se, sed non per se facto, agnovit Petrus, Non nostra potentia, &c. Act. 3. 12. Tertium genus virtutum cernitur in Sacramentis. Quorum causam primam Deum esse, vel quatenus gratiam conferant, vel infallibilitatem significent; secundam causam esse Christum ut hominem, quia Christi humanitas conjuncta est cum Divinitate hypostaticè, fatetur {a}Cardinalis: Est & hæc (inquit) potestas Excellentia. Idem dici potest de quarto genere potestatis, nempe judiciaria: quae est Christo propria (inquit Suarez) pariter ad praemium & pœnam. Cui quintum genus adjungimus, mediationis: de quo orthodoxè admodum Cardinalis, Proprium est Christo, ut per ejus Merita petamus aliquid immediatè à Deo; ipse enim solus est immediatus Intercessor noster apud Deum. Hactenus Pontificii Doctores, partim de Regia, partim de Prophetica, partim etiam de Sacerdotali potestate Christo propria, non obscurè fatentes hasce potestates excellentia esse usquè adeò Christo peculiares, ut eas alicui creatae naturae tribuere, esset Christum novum fingere, & verum Christum juribus suis [illegible, ~8 letters].
units.tr: We will review the various kinds of what are called the Virtues of Excellence proper to Christ, drawing on the Papists' own confessions. First, (as Suarez says in his treatises) it belongs to the virtue of excellence proper to Christ to have power to redeem men and enlighten minds: second, to work miracles through himself. We have an example of this where Peter, acknowledging a miracle wrought by himself but not through himself, said, Not by our own power, etc. Acts 3:12. A third kind of virtue is seen in the Sacraments. Their first cause is God, either insofar as they confer grace or signify infallibility; the second cause is Christ as man, because Christ's humanity is joined with the Divinity hypostatically, the Cardinal confesses: This (he says) is also a power of excellence. The same can be said of the fourth kind of power, namely judicial, which is proper to Christ (says Suarez) equally for reward and for punishment. To this we add a fifth kind, that of mediation, concerning which the Cardinal speaks quite orthodoxly: It is proper to Christ that through his merits we ask something immediately from God; for he alone is our immediate Intercessor before God. Thus far the Papist teachers, partly about the regal, partly about the prophetic, and partly also about the priestly power proper to Christ, not obscurely confessing that these powers of excellence are so peculiar to Christ that to attribute them to any created nature would be to invent a new Christ and to rob the true Christ of his rights [illegible].
II. Thesis.

units.la: [?]Multas esse virtutes Christi etiam Meritorias, quae sunt excellentiae, quas nemo absque impietate usurpare queat.
units.tr: [?]There are many virtues of Christ, including meritorious ones, which are excellences that no one can claim without impiety.
SECT. IIII.

units.la: Testimonia Pontificiorum ejusmodi producemus, quae instituto huic nostro potissimum inserviant. Primò, {d}Nullus praeter Christum potest mereri aliis gratiam. Secundò, Salus Christus hanc gratiam habet, quà meritis suis gratiam & gloriam meretur. Tertiò, Chrisus[?] est causa meritoria justificationis nostræ, quoniam pretium redemptionis exactè persolvit, & ex rigore justitiæ (ut Theologi loquuntur) pro nostris omnium sceleribus satisfecit. Hæc Car-dinalis; ubi loquitur de solo Christo. Hujus generis instantias alias multas adferemus infrà. Sed hæ jam propositæ hoc consectarium esse subindicant, nemine refragante, nimirum, sacrilegii se scelere astringere, si quis meritorias virtutes, Christo proprias, sibi vendicaverit.
units.tr: We shall produce testimonies of the Papists of this kind, which chiefly serve our purpose. First: No one except Christ can merit grace for others. Second: Christ alone has this grace, by which through his merits he merits grace and glory. Third: Christ is the meritorious cause of our justification, since he exactly paid the price of redemption and, from the rigour of justice (as the theologians speak), made satisfaction for the sins of all of us. So the Cardinal; where he speaks of Christ alone. We shall bring many other instances of this kind below. But these already proposed indicate this consequence, which no one will gainsay: that whoever claims for himself meritorious virtues proper to Christ binds himself to the guilt of sacrilege.
III. Thesis.

units.la: Per[?] dogma suum de Condigno, Pontificii virtutem excellentiæ meritoriæ Christo propriam usurpant.
units.tr: By their dogma of condign merit, the Papists usurp for themselves the meritorious virtue of excellence proper to Christ.
SECT. V.

units.la: Meritum de Condigno (ex ipsorum Pontificiorum definitione & explicatione superiori) est opus bonum, quod secundùm æqualitatem justitiæ absolutæ, ex ejus dignitate potest[?] premium vitæ æternæ, ex rigore, exigere apud Deum. Tale verò Meritum esse opus ex-cellentia, adeóque Christo Θεανθρώπῳ[?] proprium, rationibus perquam necessariis evincemus, partim in hac, partim in subsequentibus se-ctionibus.
units.tr: Merit de condigno (according to the Papists' own definition and explanation above) is a good work which, by its worth and by the equality of absolute justice, can rigorously demand from God the reward of eternal life. That such a merit is a work of excellence, and therefore proper to Christ, the God-man [Θεανθρώπῳ], we will prove by very necessary arguments, partly in this section and partly in those that follow.

units.la: Ratio prima. Opus ex tali justitiæ æqua-litate litate condignum vitâ æternâ apud Deum, est opus excellentiæ; quoniam est necessario infinitæ virtutis; tum quia Deus, apud quem homo merèri & exigere eam dicitur, est persona infinitæ Majestatis; tum etiam quia ipsa vita æterna, quæ isti Merito retribuitur, est infinitæ durationis. Huic rationi admodum consonat, de quæstione alia, Suarezii Jesuitæ consequentia: An, scilicet, Veteris Testamenti Patres sese condigné disposuerint, ut essent condigni progenitores Christi. Respondet {c}Suarez, Nullus audebit dicere eos id meruisse de condigno; quia hoc bonum est alterius ordinis, ad quod gratia naturâ suâ non ordinatur, & quodam modo est infinitum bonum excedens proportionem meriti puræ creaturæ. Sic ille. Quomodo distat hæc ratio à nostra, quæ non tam similis est, quàm prorsus eadem? Præterea nostra ratio confirmatur ab Augustino, (supra, cap. 14. sect. 3.) qui docet, (si res ex proportione æstimatur) de passione martyrum, Præmium æternum (modo possibile esset) non nisi æterno labore comparandum esse.
units.tr: First argument. A work that is worthy of eternal life before God by such an equality of justice is a work of excellence, because it must be of infinite virtue; both because God, before whom man is said to merit and to demand that reward, is a person of infinite majesty, and because eternal life itself, which is repaid to this merit, is of infinite duration. The consequence of the Jesuit Suarez, on another question, agrees well with this argument: Whether, namely, the Fathers of the Old Testament prepared themselves so as to be worthy progenitors of Christ. Suarez answers: No one will dare to say that they merited this de condigno, because this good belongs to another order, to which grace is not ordained by its nature, and it is in a certain way an infinite good, exceeding the proportion of the merit of a mere creature. So he says. How does this reasoning differ from ours? Indeed it is not so much similar to ours as altogether the same. Moreover, our argument is confirmed by Augustine (above, chap. 14, sect. 3), who teaches, if the matter is judged by proportion, concerning the sufferings of the martyrs, that an eternal reward (if it were even possible) could be obtained only by eternal labour.

units.la: Ratio secunda. Cùm, apud Pontificios, eadem sit virtus hominis in merendo, atque est in satisfaciendo apud Deum, ex doctrina eorum de satisfactione facile erit elicere meritum, quod venditant esse Virtutem Excellentiæ. Ubi Protestantes contra doctrinam eorum de satisfactione objiciunt in hunc mo-dum:
units.tr: Second argument. Since, among the Papists, the power of man in merit is the same as his power in satisfying before God, it will be easy, from their doctrine of satisfaction, to draw out the merit which they boast to be a virtue of excellence. Here the Protestants object against their doctrine of satisfaction in this manner:

units.la: {c} Tom. 1. disp. 10. Sect. 7. § Dices; Potest &c. dum: Si nos jure satisfacimus apud Deum, cùm etiam applicatur nobis satisfactio Christi (ut Pontificii tenent) tum istæ aut duæ sunt satisfactiones, vel una: Si duæ, tum eadem culpa bis punitur: Si verò una, tum vel ea nostra est, aut Christi: Si Christi, tum nos non satisfacimus: Si nostra, tum vel Christi satisfactionem excludimus, vel cum Christo honorem dividimus. Sic Protestantes: Et ad hanc rationem, nostrâ quidem opinione solidam omnino & irrefragabilem, responsum efflagitant. Attendite: Extant Cardinalis responsiones; {f}Dua sunt (inquit) satisfactiones, sed una ab altera dependens. Sed probabilior responsio est, esse unam.
units.tr: {c} Tom. 1, disp. 10, sect. 7, § Dices; Potest, etc. If we satisfy God by our own right, and if Christ's satisfaction is also applied to us (as the Papists hold), then either there are two satisfactions or there is one. If two, then the same guilt is punished twice. If one, then it is either ours or Christ's. If Christ's, then we do not satisfy. If ours, then we either exclude Christ's satisfaction or divide the honour with Christ. Thus the Protestants. And to this argument, which is certainly solid and unanswerable in our opinion, they demand an answer. Notice: a Cardinal's answers exist. {f} There are two satisfactions (he says), but one dependent on the other. But the more probable answer is that there is one.

units.la: Quàm misera est hæc hallucinatio, Responsiones duas ingerere, eásque invicem repugnantes, sed maximè veritati ipsi! Quia licet satisfactio Christi sit satisfactio imputativa Petri, quia pro Petro exhibita, propterea quòd noster Secundus Adam sustinuit personam totius humani generis; tamen satisfactio Petri personalis non poterit magis esse Christi satisfactio, quàm Petrus poterit esse Christus. Quid verò, an Pontificii omnes pariter desipiunt? Imò verò, Theologi Lovanienses (fatente {s}Cardinale) docuerunt passiones Sanctorum non esse justas compensationes pro pœnis quas nos debemus Deo, hoc est, veras satisfactiones. Nec mirum: Nihil enim injustius, aut à religione magis abhorrens, quàm Divinum Christi θεανθρώπου[?] sanguinem, peccatorum omnium expiatorium, cum humana fæce peccabili, in eadem satisfactionum remuneratione commiscere. Dein, quàm ridiculum est, eas satisfactiones negare esse duas, quarum si una sufficiens sit, alteram superfluficientem & superfatisfactoriam esse necesse est!
units.tr: How wretched is this delusion, to offer two answers that contradict each other, and above all to truth itself! For although Christ's satisfaction is an imputed satisfaction for Peter, because it was offered on Peter's behalf, since our Second Adam sustained the person of the whole human race, yet Peter's personal satisfaction cannot be Christ's satisfaction any more than Peter can be Christ. But are all the Papists equally foolish? Indeed, the Louvain theologians (as the Cardinal admits) taught that the sufferings of the saints are not just compensations for the punishments which we owe to God, that is, true satisfactions. Nor is this surprising: for nothing is more unjust, or more repugnant to religion, than to mingle the divine blood of Christ, the God-man, the expiation of all sins, with sinful human dregs in the same reckoning of satisfactions. Then, how ridiculous it is to deny that these satisfactions are two, when, if one is sufficient, the other must be superfluous and over-satisfactory!

units.la: Hæc figmenta Adversariorum {h}Gregorius Pontifex, si nunc in vivis esset, ex animo execraretur: cujus erat hæc sancta & Divina professio; Ipsa Redemptoris nostri passio longè ipsa diversa à nostra: (nempe illa quam martyres sustinent) quoniam ipse sine culpa pertulit, quòd nos cum culpa toleramus. Quibus verbis, nec duas satisfactiones unam esse patitur; nec nostram, quæ est cum culpa, satisfactionem esse pro pœna. Ergo commeritoria vestra virtus ad consequendam vitam æternam, ex condignitate vestri operis, quæ erat Christi sanguinis pretio empta, nihil aliud est quàm Meriti Christi absolutissimi fœda conspur-catio.
units.tr: Pope Gregory, if he were still alive, would curse these fictions of our adversaries from his heart; it was his holy and divine profession: The passion of our Redeemer is very different from ours (namely, that which the martyrs endure), since he suffered without sin what we bear with sin. By these words he permits neither that two satisfactions are one, nor that our satisfaction, which is with sin, is a satisfaction for punishment. Therefore your merit-giving virtue for obtaining eternal life, from the worthiness of your work, which was bought with the price of Christ's blood, is nothing other than a foul defilement of the most absolute merit of Christ.
Fourth Thesis.

units.la: Pontificios, ut suam merendi virtutem stat- tuant, verè propria Christi merita nequiter excludere. SECT. VI.
units.tr: That the Papists, in order to establish their power of merit, wickedly exclude the true and proper merits of Christ. SECT. VI.

units.la: EXactam & accuratam dogmatiis Pontificii Explicationem tradidit, præ cæteris, Vasquez Jesuita; quæ omnes amphiboliæ technas tollat, tenebrasque dispellat: ex qua omnibus perspicuum fiat, Per hoc eorum figmentum virtutis suæ merendi ex seipsis, vera & propria omnia Christi merita, quibus opera nostra nosque ipsi grati Deo facti simus, penitus excludi. Exempli gratiâ,
units.tr: Vasquez the Jesuit, above all others, has delivered an exact and accurate explanation of the Papists' doctrine, which removes all the devices of ambiguity and dispels the darkness; from it, it becomes plain to all that by this fiction of their own power of merit, all the true and proper merits of Christ, by which our works and we ourselves were made pleasing to God, are wholly excluded. For example:

units.la: 1. Si ab eo quis quærat, an ex propri-[?]Christi Meritis opera nostra gratiam apud Deum obtineant; negabit: {1}Dici non potest (inquit) opera nostra crescere in dignitate ex-per-sa Christi: Quoniam, aut hoc fieret, quòd Deum favore Meritorum Christi acceptas opera ad majorem gloriam, quàm aliàs haberent: at non hoc; quia opus, aliàs non dignum, non potest fieri dignum magis, quàm aliàs esset, solo extrinseco favore, quamdiu in se non mutatur, &c. His positis, si quis Vasquem interroget, utrùm quicquam ad dignitatem operum nostrorum valeat, quòd Christus sit Caput nostrum; negabit: {k}Non ut opera nostra (inquit) sint magis digna ex eo, quòd Christus est Caput nostrum, & itâ nos eadem reputamur persona cum eo, & propterea dicitur Christus offerre opera nostra tanquam propria, & sic digna sint vitâ æterna. — Caterum nec hoc modo defendi potest hoc augmentum dignitatis in nostris operibus; quoniam opera nostra dicuntur accipere dignitatem à persona, à qua proximè procedunt. — Alioqui sequeretur, opera nostra infiniti esse valoris, eò quòd, quatenus procedunt à Christi Gratia, ipsi Christo tanquam Capiti tribuuntur.
units.tr: 1. If someone asks him whether our works obtain favour before God through the merits of Christ, he will deny it: It cannot be said (he says) that our works grow in dignity through the merits of Christ. For either this would happen because God accepted the works, by the favour of Christ's merits, for a greater glory than they otherwise would have; but this is not so, because a work which is not otherwise worthy cannot become more worthy than it otherwise would be, by extrinsic favour alone, as long as it is not changed in itself, etc. Given this, if someone asks Vasquez whether anything contributes to the worth of our works that Christ is our Head, he will deny it: {k} Not so that our works (he says) should be more worthy because Christ is our Head, and so we are reckoned as one person with him, and therefore Christ is said to offer our works as if they were his own, and so they are worthy of eternal life. — Yet neither can this increase of dignity in our works be defended in this way, since our works are said to receive their dignity from the person from whom they immediately proceed. — Otherwise it would follow that our works are of infinite value, because, in so far as they proceed from the grace of Christ, they are attributed to Christ himself as Head.

units.la: 2. Mos hic obtinet apud homines, ut ex favore Regis erga Titium, gratia ejus in Sempronium quoque conferatur: Quæritur num eadem ratio valeat apud Deum: Negabit {1}Vasquez:Nec dicimus (inquit) gratiam justificantem, eò quòd à Christo nobis donatur, magis gratos nos facere Deo, aut opera nostra; sicut inter homines sit, apud quos res (ut annulus) à Rege donata magis grata est, quia à nobiliori persona donatur. Apud Deum autem justitia & sanctitas intrinseca magis eos gratos facit suâpte naturâ, ex eo quod in se est, & non ex favore extrinseco.
units.tr: 2. It is the custom among men that, by the king's favour toward Titius, his grace is also conferred upon Sempronius. The question is whether the same reasoning holds before God. Vasquez will deny it: Nor do we say (he says) that justifying grace, because it is given to us by Christ, makes us more pleasing to God, or our works; as it is among men, among whom a thing (such as a ring) given by the king is more pleasing because it is given by a more noble person. But before God, intrinsic justice and holiness make them more pleasing by their own nature, from what they are in themselves, and not by extrinsic favour.

units.la: 3. Petimus utrùm virtutem propriorum Meritorum Christi hîc intercedere necesse sit: {2}Negabit:Cùm opera justorum(inquit)condignè mereantur vitam æternam, tanquam æqualem mercedem, non opus est interventu alterius meriti condigni, quale est meritum Christi, ut eis reddatur vita æterna: quinimo habet peculiare aliquod meritum hominis justi, respectu ipsius, quod non habet meritum Christi; nempe, reddere hominem justum & dignum vita æterna, ut eam digne consequatur. Et rursus; Nostra autem merita ita sunt perfectè meritoria vitæ æternæ, ut haud digne denegari possit: ergo frustra intercederent iterum merita Christi, ut illis æterna vita tribueretur.
units.tr: 3. We ask whether it is necessary for the power of the proper merits of Christ to intervene here. Vasquez will deny it: Since the works of the just (he says) merit eternal life de condigno, as an equal reward, there is no need for the intervention of another condign merit, such as the merit of Christ, in order that eternal life be rendered to them. Indeed, the merit of the just man has a certain peculiar quality with respect to himself which the merit of Christ does not have, namely, to make the just man worthy of eternal life so that he may attain it worthily. And again: Our merits are so perfectly meritorious of eternal life that it cannot rightly be denied; therefore the merits of Christ would intervene in vain, that eternal life might be granted to them.

units.la: 4. Si fortè nos absolutè & formaliter justos quis dixerit per justitiam Christi satisfactoriam, quâ absoluti simus à peccatis, & opera nostra acceptationem obtineant apud Deum; & roget, quid Vasquez sentiat; negabit: {n}Meritum autem Christi (inquit) licèt dignißimum sit quod obtineat pro nobis gloriam à Deo; tamen non habet hanc efficaciam & virtutem, ut reddat nos formaliter justos, & dignos vitâ æternâ, sed per virtutem ab ipso derivatam hunc consequuntur effectum homines in seipsis; & itâ nunquam petimus à Deo per merita Christi, ut nostris dignis & meritoriis operibus reddatur merces vitæ æternæ; sed, ut per Christum detur nobis ea gratia, per quam digne possimus vitam æternam promereri. Tandem festinat ad conclusionem: {*}Merita nostra (inquit) eam vim habent, ut reddant nos formaliter dignos vitâ æternâ,—sed Christus dignus est qui propter illa nobis impetret, quicquid ipse pro nobis petierit. Frustra igitur videtur hæc posterior imputatio sub duplici titulo dandi vitam aeternam: siquidem nobis, quibus donanda est, per merita nostra inest dignitas talis praemii; ac proinde vita aeterna est merces nostra, ratione dignitatis operum nostrorum, non autem ratione dignitatis operum Christi. Hactenus Vasquez. Idcirco quae potest esse execrabilior derogatio à meritis Christi propriis, quàm, homines ex fictitia merendi virtute ità condignitatem suam defendere, ut propria Christi virtus constituendi nos gratos apud Deum, ut propria ejus virtus sufficienter operandi in nobis actus bonos, ut virtus quoque ejus absolutè supplendi nostros necessarios defectus, quâ coram Deo gratiores habeamur, ut virtus ejus quâ jus haereditarium obtineamus ad regnum coeleste; ut hae, inquam, singulae virtutes, quae sunt in Christo absolutissimae, meritorum nostrorum condignitate penitus extrudantur? Hactenus adversus Pontificiorum sacrilegam audaciam; (nam rationes alias singulae sectiones sequentes suppeditabunt abunde) nunc Protestantium causa afferenda est, nè ejusdem criminis sacrilegii nos Adversarii insimulent, cujus illos reos esse jam deprehendimus. est, ac di. di. Id. atio ex su- con- oria obis lutè quâ ejus um quæ no- ur; am tio- inc em nt,
units.tr: 4. If perhaps someone should say that we are absolutely and formally just through the satisfactory justice of Christ, by which we are absolved from sins and our works obtain acceptance before God, and asks what Vasquez thinks, he will deny it: {n} The merit of Christ (he says), although it is most worthy to obtain glory for us from God, does not have such efficacy and power as to make us formally just and worthy of eternal life; rather, through a power derived from him, men in themselves attain this effect. And so we never ask God through the merits of Christ that the reward of eternal life be given to our worthy and meritorious works; but that through Christ that grace be given to us by which we may worthily merit eternal life. Finally he hastens to his conclusion: {*} Our merits (he says) have the force to make us formally worthy of eternal life; but Christ is worthy to obtain for us, on account of those merits, whatever he has sought for us. Therefore this later imputation under a double title of giving eternal life seems vain: since, in us, to whom it is to be given, there is by our merits a worthiness of such a reward; and accordingly eternal life is our reward, by reason of the worthiness of our works, and not by reason of the worthiness of the works of Christ. So far Vasquez. Therefore, what could be a more execrable detraction from the proper merits of Christ than that men, by a fictitious power of merit, so defend their own worthiness that the proper power of Christ to make us pleasing before God, his proper power to work good actions in us sufficiently, his power also to supply absolutely our necessary defects, by which we are held more gracious before God, and his power by which we obtain a hereditary right to the heavenly kingdom, are all, I say, these single powers which are most absolute in Christ, thrust out entirely by the worthiness of our merits? So far against the sacrilegious audacity of the Papists; (for the following sections will supply other arguments abundantly). Now the cause of the Protestants must be set forth, lest our adversaries accuse us of the same sacrilegious crime of which we have already found them guilty.

units.la: Protestantium contraria doctrina ab adversariorum calumniis vindicatur.
units.tr: The contrary doctrine of the Protestants is vindicated against the calumnies of the adversaries.
Fifth Thesis.

units.la: Negare Christum meruisse nobis virtutem Merendi, non est detrahere à Christi Meritis: Et est hæc veritas Principiis Theologicis maximè consentanea.
units.tr: To deny that Christ merited for us the power of merit is not to detract from the merits of Christ; and this truth is most consonant with theological principles.
SECT. VII.

units.la: PLurima esse genera operum etiam Meritorum excellentia, in quibus nemo absque nefaria impietate prætexere possit Christum nobis meruisse virtutem merendi, Adversariorum nostrorum confessiones prolixè testantur. (supra in hoc capite) Primum genus est eorum, quæ extra nos sunt; Solus Christus potest mereri gratiam aut gloriam: Solus potest persolvere pro nobis redemptionis pretium quod ex rigore justitiæ requiritur. Secundum eorum, quæ ad justificationem nostram pertinent, Adversarii ipsi fatentur, {•}Ex meritis Christi nos habere justificationem & dispositiones ad eam, ut fidem, orationem, contritionem, dilectionem, quæ singula Deus nobis denegare posset, quia an-te justificationem sumus indigni. Sic Christus nobis bis meruit auxilium gratia prævenientis & operantis primum motum voluntatis. Hactenus Vasquez.
units.tr: That there are very many kinds of excellent works, even meritorious ones, in which no one can pretend, without wicked impiety, that Christ has merited for us the power of merit, our opponents' own confessions abundantly testify (above in this chapter). The first kind is of those things which lie outside us: Only Christ can merit grace or glory; only he can pay for us the price of redemption which is required by the strictness of justice. The second kind concerns those things which pertain to our justification, and the Adversaries themselves admit that we have from the merits of Christ justification and the dispositions towards it, such as faith, prayer, contrition, and love, each of which God could deny us, since before justification we are unworthy. Thus Christ has merited for us twice the help of prevenient and operating grace and the first motion of the will. Thus far Vasquez.

units.la: Quæ singula Merita ita faciunt Christo propria, ut non modò atrocem injuriam Christo factam esse sentirent, si quis diceret Christum nobis meruisse virtutem de Condigno merendi pro aliis gratiam aut gloriam, aut dispositiones ad justificationem: verùm etiam in eum, (nec immeritò) tanquam profanum temeratorem prærogativæ Christi, acerbè inveherentur. Tantùm igitur abest, ut nos, negando istam Papisticam Merendi virtutem, aliquid de Christi veris ac propriis Meritis detractum aut delibatum velimus; ut planè jam constet, contrarias affirmationes Papisticas ejusdem impietatis convinci.
units.tr: These individual merits belong so properly to Christ that those who held them would not only feel that a monstrous injury had been done to Christ if anyone said that Christ had merited for us the power of condign merit, grace or glory for others, or the dispositions to justification; they would also rail against such a person, and not undeservedly, as a profane violator of Christ's prerogative. So far, then, are we from wishing anything to be taken away from or diminished in Christ's true and proper merits by denying this Papistical power of merit, that it is now plainly established that the contrary Papistical affirmations are convicted of the same impiety.

units.la: Majoris confirmationis gratiâ, hîc lubet in Vasquis confessione {*} superiori insistere: Si concedamus (inquit) opera nostra à Deo remunerari ultra ipsorum dignitatem, planè consequitur, illam accessionem remunerationis nobis donari intuitu Meritorum Christi, non autem intuitu nostrorum operum. Hæc Jesuita. Ergò intuitus dignitatis operum nostrorum, quoad Meritum, cum dignitatis Meritorum Christi intuitu non potest consistere: tantóq; minùs, quòd ex antiquorum Patrum communi consensu supra edocti fuimus, (cap.14.sect.3.) Essentialem beatitudinem, omnem actionum atque etiam passionum nostrarum dignitatem superare.
units.tr: For the sake of greater confirmation, it pleases us here to dwell on Vasquez's confession quoted above: If we grant (he says) that our works are rewarded by God beyond their worth, it plainly follows that this addition of reward is given to us on account of the merits of Christ, and not on account of our works. Thus the Jesuit. Therefore regard for the worth of our works, as far as merit goes, cannot stand together with regard for the worth of Christ's merits; and all the less so because, as we were taught above (ch. 14, sect. 3) from the common consent of the ancient Fathers, essential blessedness surpasses all the worth of our actions and even of our sufferings.
VI Thesis.

units.la: Bonum opus, ut nostrum, extenuare, est revera Dei Gratiæ gloriam amplificare.
units.tr: To diminish a good work, as ours, is in truth to amplify the glory of God's grace.
SECT. VIII.

units.la: Plùs valet opus ad amplificandam Dei gloriam, quò plus ejus bonitati, & potentiæ tribuitur. At cùm Pontificii in cooperatione boni operis partem potiorem sibi arrogent: Protestantes opus bonum, quatenus bonum, Deo in solidum ascribant, tanquam donum ejus spirituale & supernaturale, & quidem gratuitum, itâ ut non possit esse Meritorium apud Deum. Proinde dogma hoc, quod sta-tuit Christum meruisse nobis virtutem Merendi, tam est utique absonum, absurdum, ac planè impium, ac si asseruerint, Christum meruisse à Deo, nè Christiani, absque opinione Meritorum suorum, spiritualia, supernaturalia, & gratuita ejus dona agnoscant.
units.tr: A work has the more power to amplify God's glory, the more is ascribed to his goodness and power. But whereas the Papists claim the greater part for themselves in the cooperation of a good work, the Protestants ascribe the good work, as far as it is good, wholly to God, as his spiritual and supernatural gift, and indeed a free one, so that it cannot be meritorious before God. Therefore this doctrine which holds that Christ has merited for us the power of merit is as absurd, unreasonable and plainly impious as if they asserted that Christ had merited from God that Christians should acknowledge his spiritual, supernatural and free gifts only with the opinion of their own merits.

units.la: Enimvero, inquient, Meritorum nostrorum dignitatem hoc pacto minuere, erit Christi quoque erga nos Gratiam extenuare. Imò vero, inquam, non magis, quàm Spiritus Sanctus gloriam Dei deprimit per istas μειώσεις & extenuationes, quæ frequenter admodum in Scripturis occurrunt: viz. in re militari, post adeptam victoriam, Non nobis, Domine, non non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam, Psal. 115. 1. quamvis tamen illi fortiter & animosè pugnâssent: Item in opere miraculoso Petrus, Non hic nostrà virtute ambulare factus, sed in nomine Jesu, Act. 3. 12. & tamen Petrus verba sanandi proferebat: Necnon in functione Ecclesiastica Paulus, Non ego, sed Gratia Dei mecum, 1.Cor.15.10. quanquam & ille tunc se laborâsse asserit, etiam plus omnibus: Denique in re maximè spirituali, quae est ipsa inhaerens sanctificatio, idem Apostolus, Vivo ego, jam non ego, sed vivit in me Christus, Gal. 2. 20. Et rursus, Gratiâ Dei sum quod sum, 1. Cor. 15. 10. Hoccine verò erat virtutem Dei obfuscare aut obscurare, & non potiùs magnificè illustrare?
units.tr: "Indeed," they will say, "to diminish our merits in this way will also be to diminish Christ's grace towards us." Nay rather, I answer, no more than the Holy Spirit diminishes God's glory through those depressions and self-abasements [μειώσεις] which occur quite frequently in Scripture. For instance, in military affairs, after victory has been gained: "Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory," Ps. 115. 1, although they had fought bravely and spiritedly. Likewise in a miraculous work, Peter: "Not by our own power or holiness have we made this man to walk, but by the name of Jesus," Acts 3. 12, and yet Peter was pronouncing the words of healing. Also in ecclesiastical ministry, Paul: "Not I, but the grace of God with me," 1 Cor. 15. 10, although he there also asserts that he laboured more than all. Finally, in the most spiritual matter of all, which is inherent sanctification itself, the same Apostle: "I live, yet not I, but Christ liveth in me," Gal. 2. 20. And again: "By the grace of God I am what I am," 1 Cor. 15. 10. Was this indeed to obscure or darken God's power, and not rather to illustrate it magnificently?
VII. Thesis.

units.la: Modum obtinendi vitam aeternam à Protestantibus propositum, extollere; alterum verò à Pontificiis jactatum, extenuare & revera tollere gloriam Meritorum Christi.
units.tr: To exalt the way of obtaining eternal life proposed by the Protestants; but to diminish the other, boasted of by the Papists, and in truth to take away the glory of Christ's merits.
SECTION IX.

units.la: DUo sunt in quibus de crimine derogationis à Gratia Christi Pontificios postulamus: unum est contra Gratiam Christi meritoriam: alterum, contra Gratiam ejus operantem. Quæ ut clariùs omnibus innotescant, (Quemadmodum ex collisione lapidum ignis, itâ ex diversarum opinionum collatione veritas elicitur) à Gratia Christi Meritoria ordiemur. Cùm agitur de extrinseca Christi justitia Meritoria, eam Pontificii excludere à sufficienti justificatione nostra non dubitant: quam nos imputativam dicimus. Sed malim Vazquis Jesuitæ, de sententia nostra, confessionem Lectori tradi, quàm ullam asseverationem meam. ʳ Dona gratia Dei, (inquit) tam auxilii excitantis, & adjuvantis ad promerendam vitam æternam, quàm gratia & justitia inhærentis ad eluendas maculas peccati, nobis omnia propter merita Christi dantur, atque non possumus non aliquam applicationem & imputationem meritorum Christi circa singula agnoscere: quam sanè Hæretici nostri temporis (Protestantes vult) ingenuè fatentur, nisi quòd, ut dignitatem horum donorum [scilicet inhærentis justitiæ] extenuent, usquè adeò hanc imputationem meritorum Christi [nempe quæ sunt Christo propria] nobis extollunt, ut existiment justitiâ eorum, non autem justitiâ nobis inhærente, tanquam formâ nos justificari; & eis etiam, non autem operibus nostris, nos mereri coram Deo. Hanc ille confessionem edidit, quâ apertissimè fatetur verum discrimen inter nos & Pontificios in eo consistere, quòd Protestantes nulla admittentes Merita nostra ex inhærente justitia, tantùm ipsius Christi meritis nitantur, tam quoad gratiam, quàm quoad gloriam obtinendam apud Deum, Contrà, Pontificii, posthabitis Christi meritis, in suorum Meritorum condignitate acquiescant. Res igitur jam in confesso est: Protestantes extenuare dignitatem operum suorum, negando ea esse Meritoria, ut propria Christi merita extollant. Quid mirum igitur est, si Protestantes à pseudo-catholicis Hæretici appellentur? Hactenus rationibus causam nostram confirmavimus, quæ nunc Patrum antiquorum suffragiis corroboranda est.
units.tr: There are two points on which we charge the Papists with the crime of detracting from the grace of Christ: the one is against the meritorious grace of Christ, the other against His operative grace. So that these may be more clearly known to all (just as fire is struck out from the collision of stones, so truth is elicited from the comparison of diverse opinions), we shall begin with the meritorious grace of Christ. When the extrinsic meritorious righteousness of Christ is in question, the Papists do not hesitate to exclude it from being sufficient for our justification; we call this the imputed righteousness. But rather than offer any assertion of my own about our view, I would prefer to hand the reader a confession from the Jesuit Vazquez. "The gifts of God," he says, "both the helping and exciting grace for earning eternal life, and the grace and inherent righteousness for washing away the stains of sin, are all given to us on account of the merits of Christ; and we cannot but acknowledge some application and imputation of the merits of Christ to each of these." And indeed, he says, "our heretics of this time" (he means the Protestants) "freely confess this, except that, in order to diminish the worth of these gifts [namely inherent righteousness], they so exalt this imputation of the merits of Christ [that is, of what belongs to Christ] to us, that they think we are justified by His righteousness and not by the righteousness inherent in us as a form; and that we merit before God by it, and not by our works." He made this confession, by which he most plainly admits that the true difference between us and the Papists consists in this: the Protestants, admitting no merits in us arising from inherent righteousness, rest wholly on the merits of Christ Himself, both as to obtaining grace and as to obtaining glory before God. On the contrary, the Papists, setting aside the merits of Christ, rest satisfied in the worthiness of their own merits. The matter is therefore now admitted: the Protestants diminish the worth of their own works by denying that they are meritorious, in order to exalt the proper merits of Christ. What wonder, then, if the Protestants are called "heretics" by the pseudo-Catholics? Hitherto we have confirmed our cause by arguments; it must now be strengthened by the testimony of the ancient Fathers.

units.la: Ad Patrum antiquorum consensum, tan- quam Ecclesiæ Catholicæ judicium, provocamus.
units.tr: We appeal to the consent of the ancient Fathers as the judgment of the Catholic Church.
I. THESIS.

units.la: Dogma illud de virtute nostra merendi, tanquam ex Meritis Christi, unanimi Antiquitatis consensu, tanquam turbine, prosternitur & labefactatur.
units.tr: That dogma concerning our power of merit, as if it were from the merits of Christ, is overthrown and undermined, as by a whirlwind, by the unanimous consent of antiquity.
SECT. X.

units.la: Judicium consulimus tam Catholicæ, quàm Romanæ, Ecclesiæ: sed primò ac præcipuè de Patrum testimoniis inquirimus, quorum quidem Argumenta nobis, pro causa nostra, insolubilia esse videntur.
units.tr: We consult the judgment of the Catholic Church as well as of the Roman Church, but first and above all we inquire into the testimonies of the Fathers, whose arguments seem to us, for our cause, insoluble.

units.la: Primum Argumentum, quod ex Patribus deprompsimus, est, Quòd illi Bonum opus omne, quatenus bonum, Dei donum esse testati sunt: ex quo nonnulli eorum concluserunt, primò, Neminem dignum esse vitâ aeternâ; secundò, Dona esse tam eorum opera, quàm praemia, tertiò, Ea dona esse Dei, ac proinde non habere remunerationem ex debito; & similia. Patres quos citavimus (cap.8.) sunt Augustinus, Chrysostomus, Bernardus, Origenes, respectivè.
units.tr: The first argument that we have drawn from the Fathers is that they testified that every good work, insofar as it is good, is a gift of God. From this some of them concluded: first, that no one is worthy of eternal life; second, that their works are gifts as much as rewards; third, that these gifts are God's, and therefore do not have a reward owed as a debt; and similar things. The Fathers whom we cited (chap. 8) are Augustine, Chrysostom, Bernard and Origen, respectively.

units.la: Secundum Patrum Argumentum: Cùm Adversarii Meritum de Condigno esse definiunt, primò, quatenus est opus bonum à libero arbitrio profectum; deinde, quatenus facit Deum proprie debitorem: contra primum Patres docuerunt, primò, Homines dando egentibus magis Deo obstrictos esse; secundò, Non debere nos extollere, vel omnia faciendo, quia nihil magni facimus; tertiò, Væ, nisi faciamus; quartò, Plura deesse, quæ non fecimus; quintò, Non labore merita pensitanda esse. Pro his produximus Chrysostomum, Theophylactum, Bernardum, & Bedam. (cap.9.) Deinde, quod ad alterum, primò, Non debere nobis Deum accipiendo quid, sed promittendo; secundò, Nullum opus nostrum facere Deum debitorem; tertiò, Imò ex nostro opere bono nos factos esse Deo debitores; quartò, Vitam æternam nobis ex jure non deberi.
units.tr: The second argument of the Fathers: when our opponents define merit of condignity as (first) a good work proceeding from free will, and (then) as something that makes God properly a debtor, the Fathers taught against the first point: (1) that by giving to the needy men are more bound to God; (2) that we should not exalt ourselves, either because we do everything, or because we do nothing great; (3) woe to us if we do not act; (4) many things are lacking that we have not done; (5) merits are not to be weighed by labour. For these points we brought forward Chrysostom, Theophylact, Bernard and Bede (chap. 9). Next, as to the second point: (1) God is not to be thought of as receiving anything from us, but as promising; (2) no work of ours makes God a debtor; (3) rather, by our good work we are made debtors to God; (4) eternal life is not owed to us by right.

units.la: Hæc Augustinus, Origenes, Basilius, Chryfoftomus, Beda, & Bernardus, respectivé. (su-prà, cap. 11.)
units.tr: These things were said by Augustine, Origen, Basil, Chrysostom, Bede and Bernard, respectively (above, chap. 11).

units.la: Tertium Argumentum est, quo indignitatem operantium observant atque deplorant, contra defensionem Meriti de Condigno, cui Adversarii tribuunt condignitatem fecundum æqualitatem justitiæ ad præmium coeleste, quod nolunt sibi ex acceptatione & misericordia Dei concedi. In quo aperte contradicunt Patribus, qui indignitatem nostram confitentes, misericordiam Dei acceptationem in remunerandis operibus justorum profitentur. Quæ utraq; isti prisci Ecclesiæ proceres propriis phrafibus suis, quæ sunt judiciorum suorum expressa Symbola, explicarunt. Primo, Humiliet quisq; fe, quia potest incurrere crimen nescius. Secundo, Acerrima erit judicii Divini exactio. Tertio, Etiam tres pueri in fornace dicebant, Impietatem fecimus. Et, Quàm facile est gravibus peccatis implicari, quæ à nobis levia æstimantur! Quarto, Nos tundamus pectus nostrum, & dicamus, Domine, propitius esto. Quinto, Justitia noftra injustitia est ad examen justitia Divina deducta. Sextò, Nihil in nobis mundum aut innocens; Nulla sufficiunt merita, nisi Deus misericorditer defectus nostros non reputet. Septimo, Non sufficit opus Sanctorum ad gloriam consequendam. Octavo, Semper deficiunt nobis bona ad quæ Sancti perseverant. De his copiosissimè Patres præallegati, supra, cap. 10. fect. 2. & infrà, cap. 20. fect. 11.
units.tr: The third argument is that by which they note and lament the unworthiness of those who work, against the defence of merit of condignity, to which our opponents ascribe a condignity according to equality of justice with the heavenly reward, which they are unwilling to grant to themselves from God's acceptance and mercy. In this they plainly contradict the Fathers, who, confessing our unworthiness, profess that in the rewarding of the works of the righteous God's acceptance is mercy. These ancient leaders of the Church explained both of these points in their own phrases, which are the clear symbols of their judgments. First: "Let each one humble himself, because he may fall into a crime without knowing it." Second: "The exaction of divine judgment will be most severe." Third: "Even the three boys in the furnace were saying, We have done wickedness." And: "How easy it is to be entangled in grave sins, which we regard as slight!" Fourth: "Let us beat our breast and say, Lord, be merciful." Fifth: "Our righteousness, brought to the test of divine justice, is unrighteousness." Sixth: "Nothing in us is clean or innocent; no merits suffice unless God, in mercy, does not reckon our defects." Seventh: "The work of the saints does not suffice for obtaining glory." Eighth: "The good things in which the saints persevere always fail us." On these matters the Fathers already cited are most copiously full: above, chap. 10 sect. 2, and below, chap. 20 sect. 11.

units.la: Hæc de primo genere. Sequitur de Acceptatione & misericordia in retributione, in hæc verba; Primò, Retributiones propter solam dei benignitatem præstantur. Secundò, Justitia nostra non sufficit ad beatitudinem; Spes est in misericordia; Beati erimus dignatione Domini honorati. Tertiò, In illa die nullum opus nostrum dignum reperietur. Quartò, Opus dignum exhibere non possumus; Deus justos remuneratur in misericordia. Quintò, Non in meritis nostris, sed in misericordia coronamur. Sextò, Plus attendas quæ desunt, quamvis pie vivu[?]; Justitia nostra, ut pannus menstruata mulie-ris; Digni sumus, non dignitate nostrâ, sed dignatione Dei. Patres qui ad primam partem loquuntur, allegati fuerunt, Ambrosius, Athanasius, Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Gregorius Pontifex, Hilarius, Author operis impersecti, & Beda. (cap. 10.) Pro posteriori, Basilius, Hilarius, Cyprianus, Hieronymus, Gregorius Pontifex, Bernardus, & Beda. (supra, cap. eodem.)
units.tr: These are the things of the first kind. There follows, concerning acceptance and mercy in retribution, in these words: First: "Rewards are bestowed solely by God's kindness. Second: Our righteousness does not suffice for blessedness; hope is in mercy; we shall be blessed, honoured by the Lord's condescension." Third: "On that day no work of ours will be found worthy." Fourth: "We cannot show a worthy work; God rewards the righteous in mercy." Fifth: "We are crowned not on account of our merits, but in mercy." Sixth: "Pay more heed to what is lacking, though one lives piously; our righteousness is like a menstruous woman's rag; we are worthy, not by our own worthiness, but by God's condescension." The Fathers who speak to the first part, cited, were Ambrose, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Augustine, Gregory the Pope, Hilary, the author of the unfinished work, and Bede (chap. 10). For the latter point: Basil, Hilary, Cyprian, Jerome, Gregory the Pope, Bernard and Bede (above, the same chapter).

units.la: Quartum Argumentum Patrum, Quia opera nostra Remuneratorem nostrum Deum nullo bono aut commodo afficiunt. A repetitione sententiarum libenter abstineo. Pro hoc Argumento laudamus inter Patres Gregorium, Nazianzenum, Chrysostomum, Basilium, Augustinum, Prosperum, Ambrosium, Tertullianum, (supra, cap. 15.)
units.tr: The fourth argument of the Fathers: because our works do not bring any good or advantage to God, who rewards us. I gladly abstain from repeating the sentences. For this argument we praise among the Fathers Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Basil, Augustine, Prosper, Ambrose and Tertullian (above, chap. 15).

units.la: Quintum Patrum Argumentum, Quia cùm Adversarii argutentur pro suo Merito de condigno, ex nomine Mercedis proprie accepto, Patres tamen, ubi de aeterna vita agitur, Mercedis nomen comparatè rejecerunt, & proprie eam Hæreditatem esse statuerunt: viz. Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Fulgentius, Chrysostomus, Origenes, Marcus Eremita, Bernardus, ut videre licet supra, cap.3. sect. 2. & cap. 16. Quanquam nec habet vox Merces in se vim Meriti, ut ibidem probavimus.
units.tr: The fifth argument of the Fathers: since our opponents argue for their merit of condignity from the name "reward" taken in its proper sense, the Fathers, however, when they speak of eternal life, comparatively rejected the name "reward" and declared that eternal life is properly an "inheritance": namely Jerome, Theodoret, Theophylact, Fulgentius, Chrysostom, Origen, Mark the Hermit and Bernard, as may be seen above, chap. 3 sect. 2, and chap. 16. Although the word "reward" does not in itself have the force of "merit", as we proved in the same place.

units.la: Aliud Argumentum est, Quòd fatentur Patres, Æternam vitam esse supra omnem dignitatem operum; quorum loca referemus, ubi agetur de martyrio: (infrà cap. 18.) quæ erit convictio Adversariorum validissima. Interea ex his præmissis concludimus, Adversarios nostros, aut Patribus supra nominatis singulis notam inscitiæ ac impietatis inurere oportere, quòd suam hanc virtutem de condigno merendi debellaverint atque convulserint: aut se, in ea propugnanda propagandaq;, impostores ac veteratores esse confiteri. In plerisque Argumentis testis Augustinus introducitur, quem partibus suis Pontificii adsciscunt.
units.tr: Another argument is that the Fathers confess that eternal life is above all dignity of works. We shall cite their passages when we treat of martyrdom (below, chap. 18), which will be a most powerful conviction of our opponents. Meanwhile from these premises we conclude that either our opponents must brand each of the Fathers named above with a mark of ignorance and impiety, because they have overthrown and shaken this their virtue of merit of condignity, or they must confess themselves to be impostors and cheats in defending and propagating it. In most of the arguments the witness introduced is Augustine, whom the Papists claim for their side.

units.la: Augustini judicium in hac causa à Ponti- ficiis objicitur, & à Protestantibus vindicatur.
units.tr: The judgment of Augustine in this matter is objected to by the Papists, and is vindicated by the Protestants.
SECT. XI.

units.la: {¶} Ubicunque Augustinus merita damnat, loquitur de Meritis quae ex nobis sunt, sine gratia Dei. In Epist. 105. ad Sixtum, Ipsa, inquit, vita aeterna, quae sine fine habebitur, & ideo meritis redditur, tamen quia eadem merita, quibus redditur, non à nobis partâ sunt per nostram sufficientiam, sed in nobis fa-cta per gratiam, etiam ipsa Gratia nuncupatur, non ob aliud, nisi quia gratis datur; nec ideo quia meritis non datur, sed quia data sunt & ipsa merita, quibus datur. Et infrà; Cui debetur vita aeterna, vera justitia est; si autem vera justitia est, non ex te est, sed à Patre luminum descendens.— Si ergo, ò homo, accepturus es vitam aeternam, justitiae quidem stipendium est, sed tibi gratia est, cui gratia est ipsa justitia. Tibi enim tanquam debita redderetur, si ex te tibi esset justitia cui deberetur. Quid ex his? Habemus ex hoc loco, (ait Cardinalis) nostram justitiam, cui redditur vita aeterna, veram esse justitiam, ac per hoc esse verè Meritoriam.— Habemus deinde, Augustinum, cùm dicit vitam aeternam non deberi ex meritis, sed gratis donari, loqui de homine, quatenus est sine gratia & solis suis viribus operatur. Nam dicit Augustinus vitam aeternam ut stipendium justitia reddi operibus, quæ homo per gratiam operatur. Hæc ille: qui nimiùm altercando veritatem amittit, non satis discernens statum Quæstionis. Nec enim negamus Bona opera ab Augustino Merita dici; sed, an ea dicantur propriè Merita, id est, de Condigno, id quæritur. De Condigno vero Meritum non est, nisi (ut Adversarii ipsi verè statuunt) quod ex æqualitate justitiæ potest æternam vitam, tanquam sibi debitam, vendicare apud Deum. Cui Augustinus, in locis citatis, vel maximè adversatur: nos igitur Augustini testimonium in Adversariorum pectora facilè retorquebimus.
units.tr: {¶} Wherever Augustine condemns merits, he speaks of merits that come from us, without the grace of God. In Epistle 105 to Sixtus he says: Eternal life itself, which will be possessed without end, is rendered as a reward for merits. Yet because the very merits for which it is rendered are not produced by us through our own sufficiency, but are wrought in us by grace, they too are called grace, for no other reason than that they are given freely; not because eternal life is not given on account of merits, but because the merits by which it is given are themselves given. And further on: Eternal life, which is owed, is true righteousness; but if it is true righteousness, it is not from you, but comes down from the Father of lights. So if you, O man, are to receive eternal life, it is indeed the wages of righteousness, but it is grace to you, since righteousness itself is grace to you. For it would be rendered to you as a debt, if the righteousness for which it was owed were from you. What follows from this? From this passage, the Cardinal says, we have that our righteousness, to which eternal life is rendered, is true righteousness, and therefore truly meritorious. Next, we have Augustine, who, when he says that eternal life is not owed on account of merits but is freely given, is speaking of man as he is without grace, working by his own powers alone. For Augustine says that eternal life is rendered as the wages of righteousness to works which man performs through grace. So he says; but he, by arguing too much, loses the truth, not sufficiently distinguishing the state of the question. For we do not deny that Augustine calls good works merits; the question is whether they are called merits properly, that is, of condignity. Now a merit of condignity exists only (as our opponents themselves rightly hold) when, by equality of justice, it can claim eternal life from God as owed to itself. Augustine strongly opposes this in the passages cited. We will therefore easily turn Augustine's testimony back upon the breasts of our opponents.

units.la: Cui vita æterna non ut debita redditur, illud non est propriè Meritorium de Condigno: sed operi, facto in gratia, vita æterna non ut debita redditur: ergò non est illud opus bonum Meritorium de Condigno. Minorem Augustinus adstruit: sic enim de homine regenerato arguit, Tibi æterna vita tanquam debita redderetur, si ex ea esset justitia cui deberetur, aperté indicans vitam æternam non esse debitam. Ubi (ut & alibi frequentissimè) cum agere de operibus in gratia factis, palàm est: & passim nos docet inter retributiones gratiæ Divinæ discernere, æquè ac in Psal. 102. in illa verba, NOLI OBLIVISCI RETRIBUTIONES DOMINI: Nè fis superbus, primò, cùm peccator (nempe extra gratiam) vocatus es, ut justificareris; ficaveris; secundò, cùm tibi vires subministrata sunt (utiq; intra statum gratiæ) ut in finem perseverares; tertiò, cùm Deus coronat te (viz. in statu gloriæ) in misericordia & miseratione.
units.tr: A work to which eternal life is not rendered as owed is not properly meritorious of condignity. But a work done in grace is a work to which eternal life is not rendered as owed. Therefore that good work is not meritorious of condignity. Augustine supports the minor premise. For he argues in this way about the regenerate man: Eternal life would be rendered to you as owed, if righteousness were from it to which it is owed, plainly indicating that eternal life is not owed. Here (as very often elsewhere) he is clearly speaking of works done in grace, and everywhere he teaches us to distinguish the rewards of divine grace. This is so also in Psalm 102, in the words Do not forget the rewards of the Lord, Do not be proud: first, when you, a sinner (that is, outside grace) were called, that you might be justified and glorified; secondly, when strength was supplied to you (certainly within the state of grace) that you might persevere to the end; thirdly, when God crowns you (namely in the state of glory) with mercy and compassion. Psal. 102.

units.la: Sed justitiam nostram veram vocat. Antecedens hoc nos quoque fatemur: an igitur erit Meritoria de Condigno? Consequentiam hanc pernegamus. Nam illius fides, qui in hunc modum orabat, Credo Domine, Adjuva infidelitatem meam, vera utiq; fides erat, quamvis languida. Justitiam nostram pariter imperfectam esse, & quæ, ex se, coram judicio Divino consistere nequeat, passim docet Augustinus. Instantia una sufficiet: {r}Charitas pleniffima, quamdiu hic vivitur, est in nemine: quamdiu autem augeri potest, profectò illud quod minus est quàm debet, ex vitio est: Ex quo vitio NEMO EST JUSTUS IN TERRA, QUI FACIAT BONUM, ET NON PECCET: Ex quo vitio NON JUSTIFICABITUR IN CONSPECTU DEI OMNIS VIVENS. Sed fac eam perfectam esse; nihilominus negat ei deberi vitam æternam: ratio; Quia justitia tua ex te non est, sed à Deo.
units.tr: But Augustine calls our righteousness true. We too concede this premise: will it therefore be meritorious of condignity? We flatly deny this consequence. For the faith of the man who prayed in this way, Lord, I believe; help my unbelief, was certainly true faith, though weak. Augustine teaches throughout that our righteousness is likewise imperfect, and that it cannot, of itself, stand before the divine judgment. One instance will suffice: Perfect charity is in no one as long as we live here; and as long as it can still grow, surely what is less than it ought to be comes from fault. From this fault, THERE IS NO ONE ON EARTH WHO DOES GOOD AND DOES NOT SIN. From this fault, NO ONE LIVING WILL BE JUSTIFIED IN THE SIGHT OF GOD. But grant that it is perfect; still he denies that eternal life is owed to it. The reason: Because your righteousness is not from you, but from God.

units.la: Protestantium vindicatio, atque applicatio Sententia Augustini.
units.tr: The Protestant vindication and application of Augustine's opinion.
SECT. XII.
