units.la: {t}AUgustinus; Si intelligerent Pelagiani sic merita nostra, ut etiam ipsa dona Dei esse cognoscerent, non esset improbanda eorum sententia. — Nam talia cogitanti verissime dicitur, Dona sua coronat Deus, non merita tua; si tibi à teipso, non ab illo sunt merita tua. Et alibi; Non coronat merita tua, tanquam merita tua, sed tanquam dona sua. Hinc Bellarminus, Ergo tantum damnat merita quae non sunt in nobis ex Deo.Esto; veruntamen nunquam exi-stimavit ea esse proprie dicta Merita, ne eorum quidem Sanc-torum, qui ex gratia gloriosissimè operantur. Illéne enim ut somniaret unquam, ullum esse nostrum Meritum quod ex æqualitate justitiæ vitam æternam ex Condignitate & debito vendicet apud Deum, qui primò, vitam æternam justis ex debito reddi negat? secundò, qui non permittit Deum, nisi promittendo, debitorem esse? tertiò, qui vitam æternam præmium operibus supra condignum esse docuit? quartò, qui quodvis bonum opus coronari non nisi in Misericordia judicat? quintò, qui denique statuit (si res ex proportione exacta agatur) neminem vitam æternam, nisi æterno suo labore consequi debere? Sextum addam, de Dono; ex quo volupe est videre quantum Augustinus Vegæ vestro facessat negotii: Augustinus (inquit) sic argumentatur: Fides non est meritum, quia est Dei donum: tum Vega, post aliquot velitationes, quasi tergum dans, Sed hæc satis sunt, inquit, pro pietate, quam debemus tanto Doctori; non enim necesse est omnia ipsius argumenta demonstrativa, aut efficacia esse credere. Hæc Vega,ut decuit strenuum athletam scilicet. Sed Augustinus se sibi satis constantem causæ nostræ Patronum hactenus exhibuit, pòst etiam magís magísque eundem se esse demonstrabit.
units.tr: Augustine: If the Pelagians recognised that our merits are such that they are also God's own gifts, their opinion would not be condemned. For to one who thinks this, it is most truly said: God crowns his own gifts, not your merits; if your merits are from yourself, and not from him, they are your merits. And elsewhere: He does not crown your merits as your merits, but as his own gifts. Hence Bellarmine: Therefore he condemns only those merits which are not in us from God. Granted. Yet he never thought these were properly called merits, not even those of the saints who most gloriously work through grace. For would he ever have dreamed that any merit of ours, by an equality of justice, claims eternal life from God as a matter of condignity and debt? He who first denies that eternal life is rendered to the just as a debt? Who does not allow God to be a debtor except by promising? Who taught that eternal life is a reward for works beyond condign? Who judges that any good work is crowned only in mercy? And who finally holds that, if the matter is treated by exact proportion, no one ought to attain eternal life except by his own eternal labour? I will add a sixth, concerning the gift; from which it is a pleasure to see how much trouble Augustine saves your Vega: Augustine (he says) argues thus: faith is not merit, because it is God's gift. Then Vega, after some skirmishes, as if turning his back: But these are enough, he says, for the reverence we owe to so great a Doctor; for it is not necessary to believe that all his arguments are demonstrative or effective. Thus Vega, as befits a vigorous athlete, of course. But Augustine has hitherto shown himself a patron of our cause, consistent enough with himself, and hereafter he will show himself to be the same more and more.
I. Thesis.

units.la: Dogma Pontificiorum de virtute merendi ex Condigno, tanquam ex Meritis Christi, non erat per multa secula Fidei doctrina, vel in ipsa Romana Ecclesia.
units.tr: The Papists' doctrine of the power of merit by condignity, as from the merits of Christ, was not the doctrine of the faith for many ages, even in the Roman Church itself.
SECTION XIII.

units.la: QUæ fuerit antiquitas Romanæ Ecclesiæ doctrina, tum ex celebrium Autorum scriptis, tum etiam ex ejus praxi, ab antiquis retro temporibus ad hodiernæ Liturgiæ Romanæ usum, constare facile potest. Quod ad doctrinam, non necesse est ut seriem tem-porum percurramus: In paucis Autoribus Romanensibus, exceptione majoribus, insistere sat erit: viz. Leone primo & Gregorio primo Pontificibus Romanis, Anselmo Episcopo,& Bernardo Abbate. Pontifex Leo, Deus, inquit, quid cordibus nostris insinuat, quidve commendat, nisi ut de justitia sua nemo præsumat, & de ipsius misericordia nemo diffidat? quæ tunc evidentius præminet præeminet[?] quando peccator sanctificatur, & abjectus origitur[?]. Neque enim de qualitate nostrorum operum pendes[?] cœlestium mensura donorum. Quod unicum testimonium potest ampla & luculenta esse detectio vanitatis Bellarminianæ defensionis; qui solebat, primò, dicta Patrum interpretari de operibus extra gratiam factis; At Leo agit de sanctificato. Secundò, Cardinalis contendebat pro dignitate operis in se; Leo autem negat donum cœleste pendere de ulla operis qualitate. Denique, urgebat ille commensurationem inter opera & præmia; iste verò proprie dictam operis mensuram penitus excludit. Gregorius Pontifex cognomento Magnus, &c. si cum successoribus suis comparetur, verè Maximus, primò quæstionem hanc sibi proponit,{a} Si illa Sanctorum felicitas est misericordia, & non meritis acquiritur, Ubi erit quod scriptum est, REDDET UNICUIQUE SECUNDUM OPERA EJUS? Nam si SECUNDUM OPERA reddatur, quomodo MISERICORDIA æstimatur? Ad hanc objectionem responsum suum illico adaptans, Aliud est, inquit, SECUNDUM OPERA, aliud PROPTER OPERA reddere. Hæc ille. De quo testimonio supra cap. 2. sect. 2. in quo jam negat felicitatem propter opera reddi, tanquam propter causam meritoriam.
units.tr: What the antiquity of the Roman Church's doctrine was can easily be established, both from the writings of its famous authors and from its practice, from ancient times down to the use of the present Roman liturgy. As for doctrine, we need not run through the whole sequence of centuries. It will be enough to dwell on a few Roman authors, outstanding above the rest: the Roman Pontiffs Leo I and Gregory I, Bishop Anselm, and Abbot Bernard. Pope Leo says: "God, what does he impress on our hearts, or commend to them, except that no one should presume on his own righteousness, and no one should despair of his mercy? That mercy stands out all the more clearly when the sinner is sanctified and raised up from the dust. For heavenly gifts do not depend on the quality of our works, nor are they measured by them." This single testimony can be a full and clear exposure of the emptiness of Bellarmine's defence. He was accustomed, first, to interpret the sayings of the Fathers as referring to works done outside grace; but Leo is speaking of the one who has been sanctified. Second, the Cardinal contended for the worth of the work in itself; but Leo denies that the heavenly gift depends on any quality of the work. Finally, the Cardinal urged a commensuration between works and rewards; but Leo entirely excludes a measure of works, properly so called. Gregory the Great, if he is compared with his successors, is truly the Greatest. First he puts this question to himself: "If that happiness of the saints is mercy, and is not acquired by merits, where will be what is written, 'He will render to each according to his works'? For if it is rendered according to works, how is mercy esteemed?" Answering this objection at once, he says: "It is one thing to render according to works, another to render on account of works." So he. On this testimony, see above, chapter 2, section 2, where he already denies that happiness is rendered on account of works as a meritorious cause.

units.la: Idem Pontifex, à Thesi ad Hypothesin descendens,{b} Ipsa justitia nostra, inquit, ad examen justitiæ Divinæ deducta, injustitia est, & sordet in distinctione Judicis, quod fulget in æstimatione operantis. Item, Ipsa nostra perfectio culpâ non caret, nisi hanc severus Judex in subtilis hance[?] examinis misericorditer penset. Item de seipso, {y}De sola misericordia tua impetro, inquit, quod non de meritis spero. Item, {z}Justus noster Advocatus justos nos defendet in judicio, quia nosipsos cognoscimus & accusamus injustos: non itaque nostris actionibus fidamus, sed in Advocati nostri allegatione confidamus. Hæc ille. Et sunt id genus alia testimonia plurima, quæ Pontificiorum Meritorum de Condigno defensioni opponuntur. Illi enim, Ex Meritis, Iste autem, Non ex meritis felicitatem acquirimus. Illi, Propter opera, ut causam Meritoriam: Iste, non Propter, sed, Secundum operæ reddituræ remuneratio. Illi, Merita nostra digna sunt, quibus formaliter justi sumus coram Deo: Ille, Non ita est, nam justitia nostra sordet, &, Sumus injusti. Illi denique, Non opus est nobis intuitu meritorum Christi, extra nos in judicio Dei, ut vitam æternam consequamur: At ille, Non actionibus nostris, sed in Advocati nostri allegatione confidendum est. Sic Romanus Pontifex hodierno Romanorum dogma, de virtute nostra Merendi, tanquam ex Meritis Christi nobis comparata, falsitatis convincit.
units.tr: The same Pontiff, passing from thesis to hypothesis, says: "Our very righteousness, when brought to the examination of divine justice, is unrighteousness, and it is foul in the judgment of the Judge, though it shines in the estimation of the one who does it." Likewise: "Our very perfection is not free from fault, unless the stern Judge weighs it mercifully in his subtle examination." Likewise, of himself: "I obtain from your mercy alone what I do not hope for from my merits." Likewise: "Our righteous Advocate will defend us as righteous in judgment, because we know and accuse ourselves as unrighteous. Therefore we do not trust in our actions, but we trust in the plea of our Advocate." So he. There are many other testimonies of this kind, which are set against the Papists' defence of merit de condigno. For they say, "From merits"; he says, "We do not acquire happiness from merits." They say, "On account of works, as the meritorious cause"; he says, "Not on account of, but according to, the reward due to works." They say, "Our merits are worthy, by which we are formally righteous before God"; he says, "It is not so, for our righteousness is foul, and we are unrighteous." They finally say, "We have no need, with regard to the merits of Christ outside us, in God's judgment, to obtain eternal life"; but he says, "We must trust not in our actions, but in the plea of our Advocate." Thus the Roman Pontiff convicts of falsehood the present Roman dogma of our power of merit, as though it were acquired for us from the merits of Christ.

units.la: Bernardus ante aliquot secula in ævo tenebricoso, velut cœleste fidus, claruit, ejus The-fis. fis hæc fuit, ubi agitur de proprié dictis Meritis,{a} Si proprie appellentur ea quæ dicimus nostra Merita, spei quidem seminaria sunt, charitatis incentiva, occulta prædestinationis indicia, futuræ felicitatis præsagia, via regni, non causa regnandi. Sic ille, operum bonorum prærogativas describens, & illas quidem egregias: quarum ultima est, Quòd sint via regni, quam-vis non causa regnandi. De quo plura infrà.
units.tr: Bernard shone some centuries ago in a dark age, like a heavenly star. His thesis, where he treats of merits properly so called, is this: "If those things we call our merits are properly so named, they are indeed seedbeds of hope, incentives of charity, hidden indications of predestination, forecasts of future happiness, the way to the kingdom, though not the cause of reigning." So he, describing the prerogatives of good works, and those indeed excellent ones. The last of these is that they are the way to the kingdom, although not the cause of reigning. More on this below.

units.la: Pòst, idem Bernardus, ubi ad Hypothesin accedit, {b}Nostra, inquit, siqua humilis est justitia, recta forsan, sed non pura: nisi forsitan nos meliores esse credimus patribus nostris, qui non minus veraciter quàm humiliter dixerunt, OMNES JUSTITIÆ NOSTRÆ SUNT TANQUAM PANNUS MENSTRUATÆ MULIERIS. Hæc ille. Ex comparatione hujus doctrinæ cum Pontificiorum dogmate superiori, facilè Lector intelligat, ea non minùs inter se discrepare quàm antitheta hæc; viz. primò, Opera nostra non sunt meritoria causa regnandi, &c, Sunt meritoria causa regnan-di de Condigno: secundò, Justitiæ nostræ non sunt pura, nec sumus in hoc meliores patribus nostris, &c, Sumus ex operibus formaliter justi, & eatenus patribus nostris meliores. Hactenus de professione ipsa, sequitur praxis Romanæ Ecclesiæ, per multa sæcula recepta, & ad hodiernum diem celebrata. Mitto testimonia Anselmi & Bedæ, quæ sparsim in hoc Tractatu habentur.
units.tr: Afterwards, the same Bernard, when he comes to the hypothesis, says: "Our justice, if it is some humble justice, is perhaps right but not pure, unless perhaps we think ourselves better than our fathers, who said no less truthfully than humbly, ALL OUR RIGHTEOUSNESSES ARE LIKE A MENSTRUOUS CLOTH." So he. From comparing this teaching with the Papists' dogma above, the reader can easily see that they differ from each other no less than these antitheses: first, "Our works are not the meritorious cause of reigning" against "They are the meritorious cause of reigning de condigno"; second, "Our righteousnesses are not pure, nor are we in this better than our fathers" against "We are formally righteous from works, and so far better than our fathers." So far on the profession itself. There follows the practice of the Roman Church, received through many centuries and observed down to the present day. I pass over the testimonies of Anselm and Bede, which occur scattered through this treatise.
II. Thesis.

units.la: Hodierna Ecclesia Romana praxis dogmati ejusdem Ecclesiae repugnat.
units.tr: The present-day practice of the Roman Church contradicts the doctrine of that same Church.
SECT. XIIII.

units.la: EXtant hodie in Collecta, in Commemoratione pro defunctis, haec verba; Memento Domine, &c. Et famulis tuis, de multitudine miserationum tuarum sperantibus, partem aliquam & societatem digneris cum tuis sanctis: in quorum consortium nos, non Æstimator meriti, sed venia Largitor, admittas, per Christum Dominum nostrum. Haec sunt Collectae verba, quae plane contradicunt dogmati superiori ejusdem Ecclesiae, Ex meritis Christi habemus nos virtutem merendi, juxta aequalitatem justitiae, quae exigat praemium vitae aeternae apud Deum. Haec duo si inter se conferantur, quis satis mirari potest horum hominum stuporem, qui in orando Deum non esse Æstimatorem meritorum suorum docent, in definiendo tamen & concludendo Æstimatorem meritorum suorum esse decernunt? Rursus, doctrinā hac, Merendi virtutem suam per Merita Christi jactant; oratione tamen, per Christum (adeoque per ejus Merita) veniam deprecantur, nè ex Meritis suis dijudicentur. Dicent fortasse, Professionem eorum de Meritis esse de Fide; Orationem autem Spei duntaxat esse sobolem. Monstra narrant. Spes enim non est nisi Fidei filia, sicut scriptum est, Fides est rerum sperandarum, Hebr. 11. 1. Fides autem quam Pontificii venditant, sic se habet; Opus nostrum meritorium exigit à Deo vitam aeternam. Spes vero eorum quid expetit? Ut nos in consortium Sanctorum admittat, non ut Æstimator meritorum. Hem, filia jam devoravit matrem. Sintne igitur Adversarii nostri irridendi, an miserandi potius, difficile est dicere.
units.tr: Today the following words still stand in the Collect for the commemoration of the dead: Remember, O Lord, etc. And grant to thy servants, who hope in the multitude of thy mercies, some part and fellowship with thy saints, into whose company admit us, not as the assessor of merit but as the bestower of pardon, through Christ our Lord. These are the words of the Collect, and they plainly contradict the earlier doctrine of the same Church: From the merits of Christ we have the power of meriting, according to the equality of justice, which requires the reward of eternal life from God. If these two are set side by side, who can sufficiently marvel at the stupidity of these men? In praying they teach that God is not the assessor of their merits, yet in defining and concluding they decree that he is. Again, in their doctrine they boast that they have the power of meriting through the merits of Christ, yet in prayer they beg pardon through Christ (and therefore through his merits), lest they be judged by their own merits. They may perhaps say that their profession about merits belongs to faith, while the prayer is only the offspring of hope. What monsters they relate! For hope is nothing but the daughter of faith, as it is written, Faith is the substance of things hoped for, Heb. 11. 1. But the faith which the Papists peddle is this: Our meritorious work demands eternal life from God. What, then, does their hope seek? That he would admit us into the fellowship of the saints, not as the assessor of merits. Alas, the daughter has already devoured the mother. Whether our adversaries are to be mocked or rather pitied, it is hard to say.

units.la: Hofius Cardinalis hujus generis praxeis alias commemorat: unam ex Anselmo, à Fratribus Francisci ordinis observatam, erga morti proximos: {*}Unde cuivis (inquit Hofius) perspicere licet, qui mos fuerit in Ecclesia Dei. Verba haec sunt, Morituri, ut non alia in re, quàm in Christi passionis & mortis merito, omnem suam spem & fiduciam collocarent, admonebantur.
units.tr: Cardinal Hosius mentions other practices of this kind: one, taken from Anselm, observed by the Friars of the Franciscan order towards those close to death. "From this," says Hosius, "anyone may see what custom prevailed in the Church of God." His words are these: Those about to die were admonished to place all their hope and confidence in nothing else but the merit of Christ's passion and death.

units.la: Addit aliam:{4} Vidimus (inquit) Sacerdotale Romanum, in quo sunt hæ Interrogationes, & Responsa: {*}CREdis, non proprio meritis, sed passionis Domini nostri Jesu Christi virtute & merito, ad gloriam pervenire? Respondet infir-mus, CREdo. Non igitur spei tantùm, sed
units.tr: He adds another: We have seen (he says) the Roman Priest's Book, in which are these questions and answers: Do you believe that, not by your own merits but by the virtue and merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, you will come to glory? The sick person answers, I believe. Therefore not only hope but

units.la: jussit Index Expurgatorius Madriti impressus apud Alphonsum Gomezium Regium Typographum, Anno 1584. und[?] cum alia Interrogatione & Responsione, viz. CREdis quòd Dominus noster Jesus Christus pro nostra salute mortuus sit? & quòd ex propriis Meritis, vel alio modo nullus possit salvari, nisi in Merito Passionis ipsius? Respons. CREdo. & fidei hæc vox est. Pergit Hofius, Et in fine dicit Sacerdos, SI Dominus voluerit te secundum peccata tua judicare, dicas, Domine Deus, ego pono mortem Domini nostri Jesu Christi inter me & judicium tuum, — & in manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum. Et post, cum consimilem professionem à quodam Dominicano factam commemorâsset, Hæc est, inquit, fides Catholica, quæ neminem fallere potest. Hactenus de hoc Argumento. Ad proximum festinamus.
units.tr: the Index Expurgatorius printed at Madrid by Alphonsus Gomezius, royal printer, in the year 1584, has ordered it, along with another question and answer: Do you believe that our Lord Jesus Christ died for our salvation, and that no one can be saved by his own merits or in any other way than in the merit of his passion? Answer: I believe. And this is the voice of faith. Hosius goes on: And at the end the priest says: If the Lord wishes to judge you according to your sins, say, Lord God, I place the death of our Lord Jesus Christ between me and your judgment, and into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit. And afterwards, having recalled a similar profession made by a certain Dominican, he says: This is the Catholic faith, which can deceive no one. So much on this subject. Let us hasten to the next.
CHAP. [?]

units.la: Maior ex Scriptoris facile evincitur, in quo hæreticum, tanquam nobilissimum [illegible, ~10 letters] dum perveniendi ad vitam æternam, [illegible, ~12 letters] ut enim [illegible, ~8 letters] vestros [illegible, ~8 letters] nullos [illegible, ~4 letters] ulla dis-tro.
units.tr: The greater part of this is easily proved from the writer, in which the heretic, as most noble [illegible], while attaining eternal life, [illegible] for indeed [illegible] your [illegible] none [illegible] any [illegible].
CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Undecimum nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, tanquam ex Meritis Christi, ex parte Martyrii, ut est nobilissimum medium perveniendi ad vitam aternam. Argumentatio.
units.tr: The eleventh argument of ours against merit of condignity, taken from the merits of Christ, on the part of martyrdom, as the most noble means of attaining eternal life. Argumentation.
SECT. I.

units.la: QUicquid excellentiæ competit omni operi bono, id utique Martyrio est tribuendum: At hoc excellentiæ, viz. De Condigno Meritorum esse vitæ æter-na, non est tribuendum Martyrio: Propterea, De Condigno Meritorum esse vitæ æternæ, non competit omni operi bono.
units.tr: Whatever excellence belongs to every good work must surely be attributed to martyrdom. But this excellence, namely that it is of condign merit to eternal life, is not to be attributed to martyrdom. Therefore being of condign merit to eternal life does not belong to every good work.

units.la: Major ex Scripturis facilè evincitur, in quibus Martyrium, tanquam nobilissimum medium perveniendi ad vitam æternam, sæpe anteponitur cæteris omnibus: Cui etiam Adversarios nostros assensuros esse nullùs dubito.
units.tr: The major premise is easily proven from Scripture, in which martyrdom, as the most noble means of attaining eternal life, is often placed above all others. I do not doubt that our opponents will also assent to this.
First thesis.

units.la: Patres antiquos non tribuisse Martyribus virtutem Merendi, tanquam ex Meritis Christi. In quo habemus veluti clarissimum speculum Catholica veritatis.
units.tr: The ancient Fathers did not attribute to martyrs the power of merit, as derived from the merits of Christ. In this we have, as it were, the clearest mirror of Catholic truth.
SECT. II.

units.la: CAtholicæ veritatis θεοφόροι[?], antiqui Patres, in Expositionibus suis in {*}locum Apostoli, ubi de passionibus Christianorum Apostolus clarè docuit, Non esse Condignas afflictiones hujus temporis ad gloriam futuram, Catholica sua judicia & Orthodoxa largiter exhibuerunt: (suprà:) quibus monstrum hoc, quod dicitur de Condigno ex justitia aqualitate apud Deum mercedem exigere, planè profligârunt. Juvat eorum rationum momenta aliquot saltem attingere.
units.tr: The God-bearing [θεοφόροι] ancient Fathers, in their expositions of the passage where the Apostle clearly taught that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, set out their Catholic and orthodox judgments at length (as above). By these they utterly overthrew that monstrosity which says that by condign merit, from equality of justice, one exacts a reward from God. It helps to touch on at least some of the weight of their reasons.

units.la: Ratio prima, ex testimoniis iis quibus Patres dignitatem bonorum operum deprimunt, in hunc modum. Primò, {a}Universo orbi renunciantes, nihil dignum fecimus. Secundò, {b}Nihil potest quis pati dignum gloriâ. Tertiò, {c}Etsi millies moriamur, nihil dignum gerimus pro bonis quæ accepimus, nedum futuris. Quartò, {d}Nihil dignum regnis cælestibus. Quintò, {e}Æterna requies æterno labore digna. Itâ ut (quod alibi objicere solent Pontificii) si vox Dignum infert Meritum de Condigno, Patres dum toti-es pronunciant opera bona non digna esse vitæ æternæ, eâdem vitâ condigna esse perme-gant. (Hæc supra, cap. 14.)
units.tr: The first reason is drawn from the testimonies by which the Fathers depress the dignity of good works, in this manner. First, Having renounced the whole world, we have done nothing worthy. Second, A man can suffer nothing worthy of glory. Third, Even if we die a thousand times, we do nothing worthy in return for the good things we have received, let alone future ones. Fourth, Nothing worthy of the heavenly kingdoms. Fifth, Eternal rest is worthy of eternal labour. So that (as the Papists are wont to object elsewhere) if the word worthy implies merit of condignity, the Fathers, while they so often declare that good works are not worthy of eternal life, go on maintaining that they are worthy of that same life. (These things above, ch. 14.)

units.la: Ratio secunda ex sententiis, in quibus expressè bona opera Meritoria esse Patres inficiati sunt: (supra, cap. 10, & cap. 14.) viz. Primò, {f}Non secundùm merita nostra, sed secundùm misericordiam Dei cœlestium decretorum in hominès firma processit. Secundò, {g}Major erit gloria quàm ut quis eam mereatur. Tertiò, {h}Licèt totis viribus desudemus, nihil tamen merito condignum comperiamus. Quartò, {i}Ineffabiliter omne meritum excedit vita æterna. Quintò, {k}Nihil sunt merita omnia ad tantam gloriam. Sextò, {l}Non sunt omnes passiones Condignum Meritum ad eam gloriam. Ergò ludicrum erat Bellarmini subterfugium, cùm dixit, Passiones non condignæ esse æternâ gloriâ, non respectu meritoriæ dignitatis, sed respectu levitatis & brevitatis earum, comparatione habitâ ad æternitatem & immensitatem præmii. Falsò omnino: nam in his Meritum & Dignitas operum expressè excluduntur.
units.tr: The second reason is drawn from sentences in which the Fathers expressly denied that good works are meritorious (above, ch. 10 and ch. 14). Namely: First, Not according to our merits, but according to the mercy of God, the firm decree of heaven proceeded toward men. Second, The glory will be greater than that anyone could merit it. Third, Although we sweat with all our strength, we nevertheless find nothing condign by merit. Fourth, Eternal life exceeds all merit beyond words. Fifth, All merits are nothing for so great a glory. Sixth, Not all sufferings are condign merit for that glory. Therefore Bellarmine's evasion was ridiculous, when he said: The sufferings are not worthy of eternal glory, not with respect to meritorious dignity, but with respect to their lightness and brevity, the comparison being made to the eternity and immensity of the reward. Entirely false, for in these passages the merit and dignity of works are expressly excluded.

units.la: Ratio tertia, ex modo quo usi sunt ad Meritum de Condigno expugnandum, ubi, omissis operibus, personas ipsas operantes indignas æstimant præmio æterno. Primò, {m}Non ex dignatione Dei coronamur. Secundò, {n}Vitam dono Deus indignis. Tertiò, {o}Si per totam vitam tormeritatoleraremus, non digni essemus, &c. Quar-tò, {P}Etsi omnia praecepta utriusque Testamenti quis praestiterit, tamen non est dignus illa gloriâ. (supra, cap. 14.)
units.tr: The third reason is drawn from the manner in which they used to overthrow the merit of condignity, where, leaving aside the works, they judge the persons themselves who work to be unworthy of the eternal reward. First, We are not crowned by the favour of God. Second, God gives life as a gift to the unworthy. Third, If we endured torments through the whole of life, we would not be worthy, etc. Fourth, Even if someone has performed all the precepts of both Testaments, yet he is not worthy of that glory. (above, ch. 14.)

units.la: Ratio quarta argumentandi cernitur in his Patrum phrasibus, viz. Primò, monendo ut Martyres considerent se non plus pati, quàm pro peccatis merebantur. Sic Hieronymus. Et iisdem prorsus verbis Primasius. Quibuscum Isidorus Hispalensis consentit. Denique, Dicitur ab Apostolo, NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES HUJUS TEM-PORIS &c. ad deprimendam Patientium superbiam. Hæc singula pleniùs exprimuntur su-prà [?], cap. 14.
units.tr: The fourth reason is discerned in these phrases of the Fathers. First, in exhorting martyrs to consider that they suffer no more than they deserved for sins. So Jerome; and Primasius with exactly the same words. Isidore of Seville agrees with them. Finally, It is said by the Apostle, NON SUNT CONDIGNÆ PASSIONES HUJUS TEMPORIS, etc., to humble the pride of the sufferers. These individual points are set out more fully above, ch. 14.

units.la: Antiquorum Patrum testimonia insuper alia, quæ probant Martyrium ipsum non esse opus Meritorium Condignum vitâ æternâ, ex Psal. 116.
units.tr: Other testimonies of the ancient Fathers also prove that martyrdom itself is not a meritorious work condign to eternal life, from Psalm 116.
SECT. III.

units.la: PSalm. 116. (secundùm vulgatam, 115) Quid retribuam Domino pro omnibus quæ accepi? Calicem Salutis accipiam, & nomen Domini invocabo. —Pretiosa mors Sanctorum in conspectu ejus. Non hîc contendimus de genuino & literali hujus textûs sensu, sed de antiquorum Patrum judiciis (quod ad Martyrium spectat) quæ scriptis suis confignârunt. Nec enim Adversarios nostros latet, Sanctos Patres interpretatos esse hunc locum de {q}Martyrio fidelium, tam ex occasione verborum istorum, Pretiosa mors Sanctorum, &c., Accipiam calicem salutis, quàm etiam propter allusionem ad verba Christi de martyrio Discipulorum suorum, Bibetis revera de calice quem ego bibiturus sum, Matth. 20. Nostrum erit Patrum Testimonia in medium producere.
units.tr: Psalm 116. (according to the Vulgate, 115) What shall I render to the Lord for all the things he has given me? I will take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in his sight is the death of his saints. Here we are not contending about the genuine and literal sense of this text, but about the judgments of the ancient Fathers, as far as martyrdom is concerned, which they committed to writing. For it is not hidden from our opponents that the holy Fathers interpreted this passage of the martyrdom of the faithful, both from the occasion of these words, Precious is the death of the saints, etc., I will take the cup of salvation, and also on account of the allusion to the words of Christ about the martyrdom of his disciples, You will indeed drink of the cup that I am about to drink, Matt. 20. It will be our task to bring forward the testimonies of the Fathers.

units.la: {r}Quid retribuam Domino, quòd me propriâ suâ imagine honestavit, Angelorum gloria vestivit? Pergit Chrysostomus, multa alia salutis nostræ media infignissima commemorans: & tandem, Propheta, inquit, cùm cogitando circumlustrâsset omnia, nullâque Deo digna perfectâque retributio occurreret, unum animadvertit præclarius [?], nempe, opus Martyrii, & de hoc infert, dicens, CALICEM SALVTIS ACCIPIAM.
units.tr: What shall I render to the Lord, who has honoured me with his own image and clothed me with the glory of angels? Chrysostom goes on, recalling many other most outstanding means of our salvation; and at last: The prophet, he says, when by thinking he had surveyed all things, and no retribution worthy of God and perfect presented itself, noticed one thing more excellent, namely the work of martyrdom, and from this he infers, saying, I WILL TAKE THE CUP OF SALVATION.

units.la: Augustinus ; {s}Mortem tuam (Martyrem alloquitur) Christus emit sanguine suo, quem effudit in salutem hominum, ne homines suam pro nomine ejus effundere dubitarent, qui confiteantur conditionem suam tanto pretio comparatam. Plura alia addit; ad extremum, rediens ad CALICEM SALVTIS, Revera, inquit, quicquid quisquis bene cogitat quod voveat Domino, hoc exigitur, hoc debetur. Ex his discimus, Martyrium mortem dici pretiosam, quia pretio Christi sanguinis empta est; esseque Christo, ratione istius pretii, debitam: nec Meriti (hoc enim negat) sed Gratitudinis opus, ut laudis holocaustum.
units.tr: Augustine: Christ bought your death (he addresses the martyr) with his blood, which he poured out for the salvation of men, lest men should hesitate to pour out their own for his name, those who confess that their condition was bought at so great a price. He adds many other things; at last, returning to THE CUP OF SALVATION: Truly, he says, whatever anyone who thinks rightly vows to the Lord, this is demanded, this is owed. From these things we learn that martyrdom is called death precious because it was bought by the price of Christ's blood, and that it is owed to Christ by reason of that price; and it is not a work of merit (for he denies this) but of gratitude, as a burnt offering of praise.

units.la: {t}Prosper, quasi Augustini premens vestigia: QVID RETRIBVAM DOMINO? Nihil invenit quod redderet, nisi quod à Domino acceperat: ACCIPIAM CALICEM SALVTIS, nempe mortem pretiosam, quia emit eam [Christus] sanguine suo;ea tamen servorum mors servis prodest, non Domino.
units.tr: Prosper, as if closely following in the footsteps of Augustine: WHAT SHALL I RENDER TO THE LORD? He found nothing that he could return except what he had received from the Lord. I WILL TAKE THE CUP OF SALVATION, namely a precious death, because [Christ] bought it with his blood; yet that death of servants profits servants, not the Lord.

units.la: {u}Theodoretus CALICEM SALVTIS, pro pietate, MORTEM appellat: docet igitur nos audacter pro Christo subire mortem, & hanc remunerationem pro variis officiis dare. Siquidem mortem illam admiratione dignam subiverimus, gloriam & honorem à Deo consequemur. Si vero, hostibus superiores facti, illorum aciem profligaverimus, hymnum de gratiarum actione osseremus, servitutem confitentes.
units.tr: Theodoret calls the cup of salvation death, for piety. He therefore teaches us to undergo death boldly for Christ, and to give this as a recompense for various duties. For if we undergo that death, admirable as it is, we will obtain glory and honour from God. But if, having become superior to our enemies, we have routed their battle line, we will offer a hymn of thanksgiving, confessing our servitude.

units.la: Adeste igitur quotquot estis Meriti vestri De Condigno gloriabundi buccinatores vindicésque: observate tot tantorúmque Patrum admirabilem consensum: dein (per Deum vos oro) rationum eorum momenta singula diligenter perpendite, & dicite, si potestis, an ista Catholicae religionis praeclarissima lumina, modò Protestantes fuissent, expressius, accuratius, nervosius vestram Condignitatem Meritoriam refellere & revincere potuissent. Istam enim Meritoriam condignitatem ex aequalitate justitiae, quam Pontificii Largitioni calicis aquae frigidae adscribendam judicârunt, Patres Catholici Passioni, seu Calici sanguinis, Martyrum ipsorum denegârunt.
units.tr: Come forward, then, all of you who are boastful trumpeters and champions of your merit of condignity: observe the admirable agreement of so many and such great Fathers; then (I beg you, by God) weigh carefully each single point of their reasons, and say, if you can, whether these most excellent lights of the Catholic religion, had they been Protestants, could have refuted and convicted your meritorious condignity more expressly, more accurately, more forcefully. For this meritorious condignity from equality of justice, which the Papists judged should be ascribed to the largesse of the cup of cold water, the Catholic Fathers have denied to the passion, or cup of blood, of the martyrs themselves.

units.la: CAP. XIX. Duodecimum nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, ex parte debita nostrae gratitudinis erga Deum in omni opere bono. Argumentatio.
units.tr: CHAP. XIX. Our twelfth argument against the Merit of Condignity, drawn from the debt of our gratitude to God in every good work. Argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: NUllum opus gratitudinis erga Deum, potest esse apud Deum Meritorium de Condigno: Sed omne opus bonum est opus gratitudinis erga Deum: Ergo nul-lum opus bonum potest esse Meritorium de Condigno apud Deum. Has praemissas Theses subsequentes comprobabimus.
units.tr: No work of gratitude towards God can be meritorious de condigno before God. But every good work is a work of gratitude towards God. Therefore no good work can be meritorious de condigno before God. We will prove these premises by the following theses.
Thesis I.

units.la: Omnes teneri, in omnibus gratias Deo agere.
units.tr: All are bound to give thanks to God in all things.
SECT. II.

units.la: Scripturæ satis sunt in se manifestæ. 1. Sine intermissione orate, & in omnibus gratias agi-u, 1. Thess. 5. Et revera, omne opus bonum est (vel expressè, vel implicitè) opus gratitudinis nostræ erga Deum, ut Apostolus innuit, 1. Cor. 10. 31. Sive editis, sive bibitis, sive quicquid agitis, omnia facite in Dei gloriam. Nec mirum, quia è contrà, (ut {a}Schola docet) Ingratitudo Materialis est in omni peccato.
units.tr: The Scriptures are plain enough in themselves. 1. Pray without ceasing, and in everything give thanks, 1 Thess. 5. And indeed every good work is (either expressly or implicitly) an act of our gratitude towards God, as the Apostle hints, 1 Cor. 10:31: Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Nor is this surprising, since on the contrary (as the School teaches) material ingratitude is in every sin.
Thesis II.

units.la: Actui gratitudinis non potest subesse virtus proprie Merendi de Condigno apud Deum. A Patribus probatur ex variis proprietatibus gratitudinis.
units.tr: No power properly of meriting de condigno before God can underlie an act of gratitude. The Fathers prove this from the various properties of gratitude.
SECT. III.

units.la: Huic Thesi solus Vasquez{b} (quod sciam) se opposuit. Etsi (inquit) aliqua opera ex affectu gratitudinis Deo exhibere homo teneretur, tamen sine dubio à Deo mereretur: nam qui gra-tus est Deo, ex ipso opere gratitudinis, dignus est vitâ aeternâ. Sic ille, sub praetextu gratitudinis opinionem meriti obtrudens; veluti subdoli piscatores, cùm escam piscibus praebent, sed non sine hamo. Ad Patres appellamus.
units.tr: Only Vasquez{b} (so far as I know) has opposed this thesis. Although (he says) a man is bound to offer some works to God from a feeling of gratitude, nevertheless without doubt he merits from God: for he who is pleasing to God, by the very work of gratitude, is worthy of eternal life. So he, putting forward the opinion of merit under the pretext of gratitude; like crafty fishermen who offer bait to fish, but not without a hook. We appeal to the Fathers.

units.la: Gratitudinis proprietates plurimas descripsit Antiquitas, & nobis posteris per scripta sua commendavit, quibus contra Meritum de Condigno fidissimi veritatis antiqui testes judicium suum abunde explicârunt. Prima proprietas gratitudinis est, Agnoscere nos grates dignas non posse Deo reddere. Hanc tradidit {c}Clemens Alexandrinus: Nec possumus nos omnino gratias referre pro dignitate salutis. Sic ille. Nec igitur Gratiae possunt esse Merita Condigna. Quò spectat illud {d}Nazianzeni, Da Domino omnia, quia omnia donavit; eum tamen nunquam vinces, etiamsi omnia projicias, imò nec si teipsum adjungas.
units.tr: The antiquity described many properties of gratitude and commended them to us who come after through its writings, and by these the most faithful ancient witnesses of the truth have fully set out their judgment against the Merit of Condignity. The first property of gratitude is to acknowledge that we cannot render thanks worthy of God. Clement of Alexandria handed this down: Nor can we at all return thanks worthy of the dignity of salvation. So he. Therefore graces cannot be condign merits. To this point refers that saying of Nazianzen: Give to the Lord all things, since he has given all things; yet you will never outdo him, even if you cast away everything, indeed not even if you add yourself.

units.la: Secunda proprietas gratitudinis est, Homines Deo verbales laudes referre pro beneficiis ejus realibus. De qua {e}Augustinus, Nos gratias agimus, inquit, non damus, non reddimus, sed verbis tantùm agimus Deo; ipse verò nos gratis salvos fecit. Eandem proprietatem sapienter ponderat {f}Chrysostomus: Si velimus aliquid offerre Deo, (inquit) quid amplius possumus, quàm cùm gratias verbis referimus? at ea, quae ipse exhibet, opere praestat. Quàm imparia autem sunt verba & opera[?] Et Dominus nullarum rerum indigus est &c. Rursus; Si Domino gratiesse [?] volumus, nos ipsos illustriores facimus: quoniam non quòd celebratione nostrâ egeat, hoc fieri vult; sed, ut quicquid est lucri ad nos redeat, ac dignos nos faciat majoribus subsidiis. Ubi vocem Dignos non aliter accipi posse, quàm Habiles & Aptos (juxta sensum supra ab Adversariis agnitum) res ipsa clamat, & idem {g}Chrysostomus probat: Gratiarum actio nihil illi [Deo] addit. Sic ille. Quo argumento Patres (supra cap. 2. sect. 3.) doctrinam de Condignitate Meritorum planissimè refutârunt.
units.tr: The second property of gratitude is that men render verbal praises to God for his real benefits. Augustine says of this: We give thanks, he says, we do not give, we do not repay, but only by words do we give thanks to God; but he has saved us freely. Chrysostom wisely weighs the same property: If we wish to offer anything to God, (he says) what more can we do than when we return thanks with words? But the things he himself gives, he bestows by his work. How unequal, however, are words and works[?]. And the Lord has need of nothing, etc. Again: If we wish to give thanks to the Lord, we make ourselves more illustrious: for he does not want this done because he needs our celebration; but so that whatever gain there is may come back to us, and make us worthy of greater help. Where the word worthy cannot be understood otherwise than fit and apt (according to the sense already acknowledged by our opponents above), the matter itself cries out, and the same Chrysostom proves it: The thanksgiving adds nothing to him [God]. So he. By this argument the Fathers (above, ch. 2, sect. 3) plainly refuted the doctrine of the Condignity of Merits.

units.la: Tertia proprietas gratitudinis indignitatem nostram perstringit, ut gratias agentes intelligant se haud dignos esse quorum gratiæ acceptentur à Deo. In quem finem solerter {h}Fulgentius, Gratias debemus agere Deo, quòd nos gratuitâ ejus misericordiâ sibi subjecit, ut humiles simus, quia quamdiu sumus in hoc corpore mortali, non possumus sine peccato esse, nedum perfectam humilitatem Deo exhibere. Propterea gratia agenda sunt Deo, in quantum donat nobis ut bene operemur, nè ejus muneribus simus ingrati; & danda est opera ut ad meliora proficiamus, nè in mortiferam incidamus superbiam, si conversationem nostram putemus ex omni parte perfectam. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The third property of gratitude strikes at our unworthiness, so that those who give thanks understand that they are not worthy that their thanks should be accepted by God. To this end Fulgentius shrewdly says: We ought to give thanks to God, because by his free mercy he has subjected us to himself, so that we may be humble; for as long as we are in this mortal body we cannot be without sin, let alone show perfect humility to God. Therefore thanks are to be given to God insofar as he grants us to act well, lest we be ungrateful for his gifts; and effort is to be made to advance to better things, lest we fall into deadly pride, if we think our conduct perfect in every respect. So he.

units.la: Quarta proprietas gratitudinis est, ut homo justificatus, in operibus suis non gloriatur apud Deum. Propterea circumspectè & consultò {i}Basilius, Factus est Christus nobis, (inquit) Justitia, Sapientia, & Redemptio; ut qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Perfecta & consummata gloriatio in Deo est: quando nec propter sui ipsius justitiam quis extollitur, sed agnoscit se quidem vere destitutum justitia, verum solum in Christum fide justificatum esse. In delici-is habebat Augustinus Cypriani illud, (in haec verba Apostoli, QVID HABES QVOD NON ACCEPISTI?) In nullo gloriandum, quia nostrum nihil est. Similiter Ambrosius: Non gloriabor quia justus sum, sed quia redemptus; non quia vacuus peccati, sed quia remissa sunt mihi peccata; non gloriabor quia profui, sed quia est pro me Christus Advocatus. Sic hi Patres fidei & spei suae anchoram fixerunt in coelo: At contra dogmatizantes opus bonum de Condigno Meritorum esse ex aequalitate justitiae apud Deum, Meriti (ut illud nostrum dicitur) fundamentum in nostro arbitrio positum esse judicant.
units.tr: The fourth property of gratitude is that a justified man does not glory in his works before God. Therefore Basil, carefully and deliberately: Christ has been made to us Righteousness, Wisdom, and Redemption; so that he who glories may glory in the Lord. Perfect and complete glorying is in God: when a man is not exalted on account of his own righteousness, but acknowledges that he is truly destitute of righteousness, yet justified only in Christ through faith. Augustine took delight in Cyprian's saying (on those words of the Apostle, WHAT HAVE YOU THAT YOU DID NOT RECEIVE?): Nothing is to be gloried in, because nothing is ours. Likewise Ambrose: I will not glory because I am just, but because I am redeemed; not because I am free of sin, but because my sins are forgiven; I will not glory because I have profited, but because Christ is my Advocate for me. So these Fathers fixed the anchor of their faith and hope in heaven. But on the contrary, those who teach that a good work is of condign merit, by equality of justice before God, judge the foundation of merit (so that it may be called "ours") to be placed in our free will.

units.la: Gloriationem insuper quod attinet, sunt qui haud incommode distinguunt inter internam gloriationem & fiduciam Ex operibus, & In operibus. Hanc perniciosam judicant, nec immerito: (ut hactenus probavimus ex fucata & adulterina condignitate Operis & Operantis) istam vero nonnunquam persalutarem, quatenus gratiae & potentiae Dei operans recumbit. Veluti enim experientia Da[?]vidis de interfecto leone & urso fiduciam conciliabat Divini auxilii ad prosternendum ingentem Philistæum: ita docet Apostolus, minimè dubitandum esse nobis, quin Deus, qui coepit in nobis quodvis bonum opus, perficiet usquè in diem gloriosi aduentûs Christi. Quæ fuit ratio cur Bernardus, cùm omnino negaverat Bona opera esse propriè causam regnandi, arctè tamen tenuit, & confidenter, & sancta cum gloriatione jucundè pronunciabat, ea esse spei seminaria, charitatis incentiva, occulta prædestinationis indicia, futuræ felicitatis præsagia; denique viam regni. Et hoc quidem est in Deo gloriari, & non in nobis.
units.tr: Moreover, as regards glorying, there are those who draw a not inappropriate distinction between an inward glorying and trust in works and trust from works. They judge the former to be pernicious, and not without reason (as we have shown so far, from the counterfeit and adulterated condignity of the work and the worker); but the latter they judge to be sometimes most wholesome, insofar as it rests on the grace and power of God who works. For just as David's experience of killing the lion and the bear gave him confidence in divine help to strike down the great Philistine, so the Apostle teaches that we ought by no means to doubt that God, who began a good work in us, will complete it until the day of the glorious coming of Christ. This was the reason why Bernard, although he had altogether denied that good works are properly the cause of reigning, nevertheless held firmly to them, and confidently and with holy glorying joyfully declared that they are seeds of hope, incentives of charity, hidden signs of predestination, forerunners of future happiness; finally the way of the kingdom. And this indeed is to glory in God, and not in ourselves.

units.la: 3. Quoties ex antiquis & publicis Ecclesiarum omnium Liturgiis, Christiani instituunt Deum orare, ut ab illis actas gratias dignaretur accipere, tantum abest, ut Merita sua obtenderent, ut potiùs [illegible, ~4 letters] illum deprecationibus suis semper ex professo deprecerint. Certè Augustinus in alio Pharisæi ulcere digitum infixit: Pharisæus gratias agens (inquit) nihil sibi addo ad justitiam petebat. Quam superbiæ vomicam etiam Gregorius Nyssenus planè lancinat: Pharisæus si animadvertisset (inquit) hominis naturam, intellexisset ex *Scriptura, eam à sordibus puram non esse, nec posse inveniri inter homines, qui unum diem absque macula vivat. Ergò qui accessu-rus surus est ad Deum, ne talis affectus in animo ejus ingeneretur, non eum ad res bene gestas respicere Sermo jubet, sed recordari communium humana natura debitorum, quorum quivis prorsus particeps est; & rogare Judicem, ut delictorum impunitatem largiatur. Hæc ille. De qua re ele-ganter sanè {*}Chrysostomus, Recte factorum certissimus thesaurus oblivio.
units.tr: 3. Whenever Christians, from the ancient and public liturgies of all the Churches, set about praying God to deign to accept their deeds as good, they are so far from putting forward their merits that rather, in their prayers, they have always expressly entreated him for pardon. Surely Augustine drove his finger into another sore of the Pharisee: The Pharisee, giving thanks (he says), asked nothing to add to his righteousness. Gregory of Nyssa too plainly lances this canker of pride: If the Pharisee had considered (he says) the nature of man, he would have understood from the *Scripture that it is not pure from filth, nor can anyone be found among men who lives one day without spot. Therefore, he who is about to approach God, lest such a disposition be engendered in his mind, the Word bids him not to look to his well-done deeds, but to remember the debts common to human nature, of which each of us is wholly a partaker, and to ask the Judge to grant the pardon of his offences. So he. On this matter Chrysostom says elegantly: Forgetfulness is the most certain treasury of right deeds.
Thesis III.

units.la: Opinionem Meriti de Condigno ex necessitate & difficultate vera gratitudinis convinci falsitatis.
units.tr: The opinion of merit de condigno is convicted of falsity by the necessity and the true difficulty of gratitude.
SECT. IIII.

units.la: PRimò, Necessitas gratitudinis ex ingratitudinis atrocitate optimè elicitur. Ingratitudinis verò vitium apud Ethnicos ipsos adeò videbatur detestabile, ut Seneca rationem daturus, cur non hoc, sicut cætera vitia, in foro humano actionem inveniat, scitè & argutè, {a}Non quòd absolvimus, inquit, hoc invisum vitium: sed cùm difficilis esset incerta rei æstimatio, inter ea vitia reliquimus, quæ ad deos vindices mittimus. Sic ille de suis Ethnicis, qui inter id genus vitia paricidium numerat. Sed & ingratitudinis iniquitatem satis ostendit, adversus populum Judæ severa illa Dei exprobratio & objurgatio, quâ eos ad bestias ablegabat, à quibus edocerentur: Bos (inquit) cognovit dominum suum,& asinus præsepe ejus. Cujus generis species Schola quatuor enumerat: {b} primò, Non recognoscere beneficia; secundò, Non laudare benefactorem; tertiò, Non gratias agere; quartò, Non aliquid retribuere.
units.tr: First, the necessity of gratitude is very clearly drawn from the atrocity of ingratitude. Among the heathen themselves, ingratitude was regarded as so detestable a vice that Seneca, when he gives the reason why, unlike other vices, it has no action in the human courts, says wittily and sharply: It is not that we acquit this hated vice, but since the assessment of the thing is difficult and uncertain, we have left out those vices which we send to the gods as avengers. So he speaks of his heathens, who count parricide among that class of vices. But God's stern rebuke and reproof of the people of Judah, by which he sent them away to the beasts to be taught by them, also shows well enough the wickedness of ingratitude: The ox (he says) has known its owner, and the ass his master's crib. The school lists four kinds of this vice: first, not to recognise benefits; second, not to praise the benefactor; third, not to give thanks; fourth, not to make any return.

units.la: 2.[?] Difficultas veræ & necessariæ gratitudinis, quàm multifaria sit, ex variis ejus objectis deprehenditur, prout ea à sanctis Patribus distinguuntur.
units.tr: 2. How manifold the difficulty of true and necessary gratitude is, appears from its various objects, as the holy Fathers distinguish them.

units.la: Quod ad primum genus objectorum gratitudinis attinet, tenemur tam pro adversis, quàm prosperis gratias agere. De hoc {c}Chrysostomus divinè, de Benedictione Job: Nihil est linguâ illâ sanctius, quæ in malis Deo agit gratias: Revera non est inferior linguâ Martyrum. Sic & alii Patres; sed nota cantamus.
units.tr: As for the first kind of object of gratitude, we are bound to give thanks both for adversities and for prosperities. On this Chrysostom speaks divinely, in his work on the blessing of Job: Nothing is holier than that tongue which gives thanks to God in evils. Indeed it is not inferior to the tongue of the martyrs. So also the other Fathers; but we sing well-known things.

units.la: Secundi generis objecta sunt Multitudo & Magnitudo beneficiorum. Quoad Magnitudinem, {d}Chrysostomus instantiam dat ex Evangelio Joannis, cap. 3. SIC DEUS DILEXIT MUNDUM, UT OMNES QUI CREDUNT IN EUM NON PEREANT, SED HABERENT VITAM ÆTERNAM: Hoc miraculo obstupescens tonitrui filius, &c. Quanto miraculo plena est hæc dictio! — Dic mensuram, magnitudinem, & excellentiam ejus. {e}Augustinus, Deus ita donat, ut deficiat anima nostra in consideratione beneficiorum ejus. Ecce qualia Deus ex bonitate surus[?] est ad Deum, nè talis affectus in animo ejus ingeneretur, non cum ad res bene gestas respicere Sermo jubet, sed recordari communium humana natura debitorum, quorum quivis prorsus particeps est; & rogare judicem, ut delictorum impunitatem largiatur. Hæc ille. De qua re eleganter sanè {o}Chrysostomus, Recte factorum certissimus thesaurus oblivio.
units.tr: The objects of the second kind are the multitude and the magnitude of benefits. As to magnitude, Chrysostom gives an example from the Gospel of John, chapter 3: FOR GOD SO LOVED THE WORLD, THAT WHOSOEVER BELIEVES IN HIM SHOULD NOT PERISH, BUT HAVE EVERLASTING LIFE: astonished at this miracle, the son of thunder, etc. How full of wonder is this word! Tell me its measure, its greatness and its excellence. Augustine: God gives in such a way that our soul fails in considering his benefits. Behold what kind of ... is about to God, lest such an affection be engendered in his mind; not when the sermon bids us look back on well-done deeds, but to remember the debts common to human nature, of which each of us is wholly a partaker, and to ask the judge to grant the impunity of his offences. So he. On this matter Chrysostom says elegantly: Forgetfulness is the most certain treasury of good deeds.
Third Thesis.

units.la: Opinionem Meriti de Condigno ex necessitate & difficultate vera gratitudinis convincit falsitatis.
units.tr: The opinion of merit of condignity is shown to be false from the necessity and true difficulty of gratitude.
SECT. IIII.

units.la: PRimò, Necessitas gratitudinis ex ingrati-tudinis atrocitate optimè elicitur. Ingratitudinis verò vitium apud Ethnicos ipsos adeò videbatur detestabile, ut Seneca rationem daturus, cur non hoc, sicut cætera vitia, in foro humano actionem inveniat, scitè & argutè, {*}Non quòd absolvimus, inquit, hoc invisum vitium: sed cùm difficilis esset incerta rei æstimatio, inter ea vitia reliquimus, quæ ad deos vindices mittimus. Sic ille de suis Ethnicis, qui inter id genus vitia paricidium numerat. Sed & ingratitudinis iniquitatem satis ostendit, adversus populum Judæ severa illa Dei exprobratio & objurgatio, quâ eos ad bestias ablegabat, à quibus edocerentur: Bos (inquit) cognovit dominum suum, & asinus præsepe ejus. Cujus generis species Schola quatuor enumerat: {b}primò, Non recognoscere beneficia; secundò, Non laudare benefactorem; tertiò, Non gratias agere; quartò, Non aliquid retribuere.
units.tr: First, the necessity of gratitude is drawn out well from the atrocity of ingratitude. Among the heathen themselves, ingratitude seemed so detestable that Seneca, giving the reason why it does not, like other vices, find a remedy in human courts, said wittily and shrewdly: We do not acquit this hated vice, but since an accurate estimate of the matter was difficult, we have left it among those vices which we send to the gods as avengers. So he wrote of his heathen countrymen, who count parricide among that same class of vices. But the severe rebuke and reproof of God against the people of Judah also shows the wickedness of ingratitude, when he sent them off to the beasts to be taught by them: The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib. The Schools list four kinds of this: first, not to acknowledge benefits; second, not to praise the benefactor; third, not to give thanks; fourth, not to make any return.

units.la: 2. Difficultas verae & necessariae gratitudinis, quàm multifaria sit, ex variis ejus objectis deprehenditur, prout ea à sanctis Patribus distinguuntur.
units.tr: 2. How manifold the difficulty of true and necessary gratitude is can be seen from its various objects, as the holy Fathers distinguish them.

units.la: Quod ad primum genus objectorum gratitudinis attinet, tenemur tam pro adversis, quàm prosperis gratias agere. De hoc {c}Chrysostomus divinè, de Benedictione Job: Nihil est lingua illa sanctius, quae in malis Deo agit gratias: Revera non est inferior lingua Martyrum. Sic & alii Patres; sed nota cantamus.
units.tr: As to the first kind of object of gratitude, we are bound to give thanks for adversity as well as for prosperity. On this Chrysostom speaks divinely, concerning the blessing of Job: Nothing is holier than that tongue which gives thanks to God in evils. Truly the tongue of the martyrs is not inferior. So also the other Fathers; but we sing what is well known.

units.la: Secundi generis objecta sunt Multitudo & Magnitudo beneficiorum. Quoad Magnitudinem, {d}Chrysostomus instantiam dat ex Evangelio Joannis, cap. 3. SIC DEUS DILEXIT MUNDUM, UT OMNES QUI CREDUNT IN EUM NON PEREANT, SED HABEBUNT VITAM ÆTERNAM: Hoc miraculo obstupescens tonitrui filius, &c. Quanto miraculo plena est hac dictio! — Dic mensuram, magnitudinem, & excellentiam ejus. {e}Augustinus, Deus ita donat, ut deficiat anima nostra in consideratione beneficiorum ejus. Ecce qualia Deus ex bonitate gratiæ suæ in nos contulit, nullis nostris exigentibus meritis. Hæc Augustini sententia est ipsissima nostra professio.
units.tr: The objects of the second kind are the multitude and the greatness of benefits. As to greatness, Chrysostom gives an instance from the Gospel of John, chapter 3: FOR GOD SO LOVED THE WORLD, THAT WHOSOEVER BELIEVES IN HIM SHOULD NOT PERISH, BUT HAVE EVERLASTING LIFE: The son of thunder, astonished at this miracle, etc. How full of miracle is this saying! Tell its measure, its greatness, and its excellence. Augustine: God gives so that our soul faints in considering his benefits. Behold what kind of things God has bestowed upon us from the goodness of his grace, with no merits of ours demanding them. This sentence of Augustine is exactly our own profession.

units.la: Quod ad tertium, tenemur pro quotidianis & minimis gratias agere, ut 1. Cor. 10.19. Sive edatis, sive bibitis, sive quicquid agitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Hanc sententiam inter suos flores interserens {f}Bernardus, suaviter verba sequentia modulatur: Fragmenta ciborum colligere oportet, nè pereant. Nónne id perit quod datur ingrato? Cogitent Adversarii, & inter se reputent (utcunque pro integris panibus & beneficiis amplissimis) an pro fragmentis debitas Deo gratias reddiderint.
units.tr: As to the third, we are bound to give thanks for daily and very small things, as in 1 Cor. 10:19: Whether you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Bernard, weaving this sentiment among his flowers, sweetly tunes the following words: We ought to gather up the fragments of food, lest they perish. Does not that perish which is given to the ungrateful? Let our adversaries consider, and reflect among themselves (however much they regard whole loaves and very great benefits), whether they have rendered due thanks to God for the fragments.

units.la: Quod ad quartum, tenemur pro communibus bonis, tanquam pro propriis, gratos nos præbere. Rarior hæc forsan & sublimior speculatio, quàm quæ ab omnibus statim apprehendatur. In quo Argumento {g}Chrysostomus feliciter versatus, Hic est affectus fidelis servi, inquit, ut beneficia Domini sui, quæ communiter data sunt omnibus, quasi sibi soli præstita reputet, & quasi ipse sit omnium debitor, & pro omnibus ipse solus habeatur obnoxius. Hoc fecit Paulus, qui mortem Domini & Salvatoris nostri, quæ pro universo expensa est mundo, sibi soli præstitam dicit: quasi enim de se soloquens, ita scribit, QVOD ENIM NVNC VIVO IN CARNE, IN FI-
units.tr: As to the fourth, we are bound to show ourselves grateful for common goods as though they were our own. This is perhaps a rarer and more sublime speculation than what is grasped at once by everyone. Chrysostom has handled this argument happily: This is the disposition of a faithful servant, that he should regard the benefits of his Lord, which are given in common to all, as though they were bestowed on him alone, and that, as though he were the debtor of all, he should alone be held bound for all. Paul did this, who says that the death of our Lord and Saviour, which was paid for the whole world, was bestowed on him alone: for as if speaking of himself alone, he writes thus: FOR WHAT I NOW LIVE IN THE FLESH, I LIVE IN FI-

units.la: DE VITA FILII DEI, QUI TRADIDIT SEMETIPSUM PRO ME.
units.tr: Of the Son of God, who gave himself up for me.

units.la: Hæc autem dixi non coangustare volens amplissima & per orbem terra diffusa Christi munera, sed quasi qui pro omnibus se solum judicaret abstrictum. — Idea in Parabola boni pastoris non dicitur, Quia venit MULTAS oves quarere, sed UNAM. UNA namque est, quia sic omnibus, quasi UNI Divina beneficia conferuntur. Sic ille. Quibus verbis commendat cuivis pectori Christiano Condignitatem Meritorum Christi, non autem cuique suam, ut fanatici loquuntur & sentiunt.
units.tr: I have said these things not wishing to narrow the most ample gifts of Christ, which are spread through the whole earth, but as one who judged himself alone bound for all. — Hence in the parable of the good shepherd it is not said, that he came to seek MANY sheep, but ONE. For it is one, because divine benefits are so conferred on all as though on ONE alone. Thus he. By these words he commends to every Christian breast the condignity of the merits of Christ, but not each person's own, as the fanatics speak and think.

units.la: Quintum genus est eorum beneficiorum (de quibus {*}supra diximus ex Seneca) quae in nos nolentes collata sunt. Quae consideratio aureum illud os {h}Chrysostomi aperuit rursus, qui nos commonefacit, ut gratias agamus etiam pro iis bonis, quae nolentibus nobis dantur.
units.tr: The fifth kind is of those benefits (of which we spoke above from Seneca) which have been conferred on us against our will. This consideration again opened the golden mouth of Chrysostom, who reminds us to give thanks even for those good things which are given to us unwillingly.

units.la: Sextum genus dici potest respectu peccatorum: Ut gratias agamus pro peccatis tam remissis, quàm pro non commissis. De quo Augustini extat illud scitum & percelebre dictum, Domine, omnia mala[?] peccata dimissa esse fateor, & quae spectante te feci, & quae te duce non feci.
units.tr: The sixth kind can be named with respect to sins: that we should give thanks both for sins forgiven and for sins not committed. Of this there is that witty and very famous saying of Augustine: Lord, I confess that all the evils, the sins which I committed in your sight, and those which I did not commit under your guidance, have been forgiven.

units.la: Hæc singula gratitudinis objecta, si inter se conferantur, satis demonstrant, quàm impossibile nobis fit, non in multiplici ingratitudinis reatu implicari atque involvi: quo (nisi Judicii sui rigorem Deus, pro Pa-terna sua miseratione, propter Christi Me-rita, remittat atque dissolvat) actum esse de nobis merito suspicemur. Quæ unica confideratio omnem propriè nostra condignita-tis, ex æqualitate justitiæ apud Deum, arrogantiam Papisticam conterat prorsus atque pessundet.
units.tr: If these individual objects of gratitude are compared with one another, they sufficiently show how impossible it is for us not to be entangled and involved in a manifold guilt of ingratitude; from which (unless God, in his Fatherly mercy, for the sake of Christ's merits, remits and dissolves the rigour of his judgment) we may rightly suspect that we are undone. This one consideration utterly crushes and overthrows all Papistical arrogance of a condignity properly our own, arising from equality of justice before God.

units.la: CAP. XX. Decimum tertium nostrum Argumentum adversus Meritum de Condigno, ex parte profectus verae pietatis.
units.tr: CAP. XX. Our thirteenth argument against merit of condignity, taken from the side of true godliness progressing.
Argument.
SECT. I.

units.la: Professio, quae minus valet ad verae pietatis profectum, est minus probanda: Sed professio Meriti de Condigno minus valet ad verae pietatis profectum, quam contraria Protestantium: Idcirco est minus probanda.
units.tr: A profession that contributes less to the advancement of true piety is less to be approved. But the profession of the merit of condignity contributes less to the advancement of true piety than the contrary doctrine of the Protestants. Therefore it is less to be approved.

units.la: Major est magis manifesta, quam quae ab Adversariis negari possit: Minorem dis-sertatio sequens, Deo duce, abunde demon-strabit.
units.tr: The major premise is too evident to be denied by our opponents. The minor premise the following discourse will, God being our guide, demonstrate abundantly.

units.la: Tria sunt quae ad profectum verae pieta-tis requiri possunt; Necessitas, Dignitas, & Veritas bonorum operum.
units.tr: Three things can be required for the advancement of true piety: the necessity, the dignity, and the truth of good works.
On the necessity of good works.
I. Thesis.

units.la: Protestantes negata necessitatis bonorum operum reos à Pontificiis delatoribus atrociter peragi.
units.tr: The Protestants, having denied the necessity of good works, are atrociously harassed as guilty by Papist informers.
SECT. II.

units.la: Vellemus quidem Pontificiorum accusationes non nisi surdis auribus excepisse: sed cùm adeò ad ravim[?] usque clamitant & vociferantur, eorum criminationes sanè teterrimas, quas Protestantibus impingunt, audire vel invitu eogimur. viz. primò, {1}Eunomius fertur usquè adeò fuisse bonis moribus[?] inimicus, ut asseveraret, quòd nihil cuiquam obesset quarumlibet perpetratio ac perseverantia peccatorum, si hujus, quæ ab illo docebatur, fidei particeps esset. (Augustin. Hæref.54.) Nonne hoc idem Lutherani & Calvinistæ docent, cùm nos ab omnibus peccatis per fidem solam justificari contendimus? Sic Sanderus. Secundò, {k}Hæretici veteres docuerunt suos non debere curare bona opera, cui affinis est eorum [Protestantium] de sola fide. Sic Stapletonus. Tertiò, {l}Superiorum Gnosticorum impiam sententiam sibi hoc ævo instaurandam & propugnandam sumpserunt Sectarii omnes, qui infausto nomine Hugonotarum comprehenduntur: tur: Solam fidem justificare: Hominem damnari non posse, modò tantùm credas. Sic Fevardenti-us. Quartò, {m}Ut aeternam salutem consequaris, & sis sanctus, aiunt Protestantes omnes, nihil est necesse boni aliquid velis, moliaris, aut facias: Christo fidas, impune quidvis audeas, & ad exitum perducas. Sic Bozius. Hactenus Adversarii ipsi, omissis aliis, qui non minùs rabidè in Protestantes eodem nomine involant & invehuntur. Hæc dici potuisse, & non potuisse refelli? Imò vel facillimè.
units.tr: We would indeed wish that we had received the accusations of the Papists with deaf ears. But since they cry out and vociferate until they are hoarse, we are forced to hear their very foul charges against the Protestants, even against our will. First, Eunomius is said to have been so hostile to good morals that he asserted that the commission and persistence of whatever sins did no harm to anyone, provided he shared in the faith that he taught. (Augustine, Heresies 54.) Do not the Lutherans and Calvinists teach the same thing, when we contend that we are justified from all sins by faith alone? So Sanderus. Second, the ancient heretics taught that their followers ought not to care about good works, and the view of the Protestants about faith alone is akin to theirs. So Stapleton. Third, all the sectaries who are comprehended under the ill-omened name of Huguenots have taken up and undertaken to revive and defend in this age the impious opinion of the older Gnostics: that faith alone justifies, and that a man cannot be damned, provided only that you believe. So Fevardentius. Fourth, all the Protestants say that, in order that you may obtain eternal salvation and be holy, it is not necessary that you wish, strive for, or do anything good: trust in Christ, and you may dare anything with impunity and carry it through to the end. So Bozius. Thus far the adversaries themselves, leaving aside others who rush and rage against the Protestants under the same name no less furiously. Can these things be said and not be refuted? Indeed, they can be refuted very easily.
II. Thesis.

units.la: Immanem injuriam Protestantibus factam esse per criminationes istas, ex Protestantium scriptis ostenditur.
units.tr: That an immense wrong has been done to the Protestants by these accusations is shown from the writings of the Protestants.
SECTION III.

units.la: PRotestantes in primis duo sunt, per quorum latera professionem eorum omnium Pontificii (in locis citatis) percellere & transfodere conantur: Lutherus & Calvinus. Satis erit primo in loco, ex ipsorum tabulis obsignatis calumniam propulsare, nè præjudicio præfinito rectum præfocetur judicium. {n}Lutherus in hunc modum, In fide & dilectione sita est vita Christiana syncera. Si quaeras quae sint bona opera quae debemus; dico, Te totum, quantus es, des proximo. Item, {°} ad-venit, hominem immutat, talémque formát, qui opera legis praestet atque impleat,—& probet se fide justificatum esse. Item, {P} Nusquam Scriptura opera sine fide ; verum fidem vivam, à qua opera dimanant, ubique requirit. Item, {q} Ubi fides syncera est, absque operibus esse nequit, ut nec vivus homo ullus absque aliquo motu operan-di. Item, {r} Regnum Dei, quod nos sumus, non in sermone situm est, sed in virtute, hoc est, in operibus & exercitio: Deus non auditores, aut psittacos verba tantum expedite sonare condiscentes amat, sed imitatores & effectores sermo-nis in fide per dilectionem. Fides enim absque dilectione haudquaquam sufficiens est, imo non est fides, sed somnium quoddam & simulacrum fidei: Sicut facies in speculo visa, non est vera facies, sed imago faciei. Sic ille. Calvinus pariter, ait Apostolus, inquit, CHRISTUS FACTUS EST NOBIS A DEO SAPIENTIA, JUSTITIA, SANCTIFICATIO ET REDEMPTIO. Vocat hic SANCTIFICATIONEM, quo intelligat nos, alioqui profanos, Spiritu ejus regenerari in sanctitatem, ut serviamus Deo. Unde etiam colligimus, non posse nos gratis justificari sola fide, quin simul sancte vivamus. Ista enim gratia individuo nexu cohaerent, ut qui eas separare nititur, Christum quodammodo discerpat. Non fidem somniamus operibus vacuam,nec justificationem que sine
units.tr: There are chiefly two Protestants through whose sides the Papists, in the places cited, try to strike and pierce the profession of all of them: Luther and Calvin. It will suffice, first, to repel the calumny from their own published books, so that a judgment formed in advance does not stifle what is right. {n}Luther speaks thus: Christian life consists in faith and love, in its sincerity. If you ask what the good works are that we ought to do, I say: give yourself wholly, as much as you are, to your neighbour. Likewise, {°} [faith] comes, changes the man, and forms him so that he performs and fulfils the works of the law, and proves himself justified by faith. Likewise, {P} Scripture nowhere requires works without faith; but it everywhere requires a living faith, from which works flow. Likewise, {q} Where faith is sincere, it cannot be without works, just as no living man is without some motion of working. Likewise, {r} The kingdom of God, which we are, does not lie in speech but in power, that is, in works and exercise. God does not love hearers, or parrots who learn only to sound out words fluently, but imitators and doers of the word in faith through love. For faith without love is by no means sufficient; indeed it is not faith at all, but a certain dream and image of faith, just as a face seen in a mirror is not a true face but an image of the face. Thus he. Calvin likewise says: The Apostle says, CHRIST WAS MADE TO US BY GOD WISDOM, RIGHTEOUSNESS, SANCTIFICATION AND REDEMPTION. Here he calls it SANCTIFICATION, by which he means that we, who are otherwise profane, are regenerated by his Spirit into holiness, so that we may serve God. From this we also gather that we cannot be justified freely by faith alone without at the same time living holily. For these graces cohere in an inseparable bond, so that whoever tries to separate them tears Christ apart, in a manner of speaking. We do not dream of a faith empty of works, nor of a justification which without

units.la: {°} Idem in Dominic. 4. post Epiphan. ex Rom. 15. sine ex confess. Haec ille. Extant hujusmodi testimonia trecenta, quæ eos liberare possent ab istac calumnia: sed plura referre necesse non est, præsertim cum Adversarios nostros ipsos, veluti promptissimos Advocatos, accersere possimus. Sed in eo maximè cernitur Adversariorum calumniantium pervicacia, quòd perperam, idque sponte, dissimulant, à Protestantibus, per solam fidem, non tantùm historicam & mortuam, sed vivam, operantem, fiduciam, adeoque salvificam fidem intelligi.
units.tr: {°} The same in the Fourth Sunday after Epiphany, from Romans 15, and from the Confession. Thus he. There are some three hundred such testimonies which could free them from this calumny; but it is not necessary to report more, especially since we can summon our own adversaries as the most eager advocates. But the obstinacy of the calumniating adversaries is most clearly seen in this, that they wrongly, and deliberately, pretend that by faith alone the Protestants understand not only historical and dead faith, but living, working, trusting faith, and thus saving faith.
Thesis III.

units.la: Pontificiorum ipsorum confessiones, quibus superiores calumnia falsitatis convincuntur.
units.tr: The confessions of the Papists themselves, by which the aforesaid calumny of falsehood is refuted.
SECT. IIII.

units.la: ETiamsi Adversarii omnes omnium Protestantium libros cribraverint, ut quicquid possint lolii ex eis seligerent, nunquam tamen ex ullo eorum (quod sciam) testimonio potuerunt ostendere, non requiri ab illis necessariò pœnitentiam in iis omnibus qui justificantur. Quid enim de pœnitentia statuerint, unus {t}Bellarminus abunde satis idoneus relator esse possit: Lutherus docet (inquit) pœnitentiam esse dolorem de peccato, & propositum melioris vitæ. Melanchthon disertis verbis dicit, verum obedientiam esse tertiam partem pe-nitentia. —Sententia Calvini duas partes constituit, Mortificationem & Vivificationem: — Per Mortificationem intelligens vitiorum mortificationem, sive abnegationem sui; per Vivificationem, pium bene vivendi studium, atque affectum ad opera bona: — in quam sententiam Beza descendit. Rursus, idem ex Calvino; Confessio Augustana, per solam fidem, non excludit alias virtutes, sed meritum ipsarum. Item; Negamus, inquiunt Protestantes, fidem posse cum malis operibus consistere; nam qui habet propositum peccandi, fidem remissionis peccatorum concipere nullam potest. Item {y} Toletus Cardinalis de Protestantibus ingenuè; Dicunt Protestantes, fidem ad salutem sufficere; negant tamen, illam sine operibus esse posse. Item {z} Vega; Sanctificationem & justificationem tam conjunctas esse asseverant, ut non possit altera ab altera divelli. Etiam tu, Calvine, poenitentiam in peccatoribus requiri, ut justificentur. {a} Stapletonus denique; Omnes Protestantes ad unum, dicunt fidem, quae justificat, vivam esse, & operantem per charitatem aliaque opera. Haec illi, quae nos ex congerie confessionum aliarum multarum selegimus.
units.tr: Even if our adversaries have sifted through all the books of all Protestants, to pick out whatever tares they could from them, they have never been able to show from any of them (so far as I know) that repentance is not necessarily required of all who are justified. For what they have taught about repentance, the Jesuit Bellarmine, quite an adequate reporter, can tell us: Luther teaches (he says) that repentance is sorrow for sin and a resolve to live a better life. Melanchthon in plain words says that true obedience is the third part of repentance. The opinion of Calvin makes two parts, mortification and vivification: by mortification he understands the mortifying of vices, or self-denial; by vivification, a pious zeal for living well and an affection for good works. Beza agrees with this view. Again, from Calvin's own writings: the Augsburg Confession, by faith alone, does not exclude the other virtues, but only their merit. Likewise: "We deny," say the Protestants, "that faith can coexist with evil works, for one who has a purpose of sinning can conceive no faith in the forgiveness of sins." Likewise Cardinal Toletus frankly says of the Protestants: "The Protestants say that faith is sufficient for salvation; yet they deny that it can exist without works." Likewise Vega: "They assert that sanctification and justification are so joined that the one cannot be separated from the other." And you too, Calvin, say that repentance is required in sinners in order that they be justified. Finally Stapleton: "All Protestants, without exception, say that the faith which justifies is living, and works through love and other good works." These are their words, which we have selected from the heap of many other confessions.
Thesis IIII.

units.la: Superiorum calumniarum impietatem non solùm Pontificiorum ipsorum crudelitas, sed & Protestantium patientia redarguit atque refellit.
units.tr: The wickedness of the aforesaid calumnies is refuted and confuted not only by the cruelty of the Papists themselves, but also by the patience of the Protestants.
SECT. V.

units.la: Pontificii olim impietatis Protestantes insi-mulabant, quòd imaginem Crucifixi adora-re abhorrerent: simúlq; responsum ab eis tu-lerunt, nempe, Ipsos paratos esse Crucifixi veras vivásq; imagines fieri, cruciatus omnes sustinendo pro nomine JESU. Quod illi, ex Pontificiorum decretis morti priùs adjudicati, constanter felicitérque præstiterunt. Simile nunc responsum habeant; cùm millies mille Protestantium nullum genus tormentorum recusaverint pro fide Christi: quam quidem fidem plurimi etiam eorum sanguine suo ob-signárunt. Ut hi jam à vobis Solifidiani & bonorum operum omnium hostes audiant? Proh hominum fidem frontémque!
units.tr: The Papists formerly charged the Protestants with impiety because they refused to adore the image of the Crucified; and at the same time they gave this answer, namely, that they themselves were ready to become true and living images of the Crucified, enduring every torment for the name of Jesus. Those men, having first been condemned to death by the decrees of the Papists, bore this constantly and happily.
