Let them now have a similar answer: since thousands upon thousands of Protestants have refused no kind of torment for the faith of Christ, a faith which very many of them also sealed with their blood. Why do you now have these men, the "Solifidians" and enemies of all good works, hear this? O the faith and the brazenness of men!
V Thesis.

units.la: Protestantes æquè absolutè veræ pietatis necessita-tem requirunt, ac Pontificii: ut causæ sine qua non, per quam perducuntur ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: Protestants require the necessity of true piety just as absolutely as the Papists do, as a cause without which they are not brought to eternal life.
SECT. VI.

units.la: Causa sine qua non, ex consequente, necessitatem infert absolutissimam. Ea esse potest necessitas bonorum operum, quæ est universæ piæ & Christianæ conversationis fideli-um; quatenus hæc centies fere appellatur via in Scripturis, velut Matth. 7. Via alia lata, quæ ducit ad mortem; alia angusta, quæ ducit ad vitam. Quam necessitatem non potuisse non plurimùm facere ad profectum veræ pietatis, Pontificii non debent negare, nisi forte velint duo clarissima Romanæ Ecclesiæ lumina extinguere; qui abhorrentes à doctrina meritoria condignitatis operum, operum tamen necessitatem ad modum via docuerunt. Primò, Pontifex Gregorius, Nos, inquit, non Propter opera, sed Secundum opera judicabimur. (suprà, cap. 2. sect. 2.) Deinde Bernardus, Opera bona, inquit, sunt via regni, non causa regnandi. (suprà, cap. 17. sect. 13.) In quorum testimoniis non defuit ratio persuasionis ad pietatem, quia vocat bona opera præsagia felicitatis futura. Nec est, quòd existimemus eos, quòd volunt bona opera esse causam sine qua non, propterea negasse omnino bona opera esse causam per quam vitam æternam acquirimus. Ratio sequitur in Thesi proxima.
units.tr: A cause without which not (causa sine qua non) implies, by consequence, an absolute necessity. This may be the necessity of good works, which belongs to the whole pious and Christian conduct of the faithful, inasmuch as Scripture calls this the way almost a hundred times, as in Matt. 7: Wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction; narrow is the gate and strait is the way that leads to life. The Papists ought not to deny that this necessity contributes greatly to the advancement of true piety, unless perhaps they wish to extinguish the two most illustrious lights of the Roman Church, who, while abhorring the doctrine of the meritorious worthiness of works, nevertheless taught the necessity of works in the manner of a way. First, Pope Gregory: We, he says, will be judged not on account of works, but according to works. (above, ch. 2, sect. 2.) Then Bernard: Good works, he says, are the way to the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. (above, ch. 17, sect. 13.) In their testimonies there was no lack of a reason for persuading men to piety, since he calls good works forerunners of future happiness. Nor should we think that, because they wish good works to be a cause without which not, they therefore denied altogether that good works are a cause through which we acquire eternal life. The reasoning follows in the next thesis.
VI Thesis.

units.la: Bona opera esse necessario Actualem causam (seclusâ causâ Meritoriâ) per quam vitam æternam obtinemus.
units.tr: Good works are necessarily the actual cause (leaving aside the meritorious cause) through which we obtain eternal life.
SECT. VII.

units.la: NOn ignoramus, ab Adversariis inculcari contra nos illud, 2. Cor. 4. 17. ubi Tribulatio Sanctorum dicitur κατεργάζεται[?], Operari in nobis æternum gloriæ pondus: & Phil. 2. 12. ubi admonet Apostolus nos κατεργάζεσθε[?] salutem nostram cum timore & tremore. Agnoscimus etiam vocem Græcam significare Efficere; An igitur ex Merito de Condigno? Negavit jam antea Apostolus; Non sunt Condigna, inquit, tribulationes hujus vitæ gloriâ futurâ. Quin & eadem phrasis usurpatur, ubi nulla potest subesse ratio Meriti: Rom. 4. 15. Lex iram operatur; & 5. 3. Tribulatio patientiam operatur; & Jac. 1. 3. Probatio fidei vestra patientiam operatur: Quibus tamen inest nulla vis meritoria. Et ne quisquam putet, si omnis noster conatus ad salutem dicatur esse Ambulatio in via, hoc quicquid obesse pietati, addo Thesin proxi-mam.
units.tr: We are not unaware that our opponents press against us that passage of 2 Cor. 4:17, where the tribulation of the saints is said to work (κατεργάζεται) for us an eternal weight of glory, and Phil. 2:12, where the Apostle urges us to work out (κατεργάζεσθε) our own salvation with fear and trembling. We acknowledge also that the Greek word signifies to effect. Does it follow, then, that there is merit of condignity? The Apostle has already denied this earlier: The sufferings of this present life, he says, are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come. Indeed the same phrase is used where no merit can possibly be involved: Rom. 4:15, the law works wrath; and 5:3, tribulation works patience; and Jas. 1:3, the testing of your faith works patience. In these there is no meritorious force at all. And lest anyone think that, if all our effort toward salvation is called walking in the way, this detracts from piety in any way, I add the next thesis.

units.la: VII Thesis. Ambulare in VIA ad regnum coelo- rum, omnem vera pietatis profectum in se complectitur.
units.tr: VII Thesis. Walking in the WAY to the kingdom of heaven embraces in itself every advance of true piety.
SECT. VIII.

units.la: CHristiana conversatio non ideo toties in Scripturis via dicitur, ut in ea otiosi torpescamus; sed, ut necessario in dies magisque omni conamine ad regnum coeleste contendamus: ut patet Ephes. 2. 10. Nos fi-gmentum Dei sumus, creati in operibus bonis, ut in eis AMBULEMUS: & Rom. 6. 4. Ut in novitate vita AMBULEMUS. Sive igitur modus perveniendi ad vitam aeternam Cursus in stadio, sive Labor in vinea, sive Pugna in arena, aut aliud quid in Scripturis vocetur; est nihilominus Ambulatio in via ad haereditatem coelestem, non nostro, sed Christi merito partam & comparatam, ut Patres supra docuerunt. Recte igitur {b} Hilarius; Obedire Deo, est iter ad coelum. Non igitur desperandum est de eo, qui in hac via vitam finiverit: Gloriosissimi enim sunt illi, qui per martyrium, ceu per mare rubrum istuc perrexerint. At Per meritum de condigno eo aspirare, est extra viam iter habere. Porrò, de Metaphora Ambulandi in via (pro ea, quâ excelluit, sapientia & eruditione) graviter & eleganter homines virtutum omnium præceptis excolit. Augustinus: Quid est ambulare? Breviter dico, Proficere, nè forte non intelligatis, & peregrinus ambuletis. Semper tibi displiceat quod es, si vis pervenire ad id quod nondum es. Nam ubi tibi placuisti, ibi remansisti.— Ambula igitur tur & profice, noli retro redire, noli deviare. Redimanet, qui non proficit, retro redit, qui ad ea devolvitur unde jam abscesserat, deviat, qui apostata. Melius est [?]claudus in via, quàm cursor praeter viam. Sic ille. Quo, ad pietatis profectum, requiri amplius nihil potest.
units.tr: The Christian life is called a way so often in the Scriptures not so that we may grow lazy along it, but so that we may press on toward the heavenly kingdom each day with ever greater effort, as is clear from Ephesians 2:10, "We are God's workmanship, created in good works, that we should walk in them," and Romans 6:4, "that we should walk in newness of life." Whether the way of attaining eternal life is called a race in the stadium, a labour in the vineyard, a fight in the arena, or something else in the Scriptures, it is nonetheless a walking in the way towards the heavenly inheritance, which was won and acquired not by our merit but by Christ's, as the Fathers taught above. So Hilary rightly says: "To obey God is the way to heaven." Therefore no one should despair of those who have ended their lives on this way, for those who have made their way there through martyrdom, as through the Red Sea, are most glorious. But to aspire to it by merit of condignity is to have a journey off the way. Moreover, concerning the metaphor of walking in the way (in which he excelled in wisdom and learning), a man of weighty and elegant speech adorns the precepts of all the virtues. Augustine: "What is it to walk? I say briefly: to make progress, lest perhaps you do not understand and walk like a stranger. Always be displeased with what you are, if you wish to reach what you are not yet. For where you have pleased yourself, there you have stayed. Therefore walk and make progress; do not turn back, do not wander aside. He who does not make progress turns back; he who rolls back to where he had already departed deviates; he who does so is an apostate. A lame man on the road is better than a runner off the road." Thus he. As regards the progress of piety, nothing more can be required.
On the imperfection of good works
I Thesis.

units.la: Agnitio iniustitia operum nostrorum non arguit bona opera esse simpliciter peccata.
units.tr: The acknowledgement of the unrighteousness of our works does not prove that good works are simply sins.
SECT. IX.

units.la: QUam perfectionem Pontificii operibus tribuant, supra ostendimus, ubi proportionem in eis, ex aequalitate justitiae apud Deum, absolutam esse statuerunt. Nos autem eam imperfectionem sentimus & agnoscimus, ut gratia perfectionem sentimus & agnoscimus, ut gratiosa Dei acceptatione egeant, sine qua remunerationem beatitudinis expectare nequeunt. Idcirco Pontificii in nos irruunt & invehuntur, tanquam qui bona opera simpliciter peccata esse defendamus: ex quo sequi aiunt, bo-
units.tr: Above I showed what perfection the Papists assign to works, namely that they have declared the proportion in them to be absolute, from an equality of righteousness before God. We, however, feel and acknowledge that imperfection, and we acknowledge that works need God's gracious acceptance, without which they cannot hope for the reward of blessedness. For this reason the Papists rush at us and attack us, as if we were defending that good works are simply sins. From this, they say, it follows that good works-

units.la: VII Thesis. Ambulare in VIA ad regnum coelorum, omnem vera pietatis professionem in se complectitur.
units.tr: Thesis VII. To walk in the WAY to the kingdom of heaven embraces every true profession of piety.
SECT. VIII.

units.la: Christiana conversatio non ideo toties in Scripturis via dicitur, ut in ea otiosi torpescamus; sed, ut necessario in dies magis magisque omni conamine ad regnum coeleste contendamus: ut patet Ephes. 2. 10. Nos fi-gmentum Dei sumus, creati in operibus bonis, ut in eis AMBULEMUS: & Rom. 6.4. Ut in novitate vitae AMBULEMUS. Sive igitur modus perveniendi ad vitam aeternam Cursus in stadio, sive Labor in vinea, sive Pugna in arena, aut ali-ud quid in Scripturis [illegible, ~25 letters] ad quod in Scripturis vocetur; est nihilominus Ambulatio in via ad hæreditatem cœlestem, non nostro, sed Christi merito partam & comparatam; ut Patres supra docuerunt. Rectè igitur {b}Hilarius; Obedire Deo, est iter ad cœlum. Non igitur desperandum est de eo, qui in hac via vitam finiverit: Gloriosissimi enim sunt illi, qui per martyrium, ceu per mare rubrum istùc perrexerint. At Per meritum de condigno ad aspirare, est extra viam iter habere. Porrò, de Metaphora Ambulandi in via (pro ea, quâ excelluit, sapientia & eruditione) graviter & eleganter homines virtutum omnium præcepus excolit {*}Augustinus: Quid est ambulare? Breviter dico, Proficere, ne forte non intelligatis, & pigriús ambuletis. Semper tibi displiceat quod es, si vis pervenire ad id quod nondum es. Nam ubi tibi placuisti, ibi remansisti. — Ambula igitur & profice, noli retro redire, noli deviare. Remanet, qui non proficit, retro redit, qui ad ea devolvitur unde jam abscesserat, deviat, qui apostatat. Melius it claudus in via, quàm currit praeter viam. Sic ille. Quo, ad pietatis profectum, requiri amplius nihil potest.
units.tr: Christian conversation is not called a way so often in the Scriptures so that we may grow idle and sluggish on it. Rather, we must strive toward the heavenly kingdom every day with all our effort, as is clear from Ephes. 2. 10: We are his workmanship, created in good works, that we should walk in them. And Rom. 6.4: That we should walk in newness of life. Therefore, whether the way to eternal life is described as a race in a stadium, or labour in a vineyard, or a fight in the arena, or by some other image found in the Scriptures, it is nonetheless a walking in the way to the heavenly inheritance, which was obtained and acquired not by our merit but by the merit of Christ, as the Fathers taught above. Rightly, then, Hilary says: To obey God is the way to heaven. Therefore we must not despair of those who have finished their life on this way. Most glorious indeed are those who have pressed on along it through martyrdom, as through the Red Sea. But to aspire to merit de condigno is to have a journey outside the way. Moreover, Augustine, using the metaphor of walking in the way (in which he excelled in wisdom and learning), serious and elegantly urges men to all the precepts of virtue: What is it to walk? I say briefly, to make progress, lest perhaps you do not understand and walk more sluggishly. Let what you are always displease you, if you want to reach what you are not yet. For where you have pleased yourself, there you have remained. Walk therefore and make progress; do not turn back, do not wander aside. He who does not make progress remains; he who turns back to those things from which he had already departed is wandering; he who falls away is an apostate. The lame man who walks in the way is better off than the one who runs outside the way. Thus he. Nothing more can be required for the progress of piety than this.
On the imperfection of good works
I Thesis.

units.la: Agnitio iniustitia operum nostrorum non arguit bona opera esse simpliciter peccata.
units.tr: The acknowledgment of the unrighteousness of our works does not prove that good works are simply sins.
SECT. IX.

units.la: Quam perfectionem Pontificii operibus tribuant, supra ostendimus, ubi proportionem in eis, ex aequalitate iustitiae apud Deum, absolutam esse statuerunt. Nos autem eam imperfectionem sentimus & agnoscimus, ut gratiosâ Dei acceptatione egeant, sine qua remunerationem beatitudinis expectare nequeunt. Idcirco Pontificii in nos irruunt & invehuntur, tanquam qui bona opera simpliciter peccata esse defendamus: ex quo sequi aiunt, bonon[?] opera non esse à nobis facienda, nec à Deo mandanda, nedum laudanda.
units.tr: We have shown above what perfection the Papists ascribe to works, where they have declared the proportion in them to be absolute, from an equality of righteousness before God. We, however, feel and acknowledge that imperfection, so that they need God's gracious acceptance, without which they cannot expect the reward of blessedness. Therefore the Papists rush upon us and attack us, as if we maintained that good works are simply sins. From this, they say, it follows that good works are not to be done by us, nor commanded by God, much less praised.
Second Treatise.
We have learned from Scripture the imperfection of good works.
SECT. X.

units.la: VEritatis hujus ratio erit expedissima, si quidem observare velimus Ciceronianum illud, Videndum est quatenus. Nam in quovis renato & justificato duplex est homo, ἔσω, ἔξω[?] aliàs, vetus, & novus. Qui duo, velut Jacob & Esau in uno utero, in uno eodémque pectore hominis Christiani colluctantur. Quem statum hominis regenerati graviter deplorabat Apostolus, quòd in eodem opere bono, quoad interiorem hominem delectaba-tur, ratione tamen exterioris & carnalis hominis sui perficere non[?] inveniebat, Rom. 7. 18. Et sanè si ipse Jacob, prout cum Deo ipso, ità cum ejus lege contendere & luctari velit, illum {*}claudicare necesse est.
units.tr: The explanation of this truth will be quite straightforward, if we observe that saying of Cicero's: It must be considered how far. In every regenerate and justified man there are two men: the inward and the outward [ἔσω, ἔξω], or otherwise the old and the new. These two, like Jacob and Esau in one womb, struggle against each other in the one breast of the Christian man. The Apostle lamented this condition of the regenerate man with great sorrow: in the same good work, he delighted in it as regards the inward man, yet on account of his outward and carnal man he did not find the ability to perform it (Rom. 7:18). And indeed, if Jacob himself were to wrestle and contend with God's law as he did with God himself, he must needs limp.

units.la: Ad locum Apostoli revertor: de quo {f}Augustinus, ad secundas suas cogitationes redi-rem, Non videbatur mihi Apostolus, inquit, de seipso dicere potuisse, EGO CARNALIS SUM, cùm essem spiritualis, & quòd CAPTI-VUS. [?]US DUCEBATUR SUB LEGE PEC-CATI. — Sed potest melioribus & intelli-gentioribus esse, vel potius ipsi (quod faciendum est) verbis, ut videremur in illis Apostoli verbis gentium esse Sanctorum, contra carnales concupiscentias dimicantium. — Hinc factum est ut sic illa intelligerem, quemadmodum intellexit Hilarius, Gregorius, Ambrosius, & caeteri Ecclesiae sancti multique Doctores. Haec ille. Et revera in Apostoli verbis omnia sunt [illegible, ~8 letters] viz. Malum quod nolo, &c., Ego non operor, &c., Quod odi facio. Certè homo [illegible, ~4 letters] non potest in se hunc lucem sentire. Nec hic per Carnalem corpus ipsum intelligi necesse est, sed partem etiam superiorem, quatenus non est perfectè renovata, quae dicitur [illegible, ~9 letters]. Et Textus hunc fundet: Ipse (inquit) carne servio legi peccati, mente vero [ipse idem servio] legi Dei: sed hoc, bonum faciendo, illud vero, non perficiendo bonum: Quamvis dixit, Carne servio legi peccati, quia caro, ut vetus homo, opponitur menti, ut homini spirituali. Sic enim {s}Augustinus, Quando congruentius dicitur, CARO CONCUPISCIT, quando anima non solum carni animalem vitam praebet, verbum enim secundum carnem ipsam aliquid concupiscit, quod in potestate non est ne concupiscat, quamdiu inest peccatum in membris. Sic ille. Nempe cum duo sunt mandata, quibus homo vel regeneratissimus, quoad mortalis est, par esse nequeat: Nega-tivum sicut unum. Nec corrumpitur Affirmativum alterum. Diligue Deum tum corde, tum anima, tum viribus, cogitatione [?], ex conscientia imbecillitatis suae in praedictis bonis operibus (nam de his tantum Apostolum arguit) in duplicem querelam erumpit, ex duplici odio profectum. Primus est, Non profiteri id, quod piè vult. Alter est Contraprofiteri, etiamsi maximè nolit. Tantum abest ut regeneratus volit consentire adblandiendo sibi in malis operibus, ut odio quasi sit sibi, quod sic peccare non invenit.
units.tr: I return to the Apostle's passage. Augustine, when he had reconsidered his own thoughts on it, said: It did not seem to me that the Apostle could have said of himself, I am carnal, when he was spiritual, and that he was led captive under the law of sin. But it may be (and this is what ought to be done) that the words themselves are to be understood by better and more discerning readers, so that we may appear, in those words of the Apostle, to be among the saints who struggle against carnal lusts. For this reason I understood those words in the way that Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other holy and learned teachers of the Church understood them. So far Augustine. And indeed, in the Apostle's words everything is [illegible], namely: The evil that I would not, that I do; I do not work it; what I hate, that I do. Certainly a man cannot perceive this light in himself. Nor need we here understand by "carnal" the body itself, but also the higher part, insofar as it is not perfectly renewed, which is called [illegible]. And the text will confirm this: I myself, he says, serve the law of sin with the flesh, but the law of God with the mind: the one by doing good, the other by failing to perform the good. Although he said, I serve the law of sin with the flesh, this is because the flesh, as the old man, is set against the mind, as against the spiritual man. For so Augustine says: When it is more fitting to say, THE FLESH LUSTS, namely when the soul does not merely supply animal life to the flesh; for the word itself, according to the flesh, desires something which it is not in its power not to desire, as long as sin dwells in the members. So far he. Indeed, since there are two commandments, a man, even the most regenerate, cannot keep both equally while he is mortal: the negative is like one, and the affirmative is not corrupted by the other. Love God with the heart, with the soul, and with all strength and mind. From consciousness of his own weakness, in the aforesaid good works (for it is of these alone that the Apostle complains), he breaks out into a twofold lament, arising from a twofold hatred. The first is that he does not do what he piously wills; the second is that he does what he would by no means wish. So far is the regenerate man from willing to consent, by flattering himself, to evil works, that he hates, as it were, that he cannot find himself sinning in this way.
III. You have it.

units.la: Antiqui Patres imperfectionem bonorum operum plurimùm suae professi [?].
units.tr: The ancient Fathers very often professed the imperfection of good works.
SECT. XI.

units.la: Testimonia ex quo profecerunt astringemus ad opus bonum, ut habere admixtum in se aliquam pavitarem.
units.tr: We shall set down the testimonies from which they have advanced to the good work, so that some fear is mixed into it.

units.la: 1. {h} Bernardus, Dei perfectus neque, inquit, declinare judicium. Etsi justus fuero, non [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: 1. Bernard: "God's perfect, nor does he, says he, decline judgment. Even if I shall be just, I will not [illegible]."
Bernard [illegible].

units.la: 2. Hilarius; Corpus [?] omnium vitiorum uirorum[?] est meritis[?], qui pollui[?], nihil in malis[?] nihil immune[?] obtinemus. Ex paulo ante, ipse Apostolus, inquit, verbo licet jam fidei emendatis, atque sanctificatis, non deficere-mus malitiam dicunt Christus, cum dixit, SI CUM MALI ESTIS NOSTIS BONA DA-RE FILIIS VESTRIS, &c.
units.tr: 2. Hilary: "... we obtain nothing pure among evil things [illegible]. From the words a little before, the Apostle himself, he says, even though the words of faith are already corrected and sanctified, we would not cease from malice, as Christ says, when he said: IF THEN YOU, BEING EVIL, KNOW HOW TO GIVE GOOD GIFTS TO YOUR CHILDREN, &c."

units.la: 3. Augustinus, Plenissima, inquit, cha-ritas, dum hic vivitur, est in mentem[?] quamdiu agere possit, profecto illud quod minus est quam debet, vitio est. Ex quo vitio NON JUSTIFICABITUR IN CONSPECTU TUO OMNIS VIVENS.
units.tr: 3. Augustine: "The most full love, he says, while one lives here, is in the mind as long as it can act; surely that which is less than it ought to be is a fault. From this fault, NO ONE LIVING WILL BE JUSTIFIED IN YOUR SIGHT."

units.la: 4. Gregorius Magnus Pontifex; Ut sæpe diximus, Humana justitia injustitia est, si districtè judicetur.—Etsi ad opus virtutis excrevere, ad vitam, non ex meritis, sed ex venia concessa. Ubi hoc intelligi dictum de uno eodemque opere, ut & alibi, Quis enim non de virtutis suæ conscientia non quantulumcunque superbiat? Item, Sæpe, ut longè superius dicimus, inquit, opus nostrum causa damnationis est, quod profectus putatur esse virtutis.
units.tr: 4. Gregory the Great, Pope: "As we have often said, human justice is injustice if it is judged strictly. Even if they have grown to a work of virtue, they do so for life, not from merits but from the pardon granted. Where this is said of one and the same work, as also elsewhere: For who does not take pride, even a little, in the consciousness of his own virtue? Likewise, often, as we say much higher up, he says, our work is the cause of condemnation, because it is thought to be a progress of virtue."

units.la: 5. Bernardus, Nostra, siquis est, humilis justitia, inquit, recta forsan, sed non pura, nisi forte eos meliores esse credimus quàm Patres nostros, qui non minus veraciter quàm humiliter dixerunt, OMNES JUSTITIÆ NOSTRÆ TANQUAM PANNUS MENSTRUATÆ MULIERIS. Quomodo enim pura justitia, nisi adhuc aliis non potest ipsa docere? Hic nos de Scripturae hujus sensu gemino non disputamus tantum in Patrum judicium, de imperfectione nostra inquirimus. Quanquam etiam Salmeron Jesuita hanc rationem affert, cur non sic meritis nostris fidendum: Etsi quis justus sit (inquit) & sanctus, tamen non est illi fidendum operibus, quia justitia nostra incerta sunt, quia non pura, sed multis maculis admixta, quasi pannus menstruata mulieris. Eandem interpretationem reddiderunt Pontificii alii.
units.tr: 5. Bernard: "Our justice, if there is any, is humble, perhaps right, but not pure, unless perhaps we believe that they were better than our Fathers, who spoke no less truthfully than humbly: ALL OUR JUSTICES ARE LIKE THE CLOTH OF A MENSTRUATING WOMAN. For how can justice be pure, unless it can still teach others? Here we do not dispute only about the twofold sense of this Scripture, in the judgment of the Fathers; we inquire about our imperfection. Although Salmeron the Jesuit also gives this reason why we should not trust in our merits in this way: Even if someone is just and holy, yet he must not trust in his works, because our justices are uncertain, because they are not pure but mixed with many stains, like the cloth of a menstruating woman. Other Papists have given the same interpretation."

units.la: 8. Hieronymus, Quod si quidem, inquit, Justi in Scripturis appellantur, & non solum Justi, sed Justi in conspectu Dei juxta illam justitiam Justi appellantur, juxta quam supra dictum, SEPTIES IN DIE PECCAT JUSTUS, ET RESURGET. Et ab eo accepimus hunc aphorismum, Haec hominibus sola perfectio, si imperfectos se noverint.
units.tr: 8. Jerome: "For if indeed the just are called just in the Scriptures, and not only just but just in the sight of God, they are called just according to that justice by which it was said above, A JUST MAN FALLS SEVEN TIMES A DAY, AND RISES AGAIN. And from him we have received this maxim: This is the only perfection for men, if they know themselves to be imperfect."

units.la: 7. Chrysostomus, Etiam tres pueri, cum in ignem injecti, quid in fornace dicebant? Peccavimus, iniquitatem fecimus. Haec ille. Et rursus, in 1. Cor. 4. 4. in illa verba, NIL MIHI CONSCIUS SUM, &c. Quam saepe facile est gravibus criminibus implicari, quae nobis aut levia aut nulla aestimantur, quia multa facimus bona, non tamen bono animo; multos laudamus, non eorum laudis gratia, sed ut alios mordeamus: & fit saepenumero, ut quis bonum faciat, non ut congratuletur fratri, sed ut alium laedat: laudas[?]: deinde, & castigas interdum, non ut emen- das, sed ut vulneret[?]. Has autem consilia ab ho- minibus ignorantur.
units.tr: 7. Chrysostom: "The three boys too, when they were cast into the fire, what did they say in the furnace? We have sinned, we have done iniquity." So far he. And again, on 1 Cor. 4:4, on those words, I AM CONSCIOUS OF NOTHING AGAINST MYSELF, etc.: How often it is easy to become entangled in grave crimes, which seem to us slight or none, because we do many good things, yet not with a good mind; we praise many, not for the sake of their praise, but so that we may bite others; and it often happens that someone does good, not so as to congratulate a brother, but so as to wound another; you praise, and then at times you rebuke, not to correct, but to wound. These purposes, however, are unknown to men.

units.la: 8. {a}Augustinus, postquam Apostoli verba citasset, Quis & nos, inquit, non dicimus nos perfectè sanos esse; sed tundimus[?] pectus nostrum, & dicimus Deo, Propitius esto, nè peccem tibi. Rursus, {b}Quamlibet valdè justum discentes in hac vita, quamvis jam sit dignus JUSTI vocabulo, tamen non est sine peccato. Imò, etiam ipsò Iob (cui Dominus tale testimonium perhibet, ut Diabolus invideret) quid dicis? Quis enim mundus? nè infans cujus est unius diei vita super terram. Sed planè multi justi dicuntur sine querela, quod intelligitur sine crimine: nulla enim querela justa est de his in rebus humanis qui non habent crimen. {c}Augustinus denuo, in hoc argumento semper idem, Boni, inquit, in quantum non peccant, filii Dei sunt: in quantum autem peccant, (quod sed non mendaci confessione testantur) atq; mali sunt. Et alibi alteri occurrens objectioni; {d}Virgines in Apocalypsi, Sancti, qui se non inquinaverunt cum mulieribus, & non est inventum in ore eorum mendacium, quia irreprehensibiles erant: profectò ideo irreprehensibiles erant, quia seipsas veraciter reprehenderunt; & ideo non est inventum in ore eorum mendacium, quia si dicerent se peccata non habere, seipsas deciperent.
units.tr: 8. Augustine, after he had cited the words of the Apostle: "Who among us also does not say that we are perfectly sound? But we beat our breast and say to God, Be merciful to us, lest I sin against you. Again: While learning in this life, even one who is already very just and worthy of the name JUST, is not without sin. Indeed, what do you say of Job himself, to whom the Lord bears such testimony that the Devil was envious? For who is clean? Not even an infant whose life upon the earth is a single day. But plainly many are called just without blame, which is understood as without crime; for no blame is just concerning those in human affairs who have no crime." Augustine again, always the same in this argument: "The good, insofar as they do not sin, are sons of God; but insofar as they sin, (which they attest by a confession that is not false) they are also evil." And elsewhere, meeting another objection: "The virgins in the Apocalypse, the saints, who have not defiled themselves with women, and in whose mouth no lie was found, because they were blameless: surely they were blameless because they truly blamed themselves; and therefore no lie was found in their mouth, because if they said they had no sins, they would deceive themselves."

units.la: §. ²Beda³ Hæc est sola fidei perfectio, si omnibus quæ præcepta sunt implatis, imperfectos se esse noverint, & quamdiu peregrinantur à Domino semper inesse sibi mala quæ desleant, semper meminerint sibi deesse bona, ad quæ, gratiâ ejus adjuvante, proficiant.
units.tr: §. 2 Bede: "This alone is the perfection of faith: when a man, having fulfilled all the things that are commanded, knows himself to be imperfect, and as long as we are away from the Lord, always recognises that there remain in him evils to be lamented, and always remembers that good things are lacking to him, which by his grace helping him he may advance towards."

units.la: Videmus in testimonio Hieronymi, eosdem sanctos peccatores simul & justos: in Chrysostomi, pueros beatos, at peccantes: Augustini, justos, at non perfectè sanctos; ejusdem Augustini, justos, at non sine peccato; rursus denique, irreprehensibiles, & reprehensibiles: Bedæ, perfectos simul & imperfectos appellari. Cujus una hæc ratio esse potest, quia etsi insunt in eis rebellionis peccatum, non est tamen regnum: sed regnum Satanæ eripiunt. Hæc Patrum testimonia quomodo cohæreant cum Merito de condigno, ex æqualitate justitiæ apud Deum, Adversarii nostri nunquam hactenus expedire potuerunt.
units.tr: We see in the testimony of Jerome that the same saints are both sinners and just; in Chrysostom, that children are blessed, yet sinning; in Augustine, just, yet not perfectly holy; and again in the same Augustine, just, yet not without sin; and finally, blameless and yet blameworthy; in Bede, they are called perfect and imperfect at once. The one reason for this can be that, although the sin of rebellion dwells in them, it does not reign; rather, they snatch the kingdom from Satan. How these testimonies of the Fathers agree with merit of condignity, from the equality of justice before God, our opponents have never yet been able to explain.

units.la: Est autem ubi Pontificii respondeant?, Patres ex ignorantia perfectionis suæ hujusmodi dicta ejaculari, per humilitatem scilicet. Quod responsum Patres ipsi falsitatis revincunt; qui aiunt, Sanctus (sic enim Augustinus) hæc non mendacii confessione testari: eosdemque (sic enim Bernardus) non minus veraciter quàm humiliter locutos esse. Nec enim vera potest esse humilitas, quæ cum mendacio, tanquam matrona cum meretrice, copulatur. Priusquam quam hanc sectionem concludam, Pontificiis nostris proponam hypotyposin quandam de oratione: ut ex una hac religiosa actione perspiciant, quam facile sit multoties in uno pio opere aberrare. Autor illis erit Jesuita {b}Ruiz: Ex communi Patrum doctrina, inquit, praesertim Gregorii & Bernardi, bona qualibet opera, sive supererogationis, sive praecepta, ut plurimum maculari à nobis venialibus culpis. Exemplum sit oratio, quam maculamus irreverentia, distractione cogitationum, somnolentia, inani gloria, tepiditate, defectu fiduciae, vel nostri conatus fiducia. Haec ille; quibus addere debuit hanc, (qua de agitur) nimirum eam ex hac opinione propriè meritoria condignitatis foedissimè conspurcari.
units.tr: But perhaps the Papists will reply that the Fathers uttered such sayings out of ignorance of their own perfection, namely through humility. The Fathers themselves refute this answer as false; for they say that the holy man (for so Augustine calls him) bears witness to these things with no confession of a lie, and that the same men (so Bernard says) spoke no less truthfully than humbly. For true humility cannot exist when it is joined with a lie, like a matron with a harlot. Before I conclude this section, I will set before our Papists a sketch of prayer, so that from this one religious action they may see how easily one can go astray many times in a single pious work. Their authority will be the Jesuit Ruiz: From the common doctrine of the Fathers, especially of Gregory and Bernard, he says, any good works whatever, whether of supererogation or commanded, are for the most part stained by us with venial sins. Let prayer be an example, which we stain with irreverence, distraction of thoughts, drowsiness, vainglory, lukewarmness, lack of confidence, or confidence in our own effort. So he writes; to these he ought to have added this (which is the matter in hand), namely that by this opinion of meritorious condignity it is most foully defiled.
Fourth Thesis.

units.la: Agnitio propriae imperfectionis calcar esse potest ad studiosiorem progressum in vera pietate.
units.tr: The recognition of one's own imperfection can be a spur to a more eager progress in true godliness.
SECT. XII.

units.la: Certè proverbiale illud quod Christus usurpabat Luc. 5. 31. Sani non opus habent medico, subinnuit eos, qui sibi sani videntur, quamvis forsan morbo lethali correpti fuerint, omne valetudinis suae subsidium negligere. Dein, ubi apodosin hanc adjungit, Non veni vocare justos, docet similem eorum esse vecordiam, qui, dum se perfectè justos Pharisaicè putant, {*}non aliunde auxilium petunt. Qui verò imperfectionis suæ sibi conscii sunt, eò instantiùs precibus contendunt apud Deum, vires sibi suppeditari, ut magis magisque proficiant. Fit etiam interdum, ut qui percipiunt se in via cæspitare, aut impingere, cursum vehementius redintegrent, velociùsque accelerent.
units.tr: Certainly that proverb which Christ used (Luke 5:31), "Those who are well have no need of a physician," hints at those who seem healthy to themselves, though perhaps they have been seized by a deadly disease, neglecting every aid to their health. Then, when he adds this consequence, "I have not come to call the righteous," he teaches that those who think themselves perfectly righteous in the Pharisaic manner suffer a similar madness, in that they seek help from nowhere else. Those, however, who are aware of their own imperfection press all the more urgently with prayers before God, that strength may be supplied to them so that they may advance more and more. It also sometimes happens that those who perceive that they stumble or trip in the course renew their running more vehemently and hasten more swiftly.

units.la: Consulat, qui velit, historias omnes, quà Sacras, quáve Ecclesiasticas; audacter dicam, nullos reperiet in praxi pietatis perfectiores aut digniores extitisse, quàm qui imperfectiones, &, ut itá dicam, indignitatem suam confitebantur. Hinc profectò sunt istæ suspirationes Abrahæ, Ego, qui sum terra & cinis, Gen. 18. 27. & Jacobi, Minor sum omnibus miserationibus tuis, Gen. 32. 10. Mitto Jobum, Tres pueros, Danielem, & alios, viva & illustria sanctitatis sydera, quorum in Scripturis prolixior fit mentio.
units.tr: Let whoever wishes consult all the histories, both sacred and ecclesiastical; I will boldly say that he will find no one who has been more perfect or more worthy in the practice of piety than those who confessed their imperfections and, as I may say, their unworthiness. From this indeed came those sighs of Abraham, "I, who am dust and ashes" (Gen. 18:27), and of Jacob, "I am less than all the mercies you have shown me" (Gen. 32:10). I pass over Job, the three youths, Daniel, and others, living and illustrious stars of holiness, of whom a fuller mention is made in the Scriptures.

units.la: Ad antiquos Patres redeamus, quorum superiora exempla documento nobis esse possint, quantum hæc de nostra infirmitate confessio ad pietatis incrementum conferat; juxta dictum illud Bedæ in sectione præcedenti, Homines sentientes in se mala, ad meliora, Deo adjuvante, proficiunt. Similiter Fulgentius, cap. 19. sect. 3. Denique, nisi agnitio imperfectionis nostræ adminiculo nobis esset ad veram pietatem, nunquam sacrosan-&to Evangelio Christi dicta hæc consignata fuissent, Cùm orâtis, dicite, Dimitte nobis de-bita nostra. Ubi Primò, Autor qui dixit erat Christus, qui est ipsa veritas. Secundò, Cùm VOS orâtis, dixit,compellans Discipulos suos, in pietatis schola instructissimos. Tertiò, Dimitte DEBITA. Non igitur à delictis prorsus immunes. Quando vero & quoties orandum illis erat? CVM, inquit, orâtis: ut significet eos, quoties orant, hac petitione ac supplicatione opus habere. Nec tamen bona opera dignitate suâ spoliamus.
units.tr: Let us return to the ancient Fathers, whose examples above may serve us as a lesson of how much this confession of our weakness contributes to the growth of piety; in line with that saying of Bede in the preceding section, "Men who feel evils in themselves advance toward better things, God helping them." Likewise Fulgentius, chapter 19, section 3. Finally, unless the acknowledgment of our imperfection were a help to us toward true piety, these words would never have been recorded in the most holy Gospel of Christ: "When you pray, say, Forgive us our debts." Here, first, the author who spoke was Christ, who is truth itself. Second, he said "when YOU pray," addressing his disciples, most thoroughly instructed in the school of piety. Third, "Forgive our DEBTS." Therefore they were not altogether free from offences. But when and how often were they to pray? "WHEN," he says, "you pray": so that he signifies that they have need of this petition and supplication whenever they pray. Yet we do not thereby strip good works of their dignity.
On the dignity of good works:
I THESIS.

units.la: Protestantes veriorem & illustriorem dignitatem bonorum operum profitentur, quàm Pontificii solent.
units.tr: The Protestants profess a truer and more illustrious dignity of good works than the Papists are accustomed to.
SECT. XIII.

units.la: BOna opera duplicem dignitatem fortiun-tur: unam ex principio operandi, qui est Spiritus sanctus: alteram ex statu operantis, qui est conditio adoptionis per Christum Jesum. Prius de principio. In omni verè Christiano homine duplex est homo: internus, & exter-nus; id est, carnalis, & spiritualis. Exinde de[?]cernimus duo agendi principia in uno eo-demque opere bono. Primum est Spiritus Dei, ex quo opus bonum factum est Spiritu-ale, Supernaturale, Deóque gratum; unde vox illa Apostoli, Bonum quod [?]operor. Alterum est Natura nostra claudicans; unde diffo-na altera illa vox, Perficere non invenio. Jam vero dignitatis, quam Pontificii bonis suis operibus tribuunt, partem sibi suóque libero arbitrio arrogant: cùm tamen Protestantes supernaturalis bonitatis dignitatem, quantam quantam, Divinæ operationi ascribunt. De quo supra copiosiùs.
units.tr: Good works possess a double dignity: one from their principle of operation, which is the Holy Spirit; the other from the state of the one working, which is the condition of adoption through Jesus Christ. First, concerning the principle. In every truly Christian man there are two men: the inner and the outer; that is, the carnal and the spiritual. Hence we discern two principles of action in one and the same good work. The first is the Spirit of God, by whom the good work is made spiritual, supernatural and pleasing to God; whence that saying of the Apostle, The good that I work. The other is our nature, which limps; whence that discordant other saying, To perform it I do not find. Now the Papists arrogate to themselves and to their free will a share of the dignity which they attribute to their good works, whereas the Protestants ascribe the dignity of supernatural goodness, whatever its measure, to the divine operation. Of this we have spoken more fully above.

units.la: Respectus secundus est personæ operantis, quoad statum adoptionis, ex quo, qui bona exercet opera jus habet proprie hereditari-um tantùm ad vitam æternam: Sic Protestantes: (ex operibus autem suis æquè proprie jus mercenarium sibi vendicant Pontificii) non quòd negare debeamus aut velimus, posse Christianum bona opera facere cum intuitu mercedis vitæ æternæ, modò intelligat mercedem Divinæ munificentiæ, ac liberalitatis, non autem suæ propriè condigni-tatis meritoriæ & æqualitatis: quam antiqui Patres prorsus respuerunt, quia vita æterna est supra condignitatem operis: ut supra, cap. 13.
units.tr: The second respect is that of the person working, as to the state of adoption. From this it follows that the one who performs good works has a right properly hereditary only to eternal life. So the Protestants hold; (but the Papists, from their works, claim with equal propriety a mercenary right for themselves). Not that we ought, or wish, to deny that a Christian may do good works with an eye to the reward of eternal life, provided he understands the reward to be of divine bounty and liberality, and not of his own properly meritorious and equal worthiness, which the ancient Fathers utterly rejected, because eternal life is beyond the worthiness of the work: as above, chap. 13.

units.la: Si omnes Protestantes, in unam Synodum collecti, excogitare vellent refutationem do-ctrinæ strinæ Pontificiæ de mercede, respectu hæreditatis; accuratiorem & clariorem edere, opinor, non potuissent, quàm est ipsa {c}Lorini Jesuitæ sententia, digna, quæ omnium lectorum memoriis imprimatur: Alia est ratio, inquit, cur beatitudini conveniat nomen HÆREDITATIS, quoniam ex gratia Dei maximè pendet, & nos in labores & merita Christi introimus. Item; Eadem hæreditas nostra Essentialis, inquit, nobis morte & merito Christi advenit, & vocamur Christi Coharedes, pro nobis mortui, quatenus ipse pro nobis meruit, ut quam ille habebat NATURALEM, nos acquiramus ut HÆREDITARIAM, ad est, ejus morte comparatam. Hæc admodum consentanea sunt superioribus rationibus nostris à Patribus deductis. Nam si Essentialis beatitudo hæreditas dicatur, eò quòd maximè ex gratia pendet, tum sanè propriè Merces dici nequit, quæ operibus debetur. Deinde, si parta est hæreditas hæc pro nobis ex Christi meritis, certè opera nostra, quibus eam acquirimus, non sunt propriè meritoria. Postremò, si hæreditatem illam acquirimus tantùm ex propriis Christi meritis pro nobis, tum hoc non ex eo fit, quòd Christus nobis meruerit virtutem merendi vitam æternam: de quo copiosissimè suprà disseruimus.
units.tr: If all the Protestants, gathered into one Synod, were to devise a refutation of the Papist doctrine of reward, as regards the inheritance, I think they could not produce a more exact and clearer one than the opinion of the Jesuit Lorinus itself, worthy to be imprinted in the memory of all readers: There is another reason, he says, why the name INHERITANCE belongs to blessedness, since it depends chiefly on the grace of God, and we enter into the labours and merits of Christ. Likewise: That same essential inheritance of ours, he says, comes to us by the death and merit of Christ, and we are called co-heirs of Christ, dead for us, insofar as he merited for us, so that what he had as NATURAL, we acquire as HEREDITARY, that is, procured by his death. These things agree very well with our earlier arguments drawn from the Fathers. For if essential blessedness is called an inheritance, because it depends chiefly on grace, then surely it cannot properly be called a reward, which is owed to works. Next, if this inheritance has been obtained for us by the merits of Christ, then surely our works, by which we acquire it, are not properly meritorious. Lastly, if we acquire that inheritance only through Christ's own merits on our behalf, then this does not happen because Christ merited for us the power of meriting eternal life; of which we have treated at great length above.
II Thesis.

units.la: Qui dignitate Filiationis hæreditariæ nituntur, multò sunt vera pietatis studiosiores, quàm qui à Servorum meritoria virtute dependent.
units.tr: Those who rest upon the dignity of hereditary sonship are far more zealous of true piety than those who depend upon the meritorious power of servants.
SECT. XIIII.

units.la: Servilis & agrestis animi esse videri posset, [?]quenquam de hac Thesi dubitare: idcirco in ejus confirmatione multi non erimus. Apostolus, Rom. 8.17. ut Christianos ad ἀκμὴν[?] & culmen pietatis, quod est martyrium ipsum, provocaret atque perduceret, à jure hæreditario rationem mutuatur: Si filii (inquit) tum hæredes: hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes autem Christi: si tamen compatimur, ut & conglorificemur. Ex quo discimus, Martyrium pro Christo, debitum ei esse, non meritorium; quia (ut supra Augustinus & Prosper) Christus hanc hæreditatem, pro Dei filiis, morte suâ emerat prior. Deinde Cyprianus; Memini cum magna laude quarundam gloriosè operantium, qui tamen omne opus suum bonum Deo imputabant. Ambrosius; Deus ideo nos Filios vocat & Hæredes, ut promptiores nos faciat ad obediendum ei. Nazianzenus vocem attollit altiùs, & cùm Servos dixerit esse ἀνυπολόγους[?], quibus præclarum videtur pœnam tantùm vitare, & Mercenarios esse μισθαρνίας [?], quibus propositum est etiam ad mercedem aspirare; Filios denique dicit esse τέκνα [?], eo quòd Patrem Deum reverentur, & bonis operibus studeant, etiamsi nihil sibi quaestùs sit inde rediturum. Testimonia horum Patrum habentur integra, suprà, cap. 13. sect. 4.
units.tr: It might seem the mark of a servile and rustic mind to doubt this thesis, so we shall not spend many words confirming it. The Apostle, Rom. 8.17, in order to rouse and lead Christians to the highest point of piety, which is martyrdom itself, borrows his argument from the law of inheritance: If children (he says) then heirs: heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ: if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. From this we learn that martyrdom for Christ is owed to him, not merited; because (as Augustine and Prosper said above) Christ had earlier purchased this inheritance for the sons of God by his own death. Then Cyprian: I remember with great praise certain people who worked gloriously, yet who imputed every good work of theirs to God. Ambrose: God therefore calls us sons and heirs, so that he may make us more ready to obey him. Nazianzen raises his voice higher. Having called servants unaccountable [ἀνυπολόγους], for whom it seems splendid merely to avoid punishment, and hired labourers mercenaries [μισθαρνίας], for whom the aim is also to aspire to wages, he finally calls sons children [τέκνα], because they revere God the Father and strive after good works, even if nothing of gain will come back to them from it. The testimonies of these Fathers are given in full above, chap. 13, sect. 4.
III Thesis.
The type of the higher truth in the Israelites.
SECT. XV.

units.la: ISraelitis, per multa secula antequam nati erant, Terra Canaan, expresso Dei pacto, destinata erat; ad quam tamen non sine itineris quadraginta annorum taedio, non sine gravissimis in eremo aerumnis, non sine acerrimis cum hoste pugnis, pervenerunt tandem. Non tamen per haec media, (inquimus) ut per conditiones meritorias, haereditatem illam consecuti sunt: nam, nè opinio haec cujusquam animum occuparet, tacità quādam exprobratione objurgatoriā it obviàm illis Deus, Psal. 44. 3. Non in brachio tuo comparásti tibi terram hanc. In hoc typo licebit nobis veram proprietatem haereditariam contemplari; & necessitatem per opera acquirendi eam, etiam interdum non sine sudore & sanguine, absque tamen condignitate merendi.
units.tr: Long before the Israelites were born, the land of Canaan had been appointed for them by the express covenant of God. Yet they did not reach it until the end, and not without the weariness of a forty years' journey, not without the most severe hardships in the wilderness, and not without the fiercest battles with the enemy. We say, however, that they did not obtain that inheritance through these means, as through meritorious conditions: for, lest this opinion should take hold of anyone's mind, God meets them with a silent rebuke: Psalm 44:3, Thou didst not get this land by thine own arm. In this type we may contemplate true hereditary property, and the necessity of acquiring it by works, even at times not without sweat and blood, yet without any worthiness of merit.

units.la: De vere pietatis profectu in particulari.
units.tr: On the true progress of piety in particular.
I. Thesis.

units.la: Gratitudo erga Deum esse matrem omnis verae pietatis; ex Scripturis, & Patribus. SECT. XVI.
units.tr: Gratitude toward God is the mother of all true piety; from the Scriptures and the Fathers. SECT. XVI.

units.la: Adversarii nostri etiam atque etiam orandi sunt, ut nobiscum observent Spiritus Sancti Dialecticam in adhortando & attrahendo homines ad omne genus virtutum, ex gratitudine nostra pro mera Dei misericordia. 1. Cor. 6. 20. Empti estis pretio magno; glorificate igitur Deum in corpore & spiritu vestro, quae sunt Dei. Et Rom. 12. 1. Obsecro vos per misericordias[?] Dei, ut exhibeatis corpora vestra hostiam viventem[?] holocaustum Deo, &c. Ejusdem generis testimonia plurima in numeratis habemus; quibus puteat nullum esse aliud in Scripturis Argumentum frequentius, fortius, persuasibilius ad reducendos homines justificandos ab impietate, vel ad justificatos confirmandos atque consummandos[?] in professione sanctitatis.
units.tr: Our opponents must be urged again and again to observe with us the Holy Spirit's method of exhorting and drawing people to every kind of virtue from our gratitude for God's pure mercy. 1 Cor. 6. 20. You were bought with a great price; so glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's. And Rom. 12. 1. I beg you by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, a whole burnt offering to God, etc. We have very many testimonies of this kind at hand. There seems to be no other argument in Scripture more frequent, more forceful, or more persuasive for bringing men out of impiety into justification, or for confirming and bringing to completion the justified in the profession of holiness.

units.la: Nihil autem hic negotii habemus (nè Adversarii hoc nesciant) cum praefractis hominibus, & in peccato obduratis, (sive Papistae, sive Protestantes fuerint) qui, ut Apostolus ait, Transferunt gratiam Dei in lasciviam, Epist. Jud. verf. 4. De apibus enim, non de araneis[?] hæc nostra disputatio instituitur.
units.tr: We have no business here (lest our opponents not know it) with stubborn men, hardened in sin, whether they are Papists or Protestants, who, as the Apostle says, turn the grace of God into lasciviousness, Epistle of Jude, verse 4. Our present disputation is concerned with bees, not with spiders.

units.la: Nunquid verò hîc judicium suum Patres silentio presserunt? Imò verò eandem planè veritatem ebuccinârunt. Viz. {*}Fulgentius, Gratia agenda sunt Deo, in quantum donat no-bis ut bene operemur, nè ejus muneribus simus ingrati: & danda est opera, ut ad meliora prosi-ciamus, nè (Audiant Adversarii) in mortife-ram incidamus superbiam, si conversationem nostram putemus omni ex parte esse perfectam. Pariter {*}Basilius; Perfecta & omnimoda glo-riatio in Deo est, quando non propter suiipsius justitiam quis extollitur, sed solâ Christi justi-tiâ se justificari cognoscit. Huic accedit Chry-sostomus: Memoria beneficiorum sufficiens est quæ nos adhortetur ad amorem Dei, eundémque indies adaugeat. De his largior est recitatio in superioribus sectionibus. Sed Augustinus di-gnissimus est qui colophonem apponat, qui in illa verba, Luc. 12. 48. CUI MULTUM DATUM, MULTUM QVÆRETUR AB EO, Oportet ergò Domine, inquit, me tantò tibi magis esse gratum, & devotum; ad serviendum, promptiorem existere; quantò me de cunctis beneficiis tuis obligatiorem conspicio.
units.tr: Did the Fathers, then, keep their judgment on this in silence? Quite the contrary; they sounded out this very same truth. Thus {*}Fulgentius: Thanks are to be given to God, insofar as he grants us to act well, lest we be ungrateful for his gifts; and effort is to be made to advance toward better things, lest (let our opponents hear this) we fall into deadly pride, if we think our conduct is perfect in every respect. Likewise {*}Basil: Complete and unqualified glory is in God, when a man is exalted not on account of his own righteousness, but knows that he is justified by the righteousness of Christ alone. To this Chrysostom adds: The remembrance of benefits is enough to urge us to love God, and to increase that love day by day. A fuller account of these has been given in the earlier sections. But Augustine is the most worthy to set the finishing touch, who, on those words of Luke 12. 48, To whom much has been given, much will be required of him, says: Therefore, Lord, he says, I ought to be all the more grateful and devoted to you, and readier to serve, as I see myself the more bound to you by all your benefits.
II Thesis.

units.la: Præstantes aliquot Argumentis pugnarunt adversus Meritum de condigno, tanquam gratitudinis & veræ pietatis hostem; quibus antiqui Patres ad pietatem promovendam satis ipsi suos[?].
units.tr: Some outstanding men have argued with several arguments against merit of condignity, as an enemy of gratitude and of true piety; by these arguments the ancient Fathers themselves sufficiently promoted piety.
SECT. XVII.

units.la: Meritum de condigno, quod consistit in Meritate justitiæ apud Deum, Sancti Patres, celeberrimi veritatis præcones, jam supra accuratissimis suis suffragiis jugulârunt.
units.tr: The merit of condign, which consists in merit of justice before God, was already overthrown by the holy Fathers, the most celebrated heralds of truth, in their most careful arguments above.

units.la: 1. Et eo, quòd omne opus bonum est Dei dictum[?]; ex quo (quòd ad pietatem spectat) infinebant, Homines, suis meritis pensitantes, sanctitatis sumulatio[?] semper novis studiis priora adaugent. (supra, cap. 9.)
units.tr: 1. And because every good work is a saying of God, from which (as far as piety is concerned) they inferred that men, weighing their own merits, increase their earlier achievements by ever new efforts, a pretence of holiness. (See above, ch. 9.)

units.la: 2. Telum etiam aliud contra condignitatem Meriti vibrabant; Quia nempe opus humanum (sit licèt mors martyrii) nihil prodest Deo. Ex quo tamen instigant homines tanquam ad honorificentissimum opus Martyrii subeundum; Quòd mortem eorum Christus, in eorum salutem, prior emerat sanguine suo. (supra, cap. 15.)
units.tr: 2. They also hurled another weapon against the worthiness of merit: that a human work (even if it is the death of martyrdom) profits God nothing. Yet from this they urge people on as if to undertake the most honourable work of martyrdom, because Christ had bought their death beforehand with his own blood for their salvation. (See above, ch. 15.)

units.la: 3. Arguebant contra operis Meritum vitæ æternæ, tanquam de condigno, eò quòd vita æterna est supra condignitatem ullius operis: quâ ratione [illegible, ~1 letter]tione incenderunt Christianorum animos ad omnes persecutionum flammas spirituali fortitudine extinguendas. (supra, cap. 14.)
units.tr: 3. They argued against the merit of works in respect of eternal life, as though it were of condign merit, because eternal life is beyond the worthiness of any work; by this reasoning they kindled the minds of Christians to quench all the flames of persecution with spiritual courage. (See above, ch. 14.)

units.la: 3. Imò, (ut ad matrem ipsam omni genere pietatis gravidam revertar) gratitudinis proprietates sancti Patres maximè in eo consistere senserunt, ut agnoscamus nos non posse Deo gratos dignas dare; sed, nullis exigentibus meritis nostris, nos Dei beneficia accipere. (supra, cap. 19).
units.tr: 3. Indeed (to return to the mother herself, pregnant with every kind of piety), the holy Fathers felt that the properties of gratitude consist mainly in this: that we acknowledge we cannot give God worthy things pleasing to him, but, with none of our merits demanded, we receive God's benefits. (See above, ch. 19.)

units.la: 5. Existimârunt denique ad hanc gratitudinem pertinere, ut statuamus apud nos, Deum ex benignitate & dignatione opera nostra remunerari, (supra, cap. 10.) nec esse Deum nobis proprie Debitorem, (supra, cap. 11.) & homines tantò magis Deo gratos, & devotos, ad serviendum, promptiores existere, quantò magis se Deo de cunctis beneficiis obligatiores noverint. Quibus singulis ipsam opinionem Meriti de condigno labefactârunt: etiâ tum cùm alios ad pietatem erudiendos esse maximè judicabant.
units.tr: 5. Finally they judged that it belongs to this gratitude that we hold within ourselves that God rewards our works out of kindness and condescension (see above, ch. 10), and that God is not properly our debtor (see above, ch. 11), and that men become more pleasing to God, and more devoted and readier to serve, the more they know themselves bound to God by all his benefits. Each of these points they used to undermine the very opinion of merit of condign, even at the time when they judged that others most needed to be taught piety.
Conclusion.

units.la: Eleganter admodum & scitè olim {d}Gre-gorius Magnus Pontifex de simili genere superbiæ spiritualis: Eleazar (inquit) in prælio elephantem stravit, sed sub ipso quem extinxit occubuit. Sic qui vitia superantes, sub ipsè, qua subjiciunt, superbiendo succumbunt. Quasi enim sub hoste quem prosternit moritur, qui de culpa, quam superat, elevatur. Sic ille. Quæ autem detestabilior superbia esse potest, quàm quæ non modò Gratiam de superan-dis vitiis nimis sibi vendicat, verùm etiam Gloriam vitæ æternæ ex æqualitate justitiæ exi-git, & deberi sibi ex condignitate statuit, pertinaciterque defendit
units.tr: Very elegantly and wisely, long ago Gregory the Great, the Pontiff, said of this same kind of spiritual pride: "Eleazar," he says, "struck down an elephant in battle, but fell beneath the very beast he killed. So those who overcome vices, by taking pride in the very thing they subdue, succumb under it. For it is as if one dies under the enemy he has laid low, when he is lifted up by the fault that he overcomes." Thus he. What pride can be more detestable than that which not only claims for itself too much grace for overcoming vices, but also demands the glory of eternal life from an equality of justice, holds that it is owed to itself by condignity, and stubbornly defends this

units.la: Autori omnis operis boni, Soli Deo, {*}à Quo, per Quem, & ad Quem sunt omnia, sit Glo-ria in secula.
units.tr: To the Author of every good work, to God alone, from whom, through whom, and to whom are all things, be glory for ever.
AMEN.
FINIS.
